PREFACE 

In 1932 we were selected to publish, in official form, the newly codified laws of the State of Tennessee. Annotated editions of the Tennessee laws have since been issued by other publishers.

It was determined in 1936 to reorganize the Department of Finance and Taxation in Tennessee and a firm of accredited specialists in governmental administration was employed by the State to undertake the task. After eight months of research and reorganization work their report was submitted to the Governor in December, 1936. A new commissioner took charge of the reorganized department in 

January, 1937.

Frequent requests for a complete and authoritative handbook on taxation in Tennessee led us to commission the authors to compile such a volume. Their experience during the reorganization of the Department of Finance and Taxation eminently qualified them, in our opinion, for this task. 

Experience has convinced taxpayers, their attorneys, auditors and representatives, as it has state officials, of the need for a tax manual that would give not only the present laws, but in some measure, the history of the several laws; the rules and regulations governing the reporting and discharging of tax liability, and Supreme Court decisions with respect to tax laws. 

Accordingly, such a tax compendium is here presented. 

It is arranged by chapters containing each tax law, the history of that particular tax law, the specific rules and regulations that have been developed to date, pertinent comment with respect to the law and the Supreme Court decisions affecting that law. A general index in the front of this volume offers a quick-finding reference to each class of tax laws and the separate divisions mentioned. Separate, detailed indices will be found preceding the law itself, the explanations and discussions, and the Supreme Court decisions. It is anticipated that this newer method of indexing iii

iv 

PREFACE 

will be found more readily accessible and most practical in usage. 

It is believed that this arrangement will materially aid all taxpayers and their representatives in determining correct interpretations and the proper procedures to be followed in reporting and discharging tax liabilities. 

As a complete Tennessee tax guide it will be enthusiastically welcomed by all tax assessing and collecting officials throughout the state.

It is our intent to issue annual supplements to this volume, containing all additions or amendments to the tax laws of the State of Tennessee, that accurate, up-to-the-minute tax information may be more available. 

On behalf of the co-authors, we express their and our own appreciation for the fine measure of cooperation rendered them in facilities afforded and criticisms made appertaining to the manuscript, to Hon. Walter Stokes, Jr., Commissioner of Finance and Taxation; Hon. Roy H. 

Beeler, Attorney General of the State; and Hon. Edwin F. 

Hunt, Assistant Attorney General.

April 1, 1938

CONSTITUTION OF THE STATE OF TENNESSEE Sections Affecting Taxation (Article II) Section 28: 

Properties Taxable: Valuations; Rates— 

All property, real, personal or mixed, shall be taxed, but the Legislature may except such as may be held by the State, by counties, cities or towns, and used exclusively for public or corporation purposes, and such as may be held and used for purposes purely religious, charitable, scientific, literary or educational, and shall except one thousand dollars' worth of personal property in the hands of each tax-payer and the direct product of the soil in the hands of the producer and his immediate vendee. All property shall be taxed according to its value, that value to be ascertained in such manner as the Legislature shall direct, so that taxes shall be equal and uniform throughout the State. No one species of property from which a tax may be collected shall be taxed higher than any other species of property of the same value. But the Legislature shall have power to tax Merchants, Peddlers, and privileges, in such manner as they may from time to time direct. The portion of a Merchant's Capital used in the purchase of Merchandise sold by him to non-residents and sent beyond the State, shall not be taxed at a rate higher than the ad valorem tax on property. The Legislature shall have the power to levy a tax upon incomes derived from stocks and bonds that are not taxed ad valorem. All male citizens of this State over the age of twenty-one years, except such persons as may be exempted by law on account of age or other infirmity, shall be liable to a poll

co (Ch. 1 

tax of not less than fifty cents nor more than one dollar per annum. Nor shall any county or corporation levy a poll tax exceeding the amount levied by the State. 

Section 29: 

Counties and Municipalities: power to levy taxes— 

The General Assembly shall have power to authorize the several counties and incorporated towns in this State, to impose taxes for county and corporation purposes respectively, in such manner as shall be prescribed by law; and all property shall be taxed according to its value, upon the principles established in regard to State taxation. 

Section 30: 

Articles manufactured of the produce of the State: exempt from taxation

No article manufactured of the produce of this state shall be taxed otherwise than to pay inspection fees.

HISTORY OF FRANCHISE TAXATION IN TENNESSEE 

Senate Joint Resolution Number 38, passed April 20, 1933, provides: "A careful examination and inquiry into the financial affairs of the various State Departments is deemed necessary— 

The joint resolution further provides, that the Governor employ auditors to enable him to forthwith make investigation and audit of the various State Departments. An appropriation of $10,000.00 was made to defray the expenses incident thereto. Pursuant to the resolution, the 

Governor of Tennessee requested the Tennessee Taxpayers Association to supervise the audits and investigations to be made in accordance therewith. Under date April 29, 1935, the Tennessee Taxpayers Association accepted this responsibility. By virtue of the authority vested in the Association it entered into an agreement with the firm of 

George G. Scott & Company, Certified Public Accountants,

Charlotte, North Carolina, to make certain audits and investigations and, under date July 5, 1935 this firm submitted its written report. 

While it is not proposed to enter into detail concerning the reasons for the action taken by the General Assembly, mention should be made of the fact that the Legislative as well as the Executive branches of the Government of the State of Tennessee were unable to accurately determine the actual financial status of the State Government. There was much speculation as to whether there was, or would be, a deficit at the close of the fiscal year ended June 30, 1935. For many years the revenues of the State were inadequate to meet operating expenses and while a deficit appeared very certain, the Executive Branch of the Government was not in position to ascertain the size of such deficit with any degree of accuracy.

The auditor's report covered a period of twenty-two months, from July 1, 1933 to April 30, 1935, and indicated 17

(Ch. 2 

an estimated deficit as of June 30, 1935 in the amount of $1,545,554.42. The total net indebtedness at June 30, 1935 amounted to $2,633,327.20, and with respect to this condition the following conclusion was made by the auditors: "In order that the State be placed in position to meet its current obligations out of the general fund, it is necessary that the present amount of current indebtedness be funded by the sale of funding bonds in the amount of $2,633,327.20.''

Under date July 5, 1935, the auditors submitted a separate report covering the Department of Finance and Taxation and in this report the following observation is made: "Fields of new sources of revenue are numerous, but before consideration can be given to new taxes, a complete study of the present State and Local taxation system should be made in order that all factors may be taken into consideration to the end that the tax burden is equitably borne Following this report, the Governor apparently desired to immediately improve the fiscal affairs of the State Government, the General Assembly convening on July 15, 1935 pursuant to his proclamation, which in part is as follows: "To provide sufficient revenue to pay the expenses of the State Government and maintain its institutions, departments, offices and agencies for the biennium beginning July 1, 1935.''

The extraordinary session of the General Assembly, under date of July 26, 1935 enacted Chapter 5, Public Acts of 1935, the caption of which is as follows: "An Act to provide revenue for the State by the imposition of privilege taxes and to provide ways and means for the collection of such tax." 

The Act was approved July 29, 1935 and became effective from and after passage. Under its provisions, corporations, business trusts and partnerships engaged in that type of business for which a corporation may be formed, became liable for a "privilege" tax. The privilege subjected to taxation consisted in the right to conduct business in Tennessee in corporate form and it is interesting to observe that the word "franchise" is not used a single time in the Act to denote the kind or character of the tax commonly understood to have been levied. 

Pursuant to the passage of this Act, requiring the filing of a report on or before March 1, 1936 and the payment of

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

tax on or before June 1, 1936, the Department of Finance and Taxation created a new division known as the "Franchise Tax Division" and issued Regulations No. 5 relating to the administration of the "Franchise Tax Law." Report forms were prepared and forwarded to taxpayers affected and all corporations, business trusts and partnerships were required to execute and file "Franchise Tax Reports." 

Undoubtedly, the Legislature enacted Chapter 5, Public

Acts of 1935 as an effort toward a balanced budget for the biennium ending June 30, 1937, and to comply with the proclamation of the Governor. Various estimates of the revenue yield under this act were made. The estimates varied from one to two million dollars while, according to records in the Department of Finance and Taxation, the actual collections for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1936 amounted to $626,348.36. The total yield under this act and under Chapter 100, Public Acts of 1937, aggregates $1,265,805.53 as of June 30, 1937.

The 1935 Act was contested in the courts of the State and at the present time several cases are pending. The first suit was instituted by C. E. Corn and West Kentucky 

Coal Company, in which the constitutionality of the Act was raised. The plaintiff, C. E. Corn, was conducting business as a partnership, while the West Kentucky Coal Company is a corporation organized under the laws of the State of 

New Jersey. The Supreme Court of the State of Tennessee at the December term of 1935, held the tax invalid as to partnerships and valid as to corporations. After this decision, and the issuance of rules in accordance with the provisions of the Act, many ambiguities were removed. 

Corporations generally appeared to disfavor this form of taxation. However, it was realized that additional revenue was badly needed by the State Government and as a result of closer cooperation by corporations subject to the tax $468,164.14 was collected during the month of June, 1936. 

Undoubtedly, the present administration of the State Government, as well as the General Assembly, desired to absolutely eliminate this form of taxation in Tennessee. 

However, with increased demands being made for addi- .

(Ch. 2 

tional school facilities, old-age benefits, unemployment insurance and many other highly important and necessary public services, elimination of this tax would necessitate a different form of taxation and it was therefore decided to enact a Franchise Tax Law which would be more equitable and at the same time produce revenue sufficient to assist in the enlargement of social services to the people. 

The present Franchise Tax Law, Chapter 100, Public 

Acts of 1937, repealing Chapter 5, Public Acts of Extra Session of 1935, represents the result thus far in the field of Franchise taxation in Tennessee.

An Act to provide revenue for the State by the imposition of privilege taxes upon corporations and business trusts and to provide ways and means for the collection of such taxes.

Section 1. 

Be it enacted by the General Assembly of the State of Tennessee;

Corporations subject to tax- That all corporations organized under the laws of the State of Tennessee, other than those organized for general welfare and not for profit, and all corporations organized under the laws of any other State for profit and doing business in Tennessee, shall, without exception other than as provided in Section 2 hereof, pay to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation annually a privilege tax in addition to all other taxes, the rate and measure of which are hereinafter set forth. The tax hereby imposed shall be paid for the privilege of engaging in business in corporate form in this State and shall be in addition to all other taxes levied by any other act.

The tax hereinbefore levied shall also be paid by all business trusts, commonly known as Massachusetts Trusts,

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

for the privilege of doing business in Tennessee and the word "corporation" when used herein shall be deemed to include a business trust unless the particular context require a different meaning. 

Rate and base of tax The privilege tax hereby imposed shall be a tax of fifteen (154) cents on the One Hundred ($100.00) Dollars, or major fraction thereof, of the issued and outstanding capital stock, surplus and undivided profits of each such corporation as shown by the books and records of such corporation at the close of its last calendar or fiscal year preceding the making of the sworn report hereinafter required.

Deficits allowed- Where a corporation doing business without surplus or undivided profits has had the value of its capital stock impaired by operating deficits or other business losses, such as fire, flood, tornado, etc., and where such deficit or loss is carried upon the books and records of the corporation as an impairment of capital, the measure of the tax shall be diminished by such loss or deficit. Credits allowed- The value of the stock held by any corporation in any other corporation paying the tax herein levied upon such second corporation shall be deducted from the measure of the tax.

Property values; minimum base— 

The measure of the tax hereby imposed shall in no case be less than the actual value of the real and tangible personal property owned or used by such corporation in this State and no corporation when paying tax upon the minimum basis herein set forth shall be permitted to insist that the assessed valuation of real and tangible personal property in Tennessee is greater than the actual value thereof. 

This provision is intended to fix a minimum tax base and not to substitute the value of property owned or used in

(Ch. 2 

Tennessee for the measure of the tax hereinbefore provided.

Receiverships liable- The tax imposed by this act shall apply to corporations whose business is being conducted by a receivership or trusteeship appointed by any court of competent jurisdiction and shall continue to accrue until such time as the corporation has been actually and legally dissolved or withdrawn from this State. 

Minimum tax The minimum tax payable under this Act shall be Ten ($10.00) Dollars. 

State tax only—

The tax herein levied shall be a tax for State purposes only and no county or municipality shall have the power to levy a similar tax.

Section 2. 

Be it further enacted; 

Insurance companies; tax credits 

That there shall be credited upon the tax hereby imposed such net amounts as are paid by insurance companies to this State as a tax upon gross premiums collected by them, not including the gross premium receipts tax paid by fire insurance companies for the purpose of executing the fire marshal law. There shall be no other credits. 

Section 3. 

Be it further enacted;

Apportionment of tax base- That in the case of corporations doing business in Tennessee and elsewhere the measure of the tax as hereinabove set forth shall be apportioned to Tennessee for the purpose of taxation in the following manner: (1) If the principal business in this State is manufac-

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

turing or if it is any form of collecting, assembling or processing of goods or materials, the capital stock, surplus and undivided profits shall be apportioned to Tennessee on the basis of the ratio obtained by taking the arithmetical average of the following two ratios: (a) The ratio of the value of its real estate and tangible personal property in this State on the date of the close of the fiscal year is to the value of its entire real estate and tangible personal property, with no deductions on account of encumbrances thereon. (b) The ratio of the total cost of manufacturing, collecting, assembling or processing within this State, to the total cost of manufacturing, collecting, assembling or processing within and without the State. (2) If the principal business in this State is selling, distributing, dealing in or using tangible personal property, the capital stock, surplus and undivided profits shall be apportioned to Tennessee on the basis of the ratio obtained by taking the arithmetical average of the following two ratios: 

(a) The ratio of the value of its real estate and tangible personal property in this State on the day of the close of its fiscal year is to the value of its entire real estate and tangible personal property then owned by it, with no deductions on account of encumbrances thereon. (b) The ratio of the total sales made through or by offices, agencies, or branches located in Tennessee during the income year to the total sales made everywhere during said year. (3) If the principal business is other than the manufacture or sale of tangible property, such proportion as its gross receipts in Tennessee during the income year is to its gross receipts for such year within and without the State. 

If, because of peculiar or unusual circumstances inherent in a particular case, the application of the above formulas would work a hardship or injustice, the Commissioner, upon application of the taxpayer and upon such showing, is authorized, with the approval of the Attorney General, to adopt such other method of apportionment as would be fair and just under the facts of the case.

(Ch. 2 

When corporations are doing business in Tennessee and elsewhere, only that part of the capital, surplus and undivided profits properly allocable to Tennessee by the manner of apportionment herein above set forth, shall be used as a measure of the tax subject to the other provisions of this act with reference to a minimum measure and a minimum tax.

Borrowed Capital included; when 

If the capital stock of a corporation which is a subsidiary of another corporation or closely affiliated therewith by stock ownership is inadequate for its business needs apart from credit extended or indebtedness guaranteed by the parent or an affiliated corporation, in determining the amount of capital, surplus and undivided profits of such corporations with respect to its liability for the tax imposed by this act, there shall be included in the measure of the tax the indebtedness owed to or guaranteed by the parent or an affiliated corporation. If necessary to apportion such indebtedness the methods of allocation heretofore set forth shall be used.

There is hereby appropriated annually an amount equal to two (2%) per cent of the receipts derived from the proceeds of the tax for the purpose of administering this act.

Rules and regulations— 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation is hereby granted full power and authority to adopt such reasonable rules and regulations, not in conflict with this act or other statutes, as he may deem necessary to enforce the collection of the tax herein levied. Such rules and regulations

Reports must be filed; when- 

Every corporation liable for the tax here imposed shall, on or before July 1st of each year, file with the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation on such form as he may prescribe an accurate and complete report, verified by the oath of the President, the Vice-President, the Secretary, the Treasurer or the General Manager, which report shall contain the following data: 

Data required- (a) The name of the corporation, the State in which chartered, the location of its principal place of business in this State and the location of its principal or home office. (b) The amount of capital stock subscribed and paid in, the amount issued and outstanding, the amount of surplus and undivided profits, together with the book value of each share of such stock as shown by the books and records of the corporation at the close of its last calendar or fiscal year. (d) The location by counties of all property in Tennessee of the corporation, together with the assessed valuation thereof. (e) Such other and further information as may be required by the Commissioner for the reasonable enforcement of this act.

By the enumeration of the specific data required above it is not intended to divest the Commissioner of his right to require all information which he may deem necessary for the enforcement of this act.

(Ch. 2 

Reports confidential- Reports of corporations made hereunder shall be confidential and shall not be divulged by the Commissioner or his assistants except to a legislative Committee appointed for the purpose of examining them, to the Governor, to the Attorney General and Reporter, or in obedience to a court order. If the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation or any employee, or any person to whom such information is divulged, should divulge the contents of any report except in accordance with the foregoing exception, he shall be guilty of a misdemeanor and punished accordingly. 

Payment of tax; when—

The tax herein levied shall be paid to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation on or before July 1st of each year and shall be paid at the time the sworn report is filed. The 

Commissioner of Finance and Taxation shall examine every sworn report as promptly as possible and shall ascertain whether the tax payment which accompanies such report is the amount actually and lawfully owing by the taxpayer. If the payment tendered is insufficient, the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation shall determine the correct tax due and shall immediately notify the taxpayer of the balance due, together with any interest and penalty thereon. If the amount tendered is in excess of the correct liability under this act, the Commissioner, with approval of the Attorney General and Reporter, shall return the amount of such excess to the taxpayer by State warrant, as in the case of other refunds.

Delinquents; penalties and interest 

Any corporation delinquent in the filing of the report herein required or in the payment of the tax herein levied shall pay a penalty of ten (10%) per cent for the first month or fractional part thereof of delinquency, and penalty thereafter at the rate of one-half of one per cent (2 of 

1%) of the amount due for each month of such delinquency. 

All delinquency shall bear interest at the rate of six (6%) per cent per annum from July 1st of each year until paid. 

The penalty and interest herein provided for shall apply to any part of the tax unpaid by July 1st and no such penalty or interest can be waived.

In addition to the penalty and interest heretofore provided the Commissioner is authorized in the case of any corporation failing or refusing to make report and to pay tax to ascertain the tax liability of such corporation from any information available and to give notice of the amount of such tax liability to the corporation forthwith by registered mail. After being so notified, any corporation shall pay the tax assessed against it and if it contests the legality thereof must proceed in accordance with Section 6 of this act.

Distress warrants; issuance of- 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation is hereby authorized when any tax shall have remained unpaid for

as much as fifteen days, including assessments made by the Commissioner in the absence of the sworn statement and notice hereinabove provided for, to issue distress warrant for the amount of tax, interest and penalties due under the provisions of this act, together with all costs and commissions allowed by law for collections upon execution. Such distress warrant shall be levied upon any property of the corporation located in this State. 

Suits to enforce collection—

The Commissioner may at his option bring suit in any court of competent jurisdiction against a delinquent taxpayer for the collection of the tax, interest and penalties herein provided.

Section 6. 

Be it further enacted;

Books and records; availability for inspection- 

That the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation or his duly authorized agent shall have access to all books and records of corporations required to pay tax thereunder, to enable the Commissioner to ascertain the correctness of any fact or report made or herein required. In the event any corporation fails or refuses to permit the Commissioner or his agent to have access to necessary books and information then the Commissioner shall have power and authority to compel the attendance of witnesses and the production of books and papers in the same manner as process may now be issued by the courts to compel the attendance of witnesses and the production of books and papers. Such process shall run anywhere in the State and shall be served by the Sheriff or any lawful officer to whom it may be directed. Disobedience to such process shall be treated as contempt of court and may be punished as such on the petition of the Commissioner to the Chancery Court of the county to which such process is directed. 

Overassessment-remedy of taxpayer- Whenever any corporation conceives that any tax demanded by the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation un-

der the supposed authority of this act is illegal or not due it shall be the duty of the corporation to pay the tax and to challenge the legality or correctness thereof in a suit instituted in accordance with Section 1790, et seq. of the Code of Tennessee. In such suit for the recovery of a tax paid all questions of law and fact with reference to the illegality of the tax may be raised. No corporation shall be entitled to enjoin the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation from collecting any tax demanded by such collecting officer under the authority of this act and no such injunction shall issue under the guise of enjoining an assessment or a collection. 

The sole remedy of the taxpayer shall be a suit to recover the tax alleged to have been illegally collected or demanded. 

In such suit the Commissioner shall not be permitted to defend upon the ground that the payment was not made under duress. In any case where a court of competent jurisdiction shall decree a recovery of a tax herein such court shall be authorized to allow interest from the date of the payment to the date of the judgment at a rate not exceeding six (6%) per cent per annum.

The provisions of this section with reference to payment under protest and with reference to no injunction relief shall apply to taxes demanded by the Commissioner where the original payment of the corporation was alleged to be insufficient as well as to taxes assessed by the Commissioner in the absence of the sworn report or statement required.

The time for filing suits for the recovery of allegedly illegal taxes and the procedure in such suits shall be governed by Section 1790, et seq., of the Code of Tennessee.

FRANCHISE TAX RULES AND REGULATIONS 

Issued March 10, 1937 by Walter Stokes, Jr., Commissioner of Finance and Taxation pursuant to provisions of Chapter 

100 Public Acts of 1937. Approved March 10, 1937 by Roy H. Beeler, Attorney General. 

The law requires the filing of this report and the payment of tax on or before July 1, 1937, and annually thereafter. The minimum tax is $10.00. 

1. Extension of time for filing this report may be granted in instances where the extenuating circumstances justify such extension. Application for extension must be made in writing to the Commissioner at least fifteen days before the due date of the return. Such application must fully state the reasons for such request. When extension is granted the tax due will be subject to interest at the rate of 6% per annum. 

2. This report must be complete in every detail. Unless all information requested in the report is properly shown, the report will not be considered as having been filed under the law. Penalties and interest will accrue upon all incompleted and delinquent reports. 

3. A statement of dividends paid, accrued or credited to the account of residents of Tennessee during the period for which this report is made must be attached. This statement must show the name and address of the person, the amount of dividend paid to, or due to, or credited to such person, and the dates of credits or payments as re quired by Chapter 20, Acts of 1931 Second Extra Session. 

4. If the capital stock of a corporation which is a subsidiary or closely affiliated with another corporation is inadequate for the business needs the indebtedness due the parent or affiliated corporation must be included in the base of the tax irrespective of how such indebtedness may be classified and shown on the books of the reporting corporation. 

5. The term manufacturing costs shall be taken to mean 33

(Ch. 2 

the total cost of all goods, materials and supplies used in manufacturing, assembling or processing; the total wages and salaries paid or incurred during the year and the total overhead or manufacturing burden properly assignable according to good accounting practice to such manufacturing, assembling or processing activities. 

6. The term sales as used shall be taken to mean sales made through or by offices and branches located in this State irrespective of where the purchaser may reside. 

7. Enter in Section E the cash value and the assessed value of both real and tangible personal property located in this State, inserting the county in which such property is located. Should the space provided be inadequate for this purpose, attach separate schedule. 

8. In Section F on page 2 of the report, the value of both real and tangible personal property located in Tennessee and the value of such property located everywhere should be shown less the depreciation reserve carried on the books of the taxpayer. 

9. Deficits resulting in the impairment of the capital stock may be deducted in computing the amount subject to tax provided such deficits occur in the ordinary conduct of business, or as a result of fire, flood, tornado, etc. However, deficits not shown on the books of the corporation cannot be deducted despite the fact that they arose under the circumstances described above. 

10. The Franchise Tax Law measures the tax liability upon the amount of capital stock surplus and undivided profits including allocations thereof, and not upon the worth of capital stock, surplus and undivided profits. 

11. Any taxpayer feeling aggrieved after paying his admitted tax liability, may file with this Department a written statement setting forth in detail his contentions with respect to the tax and such taxpayer will be promptly notified upon final determination by the Commissioner. 

12. Franchise tax reports are confidential and the information contained therein cannot be divulged, therefore, legal representatives or other persons acting in behalf of corporations are required to present duly executed power

Corporations Subject to Franchise Tax- Law. Section 1. 

That all corporations organized under the laws of the State of Tennessee, other than those organized for general welfare and not for profit, and all corporations organized under the laws of any other state or county for profit and doing business in Tennessee, shall, without exception other than as provided in Section 2 hereof, pay to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation annually a privilege tax in addition to all other taxes, the rate and measure of which are hereinafter set forth. The tax hereby imposed shall be paid for the privilege of engaging in business in corporate form in this State and shall be in addition to all other taxes levied by any other Act. 

The tax herein before levied shall also be paid by all business trusts, commonly known as Massachusetts Trusts, for the privilege of doing business in Tennessee and the word "corporation" when used herein shall be deemed to include a business trust unless the particular context require a different meaning. 

The Act levies a tax upon all corporations organized for profit under the laws of Tennessee, and all corporations organized for profit under the laws of any other state or country and doing business in Tennessee. 

The term "corporation" is defined by the Act to include "business trusts" and "Massachusetts trusts" organized for profit in accordance with law. 

It is observed that the tax is imposed "for the privilege of doing business for profit in corporate form" in Tennessee.

The question arises-does the tax purport to be a tax

(Ch. 2  

upon the privilege of engaging in a particular business or is it a tax upon corporations for the privilege of engaging in business for profit in corporate form? 

If the tax is imposed on the right or privilege to transact business in corporate form, then the actual transaction of business by a corporation is not a condition of the tax. 

The tax continues to accrue until such time as the corporation has been actually or legally dissolved or withdrawn from the State.

Take the following example: 

A corporation is organized for profit in Tennessee but does not actually transact any business-it does not own any property or assets, and the charter is simply held by the stockholders for future use. 

Is the corporation liable for Franchise Tax?

This question has not been disposed of by the courts of Tennessee, but inasmuch as it does appear that the tax is imposed upon the right to transact business, then in such a case as above cited, the minimum Franchise tax of $10.00 would accrue for each and every year that the charter was held.

The Tennessee Statute is somewhat analogous to the 

Michigan Franchise tax law and in Detroit International

Bridge Company V. Corporation Tax Appeal Board-287 

U. S. 295, the court said: "Actual transaction of business by a domestic corporation is not a condition of the tax. It is imposed on the right to transact." 

Corporations organized for general welfare and not doing business for profit are not subject to the tax. National Banks and corporations performing Governmental functions of the United States, State of Tennessee or political subdivisions are also exempt.

While it is rather easy to determine the taxability of the usual commercial corporation conducting business for profit, many questions may arise as to the tax status of corporations or associations such as: 

1. Building and Loan Associations. 

2. Federal Savings and Loan Associations. 

3. Fraternal Life Insurance Associations. 

4. Mutual Fire, Life and Casualty Associations. 

5. Schools and Colleges.

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

It would appear that the above class of corporations, from their very nature and mode of conducting business, would contend that the business is not conducted for profit within the usual sense of the term, that the enhancement, if any, is a matter of contract; and, in the case of insurance companies, the object is cheaper insurance to the policy holders, and that educational institutions are largely conducted in the interest of the general public welfare. 

As regards "doing business" in Tennessee, many questions can be raised. For instance, the doing of a single act or single business transaction, such as the collection of a note from a resident of Tennessee by a foreign corporation, or the foreclosure of a mortgage, the greater weight of authority holds that such an isolated transaction does not constitute doing business. See Trentham V. Moore, 111 

Tenn. 346; Wender V. Lobertini, 151 Tenn. 476; Smith V. 

Dickinson, 81 Wash. 465, 142 Pac. 1133.

Selling by salesmen who take orders for a foreign corporation not having a branch office or other place of business within Tennessee and making delivery of its merchandise in "interstate commerce" does not appear to create liability for the tax. In the case of Robins V. Taxing 

District of Shelby County, 120 U. S. 489, the court held that no state could levy a tax or impose any other restrictions upon citizens or inhabitants of other states for selling or seeking to sell their goods in such state before they were introduced therein.

However, where offices or agencies are maintained, doing business would thus be established and franchise tax accrue. See Dennison Manufacturing Company V. 

Wright 156 Ga. 789, 129, S. E. 120.

The exercise of a taxable privilege under the Tennessee Act would result where a foreign corporation ships its product or merchandise to its agent or representative for the purpose of storage, sale and delivery. Such an arrangement constitutes doing business and is not protected by the interstate commerce clause of the Federal Constitution. See Dalton Adding Machine Sales Company V. 

Lindquist, 137 Wash. 375, 242 Pac. 643.

(Ch. 2  Rate and Measure of the Tax— Law. Section 1. 

The privilege tax hereby imposed shall be a tax of fifteen cents (154) on the one hundred ($100.00) dollars, or major fraction thereof, of the issued and outstanding capital stock, surplus and undivided profits of each such corporation as shown by the books and records of such corporation at the close of its last calendar or fiscal year preceding the making of the sworn report hereinafter required. 

Where a corporation doing business without surplus or undivided profits has had the value of its capital stock impaired by operating deficits or other business losses, such as fire, flood, tornado, etc., and where such deficit or loss is carried upon the books and records of the corporation as an impairment of capital, the measure of the tax shall be diminished by such loss or deficit. The value of the stock held by any corporation in any other corporation paying the tax herein levied upon such second corporation shall be deducted from the measure of the tax. 

The measure of the tax hereby imposed shall in no case be less than the actual value of the real and tangible personal property owned or used by such corporation in this State and no corporation when paying tax upon the minimum basis herein set forth shall be permitted to insist that the assessed valuation of real and tangible personal property in Tennessee is greater than the actual value thereof. This provision is intended to fix a minimum tax base and not to substitute the value or property owned or used in Tennessee for the measure of the tax hereinbefore provided. 

(A) Rate of Tax- 

The rate of the privilege tax is fifteen cents on each one hundred dollars or major fraction thereof; i.e., if the amount subject to the tax is $15,375.00 the tax is to be computed upon $15,400.00, resulting in a tax of $23.10. However, if the amount is $15,340.00, the tax should be computed upon $15,300.00 resulting in a tax of $22.95. 

(B) Determination of Tax Base- 

The "amount" upon which the tax is to be computed under the Act is usually "Net Worth" as this term is ordinarily understood in accounting practice; however, since the Act permits certain deductions, and the regulations require the addition of certain reserves, it is deemed necessary to discuss the method to be followed in order that the reader may obtain a more thorough understanding of this particular feature of the Act. 

It will be noted that the tax rate applies to “issued and outstanding capital stock, surplus and undivided profits" as shown by the books and records at the close of the last calendar or fiscal year preceding July 1 of each year. If business is being conducted without surplus or undivided

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

profits and the value of the capital stock has been impaired by reason of operating deficits or business losses, such as fire, flood, etc., such deficit or business loss may be deducted in computing the amount upon which the tax is levied; provided, the books and records reflect such deficit or loss. 

Regulation No. 9. 

Deficits resulting in the impairment of the capital stock may be deducted in computing the amount subject to tax provided such deficits occur in the ordinary conduct of business, or as a result of fire, flood, tornado, etc. However, deficits not shown on the books of the corporation cannot be deducted despite the fact that they arose under the circumstances described above. 

It appears that before a deduction of this character may be made, the following facts must exist: 

1. The corporation must be doing business without surplus or undivided profits. 

2. The capital stock must be impaired by a deficit or loss. 

3. The deficit must arise from operations of the business. 

4. The loss must result from fire, flood, tornado, etc. 

5. The deficit or loss must be carried upon the books and records of the corporation.

Surplus and undivided profits may be subjected to a number of accruals for the purpose of minimizing the tax. 

It is generally recognized as sound accounting practice to accrue contingent and determined liabilities and this practice is not condemned by the Act. However, attention is drawn to:

Regulation No. 10. 

The Franchise Tax Law measures the tax liability upon the amount of capital stock, surplus and undivided profits, including allocations thereof, and not the worth of capital stock, surplus and undivided profits. 

Under date of May 28, 1936, the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, by virtue of authority contained in 

Chapter 5, Public Acts of the Extra Session of 1935, issued certain rules and regulations with the approval of the Attorney General, relative to the 1935 Franchise Tax. 

Among the rules issued at that time one relates to the question here under discussion, viz.: "Reserves as shown by the balance sheet and which are not determined to be actual or accrued legal liabilities shall be restored to surplus or undivided profits in determining the tax base." 

With regard to the present law (Chapter 100-Public Acts of 1937), it is observed that the franchise tax must

(Ch. 2 

be measured by the capital stock, surplus and undivided profits "as shown by the books and records of such corporation."

The change in the wording of the new law presents a different picture as to the measure of the tax from the intent of the Legislature under the 1935 Act. (6 

It will be observed that the 1937 law distinctly states 'as shown by the books and records of such corporation.' 

Actual or accrued liabilities such as- 

1. Accrued taxes. (all classes) 

2. Accrued compensation for unemployment insurance. 

3. Accrued compensation for old-age benefits. 

4. Accrued Dividends-declared or unpaid. 

5. Accrued insurance premiums. 

6. Accrued liability under life insurance policies issued by legal reserve life insurance companies. 

7. Accrued liability for damages or other payments to be made as a result of judgment of court. 

8. All accrued operating expenses. of course are not subject to the tax; but there are many instances where reserves have been set up to take care of anticipated losses or contingencies that are not, and could not be construed as, actual legal liabilities. For instance, the following reserves could be so classified: 

1. For Bad Debts (Accounts, and Notes) 2. For Obsolescence (Property) 3. For Depreciation (Property) 4. For Depreciation in Market Values (Inventories) 5. For Depreciation in Market Values (Securities) 

6. For Contingent losses-applicable to the particular business (i.e., epidemics or fire losses in the case of Insurance Companies) 

7. For Labor Disputes, Strikes, etc. 

8. For Unearned Income in the case of installment business. 

Departmental regulation No. 10 states that the tax measure shall include surplus and undivided profits plus allocations therefrom but inasmuch as the law distinctly states that the tax measure shall be "capital stock, surplus and undivided profits as shown by the books," it is doubtful whether reserves allocated from surplus are subject to the tax. Of course such reserves should have been established by appropriate action of the proper corporate officials and be consistent with the previous practice of the corporation. Any attempt by corporations to create such reserves, or allocate the surplus or undivided profits by

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

calling it by another name, for the purpose of avoiding franchise tax, would undoubtedly be disallowed. 

The Act permits the deduction of the value of stock held in any other corporation paying the tax levied in the Act. The value of such stock as shown by the books is to be deducted from the measure of the tax, i.e., from the amount of capital stock, surplus and undivided profits. 

This particular credit is not allowed when the tax base consists of real and tangible personal property.

However, the Act further provides: . $150,000.00 "The measure of the tax shall in no case be less than the actual value of the real and tangible personal property owned or used in this State This provision is intended to fix a minimum tax base and not to substitute the value of property owned or used in Tennessee for the measure of the tax hereinbefore provided.' 

The law therefore creates three taxable bases: 

First. Capital stock, surplus and undivided profits, after certain additions thereto and certain deductions therefrom as provided in the Act. If this amount is less than the value of property, the measure of the tax becomes;

Second. The actual value of the real and tangible property owned or used by the corporation in Tennessee. If, however, this amount is less than the assessed valuation of property, the measure of the tax becomes; 

Third. The assessed valuation of the real and tangible personal property in Tennessee.

The above may be further illustrated as follows: 

1. Capital stock, surplus and undivided profits 

2. Actual value of real and tangible personal property 3.

Assessed value of real and tangible personal property .$150,000.00 100,000.00 75,000.00

The capital stock, surplus and undivided profits being the greater of the three, the tax would be computed thereon; but if items 2 or 3 were larger the tax is to be computed upon the greater of the three measures. 

The use of capital stock, surplus and undivided profits as a measure of tax liability does not present a very diffi-

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

cult matter, and generally speaking the tax will be assessed upon this measure, in most instances, due to the fact that the total net worth usually is in excess of actual value or assessed value of real and tangible personal property. However, there are instances in which this condition will not exist and it should again be noted that the tax is to be assessed upon the greater of the three items mentioned above. Unfortunately, the Act does not clearly state just what is meant by the term "actual value" of real and tangible personal property; nor is this term defined in the rules and regulations of the Commissioner. Therefore, questions will arise as to the meaning of this term. Apparently there is some justification for taking the view that for the purposes of this tax the term may be taken to mean book value of real and tangible personal property, deducting therefrom depreciation reserves; but the book value may or may not be the actual value. 

However, the Act could not have contemplated the appraisal of real and tangible personal property by the Commissioner for the purpose of this tax. 

On page 2 of the Franchise Tax Report (Section E- 

Cash and Assessed Valuation of Properties in Tennessee), the cash valuation of real and personal property is to be made by the corporation in its sworn report and not only is this valuation required, but also the assessed valuation, together with the name of the county or counties in which such property is located. In this connection the following rule should be noted:

Regulation No. 7. 

Enter in Section E the cash value and the assessed value of both real and tangible personal property located in this State, inserting the county in which such property is located. Should the space provided be inadequate for this purpose, attach separate schedule. 

Article II. Section 28 of the Constitution of Tennessee among other things, provides: -All property shall be taxed according to its value, that value to be ascertained in such manner as the Legislature shall direct so that taxes shall be uniform throughout the State.- 

---

(Ch. 2 

The Legislature has directed the value to be used and 

Section 4, Chapter 602, Public Acts 1907-Section 1349, Williams Code of Tennessee, provides as follows: 

"All property of every kind shall be assessed at its actual cash value. 

The term 'actual cash value" is defined to mean the amount of money the property would sell for if sold at a fair, voluntary sale." 

Therefore, in view of Section 1349 of the Code, in theory at least, there should be no variance between "actual cash value" and "assessed value" but this condition does not exist in practice. There is a vast difference between "actual" values and "assessed" values in the ninety-five counties in Tennessee. Opinion as to values differ between the many County Tax Assessors, and City and County assessments on identically the same piece of property differ in most instances. 

Further discussion on this subject is found at Chapter 

16. "Property or Ad Valorem" Taxation. 

No connection between local property tax values and values used for State Franchise Tax can exist. However, it is understood that there is considerable difference of opinion as to whether the law contemplated the "property" tax base in the franchise tax to consist of the local assessed valuations.

In the absence of any clear definition of the term "actual" value in the law, it does appear that the original property investment, less regular depreciation (as shown by taxpayer's records) would nearer approximate the intent of the Act and it certainly would create more uniformity than any other method in those instances where "property" is the factor used for the franchise tax measure. However, there may be instances where the book figures do not reflect the correct values of real and personal properties and, in such instances, reasonable proof should be furnished by actual appraisal or investigation by disinterested persons.

Tax Accrues Until Corporation Dissolves or Withdraws- 

Law. Section 1. 

The tax imposed by this Act shall apply to corporations whose business is being conducted by a receivership or trusteeship appointed by

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

any Court of competent jurisdiction and shall continue to accrue until such time as the corporation has been actually and legally dissolved or withdrawn from this State. 

As long as a corporation continues to operate under receivership or trusteeship, franchise tax accrues; and, should a corporation owe any tax, at the time the receiver is appointed, then such tax is a prior claim against funds coming into the hands of the receiver. 

Minimum Tax- Law. Section 1. 

The minimum tax payable under this Act shall be Ten ($10.00) Dollars.

State Tax Only- Law. Section 1. 

The tax herein levied shall be a tax for State purposes only and no county or municipality shall have the power to levy a similar tax. 

The above two subsections are deemed to be sufficiently clear and comment is unnecessary.

Tax Credits- Law. 

Section 2. 

There shall be credited upon the tax hereby imposed such net amounts as are paid by insurance companies to this State as a tax upon gross premiums collected by them, not including the gross premium receipts tax paid by fire insurance companies for the purpose of executing the fire marshal law. There shall be no other credits. 

Regulation No. 13. 

No credits are allowed under the Franchise Tax Law except the tax paid by insurance companies upon gross premiums. 

Section 2 of the present law is a radical departure from the provisions of Chapter 5 of the Acts of 1935, Section 8 of which is as follows: 

There shall be credited upon said tax the net amount or amounts paid by any entity subject to this tax hereunder to the State, as excise tax under the provisions of Sections 1316-1328, inclusive, of the Code of 1932, and there shall also be credited upon said tax such net amounts as are paid by insurance companies to this State as a tax upon gross premiums collected by them and all sums paid by State banks into the Treasury of the State of Tennessee as fees for the use and benefit of the Banking Department of the State of Tennessee, but the minimum tax payable hereunder by any entity as heretofore defined shall be $10.00. 

The excise tax for which credit shall be given hereunder is the excise tax paid for the previous year to the one in which the tax herein levied shall accrue.-

(Ch. 2 

It would appear that since the Excise Tax as levied is a "privilege" tax and Chapter 5 of 1935 levies another "privilege" tax upon the same class of taxpayers and does not provide that the tax levied therein is in addition to all other taxes, that it was the intention of the author of the Act to reach only that portion of the "privilege” escaping taxation by reason of a lack of net earnings; the net result of the two acts being an attempt to use the basis which would produce the greater revenue. It will be noted that Chapter 

100, Acts of 1937, Section 1, provides: "The tax hereby imposed shall be paid for the privilege of engaging in business in corporate form in this State and shall be in addition to all other taxes levied by any other Act." While an Excise tax levied upon "net earnings" for the privilege of "doing business" in Tennessee and a franchise tax levied for the privilege of "engaging in business" in corporate form are in effect double taxation; the courts look upon this form of double taxation without condemnation. In the recent Home Federal Savings and Loan Association case the court states: "The power of the Legislature to double tax the same privilege is conceded, and is well supported by our authorities," citing Corn V. Fort, 170

Tenn. 375; Home Building and Loan Association V. 

Graham, 155 Tenn. 524; and Camden Fire Insurance Association V. Haston, 153 Tenn. 692.

Manifestly, the elimination of the Excise Tax payment as a credit upon Franchise tax was for the purpose of producing greater revenue and at the same time aid in the creation of a more equitable tax distribution. If engaging in business in corporate form is a taxable privilege, then it logically follows, all who exercise such privilege should be taxed uniformly. Of course the corporation without net earnings has less "ability to pay" than the corporation earning large profits but ordinarily a corporation exercises its privilege just as much in producing profit as a corporation which shows a loss. 

Both are afforded the same privilege by the State. 

With respect to this tax credit under the present franchise tax law, insurance companies are the only class of corporations permitted to off-set franchise tax. This ap-

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

pears to be a reasonably sound and proper exception to the general rule, for the reason that gross receipts of insurance companies operating in other states are usually subject to the same rate of tax as that imposed by their home State. The rate of tax applicable to premiums is 

22% at the present in Tennessee and the additional burden of franchise tax would result in the prohibition of Tennessee insurance companies doing business in many other states. 

Allocation of Taxable Amount to Tennessee- Law. Section 3. 

That in the case of corporations doing business in Tennessee and elsewhere the measure of the tax as hereinabove set forth shall be apportioned to Tennessee for the purpose of taxation in the following manner: (1) If the principal business in this State is manufacturing or if it is any form of collecting, assembling or processing of goods or materials, the capital stock, surplus and undivided profits shall be apportioned to Tennessee on the basis of the ratio obtained by taking the arithmetical average of the following two ratios: (a) The ratio of the value of its real estate and tangible personal property in this State on the date of the close of the fiscal year is to the value of its entire real estate and tangible personal property, with no deductions on account of encumbrances thereon. (b) The ratio of the total cost of manufacturing, collecting, assembling or processing within this State, to the total cost of manufacturing, collecting, assembling or processing within and without the State. (2) If the principal business in this State is selling, distributing, dealing in or using tangible personal property, the capital stock, surplus and undivided profits shall be apportioned to Tennessee on the basis of the ratio obtained by taking the arithmetical average of the following two ratios: (a) The ratio of the value of its real estate and tangible personal property in this State on the day of the close of its fiscal year is to the value of its entire real estate and tangible personal property then owned by it, with no deductions on account of encumbrances thereon. (b) The ratio of the total sales made through or by offices, agencies, or branches located in Tennessee during the income year to the total sales made everywhere during said year. (3) If the principal business is other than the manufacture or sale of tangible property, such proportion as its gross receipts in Tennessee during the income year is to its gross receipts for such year within and without the State. 

If, because of peculiar or unusual circumstances inherent in a particular case, the application of the above formulas would work a hardship or injustice, the Commissioner, upon application of the taxpayer and upon such showing, is authorized, with the approval of the Attorney General, to adopt such other method of apportionment as would be fair and just under the facts of the case. 

When corporations are doing business in Tennessee and elsewhere, only that part of the capital, surplus and undivided profits properly

allocable to Tennessee by the manner of apportionment hereinabove set forth, shall be used as a measure of the tax subject to the other provisions of this Act with reference to a minimum measure and a minimum tax.

If the capital stock of a corporation which is a subsidiary of another corporation or closely affiliated therewith by stock ownership is inadequate for its business needs apart from credit extended or indebtedness guaranteed by the parent or an affiliated corporation, in determining the amount of capital, surplus and undivided profits of such corporation with respect to its liability for the tax imposed by this Act, there shall be included in the measure of the tax the indebtedness owed to or guaranteed by the parent or an affiliated corporation. If necessary to apportion such indebtedness the methods of allocation heretofore set forth shall be used.

A method for the determination of the tax measure or the "taxable amount" has already been suggested. With regard to the allocation of a portion of the taxable amount to Tennessee, little difficulty arises in those cases in which the entire property and the entire business of the corporation is within the State of Tennessee. In such cases the use of the statutory ratios are unnecessary, since the entire amount is subject to the tax. However, in those cases in which only a part of the property and only a part of the business of the corporation is within Tennessee the use of the ratios for the purpose of allocation become most essential; and many intricate problems will often arise.

The ratios set forth in the Act are designed to allocate a fair and reasonable proportion of the taxable amount to Tennessee. In the case of manufacturing corporations, the arithmetical average of the ratio of real and tangible personal property and the ratio of manufacturing costs bear relationship to business done and capital invested or used in Tennessee, thereby reasonably measuring the use made of the "privilege" granted by the State. This would also appear to be true with respect to corporations dealing in or using tangible personal property as well as those corporations dealing in intangible personal property. 

However, the use of ratios for the purpose of allocating a portion of the tax base cannot alter the facts inherent in a particular case. In an adjoining state the Income Tax Law allocated net taxable income upon the basis of the ratio obtained by taking the fair cash value of real estate and tangible personal property in the State to fair cash value of real

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

estate and tangible personal property everywhere. The 

Supreme Court of the United States held this allocation of income to be unreasonable, arbitrary and in violation of the Constitution. (See Hans Rees' Sons, Inc. V. State of 

North Carolina ex rel Maxwell, 283 U. S. 123 and cases there cited).

The Tennessee Legislature in enacting the Franchise Tax Law recognized the fact that specific and uniform rules of allocation are sometimes impractical, therefore, the Act vests certain discretionary powers in the Commissioner, subject to the approval of the Attorney General, permitting the adoption of "such other method of apportionment as would be fair and just under the facts of the case." 

(A) Manufacturing Corporations- 

The Act provides that if the "principal business" in Tennessee is manufacturing, collecting, assembling or processing goods and materials, the average of certain ratios shall be used. The Act does not provide criteria for the determination of "principal business." This question is one of fact rather than law. Obviously, a corporation manufacturing, collecting, assembling or processing goods or materials in Tennessee and selling its product as an incident to its manufacturing business would be classified as a manufacturing corporation; while a corporation manufacturing its products outside of Tennessee and selling in Tennessee would be classified as a selling or distributing corporation for the purpose of this tax.

When the principal business in Tennessee is manufacturing, the average of the following two ratios must be used to allocate the taxable amount: 

1. Ratio of Property. 

2. Ratio of Manufacturing Costs. 

The determination of the average percentage depends upon the accuracy of the figures which make the ratios. and, for example, in computing the property ratio, the

(Ch. 2 

book values of the real and tangible personal property after deducting depreciation reserves must be used and the manufacturing costs ratio should be computed upon the basis of total costs in Tennessee to total costs everywhere after equitable allocation of overhead burden. 

Regulation No. 8. 

In Section F, page 2 of the report, the value of both real and tangible personal property located in Tennessee and the value of such property everywhere should be shown less the depreciation reserves carried on the books of the taxpayer. 

Regulation No. 5. 

The term manufacturing costs shall be taken to mean the total cost of all goods, materials and supplies used in manufacturing, assembling or processing; the total wages and salaries paid or incurred during the year and the total overhead or manufacturing burden properly assignable according to good accounting practice to such manufacturing, assembling or process activities.

After accurate determination of property and manufacturing costs ratios, the average is applied to the tax measure, thereby allocating a portion of the amount to Tennessee.

The above example would appear to be the apportionment method to be used by "manufacturing" corporations as contemplated by the Act; but does such method appear unreasonable in the following case:

A foreign corporation has its manufacturing plant in Tennessee and for the purpose of the Franchise tax is classified as a "manufac- turing corporation. However, this corporation is qualified to do business in the State of New York, it maintains offices there, through which all of its sales are made. It maintains its bank accounts in New 

York, its general books and records are there; in fact all of the company's business is directed from New York. 

Obviously, a substantial portion of the company's capital is invested in New York, and possibly should be so apportioned inasmuch as its entire sales force is maintained there, together with other activities. 

Under such circumstances, it might be argued that, in order to more fairly and equitably assess the tax, other methods of apportionment should be adopted. (B) Corporations Selling, Distributing, Dealing in or 

Using Tangible Personal Property- 

When the "principal business" in Tennessee is selling, distributing, dealing in or using tangible personal property, the average of the following ratios must be used to apportion the taxable amount: 

1. Property Ratio. 

2. Ratio of Total Sales. 

The term "principal business" is discussed under the heading (A) Manufacturing Corporations, and is omitted here. However, in sub-section 2 of Section 3 of the Act, a new ratio is substituted for the manufacturing costs ratio. 

This ratio was inserted for the reason that a "manufacturing costs" ratio does not produce an equitable apportionment of the taxable amount when applied to selling or distributing corporations, the "sales" ratio bearing a more reasonable relationship to the use made of the taxable "privilege" in Tennessee.

Regulation No. 6. 

The term sales as used shall be taken to mean sales made through or by offices and branches located in this State irrespective of where the purchaser may reside.

(Ch. 2 

It will be noted total sales made through offices, agencies or branches located in Tennessee is the determining factor, and that the residence of the purchaser is not to be considered; for example, if a resident of Kentucky purchases merchandise direct from a corporation located in Tennessee, not withstanding the fact that delivery takes place in interstate commerce, the sale is classified as a "sale made in Tennessee."

Here also, the accurate average ratio will depend upon the correctness of the figures used. Care should be exercised in the determination of the "sales ratio" and where possible a proper classification of sales should be maintained upon the books of the corporation. This would eliminate the necessity of making a subsequent analysis of the sales accounts.

(C) Corporations-Other than Manufacturing or Sell ing- If the principal business in Tennessee is other than manufacturing or sale of tangible personal property, the taxable amount is to be apportioned by the use of only one ratio: 

1. Gross Receipts. 

The Act contains no definition of the term "gross receipts" and frequently "gross receipts" and "total or gross sales" are considered analogous, however, the term "total sales" may or may not constitute "gross receipts." 

It is apparent that the Act intends the term "gross receipts" to include not only gross or total sales, but receipts of every nature and from all sources, i.e., income from sales, dividends, discount, interest, etc. and it is assumed that the provisions of Regulation No. 6 apply with equal force and effect to gross receipts.

(D) Apportionment of Indebtedness-Borrowed Capital- The Act provides:

Regulation No. 4. 

If the capital stock of a corporation which is a subsidiary or closely affiliated with another corporation is inadequate for the business needs, the indebtedness due the parent or affiliated corporation must be included in the base of the tax irrespective of how such indebtedness may be classified and shown on the books of the reporting corporation. 

As a general rule the apportionment of indebtedness will be unnecessary since the customary practice of corporate organization is the creation of subsidiaries. Usually corporations are able to accurately determine the sum advanced to a subsidiary and in view of known facts, "ratios of apportionment" would be unnecessary. Annual Report to be Filed- Law. Section 4. 

That the administration of this Act and the collection of the tax herein levied are hereby vested in the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation who shall have the power to employ such persons as may be necessary in the administration of this Act. There is hereby appropriated annually an amount equal to two (2%) per cent of the receipts derived from the proceeds of the tax for the purpose of administering this Act. 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation is hereby granted full power and authority to adopt such reasonable rules and regulations, not in conflict with this Act or other statutes, as he may deem necessary to enforce the collection of the tax herein levied. Such rules and regulations before being effective shall be approved by the Attorney-General and shall be printed. A copy of such rules and regulations shall be furnished any interested party upon application, and shall accompany the annual report form required to be filed under this Act. 

Every corporation liable for the tax here imposed shall, on or before July 1st of each year, file with the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation on such form as he may prescribe an accurate and complete report, verified by the oath of the President, the Vice-President, the Secretary, the Treasurer or the General Manager, which report shall contain the following data: (a) The name of the corporation, the State in which chartered, the location of its principal place of business in this State and the location of its principal or home office. (b) The amount of capital stock subscribed and paid in, the amount issued and outstanding, the amount of surplus and undivided profits, together with the book value of each share of such stock as shown by the books and records of the corporation at the close of its last calendar or fiscal year. (c) A comparative balance sheet as of the beginning and close of the last calendar or fiscal year as shown by the books and records of the corporation. (d) The location by counties of all property in Tennessee of the corporation, together with the assessed valuation thereof.

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

(e) Such other and further information as may be required by the Commissioner for the reasonable enforcement of this Act. 

By the enumeration of the specific data required above it is not intended to divest the Commissioner of his right to require all information which he may deem necessary for the enforcement of this Act. 

Reports of corporations made hereunder shall be confidential and shall not be divulged by the Commissioner or his assistants except to a legislative committee appointed for the purpose of examining them, to the Governor, to the Attorney General and Reporter, or in obedience to a court order. If the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation or any employee, or any person to whom such information is divulged, should divulge the contents of any report except in accordance with the foregoing exception, he shall be guilty of a misdemeanor and punished accordingly.

The tax herein levied shall be paid to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation on or before July 1st of each year and shall be paid at the time the sworn report is filed. The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation shall examine every sworn report as promptly as possible and shall ascertain whether the tax payment which accompanies such report is the amount actually and lawfully owing by the taxpayer. If the payment tendered is insufficient, the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation shall determine the correct tax due and shall immediately notify the taxpayer of the balance due, together with any interest and penalty thereon. If the amount tendered is in excess of the correct liability under this Act, the Commissioner, with the approval of the Attorney-General and Reporter, shall return the amount of such excess to the taxpayer by State warrant, as in the case of other refunds. 

(A) Administration- 

The administration of the Act is vested in the Commissioner, or in the Department of Finance and Taxation. The provisions with respect to the employment of persons and the appropriation of 2% of the tax collected appear to have been superseded by the passage of the 

General Appropriation Act. 

(B) Adoption of Rules and Regulations- 

Authority to adopt reasonable rules and regulations is vested in the Commissioner. From the provisions of this section of the Act it would appear that the Legislature deemed it necessary to surround this power with certain conditions or limitations intended to safeguard the rights of taxpayers. The Act provides certain criteria by which the legality of a rule or regulation may be determined; 

1. It must be adopted by the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation. 

2. It must be reasonable and not in conflict with this Act or any other Statute. 

3. Its purpose must be to enforce the collection of the Franchise Tax. 

4. It must be approved by the Attorney-General of the State. 

5. It must be printed.

(Ch. 2 

6. A copy of such rules and regulations should be available to interested persons. 

7. Printed rules and regulations should accompany the annual report form required to be filed under the Act. (C) Sworn Reports to Be Filed All corporations, except those organized for general welfare and not for profit, doing business in Tennessee, whether organized under the laws of Tennessee or other states, are required to file, on or before July 1st of each year, a Franchise Tax Report upon the form or forms prescribed by the Commissioner. Two forms have been prescribed: 

1. Domestic Franchise Tax Report. 

2. Foreign Franchise Tax Report. 

Corporations organized under the laws of Tennessee are classified as "Domestic Corporations" while those formed under the laws of other states and countries are classified as "Foreign Corporations." The reports are to be prepared in accordance with the books and records and are to be "accurate and complete." Attention is directed to:

Regulation No. 2. 

This report must be complete in every detail. Unless all information requested is properly shown, the report will not be considered as having been filed under the law. Penalties and interest will accrue upon all incompleted and delinquent reports.

In view of the above regulation it becomes important to promptly and accurately execute the annual franchise tax report in order that penalties and interest may be avoided, therefore the following examples of the executed reports are submitted for the general classification of corporations: 

(1) Domestic Manufacturing Corporation (2) Domestic Selling Corporation (3) Foreign Corporation Dealing in Intangible Property.

(Ch. 2 

July 1st, extension of time for filing should be secured in accordance with: 

Regulation No. 1. 

Extension of time for filing this report may be granted in instances where the extenuating circumstances justify such extension. Application for extension must be made in writing to the Commissioner at least fifteen days before the due date of the return. Such application must fully state the reasons for such request. When extension is granted the tax due will be subject to interest at the rate of 6% per annum. 

In this connection, attention is called to the provision contained in Section 5 of the Act. It appears that the 

Commissioner cannot, under any circumstances, grant an extension of time for a period greater than ninety days after July 1st, the certification for non-payment being mandatory. 

(D) Payment of Tax- 

The tax levied by the Act, and as shown to be due by the sworn report, is to be remitted to the Commissioner of 

Finance and Taxation on or before July 1st of each year, i. e., at the time the report is filed. The tax may be paid by check, draft, postal money order, express money order, or in cash. If payment is made in any form other than cash, the checks, draft or money order should be made payable to: "Commissioner of Finance and Taxation." To avoid penalties and interest it would appear that the report and remittance should be mailed and post-marked on or before midnight July 1st.

As promptly as possible after the report has been filed and tax paid in accordance with such report, the Commissioner "shall ascertain whether the tax payment which accompanies such report is the amount actually and lawfully owing by the taxpayer.' If payment is insufficient the taxpayer is to receive notification of the balance due; if the payment is excessive, refund is to be made upon State warrant in accordance with law. 99 After filing the Franchise Tax report and paying the tax, if an error is discovered by the corporation which has resulted in the overpayment of the tax, the discovery of such error should immediately be made known to the Commissioner and claim for refund properly filed.
