provides, "if the amount tendered is in excess of the correct liability under this Act, the Commissioner, with the approval of the Attorney General and Reporter, shall return the amount of such excess to the taxpayer by State warrant, as in the case of other refunds. The 

Legislature intended this provision to safeguard and protect the taxpayer against errors resulting in excess payments; however, Chapter 100, Public Acts of 1937, does not alter the provisions of Chapter 167, Public Acts of 1935, which provides: "Any claim for refund by the State of taxes or revenues alleged to have been erroneously or illegally paid shall be filed with the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation supported by proper proof within one year from the date of payment, otherwise the taxpayer shall not be entitled to refund and said claim for refund shall be barred." 

Corporations Commencing Business During Taxable Year- 

There is no mention in the Franchise law as to the liability of new corporations and the method of determining the tax due. The tax is assessed and collected in advance for the privilege of doing business in corporate form and is due on July 1st of each year.

Obviously, new corporations should pay this "privilege' tax from the date the privilege is granted, viz., the date of incorporation. A fair and equitable basis along the following lines might be adopted:

Example-Corporation chartered February 1, 1937. 

Capital Stock $50,000.00 

1. For the period February 1 to June 30, 1937 tax to be assessed and due February 1 on 5/12ths of the $50,000.00 Capital stock. 

2. For the twelve months period, July 1, 1937 to June 30, 1938 the tax base shall be the net worth, as shown by the books on June 30, 1937 or if that is not available, the $50,000.00 capital stock might be used. 

Failure to File Annual Report and Pay Tax- Law. Section 5. 

That the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation shall certify to the Secretary of State the name of any corporation which fails or refuses to file the report and to pay the tax herein required in all cases where such report and tax payment have not been made within ninety (90) days after July 1st of each year. At the time of such certification to the 

Secretary of State, the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation shall give notice to the corporation of the action taken. Thereupon the charter of such corporation or its domestication in Tennessee shall stand as auto-

(Ch. 2 

matically revoked and the Secretary of State shall note such revocation upon his records. At any time within one year after the date of revocation such charter may be reinstated upon the payment of tax, penalty and interest due, plus filing fees due the Secretary of State. 

Any corporation subject to the tax herein levied which shall be delinquent in filing this report or in paying this tax may be enjoined from doing business in this State in a suit brought in the name of the State by the Attorney-General. 

Any corporation delinquent in the filing of the report herein required or in the payment of the tax herein levied shall pay a penalty of ten (10%) per cent for the first month or fractional part thereof of delinquency, and penalty thereafter at the rate of one-half of one per cent (2 of 1%) of the amount due for each month of such delinquency. All delinquencies shall bear interest at the rate of six (6%) per cent per annum from July 1st of each year until paid. The penalty and interest herein provided for shall apply to any part of the tax unpaid by July 1st and no such penalty or interest can be waived. 

In addition to the penalty and interest heretofore provided the Commissioner is authorized in the case of any corporation failing or refusing to make report and to pay tax to ascertain the tax liability of such corporation from any information available and to give notice of the amount of such tax liability to the corporation forthwith by registered mail. After being so notified, any corporation shall pay the tax assessed against it and if it contests the legality thereof must proceed in ac cordance with Section 6 of the Act. 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation is hereby authorized when any tax shall have remained unpaid for as much as fifteen days, including assessments made by the Commissioner in the absence of the sworn statement and notice hereinbefore provided for, to issue a distress warrant for the amount of tax, interest and penalties due under the provisions of this Act, together with all costs and commissions allowed by law for the collections upon execution. Such distress warrant shall be levied upon any property of the corporation located in this State. 

The Commissioner may at his option bring suit in any court of competent jurisdiction against a delinquent taxpayer for the collection of the tax, interest and penalties herein provided. 

(A) Certification of Delinquent Corporation-De linquent for More than 90 Days It is mandatory that the Commissioner certify, within ninety day period, all corporations failing or refusing to file the report and to pay the tax. Such certification is to be made to the Secretary of State who is required to make record of such certification upon the records of his Department; the charter or domestication of such delinquent corporation is to stand revoked. Corporations so certified and having their charters so revoked are allowed one year from the date of such revocation to re-instate. However, before re-instatement, penalty and interest must be paid to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation and filing fees paid to the Secretary of State. 

Delinquent corporations may be enjoined from doing

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

business in this State. Such action is to be brought in the name of the State by the Attorney-General. It would appear that the Secretary of State or the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation may make official request upon the Attorney-General to institute such proceedings. (B) Corporations Delinquent for Less than Ninety Days- Penalties and interest imposed cannot be waived by the Commissioner. The Act is mandatory in this regard. 

Penalty of 10% of the amount of tax payable on or before July first is imposed for the first month or fractional part of the month. If the delinquency exists for a period of two months the penalty would be 102%. In addition to the penalty imposed the tax past due is subject to interest at the rate of 6% per cent. While it is not clear as to whether the interest is to be computed upon the tax due or upon the aggregate of tax and penalty, it would appear reasonable to compute the interest only upon the tax, provided the tax is delinquent for a period of less than a year. 

In addition to the penalties and interest imposed upon delinquent corporations, the Commissioner is authorized to assess the tax based upon any information available. 

A tax so assessed appears to be subject to all penalties provided in the Act. In such cases the only remedy available to the corporation is the payment of the tax under protest and the filing of suit for recovery in accordance with Section 1790, et seq of the Code of Tennessee. 

An extension of time granted by the Commissioner beyond July first for filing the report and making payment of the tax will avoid the imposition of penalty; however, the tax due is subject to interest from and after the due date of the report and tax payment.

The Commissioner is authorized to issue distress warrant for the collection of the tax within fifteen days after July first, or after assessment is made. Such distress warrant is to cover tax, penalty, interest and costs. The

(Ch. 2 

warrant may be levied upon any property of the corporation found in Tennessee, or at the option of the Commissioner, suit may be instituted. 

Commissioner or Authorized Representatives may Examine Books and Records- Law. Section 6. 

That the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation or his duly authorized agent shall have access to all books and records of corporations required to pay tax thereunder, to enable the Commissioner to ascertain the correctness of any fact or report made or herein required. In the event any corporation fails or refused to permit the Commissioner or his agent to have access to necessary books and information then the Commissioner shall have power and authority to compel the attendance of witnesses and the production of books and papers in the same manner as process may now be issued by the courts to compel the attendance of witnesses and the production of books and papers. Such process shall run anywhere in the State and shall be served by the sheriff or any lawful officer to whom it may be directed. Disobedience to such process shall be treated as contempt of court and may be punished as such on the petition of the Commissioner to the Chancery Court of the county to which such process is directed. 

Remedy Where Illegal Assessment Made- Law. Section 6. 

Whenever any corporation conceives that any tax demanded by the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation under the supposed authority of this Act is illegal or not due it shall be the duty of the corporation to pay the tax and to challenge the legality or correctness thereof in a suit instituted in accordance with Section 1790, et seq. of the Code of Tennessee. In such suit for the recovery of a tax paid all questions of law and fact with reference to the illegality of the tax may be raised. No corporation shall be entitled to enjoin the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation from collecting any tax demanded by such collecting officer under the authority of this Act and no such injunction shall issue under the guise of enjoining an assessment or a collection. The sole remedy of the taxpayer shall be a suit to recover the tax alleged to have been illegally collected or demanded. In such suit the Commissioner shall not be permitted to defend upon the ground that the payment was not made under duress. In any case where a court of competent jurisdiction shall decree a recovery of a tax herein such court shall be authorized to allow interest from the date of the payment to the date of the judgment at a rate not exceeding six (6%) per cent per annum. 

The provisions of this section with reference to payment under protest and with reference to no injunctive relief shall apply to taxes demanded by the Commissioner where the original payment of the corporation was alleged to be insufficient as well as to taxes assessed by the Commissioner in the absence of the sworn report or statement required.

The time for filing suits for the recovery of allegedly illegal taxes and the procedure in such suits shall be governed by Section 1790 et seq. of the Code of Tennessee.

Opinion by Justice DeHaven. 

(1) These suits involve the constitutionality of chapter 

5, Acts 1935, Extraordinary Session of the General As sembly of the State of Tennessee, which is entitled:

76

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

"AN ACT to provide revenue for the State by the imposition of privilege taxes and to provide ways and means for the collection of such tax,"

Section 2 of the Act is as follows: 

"That for the privilege of engaging in business in corporate form in this State which is expressly hereby declared to be a privilege, there is hereby levied upon all domestic corporations an annual privilege tax, the measure of which is hereinafter set forth. The tax imposed also applies to corporations whose business is being conducted by and through a receivership or trusteeship appointed by any court of competent jurisdiction. "(b) For the privilege of engaging in business in this State in corporate form, there is hereby imposed upon foreign corporations doing an intrastate business an annual privilege tax to be measured as hereinafter mentioned. "C (c) For the privilege of engaging in business as a partnership, there is hereby levied on all partnerships conducting that type of activity in this State for which corporations may be formed under existing statutes in this State an annual privilege tax measured as hereinafter mentioned. (d) For the privilege of doing business in such form in this State, there is hereby levied against common law, business and/or Massachusetts trusts an annual privilege tax for the privilege of doing business in this State in such form." "( It is further provided in the Act that, "To do business in this State in any of the above mentioned forms is expressly declared to be a privilege," but that nothing in the Act shall be applicable to National banks, corporations performing governmental functions of the United States, State of Tennessee, or any political subdivision thereof, or corporations chartered under the general welfare law of the State and not for profit, or to an individual, engaging as such, in any business or line of endeavor. 

It is further provided that every corporation and partnership coming within the purview of the Act, is an "entity," and "shall pay as a privilege tax for the exercise of the privilege hereinabove defined a tax of $0.15 (fifteen cents) on the $100.00, or major fraction thereof, worth of capital invested by such entity in this State." 

Complainants, in the two above-styled causes, filed their respective bills in the Chancery Court of Davidson County, seeking a declaration under the provisions of the Declaratory Judgments Law of Tennessee as to their liability for any tax imposed by said Act. Complainants, C. H. Corn et al., alleged in their bill that they are partners in the operation of a grist mill, at Franklin, Tennessee, which

(Ch. 2 

business is conducted under the name of the Lillie Mill Company, and that a large part of the capital of the partnership is invested in wheat, corn, and other grains, the produce of the soil of Tennessee, and in flour, meal, and feed which they have manufactured from such produce, and hold for sale. Complainant, West Kentucky Coal 

Company, alleges in its bill that it is a corporation organized under the laws of the State of New Jersey, and is engaged in the business of mining and selling coal, with mines in the State of Kentucky, and owning property and doing business in the State of Tennessee, where it is legally domesticated. Both complainants averred that chapter 5, Acts 1935, Extra Session, is unconstitutional and void as a violation of various provisions of the constitutions of the State of Tennessee and of the United States, referred to in the bill. 

The defendant demurred to the bills, relying on the validity of the Act, and also upon the provision contained therein that each section, subsection, and paragraph thereto are severable, and that should any portion of the Act be held unconstitutional the same shall not affect the remainder of the Act.

The chancellor held the Act in question constitutional and valid as applying to corporations, and unconstitutional and invalid as applying to partnerships, being of the opinion that the part of the Act applying to partnerships may be elided, leaving a valid Franchise Tax Act as to corporations. To the action of the chancellor in holding the statute unconstitutional insofar as it imposes a tax on partnerships, the defendant excepted, prayed, and was granted an appeal to this Court. The complainants also excepted and have filed certain assignments of error. the action of the chancellor in holding the Act unconstitutional as to corporations, the complainant, West Kentucky Coal Company, excepted, prayed, and was granted an appeal to this Court.

To (2) Article 2, section 28, of the Constitution of the State of Tennessee provides, in part, as follows: "But the legislature shall have power to tax merchants, peddlers and privileges, in such manner, as they may from time to

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

time direct." A privilege is whatever business, pursuit, occupation, or vocation, affecting the public, the legislature chooses to declare and tax as such. Mabry v. Tarver, 20 

Tenn. (1 Humph.), 94; Jenkins v. Ewin, 55 Tenn. (8 

Heisk.), 475; Burke v. Memphis, 94 Tenn., 691; Seven 

Springs Water Co. v. Kennedy, 156 Tenn., 1; Allen v. Pullman Palace Car Co., 191 U. S., 178, 48 L. ed., 138. The term "privilege," as used in article 5, section 28, of the constitution, refers to the activity or occupation and not to the character of the person or entity that pursues the activity or occupation. Bank of Commerce & Trust Co. v. Senter, 149 Tenn., 569, 582. The tax is upon the privilege itself. 

Mayes v. Erwin, 27 Tenn. (8 Humph.), 290, 293, and not upon the form in which the business is conducted. 

The tax imposed by chapter 5, Acts 1935, Extra Session, is upon the privilege of doing business in this State as a corporation, trust, or partnership. The application of the tax is made to depend on the character of the entity engaged in business, and not on the character of the business pursued.

This Court, in Bank of Commerce & Trust Co. v. Senter, 149 Tenn., 569, has expressly determined that the right to do business in Tennessee in corporate form is a taxable privilege. This conclusion follows from the nature of a corporation and the manner of its creation. No corporation can exist without the consent or grant of the sovereign. 

Since a corporation can exist only subject to the will of the sovereign, its right to exist or to do business in corporate form is subject to such terms and restrictions as the state may place upon the right, including the payment of such taxes as the sovereign may exact for the privilege of existing or of doing business. The right of a corporation to engage in intrastate business, within a state, depends solely upon the will of the state. The state, having the power to exclude entirely, has the power to impose as a condition the payment of a license fee. Camden Fire Ins. Assn. v. 

Haston, 153 Tenn., 675; Maine v. Grand Trunk R. Co., 142 

U. S., 217, 35 L. ed., 994; Ashley v. Ryan, 153 U. S., 436, 38 

L. ed., 773.

The Act here in question undertakes to impose a tax

(Ch. 2  

on partnerships engaged in that type of business for which corporations may be formed, for the privilege of doing business in that form, but excludes from its operation individuals, engaged as such, in any business or line of endeavor.

The elements and considerations sufficient to support the validity of a franchise tax on corporations for the privilege of doing business in that form within a state, are wholly absent in the case of an individual, or simple and unlimited partnerships. They hold no franchise or special privilege conferred by the sovereign not belonging to citizens generally of common right. The right of individuals to combine their activities, as partners, is independent and antecedent to government.

The power of taxation is not conferred upon the legislature by the constitution; it passes under the general designation of "legislative power or authority." There is no limitation upon the legislature as to the amounts or objects of taxation, except that found in the restrictions and prohibitions of the constitution. Jenkins v. Ewin, 55 Tenn. (8 Heisk.), 475; City of Chattanooga v. Railroad Co., 75

Tenn. (7 Lea), 566. While the legislature has a wide range of discretion in the matter of imposing privilege taxes, it cannot arbitrarily exclude one set of individuals from the operation of a privilege tax and include another set. The 

Act here in question excludes from its operation individuals, engaging as such, in any business, but includes two or more individuals who have agreed to join their efforts, as partners, in a common enterprise. There exists some reason for imposing the tax on corporations, as hereinbefore shown, but we can see no substantial reason for imposing this tax on a simple partnership, composed of individuals, and exempting the single individuals, who may, perhaps, be engaged in the same kind of business as the partnership. The classification is arbitrary and capricious, and in violation of article 1, section 8, of the Constitution of Tennessee, and of the equal protection clause of the 

Federal amendment to the Federal Constitution.

Our conclusion is that chapter 5, Acts 1935, Extra Session, is unconstitutional and void insofar as it undertakes

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

to place a tax on partnerships for doing business in that form. (3) The chancellor elided from the Act the provision with respect to the imposition of a privilege tax upon partnerships, having held such provision invalid. The West 

Kentucky Coal Company complains of this action of the chancellor. The Act provides: 

"That the Legislature expressly declares that each section, subsection and paragraph of this Act are severable and that should any portion of this Act be held unconstitutional the same shall not affect the remainder of said Act, but such unconstitutional portion shall be elided and the Legislature declares they would have enacted this Act with such unconstitutional portions elided therefrom."' 

The Act classifies four entities and makes them subject to a tax for the privilege of doing business in this State. 

Any one of the entities so classified could have been omitted without impairing the validity of the Act as to those included. There can be no speculation as to whether or not the legislature would have passed the Act without the unconstitutional portion for it has specifically declared that it would have enacted the statute with such portion elided. 

The inclusion of partnerships in the classification is clearly severable, and the fact that such inclusion was invalid cannot affect the validity of the balance of the Act. 

State v. Scott, 98 Tenn., 253, 39 S. W., 1; State ex rel. v. 

Cummins, 99 Tenn., 667; Fite v. State, 114 Tenn., 646; H. 

G. Hill Co. v. Whitice, 149 Tenn., 168; Williams v. Standard 

Oil Co., 278 U. S., 235, 73 L. ed., 297. (4) The tax imposed by chapter 5, Acts 1935, Extra Session, is not a property tax. It is a privilege tax measured by the worth of capital invested by the entity in this State. 

The language of the Act makes this plain. In section 2 of the Act, referring to the tax, it is stated, "the measure of which is hereinafter set forth," and "an annual privilege tax to be measured as hereinafter mentioned." The measure set forth is fifteen cents on the $100, or major portion thereof, of the worth of capital invested in this State. The fact that the tax is measured by the worth of invested capital does not make it a property tax. A privilege tax imposed upon corporations for the right to engage in business does not become a property tax because it is proportional

(Ch. 2 

in amount to the worth or value of the capital invested in this State. 

In Southern R. Co. v. Watts, 260 U. S., 519, 530, 67 L. ed., 375, 389, there was involved the constitutionality of a railroad franchise tax which was based upon the value of property as ascertained for the purpose of ad valorem taxation. The court said: "" It is argued that this franchise tax is an additional property tax which is not imposed on others, and that, consequently it violates the uniformity clause of the state Constitution and the equal protection clause of the Federal Constitution. It is true that the franchise tax is measured by the value of property already subjected to the ad valorem tax. But a privilege tax is not converted into a property tax because it is measured by the value of property (compare Clark v. Titusville, 184 

U. S. 329, 333, 46 L. ed. 569, 573, 22 Sup. Ct. Rep. 382); nor by the fact that in this measure is included property not used in the transportation service.''

In Cooley on Taxation (4th ed.), sec. 838, the rule is thus stated: "If a tax is in its nature an excise, it does not become a property tax because it is proportioned in amount to the value of the property or capital stock of the corporation. A fortiori, a tax which takes no notice of the real value of the assets of the corporation is generally held to be an excise rather than a property tax."' 

In State of Maine v. Maine Central R. Co., 74 Me., 376, the court said: "Now it is perfectly well settled that the amount of a franchise tax upon a corporation may be graduated or measured by an appraisal of the whole, thereby making it a property tax. Most franchise taxes are so measured. Possessing the power to impose a franchise tax to any amount it deems proper, the legislature may measure the amount by any standard it pleases. 

The legislature was within its constitutional rights in measuring the amount of the tax by a percentage on the worth of capital invested by the entity in Tennessee. In 

Home Insurance Co. v. New York, 134 U. S., 594, 35 L. ed., 

1025, the court said: "No constitutional objection lies in the way of a legislative body prescribing any mode of measurement to determine the amount it will charge for the privilege it bestows." The court was dealing with a tax imposed on corporations for the privilege of doing business in the State of New York. In State v. Franklin 

County Savings Bank & Trust Co., 74 Vt., 246, 52 Atl., 1069, the court said: "The amount to be paid on franchises of

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

any class may be ascertained upon such basis as the legislature shall determine." In State v. Pierce Petroleum Co. (Mo.), 2 S. W. (2d), 790, the court said: "The tax is not a property tax, but an excise levied upon the privilege of transacting business in this state as a corporation. 

It may therefore be computed according to any method the legislature sees fit to adopt." Other cases of like effect could be cited, but it is needless to multiply authority on this point. 

In Foster & Creighton Co. v. Graham, 154 Tenn., 412, relied on here by complainants, the court was considering the contention that a tax upon the storage of gasoline measured by the number of gallons of gasoline withdrawn from storage was a property rather than an excise tax. 

The court was not considering a tax of the nature here imposed. (5) The fact that the tax imposed on a corporation for the privilege of doing intrastate business in this State is measured by the capital invested, thereby including capital invested in property exempt from ad valorem tax, does not render the tax invalid. National Life & Accident Ins. 

Co. v. Dempster, 168 Tenn., 416; Pacific Co. v. Johnson, 285 U. S., 480; Thomson Electric Welding Co. v. Commonwealth (Mass.), 175 N. E., 203; Cooley on Taxation (4th ed.), 861; Flint v. Stone Tracy Co., 220 U. S., 107, 55 L. ed., 389; Home Ins. Co. v. New York, 134 U. S., 594, 33 L. ed., 1025. The reason for the rule is that such tax is not a tax upon the exempt property, but is a privilege tax in the measure of which tax exempt property can be included. (6) It is insisted by the West Kentucky Coal Company that it cannot be subjected to the tax imposed by chapter 5, Acts 1935, Extra Session, because it pays an excise tax and also a privilege tax under the General Revenue Act as a coal dealer. The argument is made that this is double taxation. The privilege tax placed upon coal dealers is applicable to all who engage in that business. The excise tax is for the privilege of doing intrastate business in this State. No double taxation arises by virtue of the two taxes. Complainant's real contention, however, is that the imposition of the excise tax (Code 1316 et seq.) and the tax

(Ch. 2  

imposed under the Act here in question amounts to double taxation. The excise tax is measured by 3 per cent of net earnings, whereas the tax here in question is measured by a percentage of worth of capital invested. The legislature, in the same act, might have made the measure of the tax a percentage of both net earnings and capital invested. 

Thomson Electric Welding Co. v. Commonwealth (Mass.), 

176 N. E., 203; Judson Freight Forwarding Co. v. Commonwealth, 242 Mass., 47, 136 N. E., 375.

Under chapter 5, Acts 1935, Extra Session, the amount paid under the excise statute is expressly made a credit upon the amount of the tax ascertained by a percentage of capital invested. The net result of the whole thing is that no corporation will be required to pay more than the tax levied under chapter 5, Acts 1935, Extra Session, excepting only those corporations whose tax would be less than 3 per cent of net earnings. The contention that complainant is subject to double taxation cannot be sustained. (7) It is contended by complainants that under chapter 5, Acts 1935, Extra Session, legislative power has been delegated to the Commissioner and the Chancery Court in ascertaining the amount of the tax. The Act provides, in substance, that if the Commissioner be of the opinion that the assessed valuation fixed upon the property for ad valorem taxation be fair and adequate, he may adopt and use such valuation; but, if he deems such value inadequate and representing less than the actual value thereof, he may, after giving ten days' notice to the entity whose property is sought to be taxed, proceed to appraise the same himself, or through competent appraisers, and determine the value thereof. After determining what in his opinion constitutes a fair value for such property, he shall file a detailed statement in his office setting forth the valuation fixed and within three days send to the owner, by registered mail, a statement showing in detail the amount of his valuation. If the entity is dissatisfied with the fixing of such valuation, it is given the right to review the findings by certiorari and supersedeas to the Chancery Court in the county in which the controversy arises, application therefor to be made within thirty days following the mailing of

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

the registered statement. Upon the hearing in the Chancery Court, the value fixed by the Commissioner shall be deemed prima facie correct, but such presumption is made rebuttable. Either party may introduce evidence as to the value of the property, and the court upon consideration of the entire record shall by its judgment fix the fair value of the property. Either party may appeal to the Supreme 

Court. As a condition precedent to certiorari and supersedeas, the entity seeking the same shall agree to pay at time due the tax upon the basis of the assessment of the property for ad valorem purposes, and give bond to pay whatever tax shall ultimately become due upon the valuation fixed by final judgment. 

Section 4 of the Act is, in part, as follows: 

"That in the case of entities having property located both in this State and elsewhere, the Commissioner is hereby authorized and empowered to adopt such method as he may deem adequate and equitable both to the State and to the taxpayer in determining the amount of capital as hereinabove defined properly allocable to this State and employed by the entity in this State. In determining the amount of such capital employed by the entity in question in this State, the Commissioner shall take into consideration the extent of the tangible property of such entity in this State as compared to the extent of the entire property of the entity wherever located; the gross receipts of the entire entity; the value of goods, wares and merchandise manufactured or maintained here as compared to the gross value of goods manufactured or maintained by such entity everywhere 

In the case of all entities, the Commissioner is required to take into consideration the book value of Tennessee property as compared to the total value of all of its property as shown by its books. 

The Act contains the following provision with reference to allocation: "The legislature hereby declares that no adequate set formula can be adopted for the determination of that proportion of the capital employed in Tennessee in case of entities having property both within and without this State which said formula would be equitable to all entities under all circumstances and for that reason has not undertaken to adopt such set formula believing that the judicial right of review of the Commissioner's allocation mentioned will prove more equitable as a whole than any set formula which it might adopt, but it expressly declares that it is made the duty of the Commissioner to take into consideration in making his allocations any and all of the above mentioned comparisons and/or ratios which will be appropriate in the determination with respect to the entity under consideration of the amount of capital employed by it in this State, and all other relevant facts. 

It is further provided:

(Ch. 2 

"In case the Chancery Court or any appelate court having jurisdiction of a review under this section shall be of the opinion that the Commissioner adopted an erroneous or inequitable method for the allocation of such tax, it shall be the duty of such court, in its decision, to lay down and promulgate the principles and factors upon which in its judgment an equitable allocation may be made. Either party may appeal... 

There is no uncertainty whatever in the Act as to the yardstick of the tax, the thing by which the amount of tax is measured. That yardstick is the named percentage on capital invested, or as repeatedly stated in the Act "capital employed," in the business. The administration of the law is, of course, left to a named official of the State. The law is not self-executing. Necessarily somebody has to ascertain the amount of invested capital. Certain elements to be considered in arriving at that value are stated in the Act. If the ad valorem assessment be considered fair, then the Commissioner accepts that, if not he proceeds to ascertain the value of the property. If the entity be dissatisfied with his findings, it may appeal. The whole object of the provisions of the Act with reference to ascertainment of the value of the property, is to arrive at a just assessment. 

The appeal is optional with the entity. The action of the court must be invoked by the entity. If the provisions governing the hearing and action of the court be considered by the entity objectionable, or invalid, then it would not, of course, invoke the jurisdiction of the court. The provisions for appeal are entirely for the benefit of the entity. If it invoked the right of appeal given by the Act, it could not be heard to say that the provisions with respect to appeal are invalid. The very object of the appeal would be, of course, to obtain a more equitable ascertainment of the value of its property.

We can see no illegal delegation of authority to the Commissioner. Certain definite formula is set out in the 

Act for his guidance. He can look to other things in ascertaining the value of the property, as a particular case might demand. Had this right been withheld from him, injustice could arise. The annotator who prepared the note to Hans Rees' Sons v. North Carolina, 283 U. S., 123, 75 L. ed., 879, says, in part:

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

"In the second place, it seems undesirable, in this present formative stage, for state legislatures to adopt mandatory apportionment formula applicable to all cases; rather, a considerable discretion should be vested in the taxing authorities, not only in the acquisition of information, but also in the apportionment of income.' 

(8) It is next insisted that the Act is unconstitutional in that a tax is never less than a sum measured by the ad valorem assessment, but may be more. The specific objection is that the taxpayer cannot dispute its ad valorem assessment, but that the State is not so limited. The contention, it seems, overlooks the fact that the statutes providing for ad valorem assessments also provide an adequate remedy for any taxpayer who feels aggrieved by the assessment. Having this opportunity for review, the tax payer cannot be heard to demand another. We see no merit in this contention. (9) Complainants challenge the Act in question as a burden upon interstate commerce because, as they insist, the Act makes as one of the essential elements in ascertaining the value of the property invested in this State by the entity the gross receipts of the entire entity. The Act plainly means, we think, that the Commissioner is to take into consideration in fixing such value the extent of the tangible property of such entity in this State as compared to the extent of the entire property of the entity, the extent of the gross receipts in this State as compared to the gross receipts of the entire entity, and the value of goods manufactured or maintained here as compared to the gross value of goods manufactured or maintained by the entire entity. 

The words "gross receipts of the entire entity," appearing in the Act, must be construed with its context and the intent of the Act, and when so construed it becomes apparent that the Commissioner is to compare the gross receipts in this State with the gross receipts of the entire entity. 

When the intent of a statute is clear, general words will be restrained to that intent, and words of narrower import will be expanded to embrace and effectuate that intent. 

Gold v. Fite, 61 Tenn. (2 Bax.), 237; Brown v. Hamlett, 76

Tenn. (8 Lea), 732. Words may be modified, altered, or supplied so as to obviate repugnancy to or inconsistency with such intent. Coal Creek, etc., Co. v. Tennessee Coal,

(Ch. 2 

etc., Co., 106 Tenn., 651, 62 S. W., 162; Rose v. Wortham, 95 Tenn., 505, 32 S. W., 458. The court is to take into consideration the "words, the context, the effects, and consequences. Russell v. Colyar, 51 Tenn. (4 Heisk.), 154; 

State v. Clarksville & Russellville Turnpike Co., 34 Tenn. (2 Sneed), 89. The literal interpretation of a statute is finding out the true sense by making the statute its own expositor. State v. Mason, 105 Tenn., 232, 58 S. W., 319.

The intent of the Act is to impose a privilege tax on an entity, engaged in intrastate business, to be measured by a percentage on the worth of the capital invested, or employed by it in this State. No tax is imposed by the Act on gross receipts of the entire entity. No such intent or purpose can be found in the Act. However, the legislature did intend that, in the ascertainment of such value, the proportion of gross receipts in this State should be compared with the gross receipts of the entire entity. To take the words 'gross receipts on the entire entity" and consider them separately from their context, and treating them as requiring the Commissioner to apply the percentage fixed for the tax to the whole of the gross receipts of the entity, would be utterly inconsistent with the clear purpose and intent of the Act, and repugnant thereto. 

However, if the words just quoted, when dissociated from their context, could be held to require the Commissioner to apply the measure of the tax to the whole of the gross profits of the entity, then it would be true that such requirement would be invalid, because a burden on interstate commerce. In such case, the court, under the mandate of the legislature, would elide such requirement, it being severable.

A statute, such as the one here, which imposes a privilege tax upon corporations having property located both in this State and elsewhere, and doing business in this State, does not impose an unconstitutional burden upon interstate commerce because in the ascertainment of the value of its capital employed in this State the assessing officer is to consider, among other factors, the ratio of its gross receipts everywhere as compared to its gross receipts in the State. U. S. Glue Co. v. Oak Creek, 247 U. S.,

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

321, 62 L. ed., 1135; Maine v. Grand Trunk R. Co., 142 U. 

S., 217, 35 L. ed., 994; Cooley on Taxation (4th ed.), secs. 

395-396. We think the objection made is without merit. (10) Complainants seek to raise the question in this Court, for the first time, whether or not chapter 5, Acts 1935, Extra Session, is constitutional legislation in view of the proclamation of the Governor calling such extra session. The defendant objects to the consideration of this question because not made in any pleading, or passed on in the court below, or presented in any assignment of error in this Court. When a bill is bottomed on the unconstitutionality of a statute it is the duty of complainant to point out and state with particularity details of supposed invalidity. Ogilvie v. Hailey, 141 Tenn., 392. In Williams v. 

Realty Dev. Co., 161 Tenn., 451, the court said: "We are of the opinion that such a question cannot be made against the statute for the first time on appeal; certainly not in a case at law, wherein an appeal is in the nature of a writ of error and the hearing in the appellate court is not de novo." 

In a matter of equity tried according to the forms of the chancery court, either party may appeal to the supreme or appeals court, "and have a reexamination, in that court, of the whole matter of law and fact appearing in the record." Code 9036. The Governor's proclamation convening the General Assembly in extraordinary session on July 15, 1935, can be judicially noticed, though not appearing in the record in the cause. Section 2 of the Governor's proclamation reads: 

"To provide sufficient revenue to pay the expenses of the State government and maintain its institutions, departments, offices and agencies for the biennium beginning July 1, 1935."

The contention made is that chapter 5, Acts 1935, Extra Session, undertook "to provide revenue for the State" for an indefinite period of time, and that the Act, therefore, was beyond the power of the legislature as restricted by article 3, section 9, of the State Constitution, which reads: "He may, on extraordinary occasions, convene the general assembly by proclamation, in which he shall state specifically the purposes for which they are to convene; but they shall enter on no legislative business except that for which they were specifically called together."

(Ch. 2 

The Act in question is an act to provide revenue to pay the expenses of the State government for the present biennium. The statute does not provide that it shall die by limitation at the end of the biennium. No provision of the 

Act undertakes to extend its operation beyond the present biennium. Every presumption is, of course, in favor of the validity of the Act. It must be presumed that the legislature was undertaking by the Act to provide revenue for the period mentioned in the proclamation of the Governor. 

The duty of providing revenue for succeeding bienniums will fall upon subsequent legislatures. The question here made could not properly arise until after the expiration of the present biennium, if it was sought to enforce the tax after that time. We find no merit in the contention made. 

After a full examination of the various questions made in the cause, we are constrained to hold that chapter 5, Acts 1935, Extra Session, is constitutional and valid as to corporations, and unconstitutional and invalid as to partnerships. The decree of the chancellor is affirmed. 

Complainants will pay the costs of the appeal. 

Home Federal Savings and Loan Associations, etc. et al. 

V. 

JOSEPH S. TOBIN, ET AL December Term 1936  

1. Complainants, under the Declaratory Judgments Law, ask the

Court to decree that they are not liable for the franchise tax imposed by Chapter 5, Acts of the Extra Session of 1935. 

2. It is conceded that the Federal Act of 1933 authorized the State to impose a direct tax on these corporations, but counsel insist that it cannot exact an indirect tax. The Act does not expressly provide that a direct tax only may be imposed, and we are of opinion that it should not be construed so narrowly. 

Opinion by Justice McKinney. 

Complainants, under the Declaratory Judgments Law, ask the court to decree that they are not liable for the franchise tax imposed by chapter 5, Acts of the Extra Session of 1935.

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

The complainants are a Federal savings and loan association chartered under an Act of Congress; a building and loan association chartered under the statutes of Tennessee but converted into a Federal association prior to the institution of this suit; and a building and loan association organized and doing business under the laws of Tennessee. 

The defendants are administrative officers of the State of Tennessee.

The primary contentions of complainants are (1) that it was not the purpose of the legislature to apply the Act of 1935 to building and loan associations and Federal savings and loan associations; (2) that Federal savings and loan associations are neither domestic nor foreign corporations within the meaning of the 1935 Act; and (3) that the 

Home Owners' Loan Act of 1933, as amended, only permits the imposition of a direct tax on Federal savings and loan associations as distinguished from an indirect tax, such as that provided by the Act of 1935. 

In support of their first proposition complainants insist that the tax imposed in the 1935 Act is of the same character as that exacted in the 1931 Act, and to adjudge them liable for both would constitute double taxation, which the courts are reluctant to impose in the absence of clear language expressing such to be the legislative intent. 

The chancellor held that complainants were liable for the privilege tax but not for the franchise tax, and complainants have not appealed; so that the question of the repeal of the 1931 Act, by implication by the 1935 Act, or the liability of complainants under that Act, is not before this Court for decision.

The power of the legislature to double tax the same. privilege is conceded, and is well supported by our authorities. Corn v. Fort, 170 Tenn., 375, 95 S. W. (2d), 620; 

Home Bldg. & Loan Assn. v. Graham, 155 Tenn., 524; Camden Fire Ins. Assn. v. Haston, 153 Tenn., 692. In the

Graham case the association was held liable for both the excise and the privilege tax, and the State insists that for the reasons set forth in the opinion in that case the complainants should be charged with both the franchise and the privilege tax.

(Ch. 2 

The Act of 1935 is quite lengthy, and it is unnecessary to incorporate it in this opinion. The caption recites that its object is to provide revenue for the State, and it is conceded that this was its purpose. 

Section 1 of the Act provides that the term "entity" comprehends corporations formed under the laws of this State except such corporations as are organized under statutes pertaining to organizations and corporations for general welfare, and engaged exclusively in religious, educational, and eleemosynary objects, and all corporations chartered under the laws of other States and doing an intrastate business in Tennessee except National Banks and Federal instrumentalities not subject to tax by virtue of the Constitution of the United States. By including all corporations except those for general welfare, National Banks and Federal instrumentalities exempted from tax by the Constitution, the Act necessarily embraced all other corporations, including complainants. 

The Act of 1935 further provides, "That for the privilege of engaging in business in corporate form in this State which is expressly hereby declared to be a privilege," there is levied upon all domestic corporations and upon foreign corporations doing an interstate business in this State an annual tax of fifteen cents on the $100 worth of capital invested by such entity in this State. 

The Act of 1931 exacts a graduated privilege tax, based upon the amount of capital paid in, from "every building and loan association incorporated, organized or doing business under the laws of this State." As previously stated, the question of the liability of Federal savings and loan associations for the 1931 privilege tax is not before us, and we infer that they were not in existence when that Act was passed. But the two acts differ materially, particularly in that one exacts a tax for the purpose of engaging in the various businesses or occupations enumerated in the act, whether conducted by an individual, a partnership, or a corporation, while the 1935 Act makes the engaging in business in corporate form a taxable privilege. 

It was not a privilege when the bill was passed whereby a

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

new source of taxation was created. This the legislature had a perfect right to do.

The validity of the 1935 Act, except as it related to partnerships, has been heretofore sustained by this Court in Corn v. Fort, supra. In that case this same question was raised by the West Kentucky Coal Company, its contention being that it would be doubly taxed for the same privilege if required to pay the tax provided in the 1935 Act since it was paying a privilege tax under the 1931 Act. The court overruled this contention, holding that "no double taxation arises by virtue of the two taxes." The mere fact that the privilege tax of the Coal Company and that of the building and loan associations are computed by different methods does not effect or alter the character of the tax. We think the legislature intended to tax complainants and that the Act is a valid one. 

As to the second contention, that Federal savings and loan associations are neither domestic nor foreign corporations, we are unable to agree. The Government of the 

United States is a "state" under the broad definition accorded that word, just as the Government of Tennessee is a state. 

In Texas v. White, 74 U. S., 227, 236, 19 L. ed., 700, 721, it is said: "A State, in the ordinary sense of the Constitution, is a political community of free citizens, occupying a territory of defined boundaries, and organized under a government sanctioned and limited by a written constitution, and established by the consent of the government. It is the union of such States, under a common constitution, which forms the distinct and greater political unit, which that Constitution designates as the United States, and makes of the people and States which compose it one people and one country."

In Union Bank v. Hill, 43 Tenn. (3 Cold.), 325, 330, this 

Court said: "The word 'State,' is used in various senses. In its most enlarged sense, it means the people composing a particular nation or community; and in this sense, 'the State,' means the whole people united into one body politic, and

(Ch. 2 

'the State,' and 'the people of the State,' are equivalent expressions." 

In United States v. Perkins, 163 U. S., 625, 41 L. ed., 287, it was held that the United States Government is a foreign corporation with respect to a state. 

Finally, as to the right of this State to tax Federal savings and loan associations, the Home Owners' Loan Act of 1933, as amended, contains the following provision: "Such associations, including their franchises, capital, reserves, and surplus, and their loans and income, shall be exempt from all taxation now or hereafter imposed by the United States, and all shares of such associations shall be exempt both as to their value and the income therefrom from all taxation (except surtaxes, estate, inheritance, and gift taxes) now or hereafter imposed by the United States; and no State, territorial, county, municipal, or local taxing authority shall impose any tax on such associations or their franchise, capital, reserves, surplus, loans or income greater than that imposed by such authority on other similar local or mutual or co-operative thrift and home financing institutions.”

This Act was before the Supreme Court of the United States in Hopkins Federal Savings & Loan Association v. 

Cleary, 296 U. S., 315, 80 L. ed., 251, in which the power of

Congress to create such corporations was expressly reserved. All that the court decided was that a State association could not be converted into a Federal association unless consented thereto by the State. Such consent was conferred by the legislature of this State in the enactment of chapter 26 at its Special Session of 1935. But so far as we are advised the construction of the provision of the Home Owners' Loan Act, quoted above, or the right of a state to tax Federal savings and loan associations has not been passed upon by any Federal court. 

It is conceded that the Federal Act of 1933 authorizes the State to impose a direct tax on these corporations, but counsel insist that it cannot exact an indirect tax. The 

Act does not expressly provide that a direct tax only may be imposed, and we are of opinion that it should not be construed so narrowly. It seems to us that what Congress

Ch. 2) 

FRANCHISE TAX 

had in mind was the taxation of these associations upon the same basis as other corporations engaged in a similar business are taxed; that is, without discrimination or partiality. Since these associations are private in character and operate for profit, such an interpretation would certainly be equitable and just. We are unwilling to ascribe to Congress a purpose to discriminate against State institutions. In our opinion, the language of the Act is sufficiently comprehensive to authorize the tax here imposed. It provides that no State shall impose any tax on such associations that is not exacted of similar home institutions. The tax in question has certainly been imposed on these complaining corporations as well as on all other corporations doing business in this State. The word "on" is synonymous with "upon. The 1935 Act imposes the franchise tax "upon corporations." The meaning of both acts is simply that the taxes imposed shall become a charge against the corporation, and shall be paid by it. 

The Act also prohibits a tax on the franchise of such associations not imposed on the franchise of other corporations engaged in a similar business. There may be a technical distinction between a "franchise tax" and a "tax on a franchise," but for practical purposes we see no material difference. "," The Act further provides that no State shall impose any tax on the capital of such associations that is not imposed on the capital of similar home institutions. In the instant cause the tax imposed is fifteen cents on the $100 of capital invested in this State. We conclude, therefore, that Congress has unmistakably conferred upon this State the authority to impose the tax here involved. In this regard we note that complainants have taken an inconsistent position. 

We quote from their brief, in which, after discussing the two Acts of 1931 and 1935, they use this language: "It is submitted that the better construction is the one which favors the 1931 tax, not only for the reason that it probably renders Federal Associations liable with State Associations, but because it is more in line with the disclosed legislative intent." According to their own interpretation, both acts impose indirect taxes, notwithstanding which they ad-

(Ch. 2  

mit liability under the 1931 Act, but deny it under the 1935 

Act. 

For the reasons stated herein, the decree of the chancellor will be reversed, and a decree entered in accordance with this opinion. 

Justice DeHaven did not participate in the consideration of this cause.

HISTORY OF EXCISE TAXATION IN TENNESSEE Section 28, Article II of the Constitution of 1870, provides in part as follows: 

"But the Legislature shall have power to tax Merchants, Peddlers, and privileges, in such manner as they may from time to time direct. 

The message of Governor Peay to the 63rd General 

Assembly, under date of January 17, 1923, appears to be the inception of Excise Taxation in Tennessee. Pertinent excerpts of his message follow: "-Pursuant thereto, I inform you that a deficit existed in state accounts, December 1, 1922 of $2,586,596.69. I therefore remind you at the outset of your deliberations, that our financing must consider these imperative items, to-wit: 

1. This deficit of $2,586,596.69. 

2. This note for $1,000,000.00 maturing this year. 

3. Annual interest of $697,000.00. 

4. This principal payment of $300,000.00 in the next fiscal period. 

This large total of $5,280,596.69 must be provided before anything can fairly be appropriated for the ordinary expenses of the State Government. We assume office with certain and definite pledges to the people. 

These must be in your mind, and must constrain your conscience as they do mine. These are our pledges: 

1. Reorganization of the administrative system looking to economy and efficiency. 

2. Thorough re-organization of tax department, and complete change of its administration. 

3. Thorough re-organization of highway department, and complete change of its administration. 

4. Abolition of present back tax system. 

5. Reduction of one million dollars in land tax. 

6. Repeal of eight per cent law. 

7. Repeal of sliding scale. 8. Restoration to municipalities of power to contract with utilities for gas, electricity, and transportation. 

9. No bond issue without popular vote. 

10. Equitable taxation of income bearing personalty. 

11. Better rural schools. 

12. Less legislation.

Nothing short of a literal redemption of these pledges should be tolerated. 

Popular government will collapse unless representatives keep faith with the people. It is now suggested in the report, (report of the Tax 

Commissioner) that the State turn from taxation of real estate for revenue and look to other sources. "This proposal comes after a quarter of a million dollars in round figures have been used to build present assessments. My position has has been, that land cannot pay its present taxes. Our tax department appears to have reached the same conclusion.-Politicians cannot administer a tax department.-Eventually, the state must find its revenue 99

(Ch. 3 

from other sources than real estate, land cannot bear the taxes which the counties are imposing, and support the state Government. We should begin framing our tax system to relieve real estate from all contribution to the state."

The principal source of revenue at this time was real estate. The tax levied upon property had become so burdensome as to threaten agriculture, the chief industry. In this connection Governor Peay states: 

"" -Our farmers are becoming restless and unhappy. They are realizing the long injustice to which they have submitted and are awakening to their power at the ballot box. Heretofore, they have constituted the stable and conservative force in our society; and it is our hope and dependence that such shall continue. The future of our country is wrapped in the solution of the agricultural problem.'' 

These issues appear to have been very vital in the first days of the Peay administration and are also vital issues today in Tennessee. The Governor and the Legislators were elected to office pledged to the people to find a reasonable solution. Tennessee had come face to face with the question of adopting a new system of taxation in order that property tax might be reduced; and to provide sufficient revenue to eliminate the recurrence of annual deficits in the general fund of the state. Obviously, the solution of these problems could not be effected upon a basis of "political expediency," solution was to be found in radical reforms in tax policies and courage to fight for such changes. Governor Peay's recommendations in this regard were as follows: 

"I recommend that that you omit the direct levy for highways.

This will relieve general property of $800,000.00 in taxes. -I recommend that you omit the levy for state fairs. This will further relieve general property of $175,000.00 in taxes. -I recommend that the levy for general purposes then be fixed to save another $1,000,000.00 in taxes from general property. 

To pursue the course I recommended it will become necessary to enact the gasoline tax in lieu of the direct levy for roads. -To replace the loss of the million dollars now being collected from general property, I recommended a FRANCHISE OR EXCISE TAX be levied on corporations on the basis of their net earnings, to be collected through the new department of finance and taxation. 

This revenue is now being derived in many states. The tax will easily produce several million dollars annually in this State, without becoming burdensome. 

It will produce considerably more if assessed on other than a nominal basis of earnings. If this tax is enacted some of the other taxes now being levied on corporations should be omitted. This subject will require careful consideration upon your part and inquiry into its constitutional phases. A bill covering this tax will be submitted for your consideration.- 

---

Ch. 3) 101 

EXCISE TAX 

The record indicates the "bill covering this tax" was introduced by the Speaker of the House, Hon. F. S. Hall, from Dickson County. The bill was entitled: 

"An Act to impose an excise tax upon all corporations and joint stock associations organized for profit under the laws of Tennessee and those organized under laws of other states and countries and doing business in Tennessee.''

The Act contains seven sections and represents the first attempt in Tennessee to tax income or earnings in any form. A brief analysis of the Act is as follows: 

APPLICABLE-To corporations and joint stock associations, other than those organized for general welfare, doing business for profit in Tennessee.

PAYABLE TO-State Comptroller. 

MEASURE OF TAX-Net earnings for preceding fiscal year arising from business done wholly within the state, excluding earnings arising from interstate commerce. 

DATE PAYABLE July 1, 1923, and annually thereafter.

RATE OF TAX-Three per cent of net earnings. 

DIRECT TAX CREDITS 1. Filing fees under Chapter 434, Acts of 1907. 

2. Banking fees under Chapter 20, Acts of 1913. 

3.

Receipts tax of insurance companies under Chapter 134, Acts of 

1919 and Chapter 131, Acts of 1915. 

4. Merchants' privilege tax paid to the state.

SUPERVISION-Department of Finance and Taxation as created under Chapter 7, Acts of 1923. 

Thus, we have the first Excise Tax Act; passed February 14, 1923, approved February 14, 1923 and cited as 

Chapter 21, Public Acts of 1923. 

The record does not disclose just how Governor Peay determined his estimate of revenue yield under the new Act. 

In recommending the passage of the Act by the General Assembly he states: "The tax will easily produce several million dollars annually," however, the yield for the first fiscal year did not amount to several million dollars. Since the fiscal year 1926-27 to the fiscal year 1937-38 the yield has been less than one million dollars annually. 

The message of Governor Peay to the 64th General 

Assembly, or two years later, under date of January 6, 1925, contains the following statement regarding the Excise Tax: "The people have approved the excise tax enacted by the last General Assembly. When the constitution may permit, it should be replaced with an income tax. In the meantime it should not be disturbed except to be amended in some particular. This law was a step in the right direction and has materially aided a better distribution of the tax burden. Those opposing this law are animated by the natural indisposition of most

people to pay taxes. The law is not unjust. It is as just as any tax law. 

It is being construed and applied with all moderation. Its administration is under the Finance Department and the Commissioner heading this department is an able lawyer, splendid executive and successful man of affairs. The administration of this Act has involved many new and complicated questions and all connected with the division in charge have rendered efficient service. It should be promptly amended to dispose of the questions remaining at issue in the courts. The tax paid to the 

Federal Government by the taxpayer should not be deducted. It is not an expense of the business. The Federal Government does not allow the taxpayer to deduct the excise tax paid to the state. The rule should work both ways or not at all. You should promptly amend the law to clarify this point and specifically provide that the Federal taxes be not included in the deductions allowed under the Act." 

Despite the Governor's recommendations that the Act of 1923, "should be promptly amended to dispose of the questions remaining in the courts.—and specifically provide that the Federal taxes be not included in the deductions allowed under the Act," the legislature left the Act without amendment. As a matter of fact the Act sets forth no deductions, other than tax credits.

The message of Governor Peay to the 65th General Assembly, under date January 6, 1927, contains no direct reference to the Excise Tax law. However, the Legislature enacted an amendment inserting certain words in Section 

One of the Act. The amendment (Chapter 44, Acts of 1927) 

was passed April 25, 1927 and approved April 26, 1927. The 

Act as amended remained in force without further amendment until the session of 1937. 

During the 70th General Assembly, under date February 15, 1937, Governor Browning submitted a number of revenue acts and amendments to existing acts. A portion of his message relates to the excise tax law as follows: "Bills designed to raise revenue to the extent of $4,000,000.00 have been introduced and have been widely publicized.-I respectfully urge upon you their prompt consideration and passage when they are in the final form our concerted judgment fashions them.-The increases incident to schools and social security will approximate $7,000,000.00. I firmly believe if given the $4,000,000.00 herein asked, we can meet this demand out of current revenue.-Another means of taxation from which considerable money might be raised is an additional ad valorem levy, but this I believe entirely impractical. The counties and cities must depend largely upon this method and the State should, as far as possible, leave it to the local units which do not have the opportunity of resorting to certain sources of revenue open to the State. Moreover, it is desirable, as far as practical, to separate the sources of revenue upon which the State and the Counties may draw, and it is, I believe, the common purpose of all of us to work toward a complete elimination of the State ad valorem tax rather than to increase it.-The corporation excise tax last year yielded approximately $375,000.00. It is levied only upon the net earnings of

Ch. 3) 103 

EXCISE TAX 

associations or persons enjoying the special privileges incident to incorporation, privileges made possible by the grace and patronage of the State. The corporation excise tax has the advantage spoken of in connection with the income tax, in that it rests only upon the entity which is actually earning money beyond its expenses and ceases when business trends or temporary misfortune eliminate net profit. Under a bill now before you the 3% rate will be made 4% as a base, with a differential in favor of profits on interstate business not heretofore included, and the various credits removed. The corporation excise tax is a privilege tax and it has seemed most reasonable to place an increase at a point where it would rest only upon net profits. There is also a change in the method of allocating net earnings to Tennessee when a corporation does business in this state and another state. Such change is designed to apportion to 

Tennessee merely a fair proportion of the net earnings of such corporation so that that part of the earnings arising from business done in Tennessee will be subject to taxation under the law. This change is one recommended by every tax expert who has ever studied the taxing system of Tennessee.- 

The Legislature of 1937 followed the recommendation of Governor Browning and enacted Chapter 99, Acts of 

1937; amending Section 1316, et seq., Code of Tennessee. 

While this form of taxation is not recognized to be as equitable as a tax levied upon statutory net income, it would appear to be the nearest approach to a net income tax possible under the Constitution.

 Section 1316; 

Corporations subject to tax; rate of tax- 

All corporations, cooperatives conducted for profit, joint stock associations and business trusts, organized under the laws of the State of Tennessee, other than those organized for general welfare and not for profit, and all such entities organized under the laws of any other state or country for profit and doing business in Tennessee, shall, without exception, pay to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation annually an excise tax, in addition to all other taxes, equal to three and three quarters (334) per cent of the net earnings for their next preceding fiscal or calendar year, from business done within the State. 

Measure of tax; apportionment of earnings—

In the case of corporations, cooperatives, joint stock associations and business trusts doing business in Tennessee and elsewhere, the net earnings shall be apportioned as hereinafter set forth and the net earnings thus apportioned to Tennessee shall be deemed to be the earnings arising from business done within the State and shall be the measure of this tax. Such method of apportionment shall be as follows: 

(1) If the principal business in this State is manufacturing or if it is any form of collecting, assembling or processing of goods or material, the entire net earnings shall be apportioned to Tennessee on the basis of the ratio obtained by taking the arithmetical average of the following three ratios: (a) The ratio of the value of its real estate and tangible personal property in this state on the date of the close of the fiscal year is to the value of its entire real estate and tangible personal property, with no deductions on account of encumbrances thereon. (b) The ratio of the total cost of manufacturing, collecting, assembling or processing within the State, to the total cost of manufacturing, collecting, assembling or processing within and without the State. (c) The ratio of the gross sales to customers within

Ch. 3) 107 

EXCISE TAX 

Tennessee is to the total gross sales from all sources. (2) If the principal business in this State is selling, distributing, dealing in or using tangible personal property, the entire net earnings shall be apportioned to Tennessee on the basis of the ratio obtained by taking the arithmetical average of the following three ratios: (a) The ratio of the value of its real estate and tangible personal property in this State on the day of the close of its fiscal year is to the value of its entire real estate and tangible personal property then owned by it, with no deductions on account of encumbrances thereon. (b) The ratio of the total sales made through or by offices, agencies, or branches located in Tennessee during the income year to the total sales made everywhere during said year. (c) The ratio of the gross sales to customers within Tennessee is to the total gross sales from all sources. (3) If the principal business is other than the manufacture or sale of tangible property, such proportion as its gross receipts in Tennessee during the income year is to its gross receipts for such year within and without the State.

If, because of peculiar or unusual circumstances inherent in a particular case, the application of the above formulas would work a hardship or injustice, the Commissioner, upon application of the taxpayer and upon such showing, is authorized, with the approval of the Attorney General, to adopt such other method of apportionment as would be fair and just under the facts of the case. 

Tennessee insurance companies shall pay on net earnings proportioned to premiums on policies on persons and property in this State. 

Section 1317; 

State tax only; credits allowed 

The tax hereby imposed shall be in addition to all other taxes, and no other tax shall be a credit upon the tax hereby imposed except that insurance companies paying a privilege tax of two and one-half (22) per cent on gross premium receipts shall be entitled to a credit for such tax so paid,

(Ch. 3 

and except that all sums paid by State banks into the State Treasury as fees for the use and benefit of the State Banking Department shall be a credit upon the tax hereby levied. 

The tax herein imposed is a State tax for State purposes only and no county or municipality or taxing district shall have power to levy any like tax. 

Section 1318; 

Tax payable-when; penalties for delinquency—

The tax imposed shall be due and payable on July 1st of each succeeding year; and, if delinquent thirty days, shall be subject to a penalty of one per cent, per month, and, in addition, interest at the rate of six per cent per annum from July 1st until paid. 

Section 1319;

Distress warrants; issuance of— 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation is empowered, and it shall be his duty, after the first day of January of each year, to issue a distress warrant for the collection of the excise tax, interest and penalty due from each delinquent corporation. Said distress warrant may be addressed and delivered to the sheriff of the county wherein such delinquent corporation has its principal office or place of business, or to the sheriff of any county in which the Commissioner has reason to believe property of such delinquent corporation may be found. 

Section 1320; 

Sale of personal property The sheriff into whose hands such warrant may come, or his deputy, may execute same by distraint and sale of personal property belonging to such delinquent corporation, and the proceedings in respect thereto shall be the same as are provided by law for proceedings under an execution at law from a court of record; and the executing officer shall be entitled to the same fees, commissions, and necessary expense of removing and keeping property distrained as in case of an execution from a court of record.

Ch. 3) 109 

EXCISE TAX 

Section 1321; 

Sale of real property If the officer cannot find personal property to satisfy said distress warrant, he may levy same upon any real estate in his county belonging to such delinquent corporation; and if levied on land, said distress warrant, together with the officer's return thereon, shall be returned to the circuit court of the county wherein the land lies, and the land shall be condemned and sold under the orders of said circuit court in the same manner as in case of the levy on land of an execution issued by a justice of the peace. 

Section 1322; 

Collection of tax The supervision and collection of the tax imposed shall be under the direction of the Department of Finance and Taxation, and such department shall have authority and power to prescribe forms upon which corporations and joint-stock associations, liable for the tax imposed, shall make reports of such facts and information as will enable the Commissioner of said department to ascertain the correctness of the amount reported and paid by such corporation or joint-stock associations. 

Section 1323;

Rules and regulations; taxpayer may sue to recover— 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation is hereby authorized to make and promulgate rules and regulations, not inconsistent with this law, for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of this law, which rules and regulations, when approved by the Attorney-General, and when promulgated and published, shall have the force and effect of law.

In all matters requiring the exercise of judgment and discretion as to what may or may not be net earnings, the judgment and opinion of said Commissioner shall be final and conclusive and there shall be no review of his action except that the taxpayer shall have the right to pay any such tax under protest and to sue for the recovery thereof

(Ch. 3  

or for the recovery of a part thereof under Section 1790, et seq., Code of Tennessee.

Section 1324; 

Suits by State— 

Said Commissioner may, in the name of the State of Tennessee, institute suit or suits for the collection of said tax or any part thereof and for the penalty and interest imposed. 

Section 1325;

Availability of books and records; inspection thereof- Said Commissioner shall have access to all books and records of all such corporations and joint stock associations to enable him to ascertain the correctness of any fact or report made or herein required.

Section 1326; 

Expense of collection limited- Said Commissioner may expend so much of two and onehalf per centum of the amount received hereunder each year as may be necessary to defray the expenses and cost of litigation arising in the administration of this statute. 

Section 1327; 

Fine for failure to report–

The wilful failure or refusal of any corporation or jointstock association to pay the tax or make reports, as herein above required, shall be a misdemeanor and subject it to a fine of not less than ten dollars nor more than one thousand dollars. 

Section 1328;

Reports confidential; reciprocal inspection- 

Except in accordance with proper judicial order or as otherwise required by law, it shall be unlawful for the

in any report or return required under this statute; provided, nothing herein shall be construed to prohibit the publication of statistics, so classified as to prevent the identification of particular reports or returns and the items thereof; or the use of such reports or returns by legal representatives of the state in any suit or suits for the collection of said tax or any part thereof, or for the penalty and interest imposed by the Statute. A violation of any of the provisions of this Section shall be a misdemeanor, punishable by fine of not exceeding one thousand dollars, or by imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both, at the discretion of the court; provided, however, the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation may permit the Commissioner of Internal Revenue of the United States, or the proper officer of any State imposing a tax similar to that imposed by this Statute, or the authorized representative of either such officer, to inspect the tax return of any corporation, or may furnish to such officer or to his authorized representative an abstract of the return of any corporation or supply him with information concerning any item contained in any return or disclosed by the report of any investigation of any return: but such permission shall be granted or such information furnished to such officer or his representative, only if the Statute or regulations of the United States or of such other State, as the case may be, grant substantially similar privileges to the Governor or the proper officers of this State charged with the administration of this Statute.
