From Davidson County 

1. The complainant, a domesticated Delaware Corporation, which succeeded to the rights of its predecessor, keeps an office in Tennessee where it received from the Connecticut manufacturer the royalties on the machines manufactured in Connecticut and from those distributed throughout the United States. 

2. The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation assessed the excise tax against complainant for the years 1925, 1926 and 1927, amounting to $539.35, and payment was about to be enforced when complainant, pursuing the course prescribed by statute, paid the tax under protest and, alleging that it was illegally exacted, sued to recover the amount paid. 

The defendants, representing the State, demurrer to the bill. The Chancellor overruled the demurrer whereupon defendant refused to further plead and a decree was entered awarding complainant a recovery for the aggregate of the taxes paid by it. 

3. The tax levied by this Act is a privilege tax upon domestic and foreign corporations organized for profit and carrying on business in this state. 

4. The complainant derived no profit from the manufacture and sale of the patented article which was manufactured by license. Its income was derived altogether from the royalties on its patent right. The state could not levy a tax upon the value of the patent right and where the state attempts to tax income inquiry is allowed to the sources from which the income is derived and the same consideration that would invalidate a tax upon the source would also invalidate a tax upon the income.

Opinion by Justice Cook. 

Complainant's predecessor, a Tennessee corporation and the exclusive owner of a patent right, entered into a contract with Turner & Seymour Company, a Connecticut manufacturer, licensing it to make and sell a patented article to the exclusion of all others. The complainant, a domesticated Delaware corporation, which succeeded to the rights of its predecessor, keeps an office in Tennessee where it receives from the Connecticut manufacturer the royalties on the machines manufactured in Connecticut and from there distributed throughout the United States. The complainant does not make or supply any part of the machines 186

Ch. 3) 187 

EXCISE TAX 

or any material that goes into their manufacture, nor does it make, buy or sell any article of commerce. According to the statements of the bill, which, upon demurrer, are admitted, complainants sole business is to hold the patent right and receive the royalties from Turner and Seymour Company.

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation assessed the excise tax against complainant for the years 1925, 1926 and 1927, amounting to $539.35, and payment was about to be enforced when complainant, pursuing the course prescribed by statute, paid the tax under protest and, alleging that it was illegally exacted, sued to recover the amount paid. The defendants, representing the State, demurrer to the bill. The chancellor overruled the demurrer whereupon defendant refused to further plead and a decree was entered awarding complainant a recovery for the aggregate of the taxes paid by it. 

The defendants appealed, insisting that complainant is subject to the excise tax imposed by Chapter 21, Acts of 1923. The tax levied by this Act is a privilege tax upon domestic and foreign corporations organized for profit and carrying on business in this State. The annual tax is measured by a sum equal to 3% of the net earnings for each preceding fiscal year, arising from business done wholly within the State. Corporations not doing business in the State and those that derive no net earnings from business done in the State are not subject to the tax. Bank of Commerce & Trust Co. v. Senter, 149 Tenn. 569.

The complainant derived no profit from the manufacture and sale of the patented article which was manufactured by the licensee. Its income was derived altogether from the royalties on its patent right. The State could not levy a tax upon the value of the patent right and where the State attempts to tax income inquiry is allowed to the sources from which the income is derived and the same considerations that would invalidate a tax upon the source would also invalidate a tax upon the income. Such is the rule announced in Gillespie v. Oklahoma, 257 U. S. 501, following McCullough v. Maryland, 4 Wheat, 316 and other cases.

(Ch. 3 

Resort to analogy is rendered unnecessary by authorities directly in point. In State v. Butler, 3 Lea, 222, the court, holding that the State could not tax sales of patented articles, said: 

"If the State can forbid the use and enjoyment of the right granted except on terms of paying for the privilege *** she may as well *** forbid it entirely. In this way the privilege granted may be rendered valueless and the right purchased from the United States be entirely destroyed for all practical purposes.' 

In Long v. Rockwood, 277 U. S. Law Ed. 145, the court said: "" These causes present the question whether the State of Massachusetts may tax, as income, royalties received by one of her citizens for the use of patents issued to him by the United States. The Supreme 

Judicial Court of that State held such an imposition would amount to a tax upon the patent right itself and was prohibited by the Federal Constitution. We agree with that conclusion.'' 

Further discussion of the questions presented through the assignments of error and brief are unnecessary.

Opinion by Justice DeHaven. 

The Public Acts of the General Assembly of the state of Tennessee for the year 1923, chapter 21, as amended by chapter 44 of the Public Acts for the year 1927, imposes an excise tax upon certain corporations and joint-stock associations. These acts are brought forward in section 1316 et seq., of the Code of Tennessee. The sections relevant to this suit are as follows: "1316. TAX IMPOSED.-All corporations and joint-stock associations organized under the laws of the State of Tennessee, other than those organized for general welfare and not for profit, and all corpora- 189

tions and joint-stock associations organized under the laws of any other state or county for profit and doing business in Tennessee, shall, without exception, pay to the state comptroller annually an excise tax, in addition to all other taxes, equal to three per cent of the net earnings for their preceding fiscal year of such corporations and joint-stock associations, arising from business done wholly within the state, excluding earnings arising from interstate commerce. Tennessee insurance companies shall pay on net earnings proportioned to premiums on policies on persons and property in this state." 1322.

Supervision and collection under department of finance and taxation; forms for reports. The supervision and collection of the tax imposed shall be under the direction of the department of finance and taxation, and such department shall have authority and power to prescribe forms upon which corporations and joint-stock associations, liable for the tax imposed, shall make reports of such facts and information as will enable the commissioner of said department to ascertain the correctness of the amount reported and paid by such corporations or joint-stock associations."' "1323. Judgment and opinion of commissioner is conclusive, when; subject to revision in the courts, when. In all matters requiring the exercise of judgment and discretion as to what may or may not be net income, the judgment and opinion of said commissioner shall be final and conclusive, and there shall be no review of his action; except the constitutional right of redress in the courts under the laws." 

It appears from the original bill herein that appellant made its report to the commissioner of finance and taxation of its net earnings for the year 1931, upon the forms for returns as furnished by the then commissioner, specifically providing for a deduction of interest on "tax free" bonds in fixing the income upon which the tax in question was to be computed. This report showed the total amount of “net earnings," credited to Tennessee business, exclusive of interest on "tax free" bonds, to be $70,342.66. Appellant paid the tax on this amount. Appellant also collected during the year 1931 interest on certain "tax free" bonds owned by it. The proportionate part of said interest credited to Tennessee business amounted to $62,- 775.39. The commissioner demanded that appellant include this interest in its "net earnings" for the year 1931, and that it pay excise tax thereon. Appellant paid, under protest, the additional tax required of it by the commissioner, amounting to $1,883.26, plus interest and penalty. 

The purpose of the bill is to recover this payment from appellees.

It appears that appellant had, since the statute first became effective, paid to the comptroller 3 per cent of its net earnings for each fiscal year arising from business done wholly within the state, there being excluded therefrom,

however, the earnings of appellant collected by it on bonds of the United States, the state of Tennessee, and the political subdivisions thereof, owned by it, which state, county, and municipal bonds, and interest thereon, were by the acts authorizing their issuance specifically exempted from taxation, and which bonds were purchased by appellant, under the contract of sale and purchase, as such tax free securities. The exclusion of interest on such bonds by appellant from its net earnings, in computing the amount upon which to pay its excise tax, was specifically authorized by the then commissioner of finance and taxation at the time the statute imposing said excise tax became effective, and had been authorized by each and every succeeding commissioner down to and including the immediate predecessor of the commissioner in office when the bill herein was filed, except during the last few months of his tenure of office, and that the forms furnished for such periods specifically provided for a deduction of interest on "tax free" bonds in arriving at the income upon which said tax was to be computed.

(2) That it was the intent of the Legislature in the passage of said statute imposing said tax measured by said income that there should not be included upon which said tax was computed any income consisting of interest collected on "tax free" bonds and tax free securities. (3) That ever since said statute went into effect in 1923, it had been construed by the various commissioners of finance and taxation to mean that the income by which said tax was measured should not include interest on "tax free"

bonds, and such construction had been uniformly followed by every commissioner down to and including the defendant's immediate predecessor in office, and upon the basis of such construction appellant had purchased said bonds and thereby property rights had become fixed, which rights would be seriously impaired under the construction now insisted on by defendant. (4) That the Legislature of Tennessee had knowledge of the construction of said statute as placed thereon by the various commissioners, and by its failure to change or modify said statute so as to provide for the inclusion of interest collected on tax free bonds in net earnings for taxation purposes, it had approved and ratified said construction as the true and legislative intent. (5) That the attempt by defendant to now construe said statute to impose a tax measured by income from "tax free" bonds, was, in effect, the enactment of a new law which impaired the obligations of the contracts between appellant and the state and the political subdivisions thereof whose bonds complainant owned, and appellant specially pleads and relies on section 10 of article 1 of the Federal Constitution, and section 20 of article 1 of the Constitution of the state of Tennessee, to protect it against laws which would impair the obligations of contracts. 

A demurrer to the original bill was interposed by the appellees, and upon hearing was sustained and the bill dismissed. To the action of the chancellor in sustaining the demurrer and dismissing the bill, appellant excepted and appealed to this court. Eleven assignments of error are made. These assignments are, in effect, that the chancellor erred in holding against appellant on the five objections to the validity of the tax set up in the bill, hereinbefore set out, and, in addition, that the court erred in failing to hold that appellant's being required to include interest from United States bonds, in the income by which the tax was measured, imposed a burden on the right of the federal government to borrow money, and was, therefore, in violation of article 1, sec. 8, cl. 2, of the Federal Constitution authorizing the government "to borrow Money on the credit of the United States."

Ch. 3) 193 

EXCISE TAX 

The sole question involved in this suit is whether or not interest collected by the appellant on "tax free bonds," during the year 1931, was properly included as a part of its "net earnings" upon which the state excise tax was competent.

The language of the statute, section 1316 of the Code, is comprehensive and inclusive. The tax is levied upon "net earnings" of corporations and joint-stock associations. The phrase "net earnings" is not defined in the statute. In the case of Bank of Commerce & Trust Company v. Senter, 149 Tenn., 569, 596, 260 S. W., 144, 151, the constitutionality of the excise tax law was before this court for determination. In sustaining the constitutionality of the statute, the court said: "The term 'net earnings,' not being defined by the act, must be given its usual and ordinary meaning of what is left of earnings after deducting necessary and legitimate items of expense incident to the corporate business.",

The term "net earnings" is unambiguous in its meaning. We must conclude the Legislature intended to convey the usual and ordinary meaning of the phrase used without any forced or subtle construction. 

Undoubtedly, the interest received by appellant on tax free bonds constituted a part of its net earnings. This is not denied. The contention is that the portion of appellant's net earnings arising from tax free bonds must be excluded in calculating the amount of excise tax due it. 

The statute itself authorizes no such exclusion. The only earnings excluded by the terms of the statute are those arising from interstate commerce. The enumeration of exceptions to a general statute excludes by necessary implication all other exceptions. Evans v. McCave, 164 Tenn., 672, 52 S. W. (2d), 159, 617; Turner v. Eslick, 146 Tenn. 

236, 240 S. W., 786; Lewis' Sutherland Statutory Construction, sec. 494.

This court, in a memorandum opinion filed in this case of Bank of Commerce and Trust Company v. Senter, subsequent to the opinion for publication reported in 149 

Tenn., 569, 260 S. W., 144, said: "For the privilege of doing business in Tennessee as a corporation, a tax was levied, measured by net earnings. The phrase net earnings

(Ch. 3 

from business done wholly within the State is definite of the measure of the tax, measuring it by earnings of the corporation upon its corporate business in the State, and excluding by the last phrase earnings from interstate commerce which cannot be burdened. The express exception of earnings from interstate commerce excludes all others. Where a general rule has been established by a statute, with exceptions, the court will not curtail the former nor add to the latter by implication." 

It seems also that the Legislature intended by the act that all net earnings of a corporation, from whatsoever source derived, shall constitute the measure of the tax, except that earnings from interstate commerce shall be excluded.

The tax imposed by the act is a privilege tax and not a direct tax on property. Bank of Commerce & Trust 

Company v. Senter, 149 Tenn., 569, 260 S. W., 144. The rule seems to be settled that an excise tax statute is not unconstitutional solely because there is included in the income of the taxpayer, by which the tax is measured, interest from tax free bonds, when such inclusion is incidental and fortuitous. Flint v. Stone Tracy Co., 220 U. 

S., 107, 31 S. Ct., 342, 55 L. ed. 389, Ann. Case., 1912B, 1312; Pacific Co. v. Johnson, 285 U. S., 480, 52 S. Ct., 424, 76 L. Ed., 893; Educational Films Corporation v. Ward, 

282 U. S. 379, 51 S. Ct., 170, 75 L. Ed., 400, 71 A. L. R., 1226; Society for Savings v. Coite, 6 Wall., 594, 18 L. Ed., 897; Provident Inst. for Savings v. Massachusetts, 6 Wall., 611, 632, 18 L. Ed., 913; Home Ins. Company v. New York, 134 U. S., 594, 10 S. Ct., 593, 33 L. Ed., 1025.

The legislation here under consideration discloses only that the state of Tennessee has sought, in good faith, to conform its scheme of taxation of corporations to a permitted method. By the act in question it has adopted a form of privilege tax on corporations measured by their net income, without any form of discrimination as to the sources of the income included in the measure, differing in this respect in no material way from a similar tax upheld in Flint v. Stone Tracy Company, 220 U. S., 107, 31 S. 

Ct. 342, 55 L. Ed., 389, Ann. Cas. 1912B, 1312, and in Educational Films Corp. v. Ward, 282 U. S. 379, 51 S. Ct., 170, 75 L. Ed., 400, 71 A. L. R., 1226. 

This court, in General Securities Co. v. Williams, 161 

Tenn., 50, 54, 29 S. W., (2d), 662, 663, said:

Ch. 3) 195 

EXCISE TAX 

'Chapter 21 of the Acts of 1923 was not aimed at the income from nontaxable securities, and any resulting burden thereby was fortuitous and incidental.''

The immunity from taxation on which appellant relies is granted by sections 1086-1088 of the Code of Ten nessee. Section 1086 provides as follows: 

"Whenever the State of Tennessee shall issue any bonds upon her faith and credit for any public purpose, neither the principal nor the interest of said bonds shall be taxed by this state or by any county or municipality of this state, and it shall be so stated on the face of said bonds when issued.' 

Sections 1087 and 1088 are substantially the same, with the exception that section 1087 refers to county bonds and section 1088 refers to municipal bonds.

Under the above sections of the Code, the bonds of the state of Tennessee, and of any county or municipality thereof, held by appellant, are exempt from taxation as to both principal and interest. Likewise, the bonds of the 

United States held by appellant are exempt from taxation by the state. Weston v. Charleston, 2 Pet., 449, 7 L. Ed., 481, 488; Macallen Co. v. Massachusetts, 279 U. S., 620, 49 S. Ct., 432, 73 L. Ed., 874, 65 A. L. R., 866. Having guaranteed to the purchasers of these bonds immunity from taxation of the principal and interest, the state of Tennessee is without power subsequently to destroy the immunity and to tax the bonds or interest directly or indirectly. The act here in question, however, does not tax either the principal or interest of any bonds of the state of Tennessee, or of any political subdivision thereof, or of the United States. 

In Pacific Co. v. Johnson, 285 U. S., 480, 489, 490, 52 

S. Ct., 424, 425, 76 L. Ed., 893, the court said: "If, as appellant argues, the exemption from taxation of the bonds is contractual and extends to the income derived from them, the question still remains whether the immunity is broad enough to secure freedom from taxation of a corporate franchise, to the extent that it is measured by tax exempt income. "The rule that a tax upon a franchise, measured by net income, including that from tax immune property, is not an infringement of the immunity, was re-examined and affirmed in Flint v. Stone Tracy Company, 220 U. S., 107, 31 S. Ct. 342, 55 L. Ed., 389, Ann. Cas., 1912B, 1312, which was accepted as authority in Macallen Company v. Massachusetts, 279 U. S., 620, 49 S. Ct., 432, 436, 73 L. Ed., 874, (65 A. L. R., 866), and followed in Educational Films Corp. v. Ward, 282 U. S., 379, 51 

Sup. Ct., 170, 75 L. Ed., 400 (71 A. L. R., 1226).

(Ch. 3 

"This distinction, so often and consistently reaffirmed, is but a recognition that the franchise, the privilege of doing business in corporate form, which is a legitimate subject of taxation, does not cease to be such because it is exercised in the acquisition and enjoyment of nontaxables. The distinction is one of substance, not of form, and has been so recently discussed in Educational Films Corporation v. Ward, that it need not be elaborated here. It suffices to say that the tax immunity extended to property qua property does not embrace a special privilege, the corporate franchise, otherwise taxable, merely because the value of the corporate property or net income is included in an equable measure of the enjoyment of the privilege. The owner may enjoy his exempt property free of tax, but if he asks and receives from the state the benefit of a taxable privilege as the implement of that enjoyment, he must bear the burden of the tax which the state exacts as its price.' 

The exemption from taxation granted on the bonds of the state of Tennessee, and of its political subdivisions, under Code, sections 1086-1088, does not exempt appellant corporation from the payment of the privilege tax exacted by the state for the privilege of doing business in Tennessee, which tax equals in amount 3 per cent of its net earnings for the preceding fiscal year, excluding earnings arising from interstate commerce. 

It is earnestly insisted by appellant that the commissioner of finance and taxation, under section 1323 of the Code, is vested with the judgment and discretion of determining what may or may not be "net income," and that for nine years from the time the act became operative the several commissioners in office during that period ruled and held that the interest on tax free securities should be excluded from appellant's "net income" in computing the tax. That upon the basis of such construction appellant had purchased said bonds and thereby property interest had become fixed, which rights would be seriously impaired under the construction now insisted on by appellees. Under section 1316 of the Code, the legislative mandate is that all of the net earnings, from whatsoever source derived, shall constitute the measure of the tax, excluding only earnings arising from interstate commerce. No judgment or discretion is given by the act to the commissioner to exclude any particular type or character of net earnings from consideration in measuring the tax. The power of determining the measure of the tax is a legislative function, not delegated to the commissioner. It is

Ch. 3) 197 

EXCISE TAX 

only matters "requiring" the exercise of judgment and discretion "as to what may or may not be net income” that are left to the judgment and opinion of the commissioner. Ascertaining "net income" of a corporation often involves processes of calculation and other details. Questions may arise as to whether the items of expense claimed are legitimate or not. It is to such administrative matters. as these that the exercise of the judgment and discretion of the commissioner is permitted. His finding as an assessment is final, and no administrative board is authorized to review or set aside his action. 

In Bank of Commerce and Trust Company v. Senterm 

149 Tenn., 569, 592, 593, 260 S. W., 144, 150, one of the grounds of attack on this act was the very argument now made by appellant. The court said: 

The 

"Another assault upon the validity of the act is that it confers power upon the commissioner of finance and taxation to define net earnings as a means of finding the measure of the tax, and therefore delegates to him legislative powers in violation of the Constitution. power of determining the measure of the tax is a legislative function. 

În adopting the measure the Legislature could have given the term 'net earnings' a statutory definition, but since that was not done the phrase must be given its usual and ordinary meaning, without any forced or subtle construction. "The determination by the state's fiscal agents, of the net earnings of corporations involves, for the most part, processes of calculation, involving detail which must of necessity be left to the administrative officers who in the discharge of their duties would be required to exercise some measure of discretion to obtain efficiency." 

General Securities Company v. Williams, 161 Tenn., 50, 29 S. W. (2d), 662, is not in conflict with the above case, nor does it support the contention of appellant. In that case the insistence was that the entire excise tax statute was unconstitutional because there was no express exemption of that part of net earnings derived from interest on United States Bonds. The court refused a declaration un der the Declaratory Judgments Act (Code, 1932, Sec. 8835 

et seq.), because the record did not show that the fiscal officers of the state, in fact, had included such tax exempt securities.

It is insisted that the construction placed upon the act, as exempting tax free securities, by the several commissioners, for nine years, is entitled to great weight and should not be disturbed unless clearly erroneous. This is

(Ch. 3 

a correct statement if the language of the taxing statute be ambiguous. In Price-Bass Company, v. McCabe, 161 

Tenn., 67, 29 S. W. (2d), 249, this court construed a taxing statute as requiring the payment of greater sums than the department of finance and taxation had under its prior rulings required from taxpayers. It was held that the fact that the department had given an unambiguous statute other than the correct interpretation was not controlling. 

So, in the instant case, the statute is free of ambiguity, and the erroneous construction placed thereon by certain of the commissioners is not controlling. Menfel Box Company v. Stevens, 141 Tenn., 373, 210 S. W. 635.

It is insisted that the ruling by the defendant Dempster to the effect that interest collected on tax free bonds should be included as part of complainant's net earnings was such a change in the taxing policy of the state as to render such construction void and unenforceable. It is sufficient to say that the unauthorized and erroneous acts of former commissioners in excluding interest on tax free bonds as a part of complainant's net earnings by which to measure the tax cannot be held to bind the state. The policy of the state is reflected in the act, and that policy has not been changed. Appellant can have no advantage from the circumstances that several of the commissioners, after the act became effective, erroneously permitted it to withhold from its net earnings, reported as a measure of its tax, the interest on tax exempt bonds. The situation is in no sense parallel with that presented in Macallen Company v. Massachusetts, 279 U. S., 620, 49 S. Ct. 432, 73 L. Ed., 874, 65 A. L. R., 866

A careful consideration of all the questions raised convinces us that the decree of the chancellor must be affirmed.

[7]-Memphis Docks & Forwarding Company V. 

DANCEY FORT, COMMISSIONER 

92 S. W. 408 

Filed April 4th, 1936.

1. The complainant is a domestic corporation organized to carry on a warehousing, storage, and freighting business. Its domicile is at 

Memphis. In 1924 it leased all its buildings, machinery, tracks and docks to the St. Louis-San Francisco Railway Company for an annual rental that produces a net income. 

2. The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation assessed against complainant the excise tax imposed by law upon corporations. The tax was paid under protest and the suit followed to recover upon the charge that it was illegally exacted. 

3. The tax is measured by net earnings that result from whatever business may be done by the corporation in the event of powers conferred by the charter. 

4. We find no error in the decree of the chancellor and it is affirmed. 

Opinion by Justice Cook. 

The complainant is a domestic corporation organized to carry on a warehousing, storage, and freighting business. Its domicile is at Memphis. In 1924 it leased all its buildings, machinery, tracks and docks to the St. Louis- 

San Francisco Railway Company for an annual rental that produces a net income. 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation assessed against complainant the excise tax imposed by law upon corporations. The tax was paid under protest and this suit followed to recover upon the charge that it was illegally exacted.

The chancellor sustained defendant's demurrer to the bill and the complainant appealed. 

It is insisted through the several assignments of error that (1) complainant is not subject to the excise tax because it has leased all its corporate property and merely maintains its corporate existence for the purpose of holding title, receiving the rents, and distributing the income 199

(Ch. 3  

from rentals, and is not engaged in business. (2) That neither the ownership of property nor the rental of the property owned by the corporation is a taxable privilege and that it is not subject to the excise tax. 

It may be conceded, as insisted by complainant, that the ownership and rental of corporate property is not a taxable privilege without effecting the result. The tax is not laid upon a particular corporate business or upon a particular transaction; it is upon the privilege of doing business as a corporation and exercising the corporate powers for the purpose of producing a profit. The source of the profit and the character of business carried on in the corporate name is immaterial. The tax is measured by net earnings that result from whatever business may be done by the corporation in the exercise of powers conferred by the charter. That is made apparent by reference to the Act carried into section 1316 of the Code of 1932. Our cases of Bank of Commerce & Trust Company v. Senter, 149 

Tenn. 569, and Jorgensen-Bennett Mfg. Company v. 

Knight, 156 Tenn. 599, are in accord with that conclusion. 

It would serve no purpose to refer to and discuss cases involving the different tax statutes from other jurisdictions which have been referred to by counsel for complainant and defendant.

We find no error in the decree of the chancellor and it is affirmed.

HISTORY OF INCOME TAXATION IN TENNESSEE Constitution of Tennessee-Article II, Section 28, States:- 

"The Legislature shall have the power to levy a tax upon incomes derived from stocks and bonds that are not taxed ad valorem." 

The first official reference to income taxation is contained in the message of Governor Austin Peay to the 63rd General Assembly under date January 17, 1923 which in part is as follows: 

"" -It is a question of time before tax will be levied on personal incomes. It is the sane and inevitable solution of the problem of assessing productive personalty without confiscating its income. It is mooted if an income tax is constitutional in this State, but it will not be known until the question is tested; and I will approve a bill assessing a moderate tax on personal income. It is easy to agree that we must have a 

Constitutional Convention in this State to enable a broad and equitable system for taxing all classes of property and income, unless the constitutionality of these measures is sustained. Otherwise, land will always bear the burden of government, except as the revenue is supplemented from the antiquated practice of collecting a privilege tax from every conceivable thing. -We must have revenues from these sources, and must institute the economies in administration proposed to restore the balance in our accounts. It will be effectively done if you will cooperate in the legislation which is necessary, and it must be done to preserve the honor and integrity of the State.- 

Governor Peay had been elected to office, pledged, among other things, to provide a "reduction of one million dollars in land tax"; he apparently realized that drastic changes in State tax policies were necessary. However, the 63rd 

General Assembly did not enact either a general income tax law or a Statute taxing selected sources of income, but did reduce the State tax levy upon real property. 

Two years later the condition of State finances appear to have improved and we find in Governor Peay's message to the 64th General Assembly under date January 6, 1925, the following: -Your tasks are simplified by the improved condition of our state finances. The last Assembly was remarkably prudent in its appropriations and legislated with rare discretion.- Economy was substituted for extravagance and order has replaced disorder.- -Comparisons are convincing. January 1st, 1923, the huge sum of $3,096,472.70 203

(Ch. 4 

stood on the Comptroller's books to the credit of general and special accounts, including short term loans borrowed for current needs, and the actual funds in all depositories to liquidate these balances were $196,377.46. The deficit then existing is thus apparent. A year later, January 1, 1924, the same balance amounted to $3,015,565.77 and the funds on hand were $2,532,289.61.- -Therefore, the former deficit had been reduced under the new administration in the first year to $483,- 

276.16. It is reported with considerable satisfaction that January 1st, 1925, these same accounts showed an aggregate to their credit of $2,026,736.86. While there were funds on hand in the various depositories belonging to the state in the sum of $2,788,307.75. Thus showing that the former deficits were replaced with an excellent surplus of $761,570.89.- -Our finances are now in splendid order and our administration machinery is performing with the best success. 

The improved condition of State finances was encouraging and we find Governor Peay silent on the subject of income taxation in the message of January 6, 1925. During the preceding two years the State property tax was reduced, revenues equalled expenditures, and a surplus was accumulated, but what of the taxpayer? Obviously, the financial condition of the units of local government was not known at this time and it is doubtful if this information is available today, fourteen years after the State land tax reduction obtained during the first two years of Governor Peay's administration. The State property tax reduction necessitated the levy of certain new taxes and in addition to these new State taxes, the inevitable happened-Gov ernor Peay states: 

"" -All real property in this State has been bearing an unjustifiable share of the tax burden. The fact that is known to all and so agreed by those who are fair minded and just. This statement is particularly applicable to farm land. We know that agriculture has been unreasonably handicapped and penalized in this period of deflation, through which the country has been passing.- Two years ago we reduced the land tax. The tax rate was lowered from 36 to 30 cents. 

The property tax in consequence dropped a million dollars and more in this State. Many counties without being candid in their act, immediately increased the county tax to absorb this reduction.- -All who are informed know that the heavy burden on land is the county tax. This action on the part of the counties was regrettable and something should be done to improve county government, but the State is powerless under our present system and law in any wise to control county taxes.- -The people themselves must correct this situation. County Government is the weak spot in our system. We have seen that too well in our various audits of the automobile funds as these are being expended in the various counties. The waste and extravagance are shocking. The trouble with county government is that too many must be consulted and small politics and human weaknesses creep in to take their toll.- "" 

The result of the first two years of Governor Peay's administration, so far as taxation is concerned, resulted in

Ch. 4) 205 

INCOME TAX 

the levy of a "million dollars and more" additional tax. 

Very little, if any, tax reduction had been afforded land owners and the Governor says- We did the best we could but "the State is powerless under our present system and law in any wise to control county taxes-the people themselves must correct that situation."

In view of Governor Peay's statement as regards units of local government and the further fact that during a period of fifteen years there has been no effort made to bring about a proper relationship between the State and units of local government with respect to taxation or fiscal supervision of local government units, this observation is made; local government is the creature, part and parcel, of State Government. The responsibility of local government rests primarily upon the State Government, especially as regards fiscal affairs and taxation. Since both State and 

Local governments must rely upon taxes for the purpose of governmental operations, it is most essential that any state tax structure be formulated in conjunction with necessary requirements of local units of government, i.e., tax competition between State and Local governmental units should not be allowed to continue. 

Governor Peay in his message to the 65th General Assembly under date January 6, 1927, states: "" The last General Assembly approved an amendment to the Constitution for the taxation of farming lands and personal property on a different basis from that which is now required.- -By all means this amendment should be passed and submitted to the people for their adoption at the earliest time. Such is necessary because the present taxing clause of our Constitution is archaic in requiring all property to be taxed on the same basis.- -The framers of our Constitution did not dream of the immense values in tangible and intangible personal property now existing in the state.- This class of property is almost wholly untaxed. Nor, can it be taxed without confiscation under the present taxing provisions of our Constitution.- 

Owners of income bearing stocks and bonds are afraid to bring them into this State because the lawful tax will absorb all or most of the income. A light tax on this class of property is in accord with just and scientific principles.- -We must rewrite our tax laws so that all property may be properly classified for taxation.- ??

While the Governor did not directly refer to the income tax on stocks and bonds it is obvious that he favored any reasonable tax measure tending to further reduce the State and Local tax upon farm land; and for the first time men-

(Ch. 4  

tions the matter of classification of tangible and intangible personal property for taxation. 

Continuing the tax policies of Governor Peay we find Governor Horton giving serious consideration to the question in his message to the 66th General Assembly under date January 14, 1929: -The question of the abolition of the property tax for State purposes in Tennessee was discussed before the people prior to the August primary and November election. From every stump I guaranteed the people that if elected, and given a sympathetic Legislature, no tax would be levied on land for State revenue. The issue was plainly drawn.- This tax is now twenty cents on the one-hundred dollars of assessed property. There are many sources from which adequate funds can be obtained to take the place of this property tax without working a hardship upon the taxpayers of the State. -By taking off the land tax not only will the tax be removed from the farm and the home and the business house, but the ad valorem tax paid on all merchandise will also be removed.- -So carefully should this be considered that it is my purpose to submit within the next few days a special message dealing singly with the ways and means by which our pledges may be kept and the desired abolition of the land tax accomplished.- 

The special message of Governor Horton was delivered to the General Assembly under date January 21, 1929; as regards revenue, he states: As -Let us examine, then, the possibilities that are before us. proposition number one I submit that any reasonable method of raising State revenue is superior to the use of the property tax, and it is my earnest hope that the legislature will allow no arguments to reduce you. to the extremity of retaining that system. Certainly we cannot expect to devise a system which will satisfy every one. As old as our civilization is no one has yet reduced the mode of raising revenue to an exact science or found a formula satisfactory to all. But it is certain that the people of Tennessee are awaiting no such impossible perfection of method. They are convinced as troublesome as certain privilege and luxury taxes may be they are far more desirable than the general property tax, the abolition of which their adoption will make possible. 

I recommend that the corporation excise tax law be amended by striking out in Section 2 of Chapter 21, Acts of 1923, the provisions that "any corporation or stock association paying the tax imposed by this Act shall be entitled to a credit upon the tax imposed in the sum which such corporation has paid to the Secretary of State under the terms of Chapter 434, Acts of 1907." Such an amendment has already been submitted. Many suggestions have been made that the rate fixed by the corporation excise tax act be increased from three to four per cent of the corporate net earnings. While this may be desirable and is far preferable to a property tax, I am not at the present time convinced that it is necessary, and suggest that you hold such legislation in abeyance until and unless the alternative becomes the retention of the land tax. In such event I have no hesitancy in urging its preference. 

The elimination of the land tax will, of course, relieve the steam railroads and public utilities from their proportionate part of the property tax now received by the State. A privilege tax to compensate for this difference should be enacted.-

Senator Frank S. Hall, representing Dickson, Houston,

Humphreys and Stewart Counties, introduced a bill entitled "an Act to Provide Revenue for the State by Levying and Collecting a Tax upon incomes derived from certain Stocks and Bonds." This bill was passed April 10, 1929, approved by Governor Horton April 12, 1929, and is the first income tax statute enacted in Tennessee. The Act (Chapter 86, Public Acts of 1929) is commonly referred to as the "Hall Income Tax Law." This Act was subsequently amended by the same Legislature, Chapter 116, April 13, 1929. 

Under date November 27, 1929, Governor Horton issued a Proclamation convening the General Assembly in extraordinary session at noon December 2, 1929. The pertinent parts of the Proclamation are as follows: 

"" -The taxation of corporations, joint stock companies, associations, firms and individuals for the privilege of doing business within the State of Tennessee, the tax to be measured by net income for the preceding calendar or fiscal year, and the repeal of the Corporation 

Excise Act, Chapter 21 of the Public Acts of 1923.-Amendment of the law levying a tax upon income from stocks and bonds, same being chapter 86 and 116 of the Public Acts of 1929, so as to more effectively enforce same, expressly prohibit the back assessment of any stocks and bonds upon the income from which this tax is imposed, strike out the exemption of income from One Thousand Dollars ($1,000.00) of stocks and bonds, change of the taxable period and time of filing returns and paying tax, and divide the proceeds of the tax between the state, counties and municipalities.- 

In accordance with the Proclamation, the Legislature amended Chapter 86, Acts of 1929, allocating to the several counties and incorporated municipalities 45% of the net taxes collected (Chapter 116, Acts of extra session of 1929). 

The $1,000.00 exemption was also removed under the provisions of Chapter 27 of the extra session of 1929 and additional powers added tending to effect greater efficiency in the collection of the tax. The extra session of the Legislature did not enact the tax upon net income as suggested by the Governor, nor did it repeal the excise tax law. 

While the message of Governor Horton under date January 27, 1931 to the 67th General Assembly, contains no reference to income taxation, the following remarks with regard to finances should be noted. 

-When I came into the Governor's office, I found a deficit of $1,500,000.00 for that biennium. I have had prepared by the Tax De-

partment for your convenience and consideration a report of a survey of the general fund of the State as of December 31, 1930. It will be seen from this report that the last Legislature authorized the expenditure of $5,482,771.69 more than it provided revenue. Because of this failure to provide proper revenue to meet these expenditures, it was made necessary to call an extra session of the Legislature.- 

There was no new income tax legislation enacted at the regular session of 1931. Under date November 13, 1931, Governor Horton issued a Proclamation convening the 

Legislature in extraordinary session November 16, 1931, for the purpose of: "" -To authorize the Funding Board to borrow money to meet appropriations, for payment of which there are no funds, or insufficient funds, in the State Treasury, and for the purpose of preventing a deficit for the present biennium; and for the purpose of refunding the

It appears that the Legislature made an attempt to meet the situation (produced in the main by the reduction of the State land or property tax and the depression) through the

enactment of Chapter 20 Acts of 1931, which is a complete re-enactment of the income tax upon income from stocks and bonds and the enactment of a net income tax-Chapter 21, Acts of extra session of 1931. The net income tax statute was held to be unconstitutional in the case of Evans v. 

McCabe, 164 Tennessee 672.

The message of Governor Horton to the 68th General Assembly is silent on the matter of income taxation; however, he made the following comment: "In 1923 the property tax was 51 cents on the $100.00. This tax was abolished by the extraordinary session of 1929. For this year there is a property tax of 8 cents levied for school purposes. This has saved to the taxpayers more than twenty-six and one-half million dollars. 

At the same time there has been no general tax levied for general purposes. The Cigarette tax was increased and the excise tax was enacted. 

Both of these are limited taxes. The Tax Commission, appointed by the Governor, consisting of the Hon. Myles P. O'Connor, the State Attorney-General, and Mr. Charles P. White of the University of Tennessee, recommended to the last Legislature various revenue-producing measures. 

They were declined. A sales tax was offered; it was refused. income tax was offered and it was so changed as to make it constitutional. 

The Legislature failed to provide the necessary revenue by taxing property which should be taxed to meet the appropriations they had made.- -The responsibility is yours, and you must assume it and solve it." An

Governors Peay and Horton sought and secured state land tax reductions. The reduction aggregated more than a million dollars per annum and was accomplished by shifting the State tax on property. To replace the reduction in 

State revenue, entirely new tax statutes were enacted. The 

State land tax reduction offered an opportunity for the units of local Government to increase their tax rates thereby affording no permanent local tax reduction. Moreover, increased expenditures of counties such as payment of rights-of-way for State Highways, school levies made necessary to share State funds, etc., required increased revenues. This was possible for counties only by ad valorem taxes.

It is obvious that the tax policy of the State was unsound as the new statutes designed to produce revenues to supplant the State tax reduction on land did not provide a very staple flow of revenue for state purposes. 

Radical changes in policies of State taxation should be based upon a very careful investigation and analysis of the

(Ch. 4 

entire tax structure of State and Local Governments. 

Changes based upon political expediency inevitably result in additional burdens to taxpayers. 

The recommendations of Governor McAlister in his message to the 68th General Assembly, under date February 28, 1933, relates to the reduction of State Governmental costs. In recommending the passage of the appropriation bill without material increase, he stated: "Such a course, moreover, will require us to place new burdensome taxes upon the people, and it is conceded that they are not able to pay those that are already levied upon them by existing laws. I venture to say again that there can be no sort of doubt that it was the definite promise of all of us in the political contests that occurred in the summer and autumn of 1932 that no such new taxes would be levied, but that the necessary relief would be achieved by reducing governmental expenditures with the reasonably anticipated revenues.- -It is for these reasons that I earnestly urge you to enact this bill without any amendment that will require the levying of such additional taxes.- 

The policy of reducing governmental costs proposed by Governor McAlister and adopted by the 68th General Assembly continued throughout the biennium. In his message to the 69th General Assembly we find: "" This budget reduced the appropriations of the general fund (where practically all of our trouble lies) for the first year of the present biennium by six million dollars from what it was in the first year of the preceding biennium. This saving was in fact accomplished, and it is my earnest hope that it will be retained by your honorable bodies in the enactment of the appropriation bills at this session. -From what has just been said, it is evident that the re-enactment by your honorable bodies of the budget passed in 1933, reduced and inadequate for many governmental purposes as it undeniably is, would produce a continuing deficit in the treasury and violate again the fundamental law that we should adopt in budget making. -I -If, then, you agree with me that the time has come when the State must materially increase its revenues for the reasons already indicated, the next and vital question is where can they be found?have no pride of conviction and will welcome your investigation and use of any possible source of taxation as will bring about the desired result. In the last year the subject has been constantly on my mind and 

I have taken occasion to examine the tax systems of other States, with a view of seeing just where Tennessee may improve her own condition and where she may have overlooked sources of public revenue to which she should in times like these at last resort. -These studies of the efforts of other States in conditions similar in most respects to our own have revealed that in nearly all of them they have adopted measures for deriving additional revenue either from taxation of incomes or from what are commonly designated as sales taxes. It is conceded by economists that an income tax is the most just of all governmental levies, as it is in all instances measured by the ability of the person from whom it is exacted to pay it. smaller the income, the smaller the tax. If there is no income, there is not tax. Tennessee attempted to resort to this source of revenue in 

The

the extra session of 1931. The income tax then passed was challenged in the courts, and our Supreme Court, in the case of Evans v. McCabe, reported in 164 Tennessee, page 672, not only declared that particular statute to be unconstitutional, but in effect ruled that under the peculiar language of our antiquated constitution, no other income tax law could be constitutionally enacted. -With this source of revenue excluded, my examinations into the subject of taxation systems of other states has come upon no other source of income to which Tennessee can resort in this emergency except what is known as the sales tax, and it is with the greatest regret that I have at length concluded to recommend to your honorable bodies the enactment of such a law in Tennessee. -I do not recommend it as an indefinite part of our tax system, and I think its continuance should not be for a longer term than thirty months from the time of its enactment.- 

By 1937, conditions were such that it became necessary to provide revenue far in excess of that necessary during the period 1933-1937 to meet demands being made for oldage insurance, unemployment compensation, additional funds for public schools, etc. Governor Browning in his message to the 70th General Assembly dealing with these demands for additional governmental service, has this to say as regards additional revenues from income taxation: "Bills designed to raise revenue to the extent of $4,000,000.00 have been introduced.- -There are certain means which might in general seem desirable but which are closed to us under our Constitution. have particularly in mind a State income tax, eminently fair in principle because it places the burden upon those most able to bear it. 

Constitutional Amendment permitting this I hope for in the near future so that relief from annoying special levies may be had.An Act amending the Statute imposing tax upon the income from stocks and bonds is part of the revenue program. This bill eliminates certain exemptions in the present law and also increases the rate from 5% to 7% on the income of our citizens derived from foreign corporations. Under the proposed bill all income received by residents of Tennessee from stocks and bonds (excepting bonds of the United States, the state of Tennessee and political sub-divisions of this state) will be taxable. suggested law will represent the nearest approach to a general income tax that is possible at the present time. Today all income from stocks and bonds of corporations having 75% of their property in Tennessee is exempt from taxation. Such exemption will be eliminated under the amendment now offered for your consideration but the rate on income from domestic corporations will be 5% as compared with the 7% proposed on foreign corporate income."' INCOME TAX Reasons for Enactment- Whereas, By Article 2, Section 28, of the Constitution of the State of Tennessee it is among other things provided: "The Legislature shall have power to levy a tax upon income derived from stocks and bonds that are not taxed ad valorem," and,

Whereas, An Income tax is just in principle and should be availed of for the purpose of assisting in defraying the expenses of government; and 

Whereas, Income taxation has been put into practice both by the Government of the United States, and by many of the States, yielding revenue and not imposing any unjust or inequitable burdens upon the persons subject to such tax; and

Whereas, It is desirable and proper that the State of Tennessee should avail itself of the privileges and exercise the power conferred upon it by the Constitution of the State of Tennessee by levying a fair and equitable income tax on stocks and bonds that are not taxed ad valorem; 

Now, therefore:

Section 1. 

Be it enacted by the General Assembly of the State of Tennessee,

Rates of tax- 

That beginning with the calendar year 1937, and for each calendar year thereafter, to be computed from January 1 to January 1 of each year, an income tax in the amount of six (6%) per cent per annum, (except as provided in the next paragraph) be levied and collected on income derived by way of dividends from stocks or by way of interest on bonds of each person, partnership, association, trust and corporation in the State of Tennessee who received, or to . whom accrued, or to whom was credited, during any year, income from the sources above enumerated except as hereafter provided.

There shall be levied and collected an income tax under the terms and provisions of the preceding paragraph in the

(Ch. 4 

amount of four (4%) per cent per annum upon income from stock in any corporation assessed for ad valorem taxes on its corporate property, if seventy-five (75%) per cent of the total corporate property (including the franchise) of such corporation is assessable in Tennessee. The burden shall be on the stockholder claiming taxation under this paragraph rather than under the preceding paragraph to show to the satisfaction of the officers charged with the tax collection that at least seventy-five (75%) per cent of the corporate property is assessable in Tennessee for ad valorem taxes. 

1937 Income taxable Taxes payable under this Act on May 15, 1938 shall be measured by income received during the entire calendar year 1937 and not merely by income received subsequent to the passage of this Act. 

Section 2. 

State tax only—

That the tax herein provided for is for State purposes only, and no county or municipality shall have power to levy the same.

Section 3. 

Definitions- 

That the word "stocks" as used in this Act shall be held and construed to mean shares of stock issued by corporations chartered and organized under the laws of the State of Tennessee, or of any other State, or of the United States, or of any foreign government, and all interests in partnerships, associations, or trusts represented by transferable evidence of such interest. 

The word "bond" shall be held and construed to in- Iclude all obligations issued by any person, firm, joint stock company, business trust or corporation organized and doing business under the laws of the State of Tennessee, or any other State, evidenced by an instrument whereby the obligor is bound to pay interest to the obligee regardless of

Ch. 4) 217 

INCOME TAX 

whether the obligor is doing business in the State of Tennessee, or whether the obligation under the terms of which the interest accrues is a mortgage or lien on property located in the State of Tennessee or beyond the jurisdiction thereof; provided that the word "bond" shall not include ordinary commercial paper, trade acceptance, etc. maturing in six (6) months or less from the date of issuance. 

The word "person" and the words "it," "he" or any other singular pronoun used in this Act shall be held to include every natural person, inhabitant, resident, beneficiary of every trust or estate, partnership, joint stock company, business trust, corporation or any other form of organization in receipt of dividends from corporate stock and/or interest on bonds as herein defined, regardless of the source from which such income is derived, save and except as herein otherwise expressly provided. 

The words "corporate property" as used in this Act shall be construed to include the "franchise," "Corporate Excess" or "intangible value" of the corporation as well as all other property.

Section 4. 

Exempt income- 

That nothing contained in this Act shall be construed or held to authorize the levy of an income tax on obligations of the United States, whether evidenced by bonds or otherwise and/or on shares of stock in corporations which are arms and agencies directly of the United States, insofar as such bonds and stocks are exempt from such taxation by the Constitution or laws of the United States; or on the income derived from bonds of the State of Tennessee, or any county or municipality or other political subdivision thereof not subject to ad valorem taxation.

Section 5. 

Conditional exemptions- 

(a) No corporation shall be required to pay any income tax which otherwise would be assessable under this Act on

any stocks and/or bonds which constitute a part of the aggregate of its corporate property on which it is now assessed, or shall be, for ad valorem taxes; nor when such stocks and/or bonds constitute a part of the assets which determine the value of the shares which are now or shall hereafter be assessed for ad valorem taxes to the stockholder. (c) No person shall be assessed with this tax on any stock in any corporation where the value of the shares are assessed ad valorem to the stockholder by the State. (d) No distribution of capital by stock dividend, or liquidation or otherwise, shall be taxed as income; but earned surplus shall not be considered as capital, and shall be taxed as income when and in whatever manner it may be distributed, irrespective of when it was earned. (e) Income from stocks as herein defined shall not be assessable to the holder thereof if the income which would be otherwise assessable has been assessed to and paid by the organization issuing the same. 

But no corporation or other person (as herein defined) shall be assessed with or forced to pay this tax on behalf of the stockholders. Such person, may, if it chooses, pay the tax on behalf of its stockholders; in such case it shall have a lien on the stock or on the dividend for its reimbursement, and the stockholder shall be no longer liable. However, should this option not be exercised, it shall, at the request of the Commissioner, furnish a list of all the stockholders, with their last known address, and the amount of the dividends paid to, or due to or credited to the stockholder in any manner. (f) The stocks and bonds of the educational, religious or other like institutions organized for the general welfare and not for profit or individual gain which are exempt from taxation under the provisions of Chapter 602 of the Acts of 1907, known as the Assessment Act, shall be exempt from the taxes imposed by this Act; provided, however, if any educational, religious or other like institution issue stocks or bonds the income or profit or any part of which go to private individuals or corporations for profit or gain and

Ch. 4) 219 

INCOME TAX 

not purely for educational, religious, or charitable purposes, shall be subject to the tax herein imposed. 

Section 6. 

Returns to be filed; when 

That the calendar year 1931 shall constitute the first period for which an income tax return shall be filed under the provision of this Act with the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation by all persons, partnerships, trust, associations or corporations that are subject to this tax, said return to be filed not later than March 15, 1932; and every person liable for the tax or taxes imposed by or levied under the authority of the provisions of this Act shall on or before the 15th day of March of each year make out, on forms prescribed by the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, a statement or return setting out, in detail, the stocks and/or bonds for the receipt of income from which the taxpayers are liable for the tax or taxes imposed hereunder, each security to be set out separately, and listing opposite each such item or security, the amount of income received therefrom during the preceding calendar year; and showing the amount of the tax owing by such person to the State of Tennessee; and showing the residence of the taxpayer at the time of the filing of the return, and the residence of such taxpayers as of noon, December 31, of the year for the receipt of income during which the taxpayer is liable for the tax imposed and the return is filed. 

Any such statement or report shall be signed and verified by the oath or oaths of the individual or individuals, or by the President, Vice-President, Treasurer, Assistant Treasurer or Managing Agent in this State of the association, trust or corporation making the same. 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation shall have the power to require all such other information from any person filing a return as, in his opinion, may be necessary to effectuate the purposes of this Act. 

It shall be the duty of the Department of Finance and Taxation of the State of Tennessee to provide suitable blanks and forms on which taxpayers, subject to this Act, shall make their returns for taxation hereunder.

(Ch. 4 

 Section 7. 

Tax payment; due date—

That the tax or taxes due and payable on account of income received during any calendar year shall be paid in full on or before May 15th of the succeeding calendar year. 

Section 8. 

Citation for failure to file return- 

That the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, or any duly authorized agent, representative or employee, is hereby authorized and empowered, either at his own instance or at the instance of any citizen or taxpayer of the State of Tennessee, whenever it is within his knowledge or he has reason to suspect that any person who may not have filed any return or report, or that any person subject to the tax or taxes imposed by the terms of this Act has filed an incorrect return or report, or has not paid the proper amount of such tax, or has not filed a report or statement setting forth the full and correct amount of the tax due to the State of Tennessee by such taxpayer, to issue the citation hereinafter provided for the purpose of assessing or re-assessing such person for the tax or taxes by the terms of this Act. 

For this purpose the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, or any authorized agent, representative or employee, may issue a citation in the name of the State of Tennessee, to be served as hereinafter provided, notifying the person against whom such citation may be issued to appear before the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, or any authorized agent, representative or employee, either at the office of the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation in Nashville, or at any other place in the county of this State in which such person may have his place of residence, such citation to be issued and served not less than five (5) days prior to the date of the hearing hereafter provided, and requiring such person to show cause, if any, why he or it should not be assessed or re-assessed as provided by the terms of this Act, and in the case of these persons not filing any return, to show cause, if any, in addition to the above matters, why such return was not filed.

Section 11. 

Back Assessments for ad valorem invalid—

That stocks and bonds upon the income from which a tax is imposed under the provisions of this Act shall not be back assessed for taxation by the State or any municipality, county or political sub-division thereof and the State of Tennessee and municipalities, counties and political subdivisions of this State and the officials and representatives thereof are expressly prohibited from back assessing for ad valorem any such stocks and/or bonds for any year or years.

Ch. 4) 231 

INCOME TAX Section 13. 

Stock Dealers must Furnish list of customers— 

That when and if a broker or commission dealer does not make a physical delivery to his customers of stocks and bonds, income from which is taxable under this Act, but retains possession and/or title himself or through a nominee, agent depository of such security and receives such income or credit therefor, he shall report such income to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, and pay the tax thereon measured by the dividends or interest credited, or which should be credited, to the accounts of his customers, unless he furnishes to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation a list of his customers, with the last known address of each, to whom such dividends and/or interest have been paid or credited and the amount thereof.

Section 14. 

Trust Estates; Income from- 

That residents of Tennessee who receive income from trust estates located without the State of Tennessee, any portion of which is invested in securities, the income from which is taxable under this Act whether said trust estate be revocable or irrevocable, shall file with the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, as part of his income tax return a sworn statement of the trustee, executor or other administrator of said trust estate showing what portion of the total income received by such Tennessee resident from such estate was derived from securities, the income from which is taxable under this Act. And if such resident of Tennessee fails to file such sworn statement from the trustee, executor or other administrator, then he shall report for income taxation in the manner otherwise provided in the Act the entire amount of income received by him from such trust estate.

Trustees, guardians, administrators, executors and other persons acting in a fiduciary capacity who receive income taxable under this Act for the benefit of residents of Tennessee, shall be required to make returns under this Act and to pay the tax herein levied. Trustees, Guardians and other persons acting in a fiduciary capacity who are

(Ch. 4 

residents of Tennessee, and who receive income on behalf of non-resident beneficiaries, shall not be required to pay tax under this Act even though such income be derived from stocks or bonds which would otherwise be assessable under this Act. However, executors or administrators receiving income taxable under this Act from stocks or bonds which were the property of a decedent who resided in Tennessee shall pay tax upon the same until such time as such stocks or bonds have been distributed or transferred to distributees or legatees thereof. 

Section 15. 

Rules and Regulations- 

That the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation is further authorized and empowered to make all necessary rules and regulations not inconsistent with the terms of this Act, which rules and regulations shall have the force and effect of law, for the purpose of fully carrying out and giving effect of the provisions of this Act.

Penalty for Violation of Rules—

General Fund Revenue [4% tax]— 

The taxes collected under the provisions of this Act upon income from stocks taxable at the rate of four (4%) per cent shall be paid into the general fund of the State Treasury.

six (6%) per cent per annum, five-eights (5%) shall be paid into the general fund of the State Treasury and the remaining three eighths (%) shall be distributed among the cities and counties of the State. Where a taxpayer residing in a county but without the corporate limits of any municipality, pays a tax imposed by this Act at the rate of six (6%) per cent per annum, then three-eights (3%) of the net tax collected from such taxpayer shall be returned to the county within which such taxpayer resides.

Payment due Cities and Counties: when- 

In each instance, the payment to cities and counties shall be upon proper voucher drawn according to law and shall be made on or before June 30th of each year covering collections thereunder of taxes levied for the preceding calendar year. To carry out the provisions of this section with reference to the return of taxes to counties and cities, the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation shall keep separate accounts with regard to securities taxable at the rate of six (6%) per cent per annum and those securities taxable at the rate of four (4%) per cent per annum. 

1937 Revenue Distributed under old Act- Payments to counties and cities upon collections made during 1937 upon income received during the calendar year 1936 shall be made in accordance with the provisions of this Act prior to the amendment to Section 17 now being incorporated therein.

RULES AND REGULATIONS Income Tax 

The only departmental rules and regulations prescribed and published are as follows:

On the 1935 Report Form- Regulations. 

I. Income collected or "collectible" during the calendar year 1935 must be reported on Form I. T. No. 

H-35 on or before March 15, 1936.

II. Uncollected dividends or interest shall be regarded as "collectible" when the owner of the stocks, bonds, notes or mortgages of his own volition allows such dividends or interest to remain unpaid. 

The renewal of a note is considered a continuous transaction and the income therefrom is taxable. 

III. Stocks and bonds (as defined in this Act) must be listed and sufficiently described to admit of identification. Lists may be attached to and made a part of Form I. T. No. H-35. 

IV. No person shall be excused from making the return required by law because of the failure of the Commissioner or his representative to send or give out forms to him.

V. Income is considered to be received for the purpose of law when: (1) It is actually paid in cash, by check or other negotiable instruments, or the equivalent of cash. (2) When credited upon the books of a bank, banking institution, broker or any agent of the taxpayer. (3) When payment is made in merchandise or other commodities of intrinsic value. 

VI. Dividends credited by a broker to a customer's account, as a part of marginal or other trading, shall be returned for taxation. 235

VII. Accrued dividends or interest received by a seller of stocks, bonds, notes or mortgages shall be returned by him for taxation; but such accrued interest or dividends thus advanced by the purchaser will be held taxable to the purchaser unless he files with the department the name or names of the seller and amounts so accrued, to obtain this exemption. 

VIII. If loans are made with no charge of interest but compensation therefor is taken under the name of bonuses, discounts or charges of any other designation, the amounts thus received shall be taxable as income.

IX. Dividends paid to any person by corporations will not be recognized as liquidating dividends unless the corporation is actually undergoing some recognized form of liquidation.

X. Administrators, executors, guardians, or persons acting in any fiduciary capacity are within this statute.

XI. Residents of Tennessee who receive income from trust estates located without the State of Tennessee, any portion of which is invested in securities taxable under this Act, shall file as part of their return a sworn statement of the trustee, executor or any other administrator of said trust, showing what portion of the total income received by such 

Tennessee resident was derived from securities income from which is taxable under this Act. Unless such list is furnished, the entire income from such out of State trust will be held taxable. 

XII. Before a fiduciary can be released and a final accounting made of the estate or trust in his charge, all taxes reflected under the provisions of this Act upon the fiduciary, which have become due, must have been paid; and taxes which may become due must have been secured by a bond, deposit or otherwise, and said fiduciary must file with the department the names and addresses of the beneficiaries of the estate or trust.
