Persons Liable for Tax- Law. Section 1. 

That beginning with the calendar year 1937, and for each calendar year thereafter, to be computed from January 1 to January 1 of each year, an income tax in the amount of six (6%) per cent per annum, (except as provided in the next paragraph) be levied and collected on income derived by way of dividends from stocks or by way of interest on bonds of each person, partnership, association, trust and corporation in the State of Tennessee who received, or to whom accrued, or to whom was credited during any year income from the sources above enumerated except as hereafter provided. 

There shall be levied and collected an income tax under the terms and provisions of the preceding paragraph in the amount of four (4%) per cent per annum upon income from stock in any corporation assessed for ad valorem taxes on its corporate property, if seventy.

(Ch. 4 

five (75%) per cent of the total corporate property (including the franchise) of such corporation is assessable in Tennessee. The burden shall be on the stockholder claiming taxation under this paragraph rather than under the preceding paragraph to show to the satisfaction of the officers charged with the tax collection that at least seventyfive (75%) per cent of the corporate property is assessable in Tennessee for ad valorem taxes. 

Taxes payable under this Act on May 15, 1938 shall be measured by income received during the entire calendar year 1937 and not merely by income received subsequent to the passage of this Act. 

Under the provisions of this section, an income tax is levied upon all "persons" (persons are defined to include a natural person, inhabitant, resident, beneficiary of every trust or estate, partnership, joint stock company, business trust, corporation or any other form of organization) receiving, or to whom accrues, or to whom was credited during the calendar year beginning January 1, 1937 and subsequent years, income from stocks or interest from bonds.

Prior to the enactment of the Income Tax Law, Chapter 

20, Acts of the second extra session of 1931, stocks and bonds were subject to property taxation according to value. 

This Act amends the Assessment Act of 1907 (Chapter 

602 Public Acts of 1907) exempting stocks and bonds from property taxation and, under the present laws, stocks and bonds are not "assessable" for ad valorem property taxation. This amendment was necessary to comply with 

Section 28 of Article II of the Constitution of Tennessee. 

With respect to this matter the court held: "Chapter 86 of the Acts of 1929 so amended the Assessment Act of 1907 as to omit stocks and bonds of the kind described from the list of properties that should be assessed for taxes ad valorem, and put them in a class to themselves to be taxed only in respect of the income therefrom. That this could be constitutionally done was determined in the case of Shields v. Williams. From the date of the passage of that 

Act no authority has existed to assess this character of property ad valorem.-The decree of the Chancellor is accordingly affirmed.'' [Hamilton National Bank et al v. Alvin Shipp, County Trustee, 160 Tennessee 311.]

The Income Tax Law was enacted in accordance with the provisions of Section 28, Article II of the Constitution of 1870 and the constitutionality of the Act is well settled. 

See Shields, et al V. Williams, Commissioner, 159 Tennessee 349 and Ross V. McCabe, Commissioner, 166 Tennessee 314.

Ch. 4) 243 

INCOME TAX Income From Bonds-Rate of Tax- 

Income from bonds, other than United States, State of Tennessee or political subdivisions of Tennessee is taxable at the rate of 6%.

Stock Dividends-Rate of Tax— 

(a) Corporations having less than 75% of the total corporate property assessable in Tennessee. 

Persons receiving dividends from corporations having less than 75% of the total corporate property (including the franchise) assessable for ad valorem property tax in Tennessee, are liable for tax at the rate of 6%. (b) Corporations having 75% or more of the total corporate property assessable in Tennessee. 

Persons receiving dividends from corporations having 75% or more of the total corporate property (including the franchise) assessable for ad valorem property tax in Tennessee are liable for tax at the rate of 4%. 

The Act places the burden upon the taxpayer to show to the satisfaction of the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation that at least 75% of the corporate property of the corporation from which the dividend is received is assessable for ad valorem property tax in Tennessee. In most instances, corporations organized under the laws of Tennessee have 75% or more of their entire property in this state while corporations organized under the laws of other states and domesticated in Tennessee do not. It should be noticed that the Act refers to assessable property and care should be used in this connection to properly classify dividends for the purpose of income taxation. 

Income from bonds is taxed at six per cent (6%) and the law defines the word "bond" to include all obligations or indebtedness other than "ordinary commercial paper, trade acceptances, etc. maturing in six months or less from date of issuance." This rate of tax applies to all income from this class of investment, whereas income from "stock" investments is taxable at 4% when such income is received from corporations having 75% or more of the

(Ch. 4 

total corporate property, assessable for ad valorem property tax in Tennessee.

It might be argued that some unfairness exists in taxing income from one class of investment at 6% and income from another class of investment at 4% in corporations coming within the "75% or over" group. Such a condition could exist with regard to these two classes of income received from the same corporation, and certainly to tax income from a mortgage investment at 6% and income from a "capital stock" investment at 4% in such instances would appear to be inequitable. However, the Legislature would appear to be within its constitutional rights, in taxing income from different sources at different rates. 

The income tax applies to all taxable income received during the calendar year 1937 and subsequent years and is payable to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation on or before May 15, 1938.

It is to be observed that the law imposes a tax "for the calendar year" and no provision is made fixing any definite date in determining liability. Therefore, it must be assumed that all persons resident in Tennessee at any time during the "calendar year," receiving income from stocks and bonds, are liable for the tax. A person resident in the State for only part of the year appears to be just as liable as the person living within the State for the full year, but it is assumed that the tax liability, if any, would be assessed proportionately to the residence period-within and without the State.

To determine the legal residence of a person for the purpose of taxation, the following questions should be given consideration: 

1. Where the person spends the greater portion of his time. 

2. Where he votes. 

3. Where he is carried in the local City or telephone directories. 

4. Where he maintains his bank account. 

5. What State he has declared in writing or verbally as his legal residence. 

6. "Confirmation" with such other State.

State Tax Only— Law. Section 2. 

That the tax herein provided for is for State purposes only, and no county or municipality shall have power to levy the same.

Ch. 4) 245 

INCOME TAX 

This section of the Act prohibits counties, cities and towns to levy a similar tax upon income from stocks and bonds.

Definitions- Law. Section 3. 

That the word "stocks" as used in this Act shall be held and construed to mean shares of stock issued by corporations chartered and organized under the laws of the State of Tennessee, or of any other state, or of the United States, or of any Foreign Government, and all interest in partnerships, associations, or trusts represented by transferable evidence of such interest. 

The word "bond" shall be held and construed to include all obligations issued by any person, firm, joint stock company, business trust or corporation organized and doing business under the laws of the State of Tennessee, or any other state, evidenced by an instrument whereby the obligor is bound to pay interest to the obligee regardless of whether the obligor is doing business in the State of Tennessee, or whether the obligation under the terms of which the interest accrues is a mortgage or lien on property located in the State of Tennessee or beyond the jurisdiction thereof; provided that the word "bond" shall not include ordinary commercial paper, trade acceptance, etc. maturing in six (6) months or less from the date of issuance. 

The word "". 'person" and the words "it, """he" or any other singular pronoun used in this Act shall be held to include every natural person, inhabitant, resident, beneficiary of every trust or estate, partnership, joint stock company, business trust, corporation or any other form of organization in receipt of dividends from corporate stock and/or interest on bonds as herein defined, regardless of the source from which such income is derived, save and except as herein otherwise expressly provided. 

The words "corporate property'' as used in this Act shall be construed to include the "franchise," "'corporate excess, or "intangible value' of the corporation as well as all other property. (a) "Stocks"- The word "stocks" means and includes the shares of stock issued by all corporations; whether such corporation is organized under the laws of the United States or any state, or under the laws of a foreign government. In addition, stocks is further defined to include any instrument which may be evidence of a transferable interest in any partnership, association or trust, i.e., if under the terms of agreement between partners the interest of the partner and his participation in the earnings is evidenced by certificate or transferable evidence of such interest the income is subject to the income tax. (b) "Bonds"-__ The word "bond" includes all obligations issued under the laws of the United States, or of any state, evidenced by

(Ch. 4 

an instrument requiring the maker thereof to pay interest to the obligee; it includes mortgages, liens, etc. on property located in or outside of Tennessee. The word "bond," however, does not include commercial paper maturing in six months or less from date of issue. As regards this question, the court says: "A more serious question is presented upon the contention that under a caption indicating legislation levying a tax upon incomes derived from certain stocks and bonds it was not permissible to levy a tax upon incomes derived on all the interest bearing obligations described as bonds in the body of the Act.-So, while the word "bond'' used in the caption of Chapter 86 of the Acts of 1929, in its most accurate or obvious sense, may not point to all the obligations taxed in the Statute, still in a sense fully sanctioned by judicial approval it does not include such obligations. The body of the Act is therefore not broader than its caption.'' Shields v. Williams, supra. (c) "Person”____ The word "person" includes natural persons, inhabitants, resident beneficiaries of every trust or estate, partnerships, joint stock companies, business trusts, corporations or any other form of artificial persons. However, this term has been held to exclude resident trustees for non-resident beneficiaries. 

The complainant is a Tennessee corporation, with its situs at Memphis. It is the duly appointed and qualified guardian and trustee of certain non-resident minors and beneficiaries, and as such received certain incomes on stocks and bonds, on which taxes were paid as stated above. There is no express language in the Act that taxes the incomes of non-residents, or taxes incomes received by resident guardians or trustees or other fiduciaries for the benefit of non-resident wards or beneficiaries. The state also insists that the word "person" is broad enough to cover trustees and beneficiaries. To this we cannot agree, particularly in view of the fact that the Legislature in a subsequent section of the Act defined this word, and under the definition the parties taxed herein were not included. Bank of Commerce & Trust Co. V. 

McCabe, 164 Tennessee 591. (d) "Corporate Property"- 

The term "corporate property" means: 

1. Real Property: 

Lands and Buildings. 

2. Tangible Personal Property: 

Merchandise, Furniture and Fixtures, Machinery and Equipment, Money on Hand, Automobiles and 

Trucks, and all other tangible property.

Ch. 4) 247 

INCOME TAX 3. Intangible Personal Property: 

Accounts Receivable, Notes Receivable, Mortgages, Liens, Patent or Copyrights, Conditional Sales Contracts, Good Will, Franchise, etc. 

4. Corporate Excess: 

The excess of actual cash value of all real, tangible and intangible personal property over book value thereof.

Exempt Income- Law. 

Section 4. 

That nothing contained in this Act shall be construed or held to authorize the levy of an income tax on obligations of the United States, whether evidenced by bonds or otherwise and/or on shares of stock in corporations which are arms and agencies directly of the United States, insofar as such bonds and stocks are exempt from such taxation by the Constitution or laws of the United States; or on the income derived from bonds of the State of Tennessee, or any county or municipality or other political subdivision thereof not subject to ad valorem taxation. 

Therefore, Income received from the following sources is exempt: (a) Obligations of the United States, evidenced by bond, or otherwise. (b) Dividends on shares of stock and interest on bonds of corporations which are direct agencies of the United States Government, provided such stocks and bonds are exempt from income taxation by the Constitution or laws of the United States. (c) Interest received from bonds of the State of Tennessee. (d) Interest received from bonds of any city, county, or political subdivision of the State of Tennessee. 

Income received by a resident of Tennessee from bonds of a state, county, city or political subdivision of a state, other than Tennessee, is subject to the income tax. See 

Union and Planters Bank & Trust Company V. Fort, 170 

Tennessee 285.

Conditionally Exempt Income- Law. Section 5. 

(a) No corporation shall be required to pay any income tax which otherwise would be assessable under this Act on any stocks and/or bonds which constitute a part of the aggregate of its corporate property on

(Ch. 4 

which it is now assessed for ad valorem taxes; nor when such stocks and/or bonds constitute a part of the assets which determine the value of the shares which are now or shall hereafter be assessed for ad valorem taxes to the stockholders. (c) No person shall be assessed with this tax on any stock in any corporation where the value of the shares are assessed ad valorem to the stockholders by the State. (d) No distribution of capital by stock dividend, or liquidation or otherwise, shall be taxed as income; but earned surplus shall not be considered as capital, and shall be taxed as income when and in whatever manner it may be distributed, irrespective of when it was earned. (e) Income from stocks as herein defined shall not be assessable to the holder thereof if the income which would be otherwise assessable has been assessed to and paid by the organization issuing the same. 

But no corporation or other person (as herein defined) shall be assessed with or forced to pay this tax on behalf of the stockholders. 

Such person may, if it chooses, pay the tax on behalf of its stockholders; in such case it shall have a lien on the stock or on the dividend for its reimbursement, and the stockholder shall be no longer liable. However, should this option not be exercised, it shall, at the request of the Commissioner, furnish a list of all the stockholders, with their last known address, and the amount of the dividends paid to, or due to, or credited to the stockholder in any manner. (f) The stocks and bonds of the educational, religious or other like institutions organized for the general welfare and not for profit or individual gain which are exempt from taxation under the provisions of Chapter 602 of the Acts of 1907, known as the Assessment Act; provided, however, if any educational, religious or other like institution issue stocks or bonds the income or profit or any part of which go to private individuals or corporations for profit or gain and not purely for educational, religious or charitable purposes, shall be subject to the tax herein imposed. (a) Corporations are not liable for the income tax in instances where either stocks and bonds, from which income is derived, constitute a part of the total corporate property assessed for ad valorem property tax. For example, this subsection is operative as regards public service corporations assessed for property taxation by the Railroad and Public Utilities Commission and to the State Banks, but unless the value of such stocks and bonds is actually included in the property tax assessment, the income therefrom is subject to the income tax. With respect to quasi corporations, the method of assessment is set forth in 

Section 1404 et seq. Williams Tennessee Code. 

(c) However, it appears that in the case of individuals there is no legal alternative. All individuals are required to pay the income tax upon income from taxable stocks and bonds since such properties are expressly excluded from property taxation. See Hamilton National Bank, et al, V. 

Shipp, supra.

Ch. 4) 249 

INCOME TAX 

(d) The distribution of capital by means of stock dividend, in instances of voluntary or involuntary dissolution of corporations, is not subject to tax, however, that portion of the dividend representing surplus would be taxable. 

To illustrate: 

The A corporation decides to dissolve on January 1, 1936. At December 31, 1935 the net worth account is as follows: 

$100,000.00 Issued and Outstanding Capital Stock 

100,000.00 Earned Surplus $200,000.00 Total Capital and Surplus

Assuming that the total capital and surplus is distributed and that each stockholder received a dividend of $1,000.00; $500.00 would represent a return of "capital" and would be non-taxable; while $500.00 represents that portion of the dividend paid from "surplus" and is taxable. 

The fact that the surplus was earned in prior years has no bearing on the liability for the tax. However, in final liquidation, if only $100,000.00 was distributed, then it is assumed that the stockholder received his original investment and therefore no liability for income tax would accrue. (e) Corporations have the option of paying the income tax upon the dividends or interest payable to its stock or bond holders and if it so elects to pay the tax, the stock or bond holder is not required to report such income for taxation. If the corporation pays the tax on behalf of its stock and bond holders, the act gives the corporation a lien upon the stocks, bonds or dividends for reimbursement. The 

Commissioner of Finance and Taxation is given the right to require all corporations, who do not elect to pay the tax on behalf of its stockholders, to furnish the names, addresses and the amount of dividends and interest paid, accrued or credited, to the stockholders. (f) The income from stocks and bonds of educational, religious or similar corporations organized for general welfare is exempt from tax; however, if such income or profit, or any part of same, inures to the benefit of in-

dividuals or corporations for profit or gain, such income is taxable in the hands of the recipient. 

Returns- Law. Section 6. 

That the calendar year 1931 shall constitute the first period for which an income tax return shall be filed under the provision of this Act with the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation by all persons, partnerships, trust, associations or corporations that are subject to this tax, said return to be filed not later than March 15, 1932; and every person liable for the tax or taxes imposed by or levied under the authority of the provisions of this Act shall on or before the 15th day of March of each year make out, on forms prescribed by the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, a statement or return setting out, in detail, the stocks and/or bonds for the receipt of income from which the taxpayers are liable for the tax or taxes imposed hereunder, each security to be set out separately, and listing opposite each such item or security the amount of income received therefrom during the preceding calendar year; and showing the amount of the tax owing by such person to the State of Tennessee; and showing the residence of the taxpayer at the time of the filing of the return, and the residence of such taxpayer as of noon, December 31, of the year for the receipt of income during which the taxpayer is liable for the tax imposed and the return is filed. 

Any such statement or report shall be signed and verified by the oath or oaths of the individual or individuals, or by the President, Vice President, Treasurer, Assistant Treasurer or Managing Agent in this state of the association, trust or corporation making the same. 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation shall have the power to require all such other information from any person filing a return as, in his opinion, may be necessary to effectuate the purposes of this 

Act. 

It shall be the duty of the Department of Finance and Taxation of the State of Tennessee to provide suitable blanks and forms on which taxpayers, subject to this Act, shall make their returns for taxation hereunder.

Persons, partnerships, trusts, associations and corporations are required to prepare and file an income tax return covering the calendar year 1937 with the Commissioner of 

Finance and Taxation on or before March 15, 1938 and annually thereafter. The return is to be made upon forms prescribed by the Commissioner and must set out in detail each security from which taxable income was received, together with the correct amount of income derived from each security. The return must be made under oath, and the Commissioner is authorized to require, under oath, any other data or information he may deem necessary. 

It will be noted that this section of the Act requires taxpayers to furnish resident address as of noon December 31, of each year. This is a most essential matter and tax-

Ch. 4) 251 

INCOME TAX 

payers should be careful to furnish this information, as the law requires the State to pay over to each county and incorporated municipality a certain portion of income taxes collected. Correct apportionment of the tax collected cannot be made unless the income tax returns indicate the correct resident address as at December 31 of each year. 

Due to the fact that the Department of Finance and Taxation has not yet prescribed income tax return forms to be used for the year 1937, illustration of the completed income tax return cannot be given. 

Payment of Tax- Law. Section 7. 

That the tax or taxes due and payable on account of income received during any calendar year shall be paid in full on or before May 15th of the succeeding calendar year. 

The income tax may be paid any time after January first of each year and it is the practice of taxpayers to pay the tax at the time the return is filed, i.e., March 15th of each year. However, the entire tax due must be paid on or before May 15th of each year if penalties and interest are to be avoided.

The income tax payable on or before May 15, 1938 will represent the tax upon income received, accrued or credited during the calendar year 1937 and correspondingly during subsequent years.

To summarize: 

1. Income tax returns must be filed with Commissioner of Finance and Taxation on or before March 15th of each year. 

2. Tax may be paid at time return is filed. 

3. Tax must be paid in full on or before May 15 of each year.

Failure to File Return and Pay Tax, etc- Law. Section 8. 

That the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, or any duly authorized agent, representative or employee, is hereby authorized and empowered, either at his own instance or at the instance of any citizen or taxpayer of the State of Tennessee, whenever it is within his knowledge or he has reason to suspect that any person who may not have filed any

(Ch. 4 

return or report, or that any person subject to the tax or taxes imposed by the terms of this Act has filed an incorrect return or report, or has not paid the proper amount of such tax, or has not filed a report or statement setting forth the full and correct amount of the tax due to the State of Tennessee by such taxpayer, to issue the citation hereinafter provided for the purpose of assessing or reassessing such person for the tax or taxes by the terms of this Act. For this purpose the 

Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, or any authorized agent, representative or employee, may issue a citation in the name of the State of Tennessee, to be served as hereinafter provided, notifying the person against whom such citation may be issued to appear before the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, or any authorized agent, representative or employee, either at the office of the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation in Nashville or at any other place in the county of this State in which such person may have his place of residence, such citation to be issued and served not less than five (5) days prior to the date of the hearing hereafter provided, and requiring such person to show cause, if any, why he or it should not be assessed or re-assessed as provided by the terms of this Act, and in the case of these persons not filing any return, to show cause, if any, in addition to the above matters, why such return was not filed. 

The form of citation shall be substantially as follows:

Said citation shall first be sent by mail by the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, or any authorized agent, representative or employee, to the person at his last known address; and should the person thus cited by mail fail to appear at the time and place specified in the citation, then a second citation shall be delivered by the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation or any authorized agent, representative or employee to the sheriff of any county wherein the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation or any authorized agent, representative or employee has the reason to believe that the person against whom the citation is issued may be found. All such citations shall be served by the sheriff, or his deputy, of the county where the same is directed. 1. Citation-- 

The Commissioner or his representative is authorized to cite for hearing any person whom he has reason to believe has received income subject to tax and has failed to make return and pay the tax thereon, or any person having made an incomplete or incorrect return. 

Such citation must be: (a) Issued and served five days prior to the date fixed for hearing, requiring such person to show cause why income tax should not be assessed or reassessed.

(Ch. 4  

(b) Mailed by the Commissioner to the last known address of the person. Upon failure to respond to citation by mail may be; (c) Served by sheriff of any county in which person may be found. 

At the hearing (the time and place being fixed in the citation issued by the Commissioner) the matters under consideration are to be gone into and a full and complete hearing had thereon. The Commissioner of Finance and 

Taxation, or his representative, is authorized to: (d) Issue subpoena requiring the attendance of witnesses for the State as well as for the person named in the citation. Subpoenas shall be served by the sheriff or deputy, who is to receive the usual fee for serving such subpoena. (e) Administer oaths to any person summoned. (f) Require persons so summoned to give all evidence relative to matters under investigation.

This section of the Act authorizes the Commissioner to subpoena any and all persons who may have any knowledge bearing upon the income taxability of any resident of Tennessee. Witnesses may be required to produce any or all records in their possession containing information relative to the amount of taxable income received during a particular period by the person cited. 

Executors, Administrators, Guardians, Stock Brokers and all other persons having knowledge or information pertaining to the amount of taxable income paid to, accrued for, or credited to the account of the person cited are legally bound to disclose such information to the Commissioner or his representative.

Hearings, as here contemplated, are very expensive and the cost of such hearings is to be paid by the person subject to the tax and in addition to the tax, therefore, it is advisable to avoid such hearings if possible. It is the practice of the Commissioner to request information, relative to income received during any particular year, from all persons thought to possess such data before the taxpayer is cited for hearing. However, upon failure of such person to furnish such information and upon failure of the taxpayer to disclose the taxable income and pay the tax, the Commissioner has no alternative, he must issue the citation and hold the hearing. 

Administrators, executors and others acting on behalf of

Ch. 4) 257 

INCOME TAX 

other persons are often hesitant in disclosing information regarding the income of beneficiaries. The thought that the person subject to the tax objects, or will object, to such a disclosure, and censor them for divulging such information to the taxing authorities should not be allowed to exist as such action will eventually result in greater cost. The person liable for the tax should realize that the law compels the disclosure of such information and that its voluntary disclosure avoids additional cost and embarrassment. 

Persons against whom citations are issued are permitted: 

To be represented by counsel. (h) To subpoena witnesses in their behalf. (i) To require witnesses to produce records, memoranda, data or papers in their behalf. (j) To request a full and complete hearing relating to all matters under investigation.

Failure of the person cited to appear, and answer any question propounded by the Commissioner relative to the matter under investigation, is deemed guilty of a misdemeanor and subject to fine of not less than $50.00 nor more than $500.00 dollars for each offense. In addition, such person is subject to penalty of $100.00 per day from the date of hearing until such person actually discloses his taxable income, files the return, and pays the income tax. 

There are a number of ways in which the Commissioner may determine or verify the amount of income of any individual in Tennessee liable for this tax and, for this reason, the above procedure is seldom, if ever, used. However, since the burden is upon the person to disclose all taxable income and make settlement of the tax, care should be exercised to avoid the exceedingly high penalties which may be imposed.

The Act requires the Attorney-General, upon request of the Commissioner to sue for and collect the penalties due in accordance with this subsection. 

2. Penalties-Failure to File Return-Incorrect Return-Limitation— 

At the hearing provided for in this section, all matters relative to the income tax status of the person cited are to be

(Ch. 4  

thoroughly investigated and, after full and complete hearing, the Commissioner or his representative shall make findings in accordance with the facts. If such facts indicate that an income tax return was not filed when such a return should have been filed, or that the return as filed was inadequate, incomplete or incorrect, it becomes the duty of the Commissioner to: 

(a) Make a statement or tax return setting forth all taxable income as required by the Act. (b) Determine and assess the income tax due the State of Tennessee. (c) Assess penalty of 25% on the income tax shown to be due. 

The fees for the service of citation, and subpoenas for witnesses are to be assessed against the taxpayer as a part of the tax in cases where the facts found by the Commissioner at the hearing are such as will permit the legal assessment of income tax; in addition, witness fees, mileage expense, and all other fees and expenses incident to such hearing are to be borne by the taxpayer. However, if the facts will not permit a legal assessment of tax such fees, expenses, and costs are to be borne by the State; except the cost of serving the citation. 

Citations may be issued for the purpose of requiring persons to file return or to revise or correct any return filed pursuant to the provisions of the Act. However, this section contains a limitation in this regard: "Such citation may be issued for the purpose of making or revising, correcting and/or increasing assessments and/or returns or reports of persons for the year in which such citation may be issued and/or three years preceding such year, but no further or otherwise.'' 

This section of the law limits the time during which citation could be issued to three years plus the current year, i.e., a return filed on or before March 15, 1933, disclosing taxable income for the calendar year 1932, would not be subject to revision (except in case of fraud) after 

March 15, 1936. 

3. Interest 

This section of the Act requires the assessment of interest at the rate of 6% per annum upon any tax not paid when due, i.e., on or before May 15, of each year, and interest cannot be waived under the Act.

Ch. 4) 259 

INCOME TAX 4. Collection of Tax— 

(a) Judgment.

The finding, computation, and assessment of tax, fines, cost, penalty and interest by the Commissioner or his representative has the same force and effect as a judgment in a court of record.

After hearing, findings and computation by the Commissioner, the taxpayer may pay the amount so determined under protest and bring suit to recover. The Act does not provide an appeal from the findings of the Commissioner, and since the taxpayer may bring suit for the recovery of any amount erroneously or illegally collected, it appears that the right to enjoin an assessment is a remedy not available to the taxpayer. 

(b) Execution. 

If the amount, computed and assessed by the Commissioner, is not paid within ten days after notice of such amount is mailed to the last known address of the taxpayer, it becomes mandatory upon the Commissioner to issue execution in the name of the State for the collection of the tax.

The execution is to be addressed to the sheriff of any county in the State in which the Commissioner has reason to believe property of the taxpayer may be found. The sheriff may execute the same by distraint and sale of property. All fees, costs, and necessary expense incident thereto are to be paid by the taxpayer. 

If the sheriff is unable to find sufficient personal property to satisfy the claim, he is authorized to levy upon any real estate belonging to the taxpayer, and the land is to be sold under order of the circuit court of the county in which the land is situated.

As previously stated, there are many ways in which the Commissioner may discover unreported or erroneously reported taxable income and in view of the very costly procedure for enforcing the collection of the tax, extreme care should be used in the prompt and correct reporting of income subject to this tax.

(Ch. 4 

 Payment under Protest- Law. Section 8-A. 

That if the taxes herein provided shall be erroneously, improperly or illegally collected from any person, firm or corporation, who has paid same under protest, such person, firm or corporation may bring suit for its recovery within thirty (30) days after its payment in the county of his residence, in the same manner and to the same extent as is now provided by law for the recovery of taxes paid under protest. In bringing such suit service of process against the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation may be had by service upon the County Trustee, who is hereby required to give notice by registered mail of such service within five (5) days thereafter to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, who will thereupon undertake the defense of such suit. In the event of a judgment against the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, the Comptroller is hereby authorized and directed to issue his warrant for the payment of such judgment.

Taxpayers should be careful to determine whether income tax assessments made by the Commissioner, or his representative, are in accordance with the law and regulations. If there be any doubt or question as to the legality or correctness of the assessment, the tax should be paid "under protest." Payment under protest may be accomplished by written statement setting forth such protest at the time of tax payment, or through notation of such protest entered upon the back or face of the check, draft or warrant tendered in payment of the tax. The payment of income tax, assessed by the Commissioner, "under protest" is a condition precedent to recovery of tax erroneously, improperly or illegally collected. 

The procedure for the recovery of tax illegally collected appears to be as follows: 

Payment tax "under protest." (2) Institute ofit for recovery of tax within thirty days from date of tax payment. (c) Suit may be brought in county in which the taxpayer resides. (d) Service upon the County Trustee constitutes service upon the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation. (e) The State Comptroller is authorized to issue warrant for payment of judgment against the Commissioner. 

However, attention is drawn to Chapter 167, Public Acts of 1935, which provides: "Any claim for refund by the State of taxes or revenues alleged to have been erroneously or illegally paid shall be filed with the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation supported by proper proof within one year from the date of payment, otherwise the taxpayer shall not be entitled to refund and said claim for refund shall be barred.”

Ch. 4) 261 

INCOME TAX Chapter 108 (Section 15) Public Acts 1937 also pro vides: "The Commissioner shall have no power to order any refund unless claim for same, supported by proper proof, shall have been made within one year from the date of payment. 

It would appear, therefore, that taxpayers are limited to one year from date of payment of the tax, within which to file any claim for refund. 

Commissioner-Disposition of Revenue- Law. Section 9. 

That it shall be the duty of the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation within thirty (30) days after the receipt by him of any taxes imposed by the terms of this Act to turn over to the State Comptroller the tax or taxes collected in accordance with the terms and provisions of this Act, less the necessary expenses for the administration of this Act, which expenses shall not exceed ten (10%) per centum of the first Two Hundred Thousand ($200,000.00) dollars of taxes collected hereunder during any fiscal year, and five (5%) per centum of taxes so received in excess of the sum of Two Hundred Thousand ($200,000.00) dollars. At the time he turns over such tax to the State Comptroller, the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation shall furnish to the State Comptroller a duplicate statement giving the name of the taxpayers, their respective addresses and the amounts paid and dates of payment and the Comptroller shall cause list so furnished to him to be checked back with the original records in the office of the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation to the end that the statement so furnished to him may be audited and verified. 

This section of the Income Tax Law has little effect, if any, since the enactment of Chapter 33 (Reorganization 

Act) and Chapter 211. (General Budget Appropriation 

Act).

State in depositories designated by the State Treasurer. 

No deduction is made by the Commissioner for the administration of the Act or for any reason; the entire amount collected being deposited in accordance with law. Copies of deposit receipts, together with manifests of tax collected, are furnished daily to the Treasurer.

Stock Broker— Law. Section 13. 

That when and if a broker or commission dealer does not make a physical delivery to his customer of stocks and bonds, income from which is taxable under this Act, but retains possession and/or title himself or through a nominee, agent depository of such security and receives such income or credit therefor, he shall report such income to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, and pay the tax thereon measured by the dividends or interest credited, or which should be credited, to the accounts of his customers, unless he furnishes to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation a list of his customers, with the last known address of each, to whom such dividends and/or interest have been paid or credited and the amount thereof. 

Stock brokers or commission dealers in stocks and bonds are liable for tax on all taxable income paid to, accrued, or credited to the account of clients residing in Tennessee where such broker or commission dealer does not actually make delivery, but retains either possession or title, i.e., the broker is liable for the tax upon the income from stocks and bonds held in his possession as collateral for the balance due upon purchases made on margin. 

While this section of the law does not so provide, it appears that brokers or commission dealers would be entitled to reimbursement of the income tax, paid for their clients, in accordance with the provisions of Section 5 of this Act.

This section further provides that brokers and commission stock and bond dealers may furnish list of customers to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation

Ch. 4) 265 

INCOME TAX 

thereby avoiding the income tax liability. This section of the Act fixes no definite time for filing such a list of customers. It is, therefore, assumed that the list should be filed annually (on or before March 15) containing: 

1. Name and address of broker or commission dealer submitting the list. 

2. Name and last known address of each customer. 

3. The amount of dividends or interest paid or credited to the account of each customer. 

4. Name and address of person or corporation from whom dividends or interest was received. 

5. The date of payment or date credit was made. Fiduciaries 

Law. Section 14. 

That residents of Tennessee who receive income from trust estates located without the State of Tennessee, any portion of which is invested in securities, the income from which is taxable under this Act whether said trust estate be revocable or irrevocable, shall file with the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, as part of his income tax return a sworn statement of the trustee, executor or other administrator of said trust estate showing what portion of the total income received by such Tennessee resident from such estate was derived from securities, the income from which is taxable under this Act. And if such resident of Tennessee fails to file such sworn statement from the trustee, executor or other administrator, then he shall report for income taxation in the manner otherwise provided in the Act the entire amount of income received by him from such trust estate.

Trustees, guardians, administrators, executors and other persons acting in a fiduciary capacity who receive income taxable under this Act for the benefit of residents of Tennessee, shall be required to make returns under this Act and to pay the tax herein levied. Trustees, guardians and other persons acting in a fiduciary capacity who are residents of Tennessee, and who receive income on behalf of non-resident beneficiaries, shall not be required to pay tax under this Act even though such income be derived from stocks or bonds which would otherwise be assessable under this Act. However, executors or administrators receiving income taxable under this Act from stocks or bonds which were the property of a decedent, who resided in Tennessee shall pay tax upon the same until such time as such stocks or bonds have been distributed or transferred to distributors or legatees thereof.

Attention is drawn to the fact that residents receiving income from trust estates (revocable or irrevocable) outside of Tennessee must file with the income tax returna sworn statement of the non-resident trustee, executor or other administrator setting forth that portion of the total income taxable under this Act. Failure to file the sworn statement subjects the entire amount of income to taxation. 

As regards this provision of the Act, the Court holds:

(Ch. 4 

"Since complainant paid this tax, it was incumbent upon her to show that the income was derived from real estate or tax exempt securities, as to which the statute has no application, but in this she has failed. It is said that the duty imposed upon the resident beneficiary of the trust to file a sworn statement of the trustee, setting forth the character of securities in which the trust funds are invested, is one impossible of performance. In our opinion, the complainant is in no position to raise this question until she has made an effort to obtain such statement and failed. This is the only method by which the State can acquire this information since it has no jurisdiction over the person of the trustee. 

If the resident beneficiary, who enjoys a substantial income from the estate, can absolve herself from liability by sitting supinely by without making any effort to ascertain the character of investment held by the trustee, then, as heretofore suggested, every resident owner of such securities can avoid the tax by creating a foreign trust, and the statute would become a dead letter.'' [Lida M. Ross V. McCabe 166 Tennessee 314.]

Resident trustees, executors, administrators and other persons acting in a fiduciary capacity for residents are required to file return and pay the tax due by such resident beneficiary upon all taxable income. 

Prior to the Legislature of 1937, it appears that there was no provision requiring the tax payment by trustees, etc. on behalf of resident beneficiaries, paragraph two of

[1]-Bank of Commerce & Trust Company V. 

MCCABE. 

164 TENNESSEE 591 

Filed July 2, 1932

1. The complainant is a Tennessee corporation, with its situs at 

Memphis. It is the duly appointed and qualified guardian and trustee of certain non-resident minors and beneficiaries, and as such received certain incomes on stocks and bonds, on which taxes were paid as stated above. There is no express language in the Act that taxes the incomes of non-residents, or taxes incomes received by resident guardians or trustees, or other fiduciaries, for the benefit of non-resident wards or beneficiaries. 

2. The Federal Income tax of 1913 imposed a tax upon the income of every corporation, joint stock company or association." The Supreme 

Court, in Crocker V. Malley (1919), 249 U. S. 223, L. ed. 573, 2 A.L.R. 

1601, held that the income from a common law trust was not subject to the Federal tax. With this decision in mind, and in order that an association of this character might not escape the tax, the legislature expressly included a "business trust.'' We hold, therefore, that the legislature did not propose to tax non-resident beneficiaries and wards whose trustees and guardians reside in the state. There is no error in the decree of the chancellor, and it will be affirmed. 

Opinion by Justice McKinney. 

The bill herein was filed to recover certain taxes paid under protest exacted by the Commissioner of Finance 270

Ch. 4) 271 

INCOME TAX 

and Taxation under the Hall Income Tax Law, chapter 86, Acts of 1929. The Chancellor granted the relief prayed for, and the Commissioner has appealed and assigned the decree of the Chancellor for error.

The complainant is a Tennessee corporation, with its situs at Memphis. It is the duly appointed and qualified guardian and trustee of certain nonresident minors and beneficiaries, and as such received certain incomes on stocks and bonds, on which taxes were paid as stated above. There is no express language in the Act that taxes the incomes of nonresidents, or taxes incomes received by resident guardians or trustees, or other fiduciaries, for the benefit of nonresident wards or beneficiaries. 

Revenue acts are not to be interpreted so as to extend their provisions by implication beyond the clear import of the language used, or to enlarge their operations so as to embrace matters not specifically pointed out, but are to be construed most strictly against the State and in favor of the citizen. United States v. Merriam, 263 U. S. 179, 68 L. ed. 240; Smietanka v. First Trust & Sav. Bank, 257 U. S. 

602, 66 L. ed. 391; Gould v. Gould, 245 U. S. 151, 62 L. ed. 

211; State ex rel. v. L. & N. R. R. Co., 139 Tenn. 412.

Section 1 of the Act is as follows: 

"That beginning with the calendar year 1929, and for each calendar year thereafter to be computed from July 1 to July 1 of each year, an income tax to the amount of five per cent per annum shall be levied and collected on incomes derived by way of dividends from stocks or by way of interest on bonds of each person, partnership, association, trust and corporation in the State of Tennessee who received during any year income from the sources above enumerated, except as hereinafter provided." 

We might entertain some doubt as to the intent of the legislature in including the word "trust" but for the interpretation placed upon this word by the legislature in section 10 of the Act, which provides as follows: "That the word 'person,' as used in this Act, shall be held to include every natural person, partnership, joint stock company, business trust or corporation in receipt of dividends from corporate stocks or interest on bonds as

(Ch. 4 

herein defined, regardless of the source from which such income is derived, save and except as is herein otherwise expressly provided."

Evidently the legislature had in mind a "business trust," also referred to in the authorities as a "Common Law 

Trust" or a "Massachusetts Trust," such trusts having originated in that State, and which is neither a partnership, a joint stock association, nor a corporation. The purpose of such trusts is stated by Mr. Fletcher in his Cyclopedia of Corporations, vol. 9, p. 10459, as follows: 

'Statutory regulation of corporations, based to some extent in particular states on alleged unreasonable hostility to corporations, and the fact that the organization of corporations for one or more purposes is prohibited in some states, have resulted in an attempt, where persons desire to combine their capital for business purposes, to create a form of combination which will, without incorporation, enable the contributors of capital to escape personal liability as partners and, at the same time, secure many or most of the advantages of a corporation. These combinations of capital, organized under the terms of trust deeds, are common in Massachusetts, especially in case of real estate trusts, and have been adopted to some extent in other states.' 99 The Federal Income Tax of 1913 imposed a tax upon the income of every "corporation, joint stock company or association." The Supreme Court, in Crocker v. Malley (1919), 249 U. S. 223, 63 L. ed. 573, 2 A. L. R. 1601, held that the income from a common-law trust was not subject to the Federal tax. With this decision in mind, and in order that an association of this character might not escape the tax, the legislature expressly included a "business trust." We hold, therefore, that the legislature did not purpose to tax nonresident beneficiaries and wards whose trustees and guardians reside in this State. To remove any doubt as to the matter, the next legislature reenacted the 1929 Act, with the added provision: "Trust estates located in Tennessee shall not be required to pay tax under this Act on the income from securities held for the benefit of nonresidents of Tennessee,

Ch. 4) 273 

INCOME TAX 

even though the moneys of the trust estate or any portion thereof shall be invested in stocks and/or bonds which would otherwise be assessable under this Act." Chapter 20, section 14, 2d Extra Session, 1931.

The State also insists that the word "person" is broad enough to cover trustees and beneficiaries. To this we cannot agree, particularly in view of the fact that the legislature in a subsequent section of the Act defined this word, and under the definition the parties taxed herein were not included.

The State further insists that the Act of 1929 is amendatory of the General Revenue Act of 1907, chapter 602, and that the two, when construed in pari materia, will show a clear intent to tax trustees and beneficiaries on incomes from stocks and bonds. The Act of 1929 is complete in itself, and amended the Act of 1907 only in so far as it was necessary to remove stocks and bonds from its provisions, otherwise the two acts would have been in conflict. 

There is no error in the decree of the Chancellor, and it will be affirmed.

1. This suit involves the constitutionality of Chapter 21 of the Acts of the Extra Session of 1931. With certain exemptions, the Act provides for a graduated income tax upon incomes of all sorts. The chancellor held the Act to be invalid under Section 28 of Article II. of the Constitution of the State, and the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation has appealed. 

2. It is conceded by counsel for the Commissioner that Chapter 21 of the Acts of the Extra Session of 1931 is invalid if the tax thereby levied is a property tax. 

3. If the tax levied by Chapter 21 of the Acts of the Extra Session of 

1931 be a privilege tax, it is likewise invalid. 

4. The Constitution of 1870 placed but little check on the powers of the legislature to tax. In the light of subsequent history, a constitution now adopted would perhaps curb this power. A restraint upon the power to tax incomes, however, is inevitably implicit in Section 28 of Article II. 

The income tax clause of that section must be given such an effect unless we disregard settled rules for the interpretation of written instruments. 

The Court would be recreant to its trust, if it failed to hold the taxing power within a limitation so plain-if it should permit the taxing power to break through the solitary substantial protection afforded to the taxpayer by the constitution. 

Opinion by Chief Justice Green. 

This suit involves the constitutionality of chapter 21 of the Acts of the Extra Session of 1931. With certain exemptions, the Act provides for a graduated income tax upon incomes of all sorts. The chancellor held the Act to be invalid under Sec. 28 of Article II of the Constitution of the State, and the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation has appealed.

It is to be conceded that the power to tax is a sovereign power and that a state's power to tax is only restrained by the limitations of the constitution of that state and of the 

Constitution of the United States. 274

Ch. 4) 275 

INCOME TAX We reproduce the material portion of Sec. 28 of Article II as follows: 

"All property, real, personal or mixed, shall be taxed, but the Legislature may except such as may be held by the State, by counties, cities or towns, and used exclusively for public or corporation purposes, and such as may be held and used for purposes purely religious, charitable, scientific, literary or educational, and shall except one thousand dollars' worth of personal property in the hands of each tax-payer, and the direct product of the soil in the hands of the producer and his immediate vendee. All property shall be taxed according to its value, that value to be ascertained in such manner as the Legislature shall direct, so that taxes shall be equal and uniform throughout the State. No one species of property from which a tax may be collected shall be taxed higher than any other species of property of the same value. But the Legislature shall have power to tax merchants, peddlers and privileges, in such manner as they may from time to time direct. The portion of a merchant's capital used in the purchase of merchandise sold by him to nonresidents and sent beyond the State, shall not be taxed at a rate higher than the ad valorem tax on property. The Legislature shall have power to levy a tax upon incomes derived from stocks and bonds that are not taxed ad valorem.''

A perusal of the foregoing will disclose, as this court has previously said, that "in reference to the powers of general taxation in this State, the only limitation upon the discretion is in the principle of equality." Friedman Bros. v. Mathes, 55 Tenn., (8 Heisk.) 488, 492.

This limitation as to general taxation was lacking in an earlier constitution-the Constitution of 1834. The provision of that constitution was in these words: "All lands liable to taxation, held by deed, grant, or entry, town lots, bank stock, slaves between the ages of twenty and fifty years, and such other property as the legislature may from time to time deem expedient, shall be taxable. All property shall be taxed according to its value, that value to be ascertained in such manner as the legislature shall direct, so that the same shall be equal and uniform throughout the State. No one species of property from which a tax may be collected, shall be taxed higher than any other species of property of equal value. But the legislature shall have power to tax merchants, pedlars (peddlers), and privileges, in such manner as they may, from time to time, direct.'' 

Many abuses grew up incident to the exercise of legislative discretion as to the objects of taxation and in 1870 the Constitutional Convention undertook to make general taxation universal and equal. So broad was the language of Sec. 28 of Article II that it was deemed necessary to qualify it in certain particulars. We have the word of two contemporary judges, speaking for this court, that the clause "But the legislature shall have power to tax merchants, peddlers, and privileges, in such manner as they

(Ch. 4  

may, from time to time, direct," was included in that section by way of exception. 

In Jenkins v. Ewin, 55 Tenn. (8 Heisk.), 456, 478, Chief 

Justice Nicholson, who had been a member of the Constitutional Convention, said that the language just quoted would seem at first view to confer upon the legislature the power to tax merchants, peddlers and privileges. He added, however, its true object was to indicate that the power to tax merchants, peddlers and privileges was not to be understood as inhibited by the restriction as to the taxation of property. He continued: 

"The word 'but' is significant of the purpose intended to be accomplished; it indicates that what follows is an exception to that which had gone before, and is not to be controlled by it." 

In Friedman Bros. v. Mathes, supra, page 493, Judge

Sneed, referring to the language quoted, said that "this proviso was intended as a palpable discrimination against the occupations and classes therein mentioned," and that "the power of taxation as to them, is left to the sound discretion of the legislative department." 

A proviso and an exception are substantially the same. 

Lewis' Sutherland Statutory Construction, section 352. 

In Shields v. Williams, 159 Tenn. 349, 366, we expressed the opinion that the clause of Sec. 28, Article II, "The legislature shall have power to levy a tax upon incomes derived from stocks and bonds that are not taxed ad valorem," was an exception to preceding clauses of section 28. Whatever be the nature of an income tax, further consideration confirms this conclusion. It is easier than the conclusion announced by the court as to the privilege tax clause. 

The imperative mood is dropped, as in the privilege tax clause. The language is not that the legislature shall levy a tax upon such incomes but shall have power to levy the tax.

If the income tax is a property tax, the authority to discriminate between incomes arising from particular stocks and bonds and incomes arising from other sources makes of the income tax clause an exception to the equality and uniformity clause. If the income tax is a privilege tax, the authority to tax incomes upon prescribed conditions

Ch. 4) 277 

INCOME TAX 

makes of the clause an exception to the unconditional and unlimited authority to tax privileges generally. 

Many years ago in the Supreme Court of the United States, the question arose as to whether the power to regulate navigation was included in the power which the Federal Constitution gave to Congress to regulate commerce. 

Certain sections of the Federal Constitution impose restrictions upon the power with respect to navigation. We have the authority of Chief Justice Marshall, for the following: "It is a rule of construction, acknowledged by all, that the exceptions from a power mark its extent; for it would be absurd, as well as useless, to except from a granted power, that which was not granted-that which the words of the grant could not comprehend. If, then, there are in the 

Constitution plain exceptions from the power over navigation, plain inhibitions to the exercise of that power in a particular way, it is a proof that those who made these exceptions, and prescribed these inhibitions, understood the power to which they applied as being granted."' 

Gibbons v. Ogden, 9 Wheat, 1 6 L. Ed. 23.

In a converse situation the Supreme Court of the United States was considering the power of the State of Maryland to require importers of foreign goods to take out a license, under that provision of the Federal Constitution providing that "No State shall without the consent of Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws." The same authority expressed the opinion of the court as follows: 

"If it be a rule of interpretation to which all assent, that the exception of a particular thing from general words, proves that, in the opinion of the lawgiver, the thing excepted would be within the general clause, had the exception not been made, we know no reason why this general rule should not be as applicable to the Constitution as to other instruments. If it be applicable, then, this exception in favor of duties for the support of inspection laws, goes far in proving that the framers of the Constitution classed taxes of a similar character with those imposed for the purposes of inspection, with duties on imports and exports, and supposed them to be prohibited."' Brown, et al v. State of Maryland, 12 

Wheat., 419, 6 L. Ed., 678.

In many decisions, interpreting statutes, this court has agreed that "where a general rule has been established by statute with exceptions, the court will not curtail the former or add to the latter by implication." Lewis' Sutherland 

Statutory Construction, section 494; Kelly v. State, 123

(Ch. 4  

Tenn., 516; Burns v. City of Nashville, 132 Tenn., 429; 

Turner v. Eslick, 146 Tenn. 236.

This court has likewise followed the Supreme Court of the United States in saying that this rule is equally applicable in the construction of constitutional provisions. 

Friedman Bros. v. Mathes, supra.

It therefore seems to us, treating the assailed tax as a property tax, upon principles too well established by authority to be challenged, that when the constitution by way of exception to a general provision against inequality in taxation conferred upon the legislature the power to tax only one class of incomes, that instrument necessarily denied to the legislature the power to tax incomes of other classes. 

Likewise, treating the income tax as a privilege tax, when the constitution, after it had sanctioned the power of the legislature to tax other privileges without restriction, designated one class of incomes to be taxed, that instrument necessarily denied to the legislature the power to tax incomes of other classes.

In reply to suggestions from the court during the argument of this case, and in opposition to the expression of ideas similar to those just before indicated, counsel for the Commissioner referred to Vertrees v. State Board of 

Elections, 141 Tenn., 645. In that case we applied the rule that a constitutional limitation upon the power of taxation will not be inferred nor implied but must be distinctly and positively expressed.

The constitutional provision before us in Vertrees v. 

State Board of Elections was "All male citizens of this state over the age of twenty-one years, except such persons as may be exempted by law on account of age or other infirmity shall be liable to a poll tax of not less than fifty cents nor more than one dollar per annum." That was a general mandate to the legislature to levy a poll tax on male citizens. 

It was not an exception to a general mandate. We held that a prohibition of the levy of a poll tax upon female citizens would not be implied. The rule mentioned finds proper application in cases of that sort, to repel an inference or implication otherwise merely permissible. Where the constitutional limitation, however, upon the power of taxa-

Ch. 4) 279 

INCOME TAX 

tion is necessarily implied or inferred, the rule can not control. A necessary inference is a logical deduction and it is a necessary inference that one exception to a general grant or denial of power excludes other exceptions. 

We refer again to Brown et al v. State of Maryland, supra, so like the case before us. Prior to the adoption of the Federal Constitution the states had full power to tax imports. Lane County v. Oregon, 7 Wall., 71, 19 L. Ed., 101. As noted above, the Federal Constitution prohibited the state from taxing imports except for purposes of executing its inspection laws, and it was held that this exception negatived the power of the state to require importers to take out a license.

It is conceded by counsel for the Commissioner that chapter 21 of the Acts of the Extra Session of 1931 is invalid if the tax thereby levied is a property tax. This concession, of course, is required, for the tax levied is not at a rate uniform with taxes levied on other property and the rate prescribed by the Act increases with the amount of the income.

If the tax levied by chapter 21 of the Acts of the Extra Session of 1931 be a privilege tax, it is likewise invalid. 

Section 28 of Article II of the Constitution confirmed the legislative power to tax privileges generally "in such manner as they may, from time to time, direct." That section of the constitution, however, only authorized the legislature to tax incomes insofar as they were "derived from stocks and bonds that are not taxed ad valorem." If the Convention of 1870 contemplated an income tax as a privilege tax it must have included the income tax clause as a limitation on the power to levy such a tax. From such a viewpoint this clause is an exception or a proviso. The clause was certainly not designed to confer an additional power of privilege taxation. The preceding clause, in terms as broad as possible, had countenanced the power of the legislature to tax every privilege. The intent, however, was that only the incomes mentioned should be taxed. 

In Shields v. Williams we did not find it necessary to express our opinion as to the nature of an income tax. No such necessity arises now. The income tax clause of our

(Ch. 4  

constitution is either a special power conferred, or a special restriction imposed. In neither view can it be ignored. 

In either view it destroys chapter 21 of the Acts of the Extra Session of 1931, whether that Act undertakes to levy a property tax or a privilege tax. 

The Constitution of 1870 placed but little check on the power of the legislature to tax. In the light of subsequent history, a constitution now adopted would perhaps curb this power. A restraint upon the power to tax incomes, however, is inevitably implicit in Sec. 28 of Article II. The income tax clause of that section must be given such an effect unless we disregard settled rules for the interpretation of written instruments. The court would be recreant to its trust, if it failed to hold the taxing power within a limitation so plain-if it should permit the taxing power to break through the solitary substantial protection afforded to the taxpayer by the constitution. Affirmed.

Concurring Opinion by Judge Chambliss 

I am impelled reluctantly to concur in the conclusion announced by the Chief Justice that the decree of the Chancellor must be affirmed. Without passing on certain detail provisions of the Act plausibly challenged as discriminatory, I rest my conclusion on this ground:

It is expressly required by our Constitution that "All Property" shall be taxed uniformly according to its value. 

I understand it to be conceded for the State that, if incomes taxed by this Act are property, then the Act must fall under this uniformity clause. 

I cannot escape the conclusion that the term "All Property"—that is, all species of property-includes income from tangibles, such as land, stocks and bonds, etc. clearly taxable ad valorem, that is according to its value. Consistently with this view and suggestive that the framers of the Constitution so regarded this broad phrase "All Property," they followed the express requirement for uniformity in taxation of "All Property" with an express provision that, (however) "The Legislature shall have power to levy a tax upon incomes derived from stocks and bonds," thus

Ch. 4) 281 

INCOME TAX 

taking this class of "All Property" taxable ad valorem out from under the uniformity requirement. 

I express no opinion as to the taxability under our Constitution of incomes derived from services or intangibles, that is, classes of incomes not directly derived from property taxable ad valorem; and I find it unnecessary to place emphasis on the doctrine of implication in constriction of our Constitution. Contracts, statutes and the Federal Constitution, grant, confer, create powers and well recognized rules of construction applicable thereto must be applied, if at all with great caution to the State Constitution, to which the Legislature need not look for grant of power, but alone for limiting restrictions and prohibitions.

ALVIN SHIPP, COUNTY TRUSTEE. 

160 TENNESSEE 311 

December Term, 1929

From Hamilton County. 

1. The original bill avers that all of the property assessed by the county trustee consists of bonds, as defined in the Income Tax Statute, Public Acts of 1929, Chapter 86; and it is averred that all such property is withdrawn from assessment for ad valorem taxation, not only for the year 1929, but for preceding years. 

2. Chapter 86 of the Acts of 1929 so amended the Assessment Act of 

1907 as to omit stocks and bonds of the kind described from the list of properties that should be assessed for taxes ad valorem, and put them in a class to themselves to be taxed only in respect of the income therefrom. That this could be constitutionally done was determined in the case of Shields V. Williams. From the date of the passage of that Act no authority has existed to assess this character of property ad valorem. 

Not only so, but Section 3 of the Amendatory Chapter 116, of the Acts of 1929, expressly forbade its assessment in this manner and by consequence forbade its back assessment, for a back assessment is but one kind of assessment.-The decree of the chancellor is accordingly affirmed. 

Opinion by Justice Swiggart. 

The Hamilton National Bank and J. Howard Pardue, complainants and appellees, are the administrators of the estate of E. S. Pardue, deceased. Their original bill was filed to enjoin as void an assessment made by the appellant, as Trustee for Hamilton County, of property belonging to the estate of E. S. Pardue for the years 1926-1929, inclusive. 

The original bill avers that all of the property assessed by the county trustee consists of bonds, as defined in the Income Tax Statute, Public Acts 1929, chapter 86; and it is averred that all such property is withdrawn from assessment for ad valorem taxation, not only for the year 1929, but for preceding years.

A demurrer was filed by the county trustee on October 

1, 1929, and thereafter, on October 23rd, the original bill was amended so as to allege that the property of the estate 282

Ch. 4) 283 

INCOME TAX 

assessed by the county trustee included money on deposit as well as the bonds described in the original bill. 

The record does not recite that the demurrer was amended, and no order was entered that the demurrer should be considered as having been filed to the amended bill.

The chancellor rendered a decree overruling the demurrer on the ground "that notes and bonds as defined in said Acts of 1929 (chapters 86 and 116), upon whose income an income tax is imposed, as provided in said Acts, are not subject to assessment for ad valorem tax either for the year 1929 or any preceding year; and that the act of the defendant in undertaking to assess said properties as alleged in the bill, was without authority of law and was void."

From this decree overruling the demurrer the chancellor granted the county trustee a discretionary appeal, in support of which assignments of error have been filed in this court.

It is apparent that the chancellor did not consider the demurrer as directed to the amendment of the bill, attacking the assessment by the county trustee of money on deposit; and the authority and power of the county trustee to make such an assessment is not properly before this court on the appeal.

The transcript of the record includes the opinion filed by the learned chancellor, which is as follows: "In this cause, I have had the benefit not only of the argument of. able solicitors pro and con appearing in the cause, but also of the opinions of the State's Attorney-General and other distinguished lawyers of the capitol city who have given the subject study. "Chapter 86 of the Acts of 1929 so amended the assessment act of 1907 as to omit stocks and bonds of the kind described from the list of properties that should be assessed for taxes ad valorem, and put them in a class to themselves to be taxed only in respect of the income therefrom. 

That this could be constitutionally done was determined in the case of Shields v. Williams. From the date of the passage of that act no authority has existed to assess this character of property ad valorem. 

Not only so, but Section 3 of Amendatory Chapter 116, of the Acts of 1929, expressly forbade its assessment in this manner and by consequence forbade its back assessment, for a back assessment is but one kind of assessment. That the effect was to allow some property, which if known, might have been assessed ad valorem, but was not, to escape any taxation for the years 1926, 1927 and 1928 does not render the Act unconstitutional any more than the Act of 1885 fixing the three-year limit

(Ch. 4 

was unconstitutional. The Act is general, but its effect varies in particular instances. "Since the proceedings complained of to assess complainant's property ad valorem for 1929 and back assess it for the years 1926, 1927 and 1928 were not begun until after the passage of the Acts of 1929, Section 61 of 

Shannon's Code has no application. "The assessment being void, complainant is entitled to the remedy of injunction. "Demurrer overruled. "'11/25/29. "Garvin, "Chancellor."

The jurisdiction of the chancery court to enjoin the enforcement of an assessment which is void because the property assessed was not subject to assessment, has heretofore been recognized by this court. Nashville Labor Temple v. 

City of Nashville, 146 Tenn. 429; Express Company v. 

Patterson, 122 Tenn. 279.

In Express Company v. Patterson, supra, this court held also that the constitutional provision requiring uniformity of taxation is not self-executing, and that "before any property can be valued and assessed for taxation a proper method and machinery for such valuation and assessment must be provided." The court held in that case that because the statute had not provided a method for the assessment of the intangible assets of the complainant corporation, the county trustee was without power to make an assessment of its intangible property, and the proceeding instituted for that purpose was accordingly enjoined. 

We are of the opinion that the cases cited support the ruling made by the chancellor herein. At the time the county trustee made the assessment complained of, the provisions of the General Assessment Law, Acts 1907, chap ter 602, had been amended so as to exclude from the several classifications of personal property, subject to assessment for ad valorem taxation, stocks and bonds, the income from which is taxed by chapter 86 of the Public Acts of 1929. 

The conclusion of the chancellor that assessment for preceding years, or back assessments, were put beyond the authority of State and county offices, by this amendment of the General Assessment Law, as well as current assessments, is in harmony with the declared policy of the State as evidenced by chapter 27 of the Public Acts of 1929 (Extra

Ch. 4) 285 

INCOME TAX 

Session), section 6, which expressly forbids back assessments for ad valorem taxation of stocks or bonds, upon the income from which a tax is imposed by the Acts of 1929, chapter 86, as amended. 

The decree of the chancellor is accordingly affirmed, and the cause is remanded for further proceedings. The cost of the appeal will be adjudged against the appellant.
