INHERITANCE TAX Divested Estates- Law. Section 1271, Subdivision 7; 

Where an estate or interest may be divested by the Act or omission of the transferee, it shall be taxed as if there were no possibility of divesting.

This section is deemed to be self explanatory and comment is not made thereon. 

Arbitration of Tax- 

Law. Section 1272, Subdivision 8;

If it shall be impossible to compute the present value of any of the property transferred, or of any interest therein, or if the tax cannot be determined because of a contingency as to who will take it, the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, with the written approval of the Attorney General, may enter into an agreement with the representatives of the estate or the transferees, or both, to compound the tax upon such terms as may be deemed equitable, and the payment of any amount agreed upon shall be in full satisfaction for the tax imposed by this statute and such amount shall be payable out of the property transferred. If such an agreement cannot be reached, the taxation of the property or interest shall be held in abeyance and the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation shall require the representatives of the estate or transferees, or both, to give bond for the prompt payment of the tax at such time as the value of the property or interest, of the transferees may be determined; and such tax shall bear interest as provided in subdivision 2 preceding. The amount of said bond shall be fixed and the sufficiency of the surety determined by the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation.

This section authorizes the arbitration of the inheritance tax in instances where, due to unusual circumstances, it is impossible to accurately determine tax liability upon the filing of the report; however, before this section is effective the following facts must exist: a. It must be impossible to determine the present value of the property (or interest therein) transferred, or; b. It must be impossible to compute tax liability because of a contingency as to who will receive the property transferred. c. Or both a and b.

Executors, administrators and other persons, charged with the adminstration of estates, under circumstances described above, should notify the Commissioner and request determination of such valuation or tax liability upon an equitable basis by agreement. However, any agreement reached with the Commissioner, must be approved by the Attorney General. The tax paid under such agreement

would constitute full and legal satisfaction of the tax liability. Upon failure to reach satisfactory agreement with the Commissioner, the matter must be held in abeyance until such time as the contingencies are removed. In such cases the Commissioner must require bond for the payment of tax and interest, the amount and sufficiency of same being in his discretion.

Administration of the Act— Law. Section 1273, Subdivision 1; 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, hereinafter called the Commissioner, shall have full supervision of the auministration and enforcement of this law and of the collection of all taxes imposed thereunder, and shall make such rules and regulations as may be necessary for its proper interpretation and enforcement, and he is empowered to call upon other departments of the state government for such information and assistance as he may deem necessary; provided, however, that the cost of administering this law shall not exceed three per centum of the total tax collection. 

The Commissioner shall have power to compel the attendance of witnesses and the production of evidence, by subpoena, to administer oaths and to take testimony in relation to any matter under this statute. 

Witnesses shall receive the same fees as are paid other witnesses in courts of record, such fees to be a part of the cost of administration. 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation is charged. 

with the administration of the Act and the collection of the tax; he is authorized to: 

1. Enforce the collection of all inheritance tax. 

2. Make rules and regulations as may be necessary for the interpretation and enforcement of the Act. 

3. Call upon other departments of the State Government for information or assistance. 

4. To subpoena witnesses, compel their attendance, administer oaths and take testimony.

Witnesses summoned by the Commissioner are allowed the same fees as are paid witnesses in courts of record. 

Authority of Assistants, Deputies, etc.—

Law. Section 1274, Subdivision 2; 

The Commissioner may designate such deputies, appraisers, agents and other assistants as may be necessary for carrying out the full purpose and intent of this law. 

Such deputies, appraisers, agents and assistants, so designated by the Commissioner, shall be empowered to represent the Commissioner in inventorying and appraising estates, examining the contents of safe deposit vaults and to perform such duties as are, by this statute, re-

Ch. 5) 363 

INHERITANCE TAX 

quired of the Commissioner, including the power to issue subpoenas and administer oaths and shall make bonds for the faithful performance of their duties, such bonds to be in such amounts and with such surety or sureties as the Commissioner may prescribe. 

Designated assistants, deputies, appraisers, agents, employees, and other persons are vested with the same power and authority as the Commissioner. The Act, however, requires that the Commissioner should designate such person or persons to act in his behalf. 

It appears that the Commissioner is bound to ratify the acts of his designated representatives; but to avoid possibility of misunderstanding, or error, which may result in the subsequent assessment of tax, or tax assessment after distribution of all property, executors, administrators and trustees should be careful to ascertain whether the act or acts of such deputy, agent or employee meets with the approval of the Commissioner. In all instances requiring agreement, as contemplated in subdivision 8 of section 1272, the written ratification of an agreement made with a deputy, agent or employee, should be obtained from the Commissioner and approved by the Attorney General as a protection to the executor, administrator or trustee charged with the administration of the estate. 

Duties of County Court Clerks- 

Law. Section 1275, Subdivision 3; (a) It shall be the duty of the county court clerk of the county wherein an estate is administered by an executor, administrator or trustee, before letters of administration are issued by such court, to demand and require of such executor, administrator or trustee a bond, with good and sufficient security, in the penal sum of five hundred dollars, payable to the Commissioner, for the use and benefit of the state, and conditioned upon the payment within the time required by this statute of any tax assessed against the estate with which such fiduciary is chargeable; provided, however, that, if in the sound discretion of the county court clerk an estate distributable to beneficiaries of Class A is of less value than Ten Thousand Dollars, and an estate distributable to beneficiaries of Class B is of less value than One Thousand Dollars, such bond may be waived by the county court clerk; provided the reasons for such waiver be fully reported to the Commissioner. (b) The bond herein required of such fiduciary shall be demanded by the clerk, subject to the exceptions above named, notwithstanding the decedent may have directed that his, or her, executor, administrator or trustee serve without bond. (c) Upon the execution of such bond, the county court clerk shall forthwith deliver, or forward by mail, to the Commissioner a statement under his seal of office giving the name and date of death of the decedent and his address at time of death, the name and address of the executor, administrator or trustee qualified, together with his estimate of the

(Ch. 5 

gross value of the estate; provided, however, that the clerk shall be required to furnish such statement even though the bond may have been waived. (d) For this service, the county court clerk shall be allowed to demand and collect, in advance, five dollars, which fee shall be in addition to the usual and customary probate fees now allowed by law and shall be paid by the representative of the estate and may be deducted as a part of the costs of administration. (e) Any county court clerk who shall violate any of the provisions of subdivision 3 of this section shall be subject to a penalty of five hundred dollars, to be recovered by the Commissioner, for the benefit of the state, in any court of competent jurisdiction; provided, however, that the Commissioner may, in his discretion, waive or reduce the above named penalty in any case to not less than one hundred dollars where there appears no manifest intent to evade the statute. 

(a) Bond Required— 

Before letters of administration are issued by court, it is mandatory that the several county court clerks of the State require of such executor, administrator or trustee- -a bond. Section 1276, Subdivision 4, appears to require delivery of the bond to the Commissioner by the County Court Clerk.

The statutory requirements of such bonds are as follows: 

1. Good and sufficient security. 

2. It must be in the penal sum of $500.00. 

3. Must be payable to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation for the benefit of the State. 

4. Must be conditioned upon the payment of inheritance tax assessed upon the estate within the time fixed by the Act. 

The bond required must be furnished irrespective of the request of the decedent that no bond be required of the executor, administrator or trustee. (b) Waiver of Bond If, in the sound discretion of the clerks of the county court, the value of an estate distributable to Class A beneficiaries is less than $10,000.00, or if the value of an estate distributable to Class B beneficiaries is less than $1,000.00, the bond may be waived by such clerk; however, the Act requires the county court clerk to report his reason for such waiver to the Commissioner. 

(c) Reports to Commissioner— 

It is mandatory upon the clerk to furnish, under the seal of his office, the following information to the Commissioner:

Ch. 5) 365 

INHERITANCE TAX 

1. Name of decedent. 

2. Address of decedent at time of death. 

3. The date of the death of the decedent. 

4. The name and address of the executor, administrator or trustee qualifying to administer the estate. 

5. The estimated value of the gross estate. 

Attention is drawn to the fact that the above information is to be furnished to the Commissioner in all cases; the waiver of the bond does not excuse the county court clerk of making the report. (d) Fee Chargeable—

A fee of $5.00 is payable to the county court clerk, in advance, by the representative of the estate and is in addition to customary probate fees. This fee may be deducted from the "gross estate" as a part of the cost of administration. 

(e) Violation-Penalties— 

A penalty of five hundred dollars is imposed upon any county court clerk violating any of the provisions of this section and may be recovered by the Commissioner for the benefit of the state in an appropriate action, however, the Commissioner may reduce the penalty to one hundred dollars where there is no manifest intent to evade the Act. 

Duties of Commissioner and Executors, Administrators, etc.- 

Law. Section 1276, Subdivision 4;

Upon receipt of the aforesaid bond and/or statement from the county court clerk, the Commissioner shall furnish the representative of the estate all necessary forms and information for the proper inventorying of the property of the estate and shall furnish such representative with a copy of this statute and all instructions and information promulgated for the guidance of such representative of the estate in the performance of the duties required of him by this statute. 

Such executor, administrator or trustee shall within sixty days thereafter, prepare and file with the Commissioner a copy of the will, if will there be, and a sworn inventory of the gross estate and shall set forth therein each item of real and personal property separately, showing its full and actual cash value at the date of decedent's death, together with the names, addresses and relationships of several beneficiaries, the allowable deductions in detail and the costs of administration, separately set forth; provided, however, that the Commissioner may, upon application of the executor, administrator or trustee showing good cause, grant sixty days' additional time within which the said sworn inventory may be filed.

After qualification of the executor, administrator or trustee the county court clerk should prepare his report and submit same to the Commissioner, whereupon the Commissioner is required to furnish the representative of the estate: 

1. All necessary forms and information for inventorying the property of the estate. 

2. A copy of this statute and all instructions, rules and regulations promulgated. 

3. Furnish such other information as will assist the representative in the performance of his duties under this Act. 

Within sixty days after receipt of the forms, the representative of the estate is required to: (a) File copy of the will of testate decedents. no will, this fact should be so reported. 

If decedent left (b) Sworn inventory of the gross estate, setting forth in detail and separately each item of property and the full and actual cash value at the date of decedent's death. (c) Names, addresses and relationship of all beneficiaries. (d) Detail statement of allowable deductions and cost of administration.

This section authorizes the Commissioner, for good cause, to grant sixty days additional time for preparing and filing the return; but extension for a longer period is not authorized by the Act. 

Assessment by Commissioner- Law. Section 1277, Subdivision 5; 

Upon receipt of such sworn inventory from the executor, administrator or trustee, the Commissioner shall proceed to make an appraisal of the various items of the gross estate and to investigate deductions claimed by such representative of the estate, and shall, as soon thereafter as possible, notify the representative of the estate by mail of his appraisal and the assessment of the tax thereof. Such notice shall be sent by registered mail to the last known address of such representative and such mailing shall constitute good and sufficient notice; provided, however, the Commissioner shall give such other and further notice, if any, as may be necessary to comply with constitutional requirements. 

In making said appraisal, the Commissioner shall direct his deputies, agents or assistants to investigate the valuation placed upon each item of the estate, with a view to determining its fullness and fairness, and, in the absence of written objection upon the part of the representative of the estate, his appraisal shall be final and binding upon the estate; provided, however, that such representative shall have the right to file with the Commissioner, within thirty days from the date of such appraisal, an appeal from his appraisal, addressed to a Board composed of the Governor, the Treasurer, and the Comptroller of the State, which said Board shall have authority to consider the exceptions filed, hear proof and determine the valuation in dispute, and the findings, by a

Ch. 5) 367 

INHERITANCE TAX 

majority vote, of said Board shall be conclusive as to all parties in interest, subject only to the constitutional right of review in the courts. 

When any executor, administrator or trustee shall neglect or refuse to file the sworn inventory required under Section 1276, the Commissioner is authorized to appraise the estate and to assess the tax upon the basis of any information available. Notice of such appraisal and tax assessment shall be given by the Commissioner in accordance with the previous provision of this section and the subsequent procedure thereafter with reference to an appeal from the appraisal and with reference to the collection of the tax shall be the same as in other cases. 

In the assessment of any tax when the sworn inventory has not been filed in accordance with Section 1276 there shall be added to the amount of tax found to be due, a penalty of five (5%) per cent. Notwithstanding that the assessment made by the Commissioner in the absence of the sworn inventory required, shall be altered or revised upon appeal or in litigation, a penalty of five (5%) per cent upon the tax ultimately found to be due shall be added and collected in all cases when the sworn inventory is not filed.

Upon receipt of the inheritance tax return, the Commissioner is required to: 

1. Make appraisal of all property owned by decedent at date of death. 

2. Investigate all deductions claimed. 

3. Assess the inheritance tax due. 

4. Notify the representative of the estate by registered mail of the appraisal and tax assessment; and give such other and further notice as may be necessary.

This section requires the Commissioner to make appraisal after full and complete investigation of the properties and valuations as shown in the inventory of the "gross estate."

If the representative of the estate objects to the appraisal made, such objection must be made in writing within thirty days from the date of the appraisal and filed with the Commissioner. The written objections, however, are to be addressed to, and become an appeal to, a board composed of the Governor, the Treasurer and the Comptroller of the State. The findings by a majority vote of the board are conclusive. However, such decision is, upon appeal, subject to review by the courts.

Attention is drawn to the fact that appraisals made by the Commissioner are final and binding upon the estate unless written objections are filed with the Commissioner within thirty days from the date of such appraisal. It appears that failure to object within the thirty day period estops the right of appeal from the Commissioner to the special board. See Chandler V. Roddy. 163 Tennessee 338.

(Ch. 5 

The Commissioner is authorized to appraise the estate and to assess the tax upon the basis of any information available in instances where the representative of the estate fails or refuses to file sworn inventory. Notice of. such appraisals and assessments are to be handled in the same manner as other assessments and the taxpayer is afforded the same rights, after appraisal and assessment, as are afforded taxpayers filing the sworn inventory; however, it is mandatory upon the Commissioner and upon the courts to add a penalty of 5% of the tax found to be due for failure to file the sworn inventory.

Basis of Valuation- 

Law. 

Section 1278, Subdivision 6;

All property, real and personal, shall be appraised at its full and true value at the date of death of the decedent. 

Stocks and bonds listed on recognized exchanges shall be appraised by ascertaining their quoted value on the date of death of the decedent, or on the nearest business day of such exchange to such date. 

Property is to be appraised at its "full and true" value, i. e., at its full cash value, or full actual value. There are a number of factors which may be used as a basis for determining the "full and true" value of property and it is generally considered good practice to appraise real estate through the use of disinterested and experienced experts. 

The amount of insurance carried upon personal property strongly indicates its value.

Stocks and bonds are to be appraised upon the basis of quoted value on recognized stock exchanges. The book value of stocks and bonds, not quoted upon such exchanges, are frequently used as a basis of appraisal. 

Attention is drawn to the fact that in each case the value of the property at the date of death of the decedent must be used.

Lien for Taxes- 

Law. Section 1279, Subdivision 7;

The tax imposed by this law shall be and remain a lien upon the property transferred, and upon all property acquired by the representative of the estate, or transferees, in exchange or substitution therefor, from the date of decedent's death, until the same is paid, but such lien shall not follow personal property after it has passed to a

Ch. 5) 369 

INHERITANCE TAX 

bona fide purchaser for value; provided, however, that the provisions of this subdivision shall not authorize any transfer without the consent of the Commissioner, if such consent be a pre-requisite to the transfer thereof.

The lien upon all real estate transferred, or any portion thereof, may be discharged by the payment of such amount of tax as the Commissioner may specify and require; provided, the lien shall expire and be void unless action is brought for its enforcement within two and one-half years from the date of administration, and within four years from the death of the decedent where no administration was granted. 

Representatives of estates desiring to transfer real property prior to tax payment should apply to the Commissioner for consent.

Inheritance tax liens are void within two and one-half years from the date of administration and within four years from the death of decedent when no administration was granted, unless action is brought by the Commissioner to enforce the lien.

There is no lien against personal property passing to a bona fide purchaser for value, but such transfer is not authorized except by and with the consent of the Commissioner.

Collection of Tax and Refunds— 

Law. Section 1280, Subdivision 8;

The Commissioner shall collect the tax imposed by this law and deposit same in such depository, or depositories, as he may select, which shall have executed and filed with him a bond in an amount fixed by the Commissioner, signed by an approved surety company authorized to transact business in Tennessee, guaranteeing the safe keeping and delivery of such funds upon demand. 

In event it should become necessary to enforce the payment of any tax imposed by this statute by legal action in the courts, the Commissioner shall make use of the offices of the several district attorneys, such action to be taken under the supervision and direction of the attorney general.

It shall be the duty of the Commissioner to keep detailed records of the tax collected and to make report thereof to the Comptroller of the Treasury not later than the fifteenth day of the months of January, April, July and October each year of such collections made during the preceding quarterly period, remitting with such reports the amount so reported, which shall be and become a part of the general fund of the State.

The Commissioner is empowered to make refund of any excess, erroneous or improper tax payment received by him out of the funds in his keeping to the estate from which it is received. 

The tax imposed upon the transfer of property under this Act is payable to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation. The payment may be made by checks, draft,

(Ch. 5 

money order or in cash. If payment is made in any other than cash, the check, draft or money order should be made payable to "Commissioner of Finance and Taxation."

The Department of Finance and Taxation maintains accurate accounting records of all assessments and collections, depositing daily all income received to the credit of the State Treasurer in depositories designated by the Treasurer. No deductions of any kind whatsoever are made from such tax collections. 

The Commissioner is authorized to make use of the Attorney General of the State, as well as the offices of the several district attorneys, for the collection of the inheritance taxes.

Refunds are made upon state warrant in case of excessive, erroneous or improper tax payment. In this regard attention is drawn to Chapter 167, Public Acts of 1935, which provides: "" 'Any claim for refund by the State of taxes or revenues alleged to have been erroneously or illegally paid shall be filed with the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation supported by proper proof within one year from the date of payment, otherwise, the taxpayer shall not be entitled to refund and said claim for refund shall be barred."' 

Public Inspection of Records- Law. Section 1281, Subdivision 1; 

The Commissioner is empowered to prescribe such forms as may be necessary under the provisions of this law and shall keep such records as are indicated by good accounting practice.

The Commissioner may, by general regulations, prescribe how much and what portion of his records shall be open to the inspection of the public and how much and what portion shall be held as confidential, and may exchange information with the United States Government, or with other state jurisdictions under reciprocal arrangements made and approved by him.

The Commissioner is authorized to exchange information with the Federal Government and with the several states under reciprocal agreements, and he is given discretion as to what portion of such information is to be made open to the public.

Inheritance tax returns are confidential in their nature and there are no regulations by the Commissioner authorizing public inspection of such records. Persons desiring information in regard to a particular report or return should make proper application to the Commissioner.

Ch. 5) 371 

INHERITANCE TAX Tax Due- Law. Section 1282, Subdivision 1; 

The tax so imposed by this statute shall be due and payable six (6) months after the death of the transferer, but such tax may be paid sooner if assessment thereof has been completed and if the personal representative desires to make payment. The value of all property transferred to each class of beneficiary, or beneficiaries, shall be aggregated for the purpose of computing the tax and allowing the exemptions heretofore provided for in this Act. 

The inheritance tax is due and payable six months after the death of the decedent or the transferer, however, same may be paid upon assessment made in less than six months. 

The value of property transferred to both classes of beneficiaries is to be totaled or aggregated, the exemption applied to each class, and the tax computed upon the net taxable estate. 

Interest and Penalty 

Law. Section 1283, Subdivision 1; 

All taxes not paid on or before the due date (six (6) months after the death of the decedent), shall thereafter bear interest at the rate of six (6) per cent per annum, which interest cannot be waived or excused. 

To all taxes not paid within one year after the death of the decedent there shall attach, in addition to interest, a penalty of one-half of one per cent for each month of delinquency which penalty the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation is authorized to waive for good cause shown when written application for such waiver is made prior to the attaching of penalty.

Attention is directed to the fact that under the law prior to the enactment of Chapter 130, Acts of 1937, discount was allowed if tax was paid within 30 days after assessment; whereas, under the law as amended in 1937, interest is imposed at the rate of 6% in instances where the tax is not paid within six months after the death of the decedent. 

Taxes remaining unpaid in excess of one year from date of death is subject to penalty of one half of one per cent for each month of delinquency. However, the Commissioner is authorized to waive the penalty for good cause, such as unavoidable delay in the adjudication of wills, sickness, etc.

Installment Payment of Tax- Law. Section 1284, Subdivision 3; 

When it is shown to the satisfaction of the Commissioner that payment at one time of the whole tax due from an estate would work a

(Ch. 5 

hardship upon the beneficiaries, or would necessitate the sale of any portion of the estate at a sacrifice, or at an inadequate price, the Commissioner is empowered to enter into an agreement with the representative of such estate for the payment of the tax due thereon in installments. 

Should any installment payments extend beyond one year after the death of the decedent, interest thereon shall be charged at the rate of six (6%) per centum per annum from the date of death until paid. 

The Commissioner is authorized to permit the payment of the inheritance tax upon an installment basis when it is shown that payment of the whole tax would: (a) Be a hardship upon the beneficiaries. (b) Necessitate the sale of a portion of the estate at a sacrifice. (c) Necessitate the sale of a portion of the estate at an inadequate price.

Written agreements, as to installment tax payments, between the Commissioner and representatives of estates is advisable and it should be noted that all installments extending beyond one year from death of decedent is subject to interest at the rate of 6% from date of death. 

Commissioner to Issue Receipts- Law. Section 1285, Subdivision 4: 

Upon the payment of the whole tax imposed against an estate under this law, the Commissioner shall issue his receipt therefor in duplicate to the representative of the estate, one copy of which shall be filed in the office of the clerk of the court in which such estate was being administered, and no final accounting, or settlement, of such estate shall be made by said court prior to the filing of such receipt, or until the filing of a certificate by the Commissioner that no tax is due thereon; such receipt, or certificate, to be furnished by the Commissioner without cost to the estate or to the beneficiaries thereof. 

Upon the payment of a fee of one dollar to the Commissioner, which said fee shall accrue to the state, any person other than the representative of the estate shall be entitled to receive from the Commissioner a certificate to the effect that the tax upon any particular parcel, or tract, of real estate has been paid, and such certificate may be recorded in the office of the register of the county in which such real estate is situated, and it shall be conclusive proof that the tax applicable to such real estate has been paid and any lien thereon shall be thereby released.

Final accounting or settlement of estates are not to be accepted by the Court until receipt in full settlement of inheritance tax is filed in the office of the Clerk of the County Court. Executors, Administrators and Trustees should be careful to see that a copy of the Commissioner's receipt, or certificate that no tax is due, is properly filed with the Clerk of the Court before final accounting is made and discharge

Ch. 5) 373 

INHERITANCE TAX 

requested. The certificate or the receipt in full settlement of tax liability is necessary before sureties upon the bond of the representative of the estate can be released, or before title to property is perfected. 

This section further provides for the issuance of a tax receipt upon a particular parcel or tract of real estate upon the payment of one dollar. Such receipt is to be recorded in the office of the register of the County and is conclusive proof of tax payment applicable to such real estate. 

Lifetime Transfer of Property-Non-Residents— 

Law. Section 1286, Subdivision 5;

In the absence of administration in this state upon the estate of a non-resident decedent, the Commissioner may, at the request of any representative of such estate, duly appointed and qualified in the state of decedent's domicile, or at the request of any beneficiary of such estate, or at the request of a transferee or trustee under a transfer made during the lifetime of such non-resident decedent, determine whether or not any property within this state transferred by such non-resident, or forming a part of this estate, is subject to tax under this Statute, and the amount of same.

The Commissioner's certificate as to the amount of such tax and his receipt therefor may be filed in the county court of the county in which such property is located, and shall be conclusive evidence of payment of the tax imposed by this law thereon. 

In instances where transfers of property situated in Tennessee have been made during the lifetime of a nonresident decedent, and where no administration of the estate exists in Tennessee, the Commissioner is authorized to determine whether any property so transferred is liable for the tax.

The filing of the Commissioner's receipt or certificate in the county court is conclusive evidence that the tax has been paid.

Commissioner May Request Appointment of Admin istrator- 

Law. Section 1287, Subdivision 6;

In order that the tax imposed herein may be expeditiously collected, if within six months after the death of any decedent, resident or non-resident, an executor does not qualify or an administrator is not appointed in Tennessee at the instance of other persons interested in the estate, then the Commissioner may apply to the proper county court for the appointment of an administrator of such estate and it shall be the duty of such court to make such appointment forthwith.

The Commissioner is authorized to apply to the county court for the appointment of an administrator of estates upon which no person qualifies within six months after the death of any resident or non-resident. This section makes it mandatory upon such court to forthwith make such appointment.

Under Section 1277, as amended by Chapter 130, Acts of 1937, the Commissioner may appraise the property and assess the tax in instances where the representative of the estate fails to file the sworn inventory; however, before such appraisal and tax assessment is made, an administrator must be appointed and proper bond posted to safeguard the 

State revenue.

Transfer of Property before Payment of Tax Pro hibited- 

Law. Section 1288, Subdivision 1; 

No person or persons, corporation or association, having in his, or its, possession or control, property of a decedent forming a part of his estate, or property transferred in any manner as to be subject to taxation under this statute, shall deliver or transfer the same to representatives of the estate of the decedent, or to any other person or persons, corporation or association, or upon their order or request, unless notice of the time and place of the intended transfer or delivery be served upon the Commissioner at least twenty days prior thereto; nor shall any person deliver or transfer any such property without retaining a sufficient portion or amount thereof to pay any tax and interest which such property may be subject to a lien under this statute, unless the Commissioner consents in writing to such transfer. 

The prohibitions herein contained shall apply to the transfer by a corporation, association or joint stock company of the shares of its capital stock or other interest therein, including registered bonds or other registered securities.

It shall be lawful for the Commissioner to examine the property at the time of delivery or transfer. 

Failure to serve such notice, or failure to allow such examination, or failure to retain a sufficient amount to pay the tax and interest, shall, unless the Commissioner consents to the transfer, render such person or persons, corporation or association, liable to the payment of the amount of the tax for which a lien is imposed upon such property by this statute, with interest thereon and the costs of any proceeding necessary for the enforcement of same in the courts of Tennessee; Provided, that the penalty provided by this section shall not apply to any insurance company which pays the proceeds of any policy of insurance on the life of the decedent after notifying the Commissioner that such payment is to be made. 

The transfer of the property of a decedent before payment of the inheritance tax is prohibited; however, this section permits transfer under certain conditions, viz:

Ch. 5) 375 

INHERITANCE TAX 

(a) Notice to the Commissioner at least twenty days prior to transfer, and retaining sufficient amount realized from such transfer to pay the tax, or (b) Upon the written consent of the Commissioner. 

The transfer of stocks and bonds by corporations are subject to the same restrictions and should not be transferred upon their books and records except in strict accordance with the provisions of this section. 

Failure to comply with these requirements subjects the violator to certain costs and penalties. However, insurance companies are not subject to these penalties when paying proceeds of policies on the life of the decedent provided notification of such payment has been given the Commissioner. 

Safe Deposit Boxes or Vaults- 

Law. Section 1289, Subdivision 2;

No safe deposit company, trust company, bank, or other person engaged in the business of renting safe deposit vaults or other receptacles of similar character, shall rent any such vault or receptacle without first requiring all persons entitled to access thereto to agree in writing to notify the lessor of the death of any such person; and all persons having the right of access to any such safe deposit vault or receptacle upon the death of any other person having the right of access thereto before seeking access, shall notify the lessor of the death of such person.

No lessor shall permit access to any safe deposit vault or receptacle by anyone after the death of any person who, at the time of his death, had the right or privilege of access thereto, either as principal, deputy, agent, co-tenant or otherwise, without notice to the Commissioner. 

At the time of opening any such vault or receptacle after the death of any person having the right of access thereto, the Commissioner shall have the right to be present, in person or by his representative, and to examine and inventory its contents. 

Any violation of the provisions of this subdivision shall subject the violator to a penalty of five hundred dollars to be recovered by the Commissioner for the benefit of the state in any court of competent jurisdiction.

Before safe deposit boxes, vaults or other receptacles of similar character are rented, the lessor must require all persons having access thereto, to agree in writing, to notify the lessor of the death of any person having access to such safe deposit box, vault or other receptacle before entering or seeking access thereto. 

The lessor shall not permit any one to enter any safe deposit box, vault or receptacle after the death of any person entitled to access thereto without proper notice to the Commissioner.

(Ch. 5 

No particular form of notification is prescribed by this section; however, it is the practice to notify the Commissioner by letter, giving him sufficient time to furnish his representative, or give consent to the entry of such vault. 

The Commissioner is authorized to be present in person or by representative at the time such box, vault or receptacle, is entered by the person having access thereto; and to examine and inventory the contents. 

The penalty for violation of this section is fixed at five hundred dollars and may be recovered in an appropriate action instituted by the Commissioner. 

Failure or Refusal to Make Report—Penalty- Law. Section 1290, Subdivision 3; 

Failure or refusal to make any report or return provided for in this statute shall constitute a misdemeanor and shall subject the offender to a penalty of five hundred dollars to be recovered for the benefit of the state in an action brought by the Commissioner in any court of competent jurisdiction; provided, however, that upon the filing of such report or reports, the Commissioner may, in his discretion, waive or reduce the above named penalty to not less than one hundred dollars in any case where there appears no manifest intent to evade payment of the tax herein imposed, and the payment of any such penalty shall in no wise affect the liability for the tax, interest and any other penalties prescribed herein. 

The making of a false return or report or affidavit with intent to deceive, shall constitute the crime of perjury. 

The penalty for failure or refusal to make any report or return required under this Act constitutes a misdemeanor and is subject to fine of five hundred dollars, and the Commissioner is authorized to collect same in an appropriate action instituted in any court of competent jurisdiction. 

The collection of the penalty does not affect the tax liability, interest or other penalties. 

Upon the filing of reports or returns as required by the Act, and where there is no manifest intent to evade payment of the tax, the Commissioner is authorized to waive or reduce the above fine. 

Tax to Be Paid by Representative of Estate— Law. Section 1291, Subdivision 4; 

All taxes due by an estate under the provisions of this statute shall be paid by the executor, administrator or trustee out of the funds in his hands for distribution, and no part of the property of an

Ch. 5) 377 

INHERITANCE TAX 

estate subject to this tax shall be distributed until the tax thereon has been paid; provided, however, that such executor, administrator or trustee, may with the written consent of the Commissioner, be authorized to sell or transfer so much of the property of the estate as may be necessary to pay said tax.

The inheritance tax must be paid by the executor, administrator or trustee before distribution of funds in his hands; however, with the written consent of the Commissioner, a portion of the property of the estate may be sold or transferred for the purpose of providing funds for the payment of the tax.

Representatives of Estates Liable until Tax Is Paid- 

Law. Section 1292, Subdivision 5;

Executors, administrators and trustees shall be liable for all taxes payable on the estate, together with any interest or penalties herein provided for, until the same shall have been paid; provided, however, that in no case shall such executor, administrator or trustee be liable for a greater amount than was actually received by him. 

Executors, administrators and trustees are liable for all tax, penalty and interest due by the estate. The bond may be called to effect tax collection, and liability is not discharged except by full payment. 

Report of Death-Insurance Companies- Law. Section 1293, Subdivision 6; 

Every life insurance company or association doing business in this state, shall within ten days after the approval of proof of death of a person insured under a policy or policies, in such companies or association, give notice in writing to the Commissioner where the estate is being administered stating: (a) The date and amount of each policy. (b) The name and address of each beneficiary therein. (c) The time and manner of payment. 

Any insurance company doing business in the state, failing to comply with the provisions of this statute, shall thereby forfeit their charter in this state and their right to do business within the state. 

Upon certification from the insurance Commissioner, that any insurance company has failed or refused to comply with the provisions of this statute, the secretary of state shall forthwith cancel the charter of such company and shall immediately notify such insurance company that it is barred from doing business in the state. 

Life insurance companies and associations, doing business in Tennessee, are required to report the death of persons insured to the Commissioner within ten days after proof of death. The Commissioner has prescribed a form

(Ch. 5 

to be used in making the report required and such forms will be furnished upon application. 

Failure or refusal to make the report of death of policy holders subjects the charter of the company to cancellation; and prohibits the company to do business in Tennessee. 

Act Does Not Repeal Estate Tax Law- Law. Section 1294, Subdivision 1; 

This statute shall in no wise be construed impliedly or expressly to repeal or modify the Tennessee estate tax law. 

Constitutionality of Act- 

Law. 

Section 1295, Subdivision 1; 

If any section, subdivision, clause or phrase of this statute is for any reason held to be unconstitutional such decision shall not affect the remaining portion of the statute. The legislature declares that it would have passed this statute and each section, subdivision, clause, phrase and sentence thereof, irrespective of the fact that any one or more of such section, subdivision, clauses, phrases or sentences be declared unconstitutional. 

Sections 1294 and 1295 are deemed to be self explanatory and no comment is made thereon.

ALSTON. 

94 TENNESSEE, 674

April 20th, 1895 

From Lauderdale County. 

1. The right to tax the succession or inheritance of property is founded on a reasonable basis, since the right of any person to succeed to property of a deceased person, whether by will or inheritance, is a creature of statute law, and the manner in which it shall pass by no means a natural right. 

2. It must be borne in mind that the tax is not upon the property, but the right or privilege of acquiring it by succession. 

3. Upon reason and authority, we are of opinion that the tax is constitutional, and may be sustained as a tax upon the privilege or condition of receiving property by will or inheritance. 379

(Ch. 5 

4. We conclude that the tax is not unconstitutional because it discriminates between direct descendants and collateral kindred and strangers. 

5. We are of the opinion that the Act is not invalid or unconstitutional on account of the exemption. 

Opinion by Justice Wilkes. 

This cause involves the constitutionality, and, to some extent, the construction, of Chapter 174, and Section 7 of Chapter 89, of the Acts of 1893, the former being an Act to provide for a collateral inheritance and succession tax, and the latter a section of the general revenue law passed at that session.

The Court below held the Acts to be constitutional; that the interests passing under the will of John J. Alston to his widow and to his brother, Volney S. Alston, were not subject to such tax, but that other devises and legacies were subject thereto, as will be more fully explained hereafter. 

Both the State and the parties held liable appealed, but the State has assigned no errors. 

The facts as agreed upon are substantially as follows: 

Dr. John J. Alston died in Lauderdale County in June, 1894. He left a will, which was duly probated, and his widow, Mary Frances Alston, is his executrix. He owned the personal property and real estate referred to in his will. 

This will gives to his widow certain notes on Jones and others, some mill machinery, a life interest in two tracts of two hundred and thirty-five acres, one hundred and twenty acres, fifty acres, and five acres of land; all cash on hand or deposit, the rents of a storehouse in Henning, Tenn., during life, the dividends and profits on his $3,000.00 of stock in a Ripley bank for life, and possibly some other property. To his niece, Mrs. Lee A. Crutcher, and her husband, W. C. Crutcher, he gave two tracts of land during life, one containing two hundred and forty acres, and the other twelve and one half acres, with remainder to their children. He also gave to his niece and her husband certain live stock.

To Mrs. McCowan and Mrs. Griggs, two nieces, he gave a remainder interest in the tracts of one hundred and twenty acres and fifty acres, in which a life estate was given

Ch. 5) 381 

INHERITANCE TAX 

to the widow, providing that the widow might give them possession before her death if she chose to do so. 

The two hundred and thirty-five acre tract and the five acre tract of land, given to the widow for life, is directed to be sold at her death, and the proceeds to be divided one half to the testator's brother, Volney S. Alston, and the other half to two nephews, William and James Dyer.

The decree of the Court below is, substantially, that the property given to the widow, Mary F., and the brother, Volney S., is not subject to the succession or inheritance tax provided by such Acts, but that such of it as was given to William and James Dyer was subject to such tax, but nothing was decreed as to the property given to Lee A. 

Crutcher and her husband.

It is stated by counsel representing the defendants that there is a clerical mistake in the decree, in that the liabilities of the property given to William and James Dyer are adjudicated, when it was intended to adjudicate the rights of Mrs. Lee A. Crutcher and her husband, and it is agreed that it may be treated as corrected. 

William and James Dyer are not parties to the agreed case in the Court below, nor in this Court, but Mr. and Mrs. 

Crutcher are parties in both Courts, and their counsel in this Court appears for them and waives the error and submits the question as to their liability. Considering the record as thus corrected, we proceed to examine the questions presented.

It is manifest that, by the express terms of the Acts referred to, none of the property of the testator passing under his will to his widow, is subject to the tax therein provided, and we proceed to examine as to the liability of the property, personal and real, given by the will to Lee A. Crutcher and her husband, W. C. Crutcher.

The first section of Chapter 174, Acts of 1893, provides for a tax upon all estates, real, personal, and mixed, situated in the State, whether the person dying seized live in the State or not, passing either by will or inheritance, or by any deed, grant, bargain, gift, or sale made in contemplation of death, or to take effect, in possession or enjoyment, after the death of the grantor, to any person or body corporate or

(Ch. 5 

politic, in trust or otherwise, when the property thus passing goes to any other than the father, mother, husband, wife, children, and lineal descendants, provided that no estate valued at less than $250.00 shall be subject to said duty or tax, and that the term "children" shall not be construed to apply to adopted children. This Act was intended to put into operation a general system of succession or inheritance taxation, and to repeal all laws in conflict with it. It was approved April 10, 1893, and fixes the rate of taxation at $5.00 on the $100.00 of value of the property passing. 

On the same day, but whether prior or subsequent in point of time does not appear, the general revenue Act was passed for that session, being Chapter 89; and in the seventh section of the latter Act a similar tax is provided and assessed. This section differs from Chapter 174, in that it exempts property passing to the same parties mentioned in Chapter 174, and, in addition, the following persons: 

Brothers, sisters, the wife or widow of a son and husband of a daughter, and any legally adopted child; but no mention is made of exemptions of estates of less than $250.00 in value.

No error is assigned nor point made as to this variance, and, as the question of the effect of the variance is in no way presented, and, as to the parties before us, cannot arise directly, we express no opinion as to this variance and its effect, if any.

It is contended that the Acts are unconstitutional because they attempt to restrain and restrict the devolution of property by will or inheritance by placing a tax upon such devolution; and, again, because the Act is partial, in that the tax is imposed if the property is given to certain persons but not if given to others; and, again, that the tax is not equal and uniform, because small estates of less than $250.00 in value are exempt from its operation, while those of that amount or over are subject to its provisions. 

In considering these grave questions, a short history of succession and inheritance taxes may not be inappropriate. 

Such taxes were recognized by the Roman Law. Gibbons' 

Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, Volume I pp. 163-4. 

They were adopted in England in 1780, and have been much

Ch. 5) 383 

INHERITANCE TAX 

extended since that date. Dowell's History of Taxation in England, 148; Acts 20 George III., Ch. 28; 45 George III., Ch. 28; 16 and 17 Victoria, Ch. 51; Green v. Craft, 2 H. Bl., 30; Hill v. Atkinson, 2 Merivale, 45. Such taxes are now in force generally in the countries of Europe. Review of 

Reviews, February, 1893. In the United States, they were enacted in Pennsylvania in 1826; Maryland, 1844; Delaware, 1869; West Virginia, 1887; and still more recently in Connecticut, New Jersey, Ohio, Maine, Massachusetts, in 1891; 

Tennessee in 1891, Chapter 25, now repealed by Chapter 174, Acts 1893. They were adopted in North Carolina in 

1846, but repealed in 1883. Were enacted in Virginia in 

1844, repealed in 1855, re-enacted in 1863, and repealed in 1884. In New Hampshire, Wisconsin, Minnesota, and 

Vermont such laws have been passed, but held unconstitutional on various grounds. 

Upon general principles the right to tax the succession or inheritance of property is founded on a reasonable basis, since the right of any person to succeed to property of a deceased person, whether by will or inheritance, is a creature of statute law, and the manner in which it shall pass by no means a natural right. 2 Blackstone's Com., p. 10; 2 Kent's Com. (12th Ed) 325; Dos Passos Collateral 

Inheritance Tax, 20; Bretlaw v. Fox, 100 Mass. 234; Majer v. Guina, 8 How., 490; Wallace v. Meyers, 4 L. R. A., 171; 

Peters v. Lynchburg, 76 Va., 927; State v. Dalrymple, 70 

Md., 294; 3 L. R. A. 372; Pallen v. Wake Co. Com's, 66 N. C. 

361; Strode v. Com., 52 Pa., 181; Re Swift's Estate, 18 L. 

R. A., 709; 137 N. Y., 77; Curry v. Spencer, 61 N. H., 624 (60 Am. R., 337).

This idea is recognized almost universally by statutes which provide the manner in which property shall descend in the absence of any will of the deceased, and in statutes which regulate the passage of property by will. 

As the right to succeed depends upon the law of the State, it follows that the State may regulate that right as public necessity or policy may dictate, and may subject it to such burdens and reasonable conditions as may best subserve the purposes of the State. 

It must be borne in mind that the tax is not upon the

(Ch. 5 

property, but the right or privilege of acquiring it by succession. It is a condition upon which the person may take the estate of a deceased relative by inheritance or testator by his will. It is a retention by the State of a part of a deceased person's property which the State may take to meet its necessities, and which in certain cases it may take in toto, as in cases of escheated property. It is not a tax upon the right of alienation, but on the privilege of receiving by inheritance or will or otherwise, at the death of a former owner. Strode v. Com., 52 Pa. State, 181; Eyre v. Jacob, 14 Gratt., 431 (73 Am. Dec., 367); Peters v. Lynchburg, 76 Va., 929; In re Howe's Estate, 2 L. R. A., 825, and note; 

Schoolfield v. Lynchburg, 78 Va., 366; Clymer v. Com., 52 

Pa. State, 189; Carpenter v. Penn. 17 How., 463; Frederickson v. Louisiana, 23 How., 447; Tyson v. The State, 28 

Md., 577; State v. Dalrymple, 70 Md., 298 (3 L. R. A., 372); 

Matter of Howard, 5 Denio (N. Y.) 487; State v. Mann, 76 

Wis., 469; Minot v. Winthrop, 26 L. R. A., 259; State v. 

Hamlin, 25 L. R. A. 632; Scholey v. Reed, 23 Wall., 331; Re 

Knoedler's Will, 140 N. Y., 377; Re Merriam's Estate, 141 

N. Y. 479.

In Curry v. Spencer, 61 N. H., 624, reported also in 60 

Am. Rep., 337, the constitutionality of such taxes was denied on the ground that the act imposing it was discriminating, unequal, and not proportional. But they have been sustained in very many cases, only a few of which we cite. 

Majer v. Guina, 8 How., 490; Scholey v. Reed, 23 Wall., 331;

In re Howe's Estate, 2 L. R. A., 825; Wallace v. Meyers, 4 L. R. A., 171; Eyre v. Jacob, 14 Gratt., 422 (73 Am. Dec., 367) Tyson v. The State, 28 Md. 577; State v. Dalrymple, 70 Md., 294, (3 L. R. A., 372) Re McPherson, 104 N. Y., 306; Strode v. Com., 52 Pa., 181; Minot v. Winthrop, 26 L. 

R. A. 259.

In the latter case, the right to transmit property is called a privilege, and also a commodity, in the sense of the Constitution of Massachusetts, and which the State has a right to sell at a reasonable price. See also Re Romaines' Estate, 12 L. R. A. 401; Re Howe's Estate, 2 L. R. A., 825; Catlin v. Trinity College, 3 L. R. A. 206. 

Upon reason and authority, we are of opinion that the

Ch. 5) 385 

INHERITANCE TAX 

tax is constitutional, and may be sustained as a tax upon the privilege or condition of receiving property by will or inheritance.

It is next insisted that the tax is not made uniform, but bears unequally, inasmuch as a distinction and difference is made between direct descendants and collateral kindred and strangers. If this is so, it has abundant reason upon which to sustain such discrimination, for the moral claim of collaterals and strangers is less than of kindred in the direct line, and the privilege is, therefore, greater. 

It is well settled that classifications may be made of privileges for purposes of taxation, and it has generally been done in our revenue laws, the only restriction being that the classification should be natural, and not arbitrary. 

State v. Schlier, 3 Heis., 286; Fulghum v. Mayer, 8 Lea, 635; Robbins v. Taxing District, 13 Lea, 303; Demoville v.

Davidson County, 87 Tenn., 218, In re Howe's Estate, 2 L. 

R. A., 825; State v. Hamlin, 25 L. R. A., 632.

We conclude that the tax is not unconstitutional because it discriminates between direct descendants and collateral kindred and strangers.

Again, it is said the tax is unconstitutional because of the $250.00 exemption, and it is properly said the exemption is not of $250.00 out of all estates, but that estates under $250.00 in value are exempted from any tax. In other words, an estate worth $249.00 escapes taxation, but one of $250.00, or over, is subject to tax. 

It is peculiarly within the province of the Legislature to declare what privileges shall be taxed, and what exemptions may be allowed, in order to make taxes bear most lightly upon those least able to bear them, and the exemption of small estates is neither arbitrary, nor is it devoid of good reason, inasmuch as the expenses of administration are proportionately much greater in small than in large estates. 

In the various States, when such taxes was imposed, there is a similar exemption depending on the size or value of the estate. In New York the limit is $500; in Pennsylvania, $250.00; In Maryland, New Jersey, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, and California, $500.00; in Connecticut and West 

Virginia, $1,000.00; in Ohio and Massachusetts, $10,000.00.

(Ch. 5 

Doubt as to the constitutionality of this tax, on the ground of the exemption, has been expressed in State v. Mann, 76 

Wis., 469; State v. Gorman, 40 Minn., 232; Le Duc v. Hastings, 39 Minn., 110. But in many other cases the exemption has not been held to affect the validity or constitutionality of the Act. See the cases already cited, and specially the case of Minot v. Winthrop, 26 L. R. A., 264.

We are of opinion that the Act is not invalid or unconstitutional on account of the exemption. The result is, that, under the provisions of the Acts of 1893, the property given by the will of John J. Alston to his widow, Mary F. Alston, is not subject to the tax imposed by said Act. 

The live stock given to W. C. and Lee A. Crutcher is liable to such tax, as well as their life estate or interest in the tracts of two hundred and forty and twelve and one half acres of land, the said Lee A. being a niece of the testator, and W. C. Crutcher a stranger in blood. The interests given by the will to the children of W. C. and Lee A. 

Crutcher, to Volney S. Alston, to William and James Dyer, to Mrs. McCowan, and Mrs. Griggs, are all estates or interests in remainder, and, by the express terms of Chapter 174, cannot be taxed under the termination of the life estates in the same premises, and the question of their liability cannot now be properly adjudicated. 

The decree of the Court below be modified as herein indicated, and otherwise affirmed. The costs of the cause on appeal will be paid, one half by the State and the other half by W. C. and Lee A. Crutcher.

The cost of the Court below will remain as therein adjudicated.

CAMPBELL, ET AL.

December Term, 1902 1. It is conceded that, whether the will is sustained or set aside, the estate will be liable to a collateral inheritance tax of the same amount in either event, and the question is when that tax was payable, and would be delinquent.-A question then arose as to the liability of the estate for interest upon the tax, and for an attorney's fee of 15 per cent- 2. We are of opinion, however, that the estate is liable for the tax only to the extent of its clear value, and that "clear value" means net value after the payment of all debts and expenses of administration, or execution of the will, in case of testacy, and in cases where the will is contested, and expenses for attorney's fees, etc., are incurred by the executor in attempting to sustain the will, these fees and expenses must be treated as expenses of administration, and deducted from the amount of the estate, in order to reach its clear value. 

3. We are of the opinion that the tax bears interest from the date when payable, to wit, one year from the death of the decedent; and this notwithstanding the impediment in the way of paying over the whole of it, such as the pendency of litigation, the scarcity of funds, and other causes. 

4. The Court is therefore of opinion that Mr. Johnson acted under his employment by the county court clerk, and is entitled only to a reasonable fee for his services in the chancery court below, which is fixed at 5 per cent upon the amount of tax so far realized, and that may be hereafter realized.

Opinion by Justice Wilkes. 

This cause comes before us upon the record and an agreed statement of facts, and involves the question of the liability of the estate of Mrs. Mary J. Furman to an inheritance tax, the amount for which liable, and the date when it should have been paid. 

The main feature, so far as appears from the record and agreed statement of facts, is, that Mrs. Furman died April 

11, 1900, leaving an estate estimated at $150,000.00 consisting of both realty and personalty. She left no husband, father, mother or direct lineal descendant, and the debts are merely nominal in amount. She executed a will by which she provided for the payment in the first instance of her debts; second, for the erection of a monument, to cost not 387

(Ch. 5 

less than $26,000.00, and, thirdly, she willed all the remainder of her property, except her household and kitchen furniture, wearing apparel and jewelry, to her executors named in the will, in trust for the Vanderbilt University, located in Nashville, to be expended in the manner directed in the will, and for the purposes therein specified. 

The will was contested by her next of kin, and the contest is now pending, undecided, upon an issue of devisavit vel non, upon appeal in this court. 

It is conceded that, whether the will is sustained or set aside, the estate will be liable to a collateral inheritance tax of the same amount in either event, and the question is when that tax was payable, and would be delinquent. 

On the 25th of May, 1901, a bill was filed in the chancery court of Davidson county by the clerk of the county court to collect the tax, through Thos. B. Johnson, State revenue agent, as his attorney. On the 23rd of September, 1901, it was agreed that the executors should pay $4,000.00 of said taxes (being 5 per cent, upon $80,000.00 of value), and that the remainder should await the result of the litigation or further orders, and this was done. 

A question then arose as to the liability of the estate for interest upon the tax, and for an attorney's fee of 15 per cent, upon it, and the agreed case was made up to test these questions in the courts.

The chancellor held that the tax was past due and delinquent when the bill was filed; that it bore interest from one year after the death of testatrix; that, under the statute, the estate was liable to an attorney's fee of 15% on the amount already paid and yet to be paid. 

Defendants prayed an appeal to this court, and assign the several holdings mentioned as error. 

The present law providing for an inheritance and succession tax is chapter 174, p. 347, Acts 1893 (Shannon's 

Compilation, secs. 724–756). Section 729 provides: "If the collateral inheritance tax shall be paid within three months after the death of the decedent, a discount of 5 per centum on the amount of the tax shall be made and allowed; and if said tax is not paid at the end of one year from the death of decedent, at which time it shall be due, interest shall then be charged at the rate of 6 per centum per annum on such tax.''

Ch. 5) 389 

INHERITANCE TAX 

This provision is found in section 4 of the original act, and fixes the date when the tax becomes due and payable. 

By section 3 of the original act (section 728 of Shannon's Compilation) it is provided that the tax shall be a lien upon the real estate, and that the owner of any personal estate subject to the tax shall make full report and return of same to the clerk of the county court within one year from the death of the decedent, and enter into security for the payment of the tax to the satisfaction of such clerk, and, in case of failure so to do, the tax shall be immediately payable and collectible.

It is left somewhat uncertain by the connection as given in the original act whether the provision for bond is intended, except in cases where there are life estates, or periods of years intervening. We need not now decide this question, as in the present case there are no intervening estates, and the tax, in any event, was due and payable at the end of one year from the death of the decedent, and a report was a necessary incident to the settlement for and payment of the tax.

The fact that proceedings are pending to test the validity of the will can not postpone the maturity of the tax, when it appears that in either event, testacy or intestacy, the tax will be payable, and at the same rate as in the present case. 

We are of opinion, however, that the estate is liable for the tax only to the extent of its clear value, and that "clear value” means net value after the payment of all debts and expenses of administration, or execution of the will, in case of testacy, and in cases where the will is contested, and expenses for attorney's fees, etc., are incurred by the executor in attempting to sustain the will, these fees and expenses must be treated as expenses of administration, and deducted from the amount of the estate, in order to reach its clear value.

In such case, it is the duty of the executor and clerk of the county court to make an estimate of such fees and expenses, and to tentatively allow for them, and thus approximate the amount of tax to be paid; and this amount should be paid subject to revision upon final statement and settlement of accounts.

(Ch. 5  

Under section 11 of the act, provision is made, which, we think, covers the case, where the executor may have paid too much tax, and allows its recovery back from the clerk, or out of the State treasury, when overpayment is made. 

In the present instance, $4,000.00 has been paid upon an estimate of clear value of $80,000.00 but this payment was not made for some four months after the tax was due and payable. We are of opinion that the tax bears interest from the date when payable, to wit, one year from the death of the decedent; and this notwithstanding the impediments in the way of paying over the whole of it, such as the pendency of litigation, the scarcity of funds, and other causes. 

The next question that arises is as to the liability of the estate for attorney's fees, and, if liable at all, for what amount.

It is made the duty of the county court clerk to collect the tax, and for that purpose he is by the act authorized to employ an attorney, who shall have a reasonable fee for his services, to be paid, in addition to the tax, by the party liable for the tax.

It appears that the clerk of the county court of Davidson county has entered into an agreement with Thomas B. 

Johnson, one of the three revenue agents of the State, whose office it is to collect back or delinquent taxes, to look after, bring suit for, and collect such inheritance taxes as may be overdue.

Mr. Johnson claims that he has the right, by virtue of his office, and under the statute defining his duties, to look after and collect this tax, and bring suit therefor, as well as under the appointment of the county court clerk, and that, under the statute, his compensation for such service is fixed at 15 per cent upon the amount of tax realized. 

It is held in Zickler v. Union Bank & Trust Co., 104 Tenn. 

281 (57 S. W. 341), that the inheritance tax law, contained in chapter 174, Acts 1893, was designed to furnish a complete system of taxation upon the subject of collateral inheritance taxes; that is, a system, in and of itself, to be executed according to the provisions of that act. 

Under these provisions, it was the duty of the county court clerk of Davidson county to have collected this tax,

Ch. 5) 

391 

INHERITANCE TAX 

and, when suit became necessary, it should have been brought in that court; and the clerk, under the act, had the authority to employ an attorney, to be paid a reasonable compensation for his services, in that court. This suit was not brought in that court, but in the chancery court. There was, however, no demurrer or plea to the jurisdiction, and we hold that it could be maintained, under such circumstances, in the chancery court. 

But it must be conducted and treated as though it had been brought in the county court, and in accordance with the provisions of the act, by an attorney employed by the county court clerk under that act. 

The suit must therefore be treated as if brought by Mr. 

Johnson under his employment by the county court clerk, and not by him in his official capacity of State revenue agent. 

This being so, he would, under the general inheritance act, be entitled to a reasonable fee in the court below; but the act provides only a fee for services in the county court to such attorney, and contemplates that on appeal to the circuit court it shall be looked after by the district attorney, and in the supreme court by the attorney-general and reporter.

The court is therefore of opinion that Mr. Johnson acted under his employment by the county court clerk, and is entitled only to a reasonable fee for his services in the chancery court below, which is fixed at 5 per cent upon the amount of tax so far realized, and that may hereafter be realized.

This fee, however, will go to him as the employed attorney of the county court clerk, to be paid by the parties liable for the tax, but will constitute no part of the salary provided in the act relating to State revenue agents. 

Nor will the $4,000.00 taxes recovered in this suit, or the amount hereafter recovered, be treated as a fund out of which his salary of $2500.00 as revenue agent is to be paid by the comptroller. In other words, the inheritance tax collected and to be collected out of the decedent's estate will be treated as though collected under the general inheritance law, and the fees of Mr. Johnson, of 5 per cent, will be paid to him as though he did not fill the office of revenue agent for

(Ch. 5 

the State, and independent of his salary as such agent, just as they would be to any other attorney whom the county court clerk might see fit to employ.

The decree of the court below will be modified as herein indicated, and in all other respects affirmed, and the cause is remanded to the court below for further proceedings. 

The costs of the cause will be paid by the estate of Mrs. 

Furman.

Mary J. English, Admx.

Opinion by Justice McAlister. 

This suit was brought by the county court clerk of Shelby County against Mary J. English, administratrix cum testamento annexo of the estate of C. B. English, deceased, for the purpose of recovering an inheritance tax alleged to be due the State. The case was submitted to the 

Honorable J. P. Young, of the circuit court, on the following stipulation of agreed facts: "C. B. English, a citizen of Shelby County, Tennessee, died January 26, 1904. He was childless, but left as his widow Mary J. English, the administratrix cum testamento annexo. His heirs at law were
