Snook, supra; St. Louis & Southwestern Railway Company v. Nattin, 277 U. S. 157, 159. The allegations of the bill showing that a heavier burden of taxation is imposed upon railroads than upon common carriers by motor bus, examined in the light of the applicable statutes of the State, fall short of alleging a discrimination forbidden by either the commerce clause or the Fourteenth Amendment. 

Affirmed.

Texas Company V. 

FORT, COMMISSIONER, ET AL. 

Pan-American Petroleum Corporation V. 

FORT, COMMISSIONER, ET AL. 

168 TENNESSEE 679 December Term, 1934 (From Davidson County) 

1. Gasoline tax should be paid by dealers and distributors according to the amount held in storage in this State, instead of according to the number of gallons withdrawn from storage. 

2. It applied to all gasoline in storage on and after April 22, 1933 (effective date of Chapter 130, Acts of 1933). 

Opinion by Justice Chambliss. 

These causes were heard together. They present the same question. Both suits were brought to recover gasoline taxes paid under protest. The chancellor dismissed both bills on demurrer. Both complainants appealed. 

By chapter 130, Acts 1933, the Legislature amended various sections of the Code of 1932, beginning with section 1126, so as to provide that the gasoline tax of six cents per gallon (see Pub. Acts 1931, chap. 40) should be paid by dealers and distributors according to the amount held in storage in this state, instead of according to the number of gallons withdrawn from storage, as provided by the Code. (1) The constitutionality of this amendatory act is assailed on the ground that it fails to comply with the requirements contained in section 17, article 2, of the state Constitution, that "no bill shall become a law, which embraces more than one subject; that subject to be expressed in the title," and that, "All acts which . . . amend former laws, shall recite in their caption or otherwise, the title or 620

Ch. 7) 621 

GASOLINE TAX 

substance of the law . . . amended." We understand counsel for appellants to concede that reference to the sections of the Code of 1932 is a sufficient recital of the title of the act to be amended to satisfy the requirement that the amendatory act shall recite the title of the law to be amended. As said in Gamble v. State, 159 Tenn., 446, 19 

S. W. (2d), 279, 280, this "was long since decided." v. Runnels, 92 Tenn., 320, 21 S. W., 665. State (2-5) But the insistence is that the subject of the amendatory act is not "embraced in the title" of that act; that the language of the title used in restrictive and the subject so limited that it should not be construed to refer to "storing" of gasoline, which it is alleged is a new and independent subject of taxation. Close reasoning is resorted to, turning, apparently, on the construction to be given the word "said," preceding the words "gasoline taxes," and preceding the word "laws."

The caption or title of the Amendatory Act of 1933 reads, "An Act to amend Section 1126 . . . of the Code of 

Tennessee, 1932; said sections of the Code relating to the 

Gasoline Tax Laws, providing for an improved method of assessing and collecting said gasoline taxes and to strengthen the enforcement of said laws, and to repeal all laws," etc. It is insisted that the language of the caption must be limited in its application to just such "gasoline taxes" and just such "laws" as were provided for in the Code sections cited; that "storing" was not embraced within the "said gasoline taxes," or tax laws, so provided for; that therefore the amendment making "storing" a privilege brings in a new and independent subject, not within the scope of the limiting phrase "said gasoline taxes," or "said" laws.

To this we are unable to agree. The sections amended are under a subheading of the Code reading "Gasoline Tax." It is the state "Gasoline Tax" which the title of the amendment gave notice of a purpose to amend, that is, to change, correct, revise. Gamble v. State, supra. And notice was further given that it was proposed by this amendment to provide for "an improved method of assessing." etc., this gasoline tax. To "assess" is to determine and impose

(Ch. 7  

a tax; also, but not alone, to value for taxation. Levy is a synonym of assess. Webster's New International. It appears, therefore, that the title of this amendment to the Code sections cited gave notice of a purpose to change and improve the method of assessing, imposing, levying, the state gasoline taxes, so as to strengthen the enforcement of this law set forth in the Code sections cited. The details of the plan were not required to be set forth in the title. Having called attention to the particular form of privilege taxation to be dealt with, that is, gasoline taxes, it was necessary only to indicate the object aimed at by the amendment. This was clearly done. The title discloses the result aimed at; the method is for the body of the act. The "subject" only is called for in the title, not the story; the purpose to do a certain thing, not just how it is to be done. The purpose declared here was to amend the gasoline tax laws, so as to provide an improved method of assessing and collecting this tax. In the body of the amendment the details were set forth clearly, and under all our holdings this was sufficient. For example, see Van Dyke v. Thompson, 136 Tenn., 136, 189 S. W., 62; Hunter v. Conner, 152 Tenn., 258, 277 

S. W., 71; Henderson Co. v. Breeden Bros., 148 Tenn., 278, 255 S. W., 359; Couch v. State, 140 Tenn., 156, 203 S. W., 831; Petty v. Pheonix Cotton Oil Co., 150 Tenn., 292, 264

S. W., 353. The manner, modes, means, instrumentalities of enforcements, etc., may be embraced in the body of the act, though not recited in the title. State v. Yardley, 95 

Tenn., 546, 553, 32 S. W., 481, 34 L. R. A., 656; State v. 

Brown, 103 Tenn., 449, 458, 53 S. W., 727; Peterson v. State, 104 Tenn., 127, 131, 56 S. W., 834; Rhinehart v. State, 121 

Tenn., 420, 434, 117 S. W., 508, 17 Ann. Cas., 254. The generality of the title is no objection, if not made a cover for incongruous legislation, which by no fair intendment can be considered as having a necessary or proper connection with the subject expressed in the title. Cannon v. Mathes, 8 

Heisk., 504, 519. We think it cannot be fairly said that an act which amends the body of our gasoline tax laws so as to measure the tax imposed according to the amount stored, rather than the amount withdrawn from storage, has no proper connection with, is not germane to, the general sub-

Ch. 7) 

623 

GASOLINE TAX 

ject expressed in the title, "providing for an improved method of assessing and collecting said gasoline taxes.' (6, 7) It is next urged for appellants that under a proper construction of the law as amended the tax applies only to such gasoline as appellants have placed in storage since the effective date of the Amendatory Act, April 22, 1933. The state contended that the tax applied to all gasoline stored, that is in storage, by appellants on and after said effective date. The appellants paid under protest, as before stated. 

The opinion of the learned chancellor so well discusses and disposes of this issue that we incorporate and adopt this part of his opinion, as follows: "The section of the Code, section 1140, as amended by chapter 130, sec. 13, exempts from taxation gasoline stored for export to points outside the state, if the gasoline is stored in a separate tank marked 'export tank,' provided it is not stored for export for longer than a period of sixty days. Under this exemption it would hardly be insisted that gasoline which was in storage when the act became effective and remained in storage for a period longer than sixty days, would not fall within the provisions of the act taxing such gasoline. The amendatory act involved expressly purports in its caption to amend section 1140 of the Code and the amendatory matter in the body of the Act is germane to the section of the Code and the matter covered thereby. This part of the amendatory act does not violate said provision of the Constitution. "If the act as amended imposed a tax only on gasoline imported and stored after its enactment, and exempted from taxation all gasoline that had been imported before and remained in storage after the enactment of the law, it would violate the Equal Protection Clauses of the State and Federal Constitution because you would have an act under which members of each class were doing exactly the same kind of business under the same conditions and for the same purposes, yet one is taxed and the other is exempt. There would be no reasonable basis for such a classification under either the State or Federal Constitution. Moreover, this construction would make the act violate the Commerce Clause of the Federal Constitution, because the privilege tax would not apply to gasoline imported before but remaining in storage after the effective date of the amendatory act, and gasoline imported and stored after the act would be taxed. Such a construction would place a direct burden on 

Interstate Commerce and make the act unconstitutional for that reason. 

The act as amended lays a privilege tax on engaging in the business of storing gasoline, and certainly gasoline shipped into the state before, as well as gasoline shipped into the state after, the effective date of the act and stored, are in the same class so far as storage is concerned, which is the business taxed. The object of the privilege tax involved is the storage of gasoline, and this privilege was exercised and enjoyed by the defendants after the passage of the act, and it would be an anomalous construction of the challenged act that the defendants could enjoy the privilege, namely of importing gasoline before and keeping it in storage after the passage of the act, without paying the privilege tax on the business of storing, and yet be taxed on gasoline imported and stored after the passage of the act. Manifestly the tax is based on the business of keeping in storage, gasoline, and this privilege is exercised by the

(Ch. 7 

defendants on gasoline imported before and stored just as it is on gasoline imported afterwards and stored. It certainly cannot be insisted on this record that the gasoline upon which the tax was collected was not in storage after the passage of the act. Importing or the manner of getting the gasoline into the state for storage, is not an element of the business taxed, but it is the privilege of engaging in the business of storing that is taxed. Under the amended act gasoline could be imported into the state, and until it was sold, stored or distributed, the tax would not attach, and it can make no difference when the importation takes place whether before or after the effective date of the act, provided the gasoline was in storage after the effective date of the act. "It is an elementary principle of construction that if a statute is susceptible of two reasonable constructions, one that will sustain its constitutionality and one that will destroy the act, it is the duty of the Court to adopt the construction which will preserve the law. It is insisted that the tax upon the gasoline that was stored prior to the passage of the amendatory act, offends that part of our Constitution which provides that all property taxes shall be equal and uniform. 'In the case of Foster & Creighton Co. v. Graham, 154 Tenn. 412, 285 S. W., 570, 47 A. L. R., 971, it was insisted that the tax there challenged was a property tax, because the right to store gasoline was a natural right and therefore could not be taxed as a privilege. The 

Supreme Court did not agree with this insistence. It in substance ruled that there is no natural right in a citizen to store gasoline any more than to store dynamite or gunpowder, and that the State has the right to tax the storage of gasoline as a privilege. This case settled the proposition that the tax levied by chapter 130 is not a property tax on the gasoline placed in storage before the effective date of the amendatory act, but that it is a privilege tax on the engaging in the business of storing gasoline based on the number of gallons in storage. 

Again it is said that the Foster & Creighton Company Case is decisive of the question presented here of the validity of the act amending the sections of the Code relating to the gasoline tax. The act before the Court in the Foster & Creighton Company Case was an act which purported to amend an act that levied a tax on engaging in the business of producing and selling in the state or importing and selling in the state, gasoline. This act was amended so as to extend the tax to cover gasoline stored and allowed to be withdrawn from storage for sale or use, and since the gasoline stored and allowed to be withdrawn from storage was not covered by the caption of the act amended, which as stated, was an act imposing a tax on engaging in the business of producing, importing and selling gasoline, it became necessary to amend the caption of the act by including the words 'or storing or distributing' after the word 'selling.' But no such situation is presented in the case under consideration. Here the sections of the Code sought to be amended impose a privilege tax on the business of storing and withdrawing from storage, gasoline and the amendatory act is germane to this act, and it is not necessary to amend the caption of the act so as to add after the recited section of the Code, that it is an act to place a tax on the storage of gasoline because the original act contained in the sections of the Code amended already provided for a tax on storage and withdrawal of gasoline. "The case of Pan-American Petroleum Company v. Miller, 154 

Miss., 565, 122 So. 393, and the case of Gay Oil Company v. State, 170

Ark., 587, 280 S. W., 632, are cited and relied on by the complainants on the question that the amended statute involved did not apply to gasoline held in storage at the time the amendatory act went into effect. 

Both of these decisions were rendered by a divided court. When the 

Foster & Creighton Company Case was before our Supreme Court, the

Ch. 7) 625 

GASOLINE TAX 

complainant relied on a Mississippi case holding that an act imposing the privilege tax upon persons pursuing the business of extracting turpentine from standing trees, imposed a property and not a privilege tax, and was unconstitutional under a section of the Mississippi Constitution which corresponds to article 2, section 28 of our Constitution, and it was insisted that the tax under consideration in the Foster & Creighton Company Case was unconstitutional because it was a property and not a privilege tax. This insistence was rejected by our Supreme Court and it said in speaking of the Mississippi case: "The tax in that case was held by a majority of the court to be a property tax, Justice Potter and Cook dissenting, being of the opinion that the tax was levied on the occupation or business of extracting crude turpentine from the tree, that the statute said so in plain English, and we may say that we are impressed with the logic of the dissenting opinion, and will not be controlled by the opinion of the majority in determining whether the tax under consideration is a property tax or a privilege tax. We think it is the latter, and so hold.' 154 Tenn., 428, 285 S. W., 575. "This language is peculiarly appropriate to the case of Pan-American Petroleum Company v. Miller. The cogent reasoning and logic of the dissenting opinion of Mr. Justice Anderson is more impressive and persuasive than the majority opinion, and to my mind applies with peculiar force to the act under consideration."' 

Concurring with the chancellor, his decree dismissing these bills is affirmed.

Fort, Commissioner, et al

V. 

DIXIE OIL COMPANY 

170 TENNESSEE 183

December Term, 1935 

(From Davidson County) 1. Petition to stay levy of distress warrant, issued by Commissioner of Finance and Taxation and granted by Chancery Court, is dismissed. 

2. Commissioner is empowered to determine the amount of gasoline tax due from any delinquent dealer or distributor and is authorized to enforce collection by distraint. 

3. Adequate remedies, by statutory provision, permit taxpayers to recover taxes illegally collected. 

Opinion by Chief Justice Green. 

A petition for certiorari and supersedeas to stay the levy of a distress warrant, issued by the commissioner of finance and taxation, on the properties of the Dixie Oil Company, and to have said warrant adjudged null and void, was filed by that company in the chancery court of Nashville. The commissioner and the sheriff entered a motion to dismiss for want of equity on the face of the petition, which motion they treat as one to dismiss for want of jurisdiction. The chancellor overruled the motion, having previously granted the writs of certiorari and supersedeas upon the execution by the petitioner of a supersedeas bond in the sum of $5,000, but required the commissioner and the sheriff to answer. They have filed a petition for certiorari and supersedeas in this court seeking to have the writs granted by the chancellor quashed and the petition of the Dixie Oil Company dismissed.

The contention of the commissioner and the sheriff is that the chancellor was without jurisdiction to issue the writs allowed by him. If this contention be good the commissioner and the sheriff are entitled here to the writs they seek.

A special privilege tax upon the handling of gasoline 626

Ch. 7) 627 

GASOLINE TAX 

is levied by section 1126 et seq. of the Code (as amended by 

Pub. Acts 1933, chap. 130, sec. 1 et seq.). The petition of the Dixie Oil Company avers that it is a corporation engaged in the buying and selling of gasoline, kerosene, and by products of petroleum. That the commissioner of finance and taxation, prior to February 14, 1936, made an assessment against the petitioner in the sum of $2,471.70 as taxes due the state on gasoline sales; that while petitioner was disputing and denying this assessment the commissioner "arbitrarily and without just cause or right issued a distress warrant" against the properties of petitioner and that the sheriff of Davidson county levied said distress warrant and seized and locked up petitioner's place of business. Petitioner further avers that it does not owe "said assessment made against it” and that the payment of same under protest would work a tremendous hardship on petitioner. There is an allegation in the petition that "the representatives of defendant, Dancey Fort, Commissioner, are openly asserting that their real purpose is to destroy petitioner's business." There is a further allegation that private competitors are aligned with the commissioner and are working with representatives of the commissioner to destroy petitioner's business and the business of other "independent operators in gasoline." It is set out that petitioner has tendered the commissioner a bond in the sum of $10,000 for the payment of all delinquent taxes, which bond the commissioner refused to accept and release the properties of the petitioner. There is also a statement in the petition that "the legal representative of the defendants" has stated that their main purpose is to drive petitioner out of business.

It will be observed from the foregoing that the Dixie Oil Company concedes that it is in the business of buying and selling gasoline and accordingly liable for the payment of gasoline tax. The validity of the gasoline tax is not challenged. All that the petition can mean is that the commissioner has assessed an excessive tax against the Dixie Oil Company and that this has been done unjustly and arbitrarily. The tax is measured by the number of gallons of gasoline sold. The real controversy, as the petition dis-

closes, is as to the amount of the tax for which the Dixie Oil Company has incurred liability. 

There is no charge in the petition that the commissioner was guilty of fraud in the assessment of this tax. It is said that he acted arbitrarily, but no facts are set out to support this conclusion. Neither the commissioner nor the state can be prejudiced in the collection of revenues due the state by indiscreet remarks or threats of subordinate employees or representatives.

Sections 1130-1136 of the Code (as amended by Pub. 

Acts 1933, chap. 130, sec. 4 et seq.) provide for the making of certain reports by distributors of gasoline and dealers in gasoline with respect to the number of gallons sold, and section 1137 of the Code is as follows: 

"Upon the failure of any person engaged as distributor or dealer to make and deliver to the commissioner of finance and taxation the statement above provided for, or to pay the taxes due, it shall be the duty of the commissioner to revoke his permit, and immediately to proceed to inform himself as best he may regarding the matters and things to be set forth in such statement, and, from such information as he may be able to obtain, to make a statement, showing such matters and things, and determine and fix the amount of the privilege tax due the state from such delinquent person, and deliver such statement to the comptroller, of the taxes due, based upon such delinquent's report, or upon the finding, who shall proceed to collect said amount, including a penalty of one per cent per day, for not exceeding ten days, and interest, by the issuance of a distress warrant against the delinquent and the surety on his bond, and, if necessary, by suit on the bond. Upon the request of the comptroller, it shall be the duty of the attorney-general to institute and prosecute to conclusion all proper and necessary suits for the collection of the taxes.''

By the chapter 130 of the Public Acts of 1933 (section 11) authority to issue a distress warrant was conferred upon the commissioner of finance and taxation instead of upon the comptroller as in section 1137 above. 

From the foregoing, it appears that the commissioner of finance and taxation is empowered to determine the amount of gasoline tax due from any delinquent dealer or distributor and is charged with the collection of the gasoline tax and is authorized to enforce collection of this tax by distraint.

Section 1790 of the Code is as follows: 

"In all cases where not otherwise provided in which an officer, charged by law with the collection of revenue due the state, shall institute any proceeding, or take any steps for the collection of the sum

Ch. 7) 629 

GASOLINE TAX 

alleged or claimed to be due, by said officer, from any citizen, the person against whom the proceeding or step is taken shall, if he conceives the same to be unjust or illegal, or against any statute or clause of the constitution of the state, pay the same under protest. 

Sections 1791, 1792, and 1793 of the Code provide for suit for the recovery of taxes paid under protest and if adjudged to have been illegally exacted of the taxpayer, repayment of such illegal exactions is required to "be paid in preference to other claims on the treasury." 

Then follows section 1794 of the Code: 

"There shall be no other remedy in any case of the collection of revenue, or attempt to collect revenue illegally, or attempt to collect revenue in funds only receivable by said officer under the law, the same being other or different funds than such as the taxpayer may tender, or claim the right to pay, than that above provided.” 

And then section 1795 of the Code: "No writ for the prevention of the collection of any revenue claimed, or to hinder and delay the collection of the same, shall in any wise issue, either injunction, supersedeas, prohibition, or any other writ or process whatever; but in all cases in which, for any reason, any person shall claim that the tax so collected was wrongfully or illegally collected, the remedy for said party shall be as above provided, and in no other manner. ""

Considering the explicit prohibition of section 1795, we are unable to see how the issuance of the writs of certiorari and supersedeas by a Tennessee court to arrest a distress warrant in a case like this can be justified. 

The sections of the Code quoted are taken from chapter 44 of the Acts of 1873. This act was declared to be constitutional in the case of Louisville & Nashville R. Co. v. 

State of Tennessee et al, 55 Tenn. (8 Heisk.), 663, 805, and it was held in that case that the writs of certiorari and supersedeas would not issue to stay the collection of a tax. 

The act of 1873 was considered by the Supreme Court of the United States in Tennessee ex rel, Bloomstein v. Sneed, 96 U. S., 69, 24 L. Ed., 610, and Shelton v. Platt, 139 U. S., 591, 11 S. Ct., 646, 35 L. Ed., 273, and treated as affording to a taxpayer, of whom an illegal exaction had been made, an adequate remedy to protect his rights. In the more recent case of Smallwood v. Gallardo, 275 U. S., 56, 48 S. Ct., 23, 72 L. Ed., 152, that tribunal has approved a statute depriving the federal courts of authority to enjoin the col-

(Ch. 7  

lection of taxes in Porto Rico and held that the statute applied to suits brought prior to its enactment. 

In City of Nashville v. Smith, 86 Tenn. 213, 6 S. W., 273, 275, a distress warrant issued to collect from the City of Nashville a privilege tax for the operation of water works. 

The city denied its liability and took the matter before the circuit court upon petition for certiorari and supersedeas. 

It was held that the city was not liable for this tax, but it was further held that insofar as the state tax was involved, as distinguished from the county tax, the petition must be dismissed, the court saying: "For, however unjust or illegal the demand against the city may have been, the only course left open to it was to pay the state's part of the same under protest, and then sue for the recovery thereof within 30 days, thereafter. No writ of injunction, supersedeas, or prohibition or other process can lawfully issue for the prevention of the collection of revenue claimed to be due the state." 

It may be noted that chapter 44 of the Acts of 1873 was brought forward without change into the Code of 1932, and this is a sufficient answer to the contention of counsel that the provisions of that act are not applicable to present day conditions. The General Assembly of 1931 took a contrary view.

The Court discussed chapter 44 of the Acts of 1873 in 

Bank of Commerce & Trust Co. v. Senter, 149 Tenn., 569, 260 S. W., 144, 151, where the corporation excise tax was under consideration and said: "Chapter 44, Acts of 1873, Shannon's Code, 1059 et seq., provides a remedy for the taxpayer confronted by an unjust or illegal claim for taxes. The state cannot be postponed in the collection of its revenue, for the taxpayer must pay the tax under the conditions prescribed, as a condition precedent to contesting the liability for the tax or any part of it.

The proceeding under the act of 1873 was not intended as the remedy for an erroneous or unjust assessment. Where the assessment of the ad valorem is challenged, the remedy of the taxpayer is as indicated in Briscoe v. McMillan (117 Tenn., 115, 100 S. W., 111), Ward 

V. Alsup (100 Tenn., 619, 46 S. W., 573), and other cases cited. Where the state's fiscal agents make an erroneous or illegal charge and require the taxpayer to pay more than the law authorized them to collect, chapter 44, Acts of 1873, Shannon's Code sec. 1059, supplies the remedy. 

Phillips v. Lewis, 3 Tenn. Cas., 230; Atlas Powder Co. v. Goodloe, 131 

Tenn., 490, 499, 175, S. W., 547; Western Oil Refining Co. v. Dalton, 131 Tenn., 329, 174, S. W., 1138. Where the levy is in part unauthorized by law, the tax payer may pay the tax under protest and recover to the extent of the illegal exaction." 

Complaint is here made because the taxpayer had no notice of the assessment sought to be collected by the com-

Ch. 7) 631 

GASOLINE TAX 

missioner of finance and taxation and no opportunity was given for a hearing before the commissioner. We have undertaken to show in East Tennessee Brewing Co. v. Currier, 126 Tenn., 535, 150 S. W., 541, that it is sufficient, if at some stage of the proceedings the taxpayer is given an opportunity to be heard. The courts quite uniformly hold that an adequate hearing is provided by statutes similar to the act of 1873, Casco Co. v. Thurston County, 163 Wash., 666, 2 P. (2d), 677, 77 A. L. R. 622; Eddy v. Lee Tp., 73 

Mich., 123, 40 N. W., 792; Raleigh & G. R. Co. v. Lewis, 99 

N. C., 62, 5 S. E., 82; and other cases collected in a note, 77 A. L. R. 629.

We think there is no power in the courts of Tennessee to stay by injunction or supersedeas the collection of taxes due to the state when the whole substance of the taxpayer's contention is that the tax levied is excessive. 

The chancellor expressed the opinion that section 9008 et seq. of the Code providing for the review of actions of boards or commissions gave him authority herein. We have indicated a contrary view in Savage Co. v. Knoxville, 167 

Tenn., 642, 72 S. W. (2d), 1057, and Anderson v. Memphis, 167 Tenn., 648, 72 S. W. (2d), 1059. These sections are contained in article 5 of chapter 14 of the 1932 Code. In addition to what was said in the cases just mentioned, section 9014 by implication negatives the idea that the writ of certiorari here dealt with was intended to apply to revenue cases. The language of section 9014 is "At the expiration of ninety days from the filing of said transcript, the cause shall stand for trial, and shall be heard and determined at the earliest practical date, as one having precedence over other litigation, except suits involving state, county or municipal revenue."

This seems to contemplate revenue suits as suits apart from proceedings under these section of the Code. 

For the reasons stated, being of opinion that the chancellor has acted in this matter beyond his jurisdiction, the writs of certiorari and supersedeas sought by the commissioner and the sheriff are granted, and the writs of certiorari and supersedeas issued from the chancery court to stay the levy of the distress warrant are quashed.

Section 6809: 

Department enforcing law- The enforcement of this article shall be by the department of finance and taxation, through its excise division. Section 6810: 

Inspector at large and deputies to supervise— The governor shall appoint the director of the excise tax division of the department of finance and taxation, in

(Ch. 8  

office, and successors, "inspector at large," and is authorized to appoint three "deputy inspectors at large" for the department of finance and taxation, to supervise the inspection of petroleum products and substitutes therefor, but without additional compensation, all to be under the direction of the commissioner of the department. 

Section 6811: 

Reports from inspectors- It shall be the duty of all inspectors of petroleum products and substitutes therefor to make such reports and secure such data as may be requested, and obey all orders that may be issued by the inspector at large, or a deputy inspector at large, and such inspector at large or his deputy may prepare forms for reports and other information desired from the various inspectors of petroleum products and substitutes therefor throughout the state. 

Section 6812: 

Appointment of inspectors; competent- 

The governor shall appoint for each city and/or county containing a population of one thousand and over by the latest federal census an inspector of coal oil, carbon oil, petroleum, kerosene oil, gasoline, or any other product of petroleum used for illuminating, volatile or burning fluid, by whatever name known, which may be manufactured or offered for sale in the state. Said inspector shall be a competent person. 

Section 6813: 

Term of office; inspectors- 

The term of office for all inspectors shall be for two years, or until removed by, and at the pleasure of the governor; and the inspectors are empowered, if necessary to the convenient dispatch of their duties, to appoint competent deputies, for whom they shall be responsible and accountable, which deputies are empowered to perform the duties of inspector, and shall be liable to the same penalties as the inspector.

Ch. 8) 639 

INSPECTION FEES Section 6814: 

Oath and bond of inspector- Every person appointed inspector shall, before he enters upon the duties of his office, take an oath or affirmation to support the constitution of this state and that of the United States, and to perform the duties of his office with fidelity. 

Each inspector shall also enter into bond, payable to the State of Tennessee, conditioned for the proper disposition of the fees collected by him, and for the faithful performance of his duties under this article, and to account for all moneys received and collected by him as such inspector; and for inspectors in cities and/or counties of 40,000 population and under, according to the federal census last preceding the making of the bond, the penalty of the bond shall be two thousand dollars; and in cities and/or counties of over 40,000 population, according to said census, the penalty shall be five thousand dollars. The bond of each inspector in each county or municipality shall be approved by and filed with the Secretary of State and it shall also provide, in case of suit thereon, for a reasonable attorney's fee for the state's attorney. 

Section 6815: 

Removal of inspector- 

On failure of any inspector to turn over and account for the fees as herein directed within ten days after the time fixed, or for any other act or omission deemed sufficient by the governor, he shall have the right to remove such inspector from office, and appoint another. 

Section 6816: 

Inspectors not permitted to be interested in oils or fluids- No inspector or deputy inspector shall, while in office, be interested, directly or indirectly, in the manufacture or vending of any of the said illuminating oils or fluids to be inspected under this article; nor shall he, directly or indirectly, traffic therein; nor shall he for the purpose of inspection take away or appropriate any part of said oils

(Ch. 8 

or fluids to his own use, or for the use of any other person, under penalty of dismissal from office and of five hundred dollars fine, to be recovered by indictment or presentment in the manner provided for in section 6846. 

Section 6817: 

Inspection before sale, use, or storage- All benzol, gasoline, burning oil, distillate, fuel oil, gas oil, kerosene, naphtha and/or any other volatile substances, reflecting a gravity of sixteen degrees or above on the Baumé scale, produced from petroleum, natural gas, oil shales or coal, by whatever trade name known and/or substitutes therefor, sold or used and/or stored in this state, separately or in combination for any purpose whatever, by any user and/or storer, including all subordinate governmental bodies, whether manufactured in this state or not, shall be inspected, under the general supervision of the inspector at large, before being sold or offered for sale or used and/or stored in this state. 

Section 6818: 

Duty of inspectors- 

It shall be the duty of the inspectors to examine and test, within this state, all such volatile substances before being sold or offered for sale or used and/or stored in this state.

Section 6819: 

Gravity standards- The gravity, purity and tests of said volatile substances shall be determined in such manner and under such regulations as the inspector at large may specify, subject to approval of the commissioner of finance and taxation, and in accord with usages practiced or data or regulations issued by the United States Bureau of Mines. 

Section 6820: 

Notice of inspection attached- After making said examination and test, inspectors shall affix to receptacles, sale tanks, pumps, etc., containing

Ch. 8) 641 

INSPECTION FEES 

volatile substances inspected such marks of identification and/or caution notices as the inspector at large may designate, subject to such approval, in accord with reasonable trade customs and precautions governing the handling of volatile substances, and the unauthorized removal of any such notice is a misdemeanor. 

Section 6821: 

Inspection fees charged—

Each inspector who shall inspect any consignment of volatile substances described in the preceding sections, as provided in this article, shall charge the consignor or consignee thereof the sum of twenty cents for testing a barrel, or less quantity, and twenty cents additional for each barrel. Fifty gallons shall constitute a barrel. When the inspection is made of a tank containing more than fifty gallons, twenty cents shall be charged for each fifty gallons or fraction over.

Section 6822: 

Records to be kept by inspectors- Every inspector shall keep an accurate record of all such goods inspected, rejected, branded, or certified to by him, which record shall state the date of such inspection, the number of packages, barrels, casks, or tanks approved, the number rejected, the name of the person for whom inspected, the name of the person to whom consigned, with his address, the sum of money charged for such inspection; and such records shall be open to all persons interested. 

Section 6823: 

Reports and remittances of fees collected- Each inspector shall, within twenty-five days after the end of each month, render to the comptroller of the state, through the inspector at large, an itemized report of all oils inspected by him, and shall at the same time remit to the comptroller; through the inspector at large, all moneys collected by him for inspection fees.

(Ch. 8  Section 6823.1: 

Inspection fees: to whom paid- 

All volatile substance inspection fees heretofore paid to inspectors shall hereafter be payable to the State Comptroller.

Section 6823.2: 

Inspector at Large to make reasonable regulations- Inspector at large, appointed under provisions of Chapter 6, Public Acts of 1925, shall supply necessary blanks and make reasonable regulations to facilitate the administration of the Act. 

Section 6824: 

Books, instruments, etc. furnished 

It shall be the duty of the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation to furnish each inspector with blanks, books, instruments, etc., that are necessary for him to make inspection as provided in this article, and to see that proper returns are made of the moneys collected. 

Section 6825: 

Apparatus to be furnished- Also, to furnish to each inspector such apparatus as may by necessary to carry out the provisions of this article. 

Section 6826: 

Making tests; apparatus to be purchased by- 

For the purpose of making chemical and photometric tests, as provided for, it shall also be the duty of the Inspector at large to purchase, from time to time, the apparatus for making tests of volatile substances, and make an arrangement with the inspector at large to make such tests as are called for by this statute, or as in the judgment of the inspector at large are essential for better enforcement, and to afford full protection to the public. The amount to be paid to said inspector at large for making such tests not to exceed two thousand dollars per annum.

Ch. 8) 643 

INSPECTION FEES Section 6827: 

Determination of the value for purposes claimed— It shall be the duty of the inspector at large to make tests of products submitted to him, to determine the value for the purpose claimed. 

Section 6828: 

Inspectors and others to report violations to district attorney, who shall prosecute; violation by inspectors a misdemeanor; removal from office- 

It shall be the duty of any inspector, or any person having cognizance of any violation of the provisions of this article forthwith to make complaint to the district attorney for the county in which this offense is alleged to have been committed, against the person or persons so offending; and it is the duty of such district attorney to represent and prosecute, on behalf of the state, all cases of offense arising under the provisions of this article. Any inspector who willfully refuses or neglects to carry out the provisions of this section shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, and be removed from office. 

Section 6829: 

Violation a misdemeanor; fine and imprisonment- 

Any person violating any of the provisions of this article shall be punished by a fine of not less than one hundred dollars, or by imprisonment in the county jail not to exceed sixty days, or both in the discretion of the court. 

Section 6830: 

Expenses and salaries paid out of inspection funds- All expenses and salaries shall be paid by the State comptroller out of the funds collected for such inspection, after such expenses and salaries are approved by the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation.

Section 6831: 

Other laws not repealed; records. 

Nothing in this statute shall be construed as repealing or interfering in any way with any laws with reference to

(Ch. 8 

inspection of any oils not mentioned in this article. It shall be the duty of all persons handling, transporting and/or storing volatile substances described in this article to retain records and/or intelligible memoranda and/or books subject to inspection by any inspector at large covering the movements of said volatile substances. 

Section 6832: 

Inspected products to be marked- The inspector shall affix his brand or device upon each package by him inspected, designating his name and place and date of inspection.

Section 6833: 

Quantity expressed by weight, when; fluids without flash test to be branded "highly inflammable" If weights shall be established for the ascertaining of the quantity, in place of gauging by gallons, then the inspector shall mark on the package inspected by him the gross weight in place of gallons. The inspector shall, in addition, affix his brand on all containers or packages by him found to contain fluids that have no proper test with these words "highly inflammable."

Section 6834: 

Inspection in transitu; fees 

All such oils and fluids which may be used for any such purposes, sent from other states to counties in this state which are without inspectors of oils and fluids, or sent from counties in this state without the barrels and packages containing the same being branded by laws by the inspectors of the county or city from which they are sent, may be inspected in transitu, in the hands of the carrier, forwarding agent, or warehouseman, and the inspector shall demand and receive for a single barrel sent to one party forty cents; for more than one barrel up to five barrels, thirty cents a barrel; and from five barrels to any number, twenty-five cents.

Ch. 8) 645 

INSPECTION FEES Section 6835: 

Inspector may go to other counties, when; fees- 

Any inspector, or his assistant, may go to any county which is without an inspector when he has information that oils or fluids aforesaid of less test than that required are being sold for any such purposes, without the barrels and packages containing the same being branded as provided by law, and inspect and brand all the oils and fluids not branded by an inspector of this state, and he shall demand and receive thirty cents a barrel for all barrels of oils and fluids aforesaid inspected by him, the fees to be paid by the owner or the person for the time being in the possession of the same, on the demand of the inspector. 

Section 6836: 

Oil inspected in transitu and condemned to be shipped back- When oils or fluids above specified are sent from other states for consumption in this state for such purposes to counties without an inspector, and the same are inspected in transitu, and condemned as of less test than required, the inspector is authorized and directed to ship back said oils or fluids to the shippers of the same.

Section 6837: 

Inspected in transitu and condemned to be branded, how- And when oils or fluids specified above are sent to this state to counties or cities without an inspector, and the same are inspected in transitu, and found to be without a required test, the inspector shall brand the barrel or package containing the fluid "unsafe for use." All such packages or barrels which are plainly marked by the manufacturers or shippers "naphtha," "benzine," "gasoline, etc., together with the specific gravity of the same, may be permitted to go forward to their destination as not intended for any of said purposes; but all barrels or packages without a required test, and which are not so branded or plainly marked by the manufacturers or ship-

(Ch. 8  

pers, shall be considered as intended for such purposes, and shall be shipped back in like manner as condemned products.

Section 6838: 

Collection of fees on oils and fluids inspected in transitu- The inspector shall notify the shipper of the cause and his own action in the premises, and may collect the fees for oils and fluids inspected in the hands of the carrier, forwarding agent, or warehouseman, from the carrier, forwarding agent, or warehouseman, as charges on the oils and fluids, and the carrier, forwarding agent, or warehouseman may collect their fees as charges on the oils and fluids, and hold the same until paid. 

Section 6839: 

Refusal to pay fees; penalty- 

If any carrier, forwarding agent, or warehouseman shall refuse to pay the inspection fees as provided in this article, he shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, and be fined ten dollars for each refusal, the fine to go to the school fund of the state.

Section 6840: 

Obstructing inspector; penalty- 

While the inspector is in the discharge of his duties, if any dealer in or manufacturer of oils or fluids above specified, shall refuse to admit an inspector or his deputy upon his premises, so far as it may be necessary for the performance of his duties, or if he shall obstruct an inspector or his deputy in the discharge of his duties, such persons shall for each refusal be fined not less than twenty dollars nor exceeding fifty dollars.

Alteration of brands or use of branded packages a misdemeanor-

Misdemeanor to sell mixtures; penalties-

Chapter 77-Public Acts of 1933

Provided, further, that this is a special privilege tax for the State, and no county or municipality in this State is authorized to levy and collect said special privilege tax as provided herein.

ARTICLE 1. Report of Cars of Volatile Substances Placed on Sidings. 

All carriers and/or terminal organizations will, from and after this date, report monthly, on Form I. F. 10, all cars placed on sidings for unloading, containing more than five hundred (500) gallons of benzine, benzol, casing-head gasoline, gasoline, naphtha, kerosene and/or any other volatile substances. 

ARTICLE 2. Report of All Dumps of Inflammable Substances in Excess of Twenty Gallons. 

All persons as individuals or as agents and/or as employees of any corporation, company or association transporting and making dumps in excess of twenty (20) gallons of benzine, benzol, casing-head gasoline, gasoline, naphtha, kerosene or any other volatile substances will report monthly on Form I. F. 10-A. 

ARTICLE 3. Specifications for Auxiliary Tanks. 

The combined total carrying capacity of containers connected by feeder pipe to the carburetor or otherwise transported as an emergency supply shall not exceed forty (40) gallons. Additional space for expansion shall be provided in each compartment equal to at least two per cent of the capacity thereof. An adequate indicator shall be provided for each compartment.

(Ch. 8  

The containers shall be a rigid all-metal welded structure braced to withstand twisting strains, and of not less than three-sixteenths steel throughout. All welded joints shall have a strength in excess of the strength of the parts welded.

ARTICLE 4. The Handling of Volatile Substances and Explosives. 

Automatic vending and/or self-service devices for the discharge of gasoline or other volatile inflammable liquids for public use is prohibited. 

The servicing of gasoline or other similar liquids at service stations or garages, or from pumps or devices from which the public is served, regardless of their location, shall be arranged under the direct control of the owner of the service or of an employed attendant. 

ARTICLE 5. Equipment 

A Certificate of Approval shall be obtained from the Commissioner of Labor for all equipment used in the transportation of volatile inflammable oils over the bridges and highways of the State of Tennessee, and such certificate shall be granted only when equipment is found to be reliable, safe and satisfactory in performance. 

Each truck, wagon or other vehicle used in the transportation of volatile inflammable oils having a flash test less than 120 degrees F. (closed cup "Tag") over the bridges and highways of the State of Tennessee shall be given a serial number and shall be registered in the Department of Labor.

As a general rule, Certificates of Approval will be granted when equipment conforms to Specifications of Interstate Commerce Commission set out in I. C. C. Number Two.

ARTICLE 6. Use. 

Bodies, platforms and tanks approved for hauling volatile inflammable oils over the bridges and highways of the State of Tennessee shall be used for no other purpose. 

No volatile inflammable oil having a flash point less than

Ch. 8) 659 

INSPECTION FEES 

120 degrees F. (closed cup "Tag") shall be transported over the bridges and highways of the State of Tennessee in barrels, cans, tanks or drums on trucks or wagons equipped with closed or curtained bodies. 

ARTICLE 7. Marking and Painting. 

The name of the person, firm or corporation owning and/or operating equipment transporting volatile inflammable oils over the bridges and highways of the State of Tennessee shall be painted on both sides of such equipment in letters not less than three (3) inches high, also the serial number shall be painted on both sides and the back in letters not less than three (3) inches high. 

The words "Gasoline" and "Danger" shall be painted in letters not less than six (6) inches high on back of such equipment when used to transport volatile inflammable oils having a flash point less than 120 degrees F. (closed cup "Tag"), over the bridges and highways of the State of Tennessee.

Satisfactory evidence of compliance with these regulations shall, when required, be furnished to Commissioner of Labor.

[G]-Attorney-General's Opinion Dated August 13, 1936This will respond to your letter of August 3, in which you ask certain questions regarding the gasoline taxing statutes (sec. 1126 et seq. of the Code of Tennessee) and the oil inspection statutes (sec. 6809 et seq. of the Code of Tennessee).

(Ch. 8 

You also request an opinion as to whom "the inspection fee of 20 cents per barrel on volatile substances becomes due and payable." This inspection fee is imposed by section 6809 et seq. of the Code. 

Section 6817 of the Code provides that all gasoline, distillate, etc. "sold or used and/or stored in this State, separately or in combination, for any purpose whatever, by any user and/or storer, including all subordinate governmental bodies," shall be inspected. The amount of inspection fees is provided by other sections of the Statute. 

In the case of State v. Reed Oil Company, decided by the Supreme Court of Tennessee on June 9, 1926, in a memorandum opinion not designated for publication, the Court determined that the oil inspection statutes of Tennessee express the intention of the legislature not only to cause the inspection of these inflammable products in the exercise of the State police power, but express the purpose to accomplish that act by the imposition of fees far in excess of the expense of inspection. The Court further said that "the intention of the legislature to exact these fees as a means of producing revenue is, we think, clearly expressed when the acts relating to the subject are construed together." In response to the petition to rehear the Court said that it considered these oil inspection statutes as a legislative plan "to produce revenue for the State Government."

While it is true that the inspection statute does not purport to be a privilege tax statute, and was enacted under the police power of the State, it is clear that under the construction of this statute adopted by the Supreme Court of Tennessee it must be considered, not merely as a regulatory statute enacted under the police power, but as a revenue measure.

With this construction in mind, an examination of sec. 

6817 of the Code reveals that liability for the inspection fees attaches to all petroleum products coming within the purview of that section which are used or stored in this State. 

Liability does not attach merely to such products as are withdrawn from storage, but such liability attaches at the time when the petroleum products are placed in storage.

Ch. 8) 663

INSPECTION FEES 

The oil inspection statutes do not provide, as do the gasoline tax statutes, for an exemption from the inspection fees of petroleum products which are stored in Tennessee for export to other states. Such petroleum products are subject to the oil inspection fees. 

It will also be noted that the oil inspection statutes expressly provide that subordinate governmental bodies of the State of Tennessee shall be liable for the inspection fees. 

The oil inspection statutes do not apply to petroleum products moving in interstate commerce through Tennessee. 

This is true even though such products are temporarily halted in Tennessee during their movement through the State. However, petroleum products which are brought into Tennessee and are stored here are not moving in interstate commerce merely because of the intention at some later date to remove such petroleum products into another state. In order that such petroleum products shall not be subject to the inspection statutes, it is necessary that there be bona fide movement in interstate commerce, which commerce has not ended at such time as the products are temporarily halted in Tennessee. 

On October 21, 1929, Attorney-General L. D. Smith advised the Department of Finance and Taxation that "all coal oil products must be inspected which come into the State or manufactured in this State by the State coal oil inspectors before it can be sold or used by anybody, irrespective of who brings it into the State, sells it or uses it, and, therefore, the inspection fees prescribed by statute must be paid. There is nobody excepted. Neither municipalities, nor counties, nor any other organizations, can escape the payment of inspection fees, by whomsoever imported, received, sold, distributed or used." This opinion was rendered at a time when the inspection statutes in their present form were the existing law and in my opinion it represents a correct interpretation of the statutes involved, except that such opinion does not deal with the proposition of whether liability for inspection fees attaches when the petroleum products are placed in storage, or only when they are withdrawn from storage. As heretofore stated, you are advised that such tax liability attaches when petroleum products

(Ch. 8  

which come within the purview of sec. 6817 are sold or used or placed in storage in this State. 

In connection with the oil inspection fees, your attention is directed to Chapter 77 of the Public Acts of 1933. This statute levies an additional privilege tax equal to one-half of one cent for each gallon of coal oil, kerosene, benzol, benzine, gas oil, processed fuel oil or gasoline, provided such substances have not been inspected and the inspection fees thereon paid, as now required by law. From time to time there have been suggestions that the oil inspection statutes of Tennessee are invalid for one reason or another, although no good reason is assigned for the opinion with respect to their invalidity. The Department of Finance and 

Taxation, however, should proceed to enforce the oil inspection statutes (which the Supreme Court of Tennessee has characterized as designed to produce State revenue) without any fear that a complete enforcement of these statutes may result in litigation successfully attacking the constitutionality of these statutes. Any taxpayer who challenges the validity of the oil inspection statutes successfully will jump "out of the frying-pan into the fire," because such taxpayer will become liable for the additional tax equal to one-half of one cent per gallon, as provided by 

Chapter 77 of the Public Acts of 1933. 

Certain rules and regulations of the Department of Finance and Taxation, including Supplement "Q (2nd),"

Supplement "A" and "Circular G," are apparently in conflict with this opinion. At least the construction which has been given these circulars by certain oil dealers is in conflict with this opinion. For this reason it is suggested that these rules and regulations ought to be withdrawn and new rules and regulations promulgated in their place which are not in conflict with this opinion. 

[H]-Specifications or Test Requirements (ex-Regulations No. 8)— GASOLINE 

All gasoline shall be free from water and suspended matter.

Ch. 8) 665 

INSPECTION FEES 

Distillation Tests.-Distillation yields must meet the following temperature readings: 

167° Fahrenheit not less than 10% must have distilled over and be in receiving container. 

284° Fahrenheit not less than 50% must have distilled over and be in receiving container. 

392° Fahrenheit not less than 90% must have distilled over and be in receiving container. 

410° Fahrenheit not less than 97% must have distilled over and be in receiving container. 

Corrosion Test.-A clear copper strip shall not show more than a slight discoloration when submerged in sample of gasoline for three hours at 122° Fahrenheit. 

Vapor Pressure.-Vapor pressure shall not exceed ten pounds at 100° Fahrenheit. For June, July, August and

September the vapor pressure shall not exceed eight pounds at 100° Fahrenheit. Vapor pressure shall be determined by method employed by Interstate Commerce Commission. 

FLASH POINTS 

Kerosene.-Flash point of kerosene must not be lower than 115° Fahrenheit, using the Tagliabue (TAG) closed cup, nor lower than 120° Fahrenheit when Tagliabue (TAG) open cup apparatus is used. 

Cleaning Fluids.-Flash point of cleaning fluids must not be lower than 102° Fahrenheit, using the Tagliabue (TAG) closed cup apparatus. 

Fuel or Furnace Oil.—Flash point of fuel or furnace oil shall be determined by the Cleveland open cup method.

Appointment of Inspectors; Competent- 

Law. Section 6812. 

The governor shall appoint for each city and/or county containing a population of one thousand and over by the latest federal census an inspector of coal oil, carbon oil, petroleum, kerosene oil, gasoline, or any other product of petroleum used for illuminating, volatile or burning fluid, by whatever name known, which may be manufactured or offered for sale in the state. Said inspector shall be a competent person.

Term of Office: Inspectors— Law. Section 6813. 

The term of office for all inspectors shall be for two years, or until removed by and at the pleasure of the governor; and the inspectors are empowered, if necessary to the convenient dispatch of their duties, to appoint competent deputies, for whom they shall be responsible and accountable, which deputies are empowered to perform the duties of inspector, and shall be liable to the same penalties as the inspector. 

Oath and Bond of Inspector 

Law. Section 6814. 

Every person appointed inspector shall, before he enters upon the duties of his office, take an oath or affirmation to support the constitution of this state and that of the United States, and to perform the duties of his office with fidelity. Each inspector shall also enter into bond, payable to the State of Tennessee, conditioned for the proper disposition of the fees collected by him, and for the faithful performance

(Ch. 8  

of his duties under this article, and to account for all moneys received and collected by him as such inspector; and for inspectors in cities and/or counties of 40,000 population and under, according to the federal census last preceding the making of the bond, the penalty of the bond shall be two thousand dollars; and in cities and/or counties of over 40,000 population, according to said census, the penalty shall be five thousand dollars. The bond of each inspector in each county or municipality shall be approved by and filed with the Secretary of State and it shall also provide, in case of suit thereon, for a reasonable attorney's fee for the state's attorney. 

Removal of Inspectors- Law. Section 6815. 

On failure of any inspector to turn over and account for the fees as herein directed within ten days after the time fixed, or for any other act or omission deemed sufficient by the governor, he shall have the right to remove such inspector from office, and appoint another. 

Sections 6812 through 6815 applied to the so-called "coal oil inspectors" employed by the governor in the various counties throughout the State. These "inspectors" were dispensed with early in the year 1937, and the work of inspection of all volatile or petroleum substances is carried on by the regular field personnel of the Department of Finance and Taxation. 

Inspectors Not Permitted to Be Interested in the

Manufacture or Vending of Any Oils or Fluids- Law. Section 6816 

No inspector or deputy inspector shall, while in office, be interested, directly or indirectly, in the manufacture or vending of any of the said illuminating oils or fluids to be inspected under this article; nor shall he, directly or indirectly, traffic therein; nor shall he for the purpose of inspection take away or appropriate any part of said oils or fluids to his own use, or for the use of any other person, under penalty of dismissal from office and of five hundred dollars fine to be recovered by indictment or presentment in the manner provided for in section 6846. 

This section is self-explanatory and violation thereof incurs heavy penalties. 

Inspection before Sale 

Law. Section 6817 

All benzol, gasoline, burning oil, distillate, fuel oil, gas oil, kerosene, naphtha and/or any other volatile substances, reflecting a gravity of sixteen degrees or above on the Baume scale, produced from petroleum, natural gas, oil shales or coal, by whatever trade name known and/or substitutes therefor, sold or used and/or stored in this state, separately or in combination for any purpose whatever, by any user and/or storer, including all subordinate governmental bodies, whether

Ch. 8) 671 

INSPECTION FEES 

manufactured in this state or not, shall be inspected, under the general supervision of the inspector at large, before being sold or offered for sale or used and/or stored in this state. 

This section provides that all gasoline, distillate, etc. "sold or used and/or stored in this state, separately or in combination for any purpose whatever, by any user and/or storer including all subordinated governmental bodies," shall be inspected.

The Attorney General of the State very clearly defined, in his opinion dated August 31, 1936, when inspection fees are payable and by whom. "In the case of State V. Reed Oil Company (reprinted in detail in Section E of this chapter) decided by the Supreme Court of Tennessee on June 9, 1926, in a memorandum opinion not designated for publication, the court determined that the oil inspection statutes of Tennessee express the intention of the Legislature not only to cause the inspection of these inflammable products in the exercise of the State police power, but express the purpose to accomplish that act by the imposition of fees far in excess of the expense of inspection. The Court further said that "the intention of the Legislature to exact these fees as a means of producing revenue is, we think, clearly expressed when the acts relating to the subject are construed together." In response to the petition to rehear the court said that it considered these oil inspection statutes as a legislative plan "to produce revenue for the State Government."

While it is true that the inspection statute does not purport to be a privilege tax statute, and was enacted under the police power of the State, it is clear that under the construction of this statute adopted by the Supreme Court of Tennessee it must be considered, not merely as a regulatory statute enacted under the police power, but as a revenue measure.

With this construction in mind, an examination of Section 6817 of the Code reveals that liability for the inspection fees attaches to all petroleum products coming within the purview of that section which are used or stored in this State. Liability does not attach merely to such prod-

(Ch. 8 

ucts as are withdrawn from storage, but such liability attaches at the time when the petroleum products are placed in storage.

The oil inspection statutes do not provide, as do the gasoline tax statutes, for an exemption from the inspection fees of petroleum products which are stored in Tennessee for export to other states. Such petroleum products are subject to the oil inspection fees.

It will also be noted that the oil inspection statutes expressly provide that subordinate governmental bodies of the State of Tennessee shall be liable for the inspection fees. 

The oil inspection statutes do not apply to petroleum products moving in interstate commerce through Tennessee. This is true even though such products are temporarily halted in Tennessee during their movement through the State. However, petroleum products which are brought into Tennessee and are stored here are not moving in interstate commerce merely because of the intention at some later date to remove such petroleum products into another state. In order that such petroleum products shall not be subject to the inspection statutes, it is necessary that there be bona fide movement in interstate commerce, which commerce has not ended at such time as the products are temporarily halted in Tennessee."

The summary of this opinion is as follows: 

(a) Oil inspection fee liability accrues upon all engaged in importing and storing any volatile petroleum substances in this state. The fee does not apply to petroleum products moving through the state in interstate commerce. (b) The inspection fee liability is measured by the total number of gallons of volatile petroleum substances imported and stored in this state. (c) There are no exemptions from inspection fee liability on petroleum products stored in Tennessee for export to other states or on sales to the United States Government or instruments thereof, or to the State of Tennessee or counties, cities and towns of Tennessee, or any sub-governmental bodies of this state. 

In General Oil Company V. Crain, Inspector of coal oil, 209 U. S. 211, 52 L. Ed. 754, 28 Sup. Ct. 475, (reprinted in Section 3 of this Chapter) the opinion of the United 

States Supreme Court was:

Ch. 8) 673 

INSPECTION FEES 

(1) Oil shipped by a domestic corporation from its refineries in other states and destined ultimately for points outside Tennessee, was not in interstate commerce so as to be exempt from state tax or inspection laws while held at a distributing point in Tennessee for the purpose of unloading and placing in other receptacles preliminary to forwarding oil to its final destination. (2) The Company was doing business in the State and its property was receiving the protection of the state. Its oil was not in movement through the state. It had reached the destination of its first shipment and it was held there, not in necessary delay or accommodation to the means of transportation, but for the business purposes and profit of the company.

Duty of Inspectors— Law. Section 6818 

It shall be the duty of the inspectors to examine and test, within this state, all such violatile substances before being sold or offered for sale or used and/or stored in this state. 

The above section is self-explanatory and needs no comment.

Gravity Standards- Law. Section 6819 

The gravity, purity and tests of said volatile substances shall be determined in such manner and under such regulations as the inspector at large may specify, subject to approval of the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation, and in accord with usages practiced or data or regulations issued by the United States Bureau of Mines. 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation specifies and promulgates by regulation the gravity standards under which tests of volatile substances shall be made, and they are in accordance with those used by the United States 

Bureau of Mines. (See Regulation (J) Section C of this Chapter.) Notice of Inspection Attached_ Law. Section 6820 

After making said examination and tests, inspectors shall affix to receptacles, sale tanks, pumps, etc. containing volatile substances inspected, such marks of identification and/or caution notices as the inspector at large may designate, subject to such approval, in accord with reasonable trade customs and precautions governing the handling of volatile substances, and the unauthorized removal of any such notice is a misdemeanor.

Inspector, after making examinations and tests, shall affix to the receptacles, tanks, pumps, etc., such marks of identification as may be prescribed by the Commissioner.

(Ch. 8  Inspection Fees Charged- Law. Section 6821 

Each inspector who shall inspect any consignment of volatile substances described in the preceding sections, as provided in this article, shall charge the consignor or consignee thereof the sum of twenty cents for testing a barrel, or less quantity, and twenty cents additional for each barrel. Fifty gallons shall constitute a barrel. When the inspection is made of a tank containing more than fifty gallons, twenty cents shall be charged for each fifty gallons or fraction over. 

The fees chargeable are twenty (204) cents per barrel or any quantity less than a barrel, and fifty (50) gallons constitute a barrel. For example, a tank car containing 

10,560 gallons would be considered as 212 barrels and the inspection fees would amount to $42.40.

Records to Be Kept by Inspectors- 

Law. Section 6822 

Every inspector shall keep an accurate record of all such goods inspected, rejected, branded, or certified to by him, which record shall state the date of such inspection, the number of packages, barrels, casks, or tanks approved, the number rejected, the name of the person for whom inspected, the name of the person to whom consigned, with his address, the sum of money charged for such inspection; and such records shall be open to all persons interested. 

Inspectors receive their instructions from, and are under the direct supervision of, the Divisional Supervisors. 

Inspectors report daily to the divisional office as to the samples of volatile substances collected, together with the necessary identifying information. Samples are then tested at the various laboratories and technicians in charge at the laboratories or testing stations report daily their findings to the divisional supervisors.

Inspection Fees: To Whom Paid- Law. Section 6823.1

(See Section D in the Chapter on Gasoline, for a specimen of monthly report.) Inspectors do not collect any monies for inspection fees.

The amount to be paid to said inspector at large for making such tests not to exceed two thousand dollars per annum. 

The necessary books, instruments, apparatus, etc. are purchased by the Commissioner and the cost thereof (not limited to $2000 per annum) is included in the general appropriation bill Chapter 211, Acts of 1937, covering the estimated expenditures of the Department of Finance and Taxation.

Inspectors and Others to Report Violations to District Attorney, Who Shall Prosecute; Violation by

Inspectors a Misdemeanor: Removal from Office- Law. Section 6828 

It shall be the duty of any inspector or any person having cognizance of any violation of the provisions of this article forthwith to make complaint to the District Attorney for the county in which this offense is alleged to have been committed, against the person or persons so offending; and it is the duty of such district attorney to represent and prosecute, on behalf of the state, all cases of offense arising under the provisions of this article. Inspected in Transitu and Condemned to Be Branded; 

How- Law. Section 6837 

And when oils or fluids specified above are sent to this state to counties or cities without an inspector, and the same are inspected in transitu, and found to be without a required test, the inspector shall brand the barrel or package containing the fluid "unsafe for use. All such packages or barrels which are plainly marked by the manufacturers or shippers "naphtha," "benzine, "gasoline," etc., together with the specific gravity of the same, may be permitted to go forward to their destination as not intended for any of said purposes; but all barrels or packages without a required test, and which are not so branded or plainly marked by the manufacturers or shippers, shall be considered as intended for such purposes, and shall be shipped back in like manner as condemned products.

Obstructing Inspector; Penalty—

Law. Section 6840 

While the inspector is in the discharge of his duties, if any dealer in or manufacturer of oils or fluids above specified, shall refuse to admit an inspector or his deputy upon his premises, so far as it may be necessary for the performance of his duties, or if he shall obstruct an inspector or his deputy in the discharge of his duties, such persons shall for each refusal be fined not less than twenty dollars nor exceeding fifty dollars. 

Obstructing an inspector or his deputy in the discharge of his duties, or refusing admittance upon premises necessary for the performance of his duties, is punishable by a fine of not less than twenty ($20.00) dollars nor more than fifty ($50.00) dollars. 

In J. H. and Henry Coffin V. the State, 70 Tennessee 

559, (reprinted in Section E of this Chapter) the court said: "It is made the duty of the inspectors by the Acts of 1877 promptly to inspect and it is a misdemeanor for the owner to refuse him admission to his premises for the purpose, or to obstruct him in the discharge of his duties."'

Selling before Inspection a Misdemeanor- 

Law. Section 6844 

If any person, manufacturer or dealer, shall sell to any person in the state any of said oils and fluids before first either holding a true sample for inspection or having the same inspected as provided in this article, he shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, and punished as set forth in section 6829; and the oils and/or fluids if found to be rejected, may be forfeited and sold, and the proceeds go to the common school fund of the state.

This section provides that any person selling any oils or fluids before taking a true sample and holding for inspection, or having the same inspected, is guilty of a misdemeanor and punishable by fine of not less than $100.00 or imprisonment, or both, in the discretion of the court. 

In addition, such oils or fluids may be forfeited or sold.

Alteration of Brands or Use of Branded Packages a Misdemeanor- Law. Section 6845 

If any manufacturer or dealer of said oils or fluids shall, with intent to deceive or defraud, alter or erase the inspector's brand, to indicate a different test, gravity, purity or quantity than is found by the inspector or shall use with such intent packages having any inspector's brand thereon, without having the contents actually inspected, shall be fined in any sum not exceeding one hundred dollars for every such offense. 

Any person, with intention to deceive or defraud, who alters or illegally uses an inspector's brand is subject to a fine in an amount not exceeding $100.00 for each offense. 

Fines and Penalties; Disposition of- Law. Section 6846 

All prosecutions for fines and penalties under provisions of this article shall be by indictment or presentment, and when collected shall be paid into the treasury of the county where the offense is committed, onefourth of which shall be paid to the informer, and three-fourths to the State common school fund. 

Misdemeanor to Sell Mixtures; Penalties— Law. Section 6847 

No person shall mix, for sale, naphtha and other such oils or fluids, or same with any corrosive substance, or shall knowingly sell, or keep for sale, or offer for sale, such mixture, or shall sell, or offer for sale such products which are not of required test; and any such person shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, and be punished by a fine of not less than one hundred dollars nor more than five hundred dollars, and by imprisonment for less than six months nor more than three years. 

The above two sections are self-explanatory and need no comment.

Each person, firm or corporation for whom coal oil, carbon oil, petroleum, kerosene oil, gasoline, and other products of petroleum are

(Ch. 8 

inspected, shall furnish through the inspector at large to the comptroller of the treasury, as of the last days of March, June, September, and December of each year, and within five days after said dates, under oath, an itemized statement showing all the fees accrued and paid by such person, firm or corporation during the quarter just passed, which statement shall show the number of vessels, barrels and smaller packages inspected and gauged for such person, firm or corporation so reporting, and when and where, and names and residences of the inspectors making said inspections, and/or gauging, and also the kind of material inspected or gauged.

Failure to Report Is a Misdemeanor; Fine- Law. Section 6850 

Any person, firm or corporation refusing or failing to make such report, within ten days after the time fixed, shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, and fined not less than fifty dollars, nor more than two hundred dollars.

Monthly reports are required of all persons liable for inspection fees on forms prescribed by the Commissioner. 

The fees due are payable at the time the report is filed. 

Specimen of such report will be found in Section D of the Chapter on Gasoline Tax.

Each inhabitant, person, firm, corporation, syndicate, joint stock association or agent thereof, subject to the payment of the special privilege tax provided for herein, and subject to pay the special privilege tax herein provided, shall make a monthly report to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation on or by the tenth day of the succeeding month, showing the amount in gallons of each said commodity sold, delivered or distributed for the preceding month and subject to be estimated in calculating the amount of privilege tax as herein provided, and shall also make monthly remittance to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation for the amount of the special tax based upon and equal to said one-half cent per gallon for each gallon of said commodities so sold, delivered or distributed during the preceding month.
