Chapter 206, Public Laws of 1937 

AN ACT to provide an improved method of collecting State, County, Municipal or any special taxes by authorizing the voluntary sale of ad valorem tax certificates on real estate, etc. etc.

Section 1: 

That for the purpose of giving to the owner of real estate a more equitable and less expensive way for pro-

(Ch. 16  

tecting his property against interest, penalties and costs accruing when his taxes become delinquent, any ad valorem taxes assessed against real estate in Tennessee, as provided by law, for State, County, Municipal or special purposes are hereby authorized to be sold or assigned, by voluntary sale by the owner of real estate on which such taxes have been assessed; and the sale of same shall carry with the sale to the purchaser the same prior lien of the state, county and/or municipality on the real estate securing the payment of the same, together with the legal right in the purchaser to enforce said lien in the manner provided by law, for the collection of the said taxes, interest and penalties so embraced in said tax certificate; it being the intent and purpose of this Act to place the purchaser of such certificate in the same position now occupied under the law by the State, County and/or Municipality with reference to said lien.

Upon the application of the owner of any such real estate against which such taxes have been assessed and the assent of the purchaser at any time before or after such taxes have become delinquent, the county trustee, or other official charged with the collection of such taxes, is hereby authorized, empowered and directed, upon the payment to him of all taxes, interest and penalties due or accrued thereon, to issue to the purchaser of such taxes a certificate in writing, setting out the name of the owner of the real estate so applying, describing the real estate, stating the amount of taxes, interest and penalties, if any due and for what year or years same are owing, showing that same is paid by the purchaser upon the request of the owner of the real estate, and that the same prior lien of the state, county and/or municipality is transferred to the purchaser as security for the said payment. Such tax certificate shall be numbered by appropriate number and bear on its face six per cent interest per annum from the date of issuance and a penalty of two per cent per annum from the date of the certificate until the same is paid in full by the owner or his agent, which certificate shall be payable at any time by the owner of said real estate by the payment of the face of the same together with the interest

to the purchaser and constitute in his hands the same lien and/or security for the payment of such taxes, interest, penalties, costs and attorney's fees as it was to secure the payment of same to the state, county and/or municipality in such pending suit or suits. 

Section 3: 

That, no purchaser of such tax certificate by agreement with the owner of the real estate and issued by the tax collecting official shall institute any suit to enforce the lien for the amount so paid and set out in said certificate until the expiration of two years from the date when the said taxes became delinquent, nor until the expiration of one year from the date of the certificate issued by the clerk of the court where the suit is pending to enforce the lien by the state, county or municipality as set out above, and in either instance not until he has presented the same to the owner of the real estate covered thereby for payment, or served a written notice on him demanding payment, which notice shall be served thirty days before the institution of such suit, which notice may be served by mailing same to the owner at his last known address, if he is a resident of the state, or by posting such written notice at the Court House door, of the County in which the land lies, if the owner is a nonresident of the State; and if same is not paid by the expiration of the said thirty day notice, the holder of such tax certificate may file his petition against the owner of said real estate, either in a separate suit or in any tax suit pending in any court in said county, as provided by chapter 77 General Acts of 1923, and may include in one petition as many different certificates against as many different parties or tracts of land against whom he holds a certificate as he may desire for the purpose of enforcing the lien on the real estate for the amount of the said certificate together with the interest, penalties, cost and attorney's fees provided for in said certificate or certificates. Such separate suit or suits shall be brought and prosecuted in the name of the State of Tennessee for the use and benefit of the owner of such tax certificate; and authority is hereby given to any number of separate owners of tax certificates

Ch. 16) 1343 

PROPERTY TAX 

as may desire to join in the same suit as use complainants or plaintiffs, whether such certificates be upon the same or different parcels of real estate, and/or whether the real estate be owned by the same or different owners; provided that all of said real estate must be located in the county where the suit is brought and provided further, that any owner or owners of tax certificates covering any of the property involved in any such suit, who do not join as use complainants or plaintiffs may be made defendants and his or their rights determined in the same proceeding. Along with and as a part of such petition the said certificate or certificates shall be exhibited, or, if the original is lost or mislaid and cannot be found then a duly certified copy by the official issuing same may be used; and upon said petition being so filed, process shall issue and the suit shall proceed in all respects as a suit in Chancery Court filed to enforce liens for taxes under the provisions of the Act of 1923 or any other law for enforcing liens in Chancery Courts. If such suit is prosecuted to a finality and the real estate so sold, is purchased by someone other than the State, county or municipality, and title thereto divested and vested in the purchaser, than an additional five per cent attorney's fees as provided for in said certificate calculated on the face amount of said certificate, shall be added for conducting said suit and collecting same, and secured by a lien on the real estate; provided, however, that the real estate, ordered sold in said suit shall not be advertised for sale until the expiration of 60 days from the rendition of the decree of sale, during which time the owner may pay the judgment and costs; and provided, further, that at any time before the confirmation of the sale by the court, the owner may redeem the property by paying the judgment, interest, penalties, costs and attorney's fees provided for in said certificate and decrees of sale; and provided, further, that the court may decree the sale of the real estate on a credit of not less than six nor more than twelve months and in bar of the equity of redemption, as provided by law.

The fact that there may be a tax certificate outstanding against any real estate for any particular year or years

(Ch. 16  

shall not prevent the owner of the land from selling a tax certificate thereon for any other year or years, nor prevent the trustee of the county from delivering the lists of delinquent taxes, for any year not so covered by such certificate, to deputy collectors or to attorneys to file suits thereon for the collection of taxes not covered by such certificate, nor prevent the filing of suits to enforce the tax lien for any such other years, as provided by Chapter 77, of the Public Acts of 1923. All certificates on the same real estate, dated within the limitation provided by law for tax liens, shall be of equal dignity, irrespective of priority in the date of issuance. 

Section 4: 

That, no such tax certificate shall be negotiable in the sense of the Uniform Negotiable Instrument Act of the

State, but any such certificate shall be assignable and transferable by the endorsement of the holder on the back thereof, showing the date of the assignment, to whom assigned and the post office address of the assignee; and such assignment shall carry with it to the transferee of assignee all restrictions and all of the rights, prior liens and privileges held and owned by the State, county and/or municipality. But such assignment shall not become complete and effective until the endorsement thereof on said certificate has been copied on the duplicate in the hands of the official issuing and having custody of said duplicate and attested by the signature of said official. 

Upon the request of the owner of any real estate covered by any such tax certificate, or his administrator, heirs or assigns, and upon tender and payment to the owner of such certificate of the amount then due thereon, as provided by this Act, the owner of such certificate shall transfer by endorsement on the back thereof and delivery of the same to any person named by the owner of such real estate to receive such certificate. The owner of any real estate covered by any such tax certificate or his administrator, agent, heirs or assigns, may at any time discharge the lien of such certificate by paying the amount then due thereon to the official issuing such certificate, which official

Ch. 16) 1345 

PROPERTY TAX 

is hereby charged on his official bond with the duty of accepting said amount and paying it over to the owner of such certificate; and upon the acceptance of such payment it shall be the duty of such official to note the fact and time of such payment upon the original (which must be presented) and the duplicate of such certificate in his possession and to accept the original certificate duly cancelled, which he shall turn over to the owner of said real estate. 

Section 5: 

That, whenever the owner of any such real estate, on which such tax certificate exists unsatisfied either by himself, his administrator, heirs or assigns, pays the same, the holder thereof shall endorse thereon and sign a statement thereon that the same has been paid and the date of payment, and deliver up such certificate; and such cancelled certificate in the hands of the owner, his representative or assigns, shall be evidence of such payment; and when presented to the official holding the duplicate of such certificate, it shall be the duty of such official to copy on said duplicate the said endorsement, date and signature of the person acknowledging receipt of same and such endorsement and signature so copied and verified by the signature of the official on said duplicate, shall become a record in his office of the payment and cancellation of such original certificate and taxes on said property for the year or years mentioned therein; and for such service the owner of the property shall pay to the official the sum of twenty-five cents for such endorsement on each certificate. 

It is hereby declared to be the legislative intent that this Act is not intended to conflict with the provisions of Chapter 77, Acts of 1923, for the collection of delinquent taxes, but is intended to supplement the provisions of that Act for the collection of State, county municipal and/or other special delinquent taxes.

Any person purchasing land sold to satisfy the lien under any such tax certificate or under the provisions of Chapter 77, of the Acts of 1923, for any year shall have and is hereby given the right to take any taxes due on a lien on said real estate to the state, county and/or munici-

(Ch. 16 

pality, for any year prior or subsequent to the year for which such sale was made, and to be subrogated to the rights of the state, county and/or municipality to enforce the same lien against the property given by law to the State, county and/or municipality, and in the same way; or if the statute of limitations of two years applicable to his purchase, shall have run he is given the right to pay any or all of such taxes, as a payment and satisfaction of an encumbrance on his own property, so purchased. 

Section 6: 

That, if any provision, paragraph, section, sentence, clause or other part of this Act shall be held by any court of competent and final jurisdiction to be unconstitutional and void, that shall not affect the remainder of this Act, it being the Legislative intent to have passed this Act without such invalid part.

Section 7: 

That, all laws and parts of law in conflict with this Act be and the same are hereby repealed and this Act take effect from and after its passage, the public welfare requiring it. 

Approved May 21, 1937.

Chapter 214, Public Acts of 1937 

AN ACT providing that the property and bonds of housing authorities shall be exempt from taxation and assessments and authorizing certain payments in lieu of such taxes and assessments- 

Section 1: 

That it has been found and declared in the Housing Authorities law and the Housing Cooperation law (a) that there exists in the State housing conditions which constitute a menace to the health, safety, morals, and welfare of the residents of the state; (b) that these conditions necessitate excessive and disproportionate expenditures of public funds for crime prevention and punishment, public

Ch. 16) 1347 

PROPERTY TAX 

health and safety, fire and accident prevention, and other public services and facilities; (c) that the public interest requires the remedying of these conditions by the creation of housing authorities to undertake projects for slum clearance and for providing safe and sanitary dwelling accommodations for persons who lack sufficient income to enable them to live in decent, safe and sanitary dwellings without overcrowding; and (d) that such housing projects are for public uses and purposes, and are not used or held for profit, and are governmental functions of state concern.

As a matter of legislative determination, it is hereby found and declared that the property and bonds of the housing authority of such character as to be exempt from taxation.

Section 2: 

That the property of housing authorities shall be exempt from all taxes and 'special assessments of the state or any city, town or political subdivision thereof, provided, however, that in lieu of such taxes or special assessments a housing authority may agree to make payments to any city, town or political subdivision of the state for services, improvements or facilities furnished by such municipality or political subdivision for the benefit of a housing project owned by the housing authorities but in no event shall such payments exceed the estimated cost to such city, town or political subdivision of the services, improvements or facilities to be so furnished.

Section 3: 

That the bonds of a housing authority are declared to be issued for an essential public and governmental purpose and, together with interest thereon and income therefrom, shall be exempt from all taxes. 

Passed May 20, 1937.

The laws covering property taxation in Tennessee are most voluminous; there is much ambiguity and duplication. To reprint and comment upon all the statutes, pertaining to the administration of these taxes, would require many pages of this book and tend to destroy the purport of the work, viz:

To more clearly define and discuss the tax liability in Tennessee

Therefore, the many sections of the law, dealing with the administration of property taxes, are omitted. For reference purposes, however, the Reorganization Bill (Chapter 33 of the Public Acts of 1937), which materially affected tax administration, is reprinted in the front of the book.

With regard to municipal or city property taxes, the general laws of the State permit assessment and collection by county officials; but, inasmuch as the majority of cities and towns assess and collect their own taxes and revenues under special or charter provisions, discussion thereofin a general way-is impossible. 

Under the heading 'Property Tax Law,' the various sections of the code are in numerical sequence and in the 'Explanations and discussion' thereof, the following groups are used-with a cross index to the code sections.

Sources of Public Revenue- (Law: Code sections 1035, 1081) 

Revenue of the State of Tennessee, and its counties and municipalities, is derived from various sources, including taxes on polls and property. 

Property Subject to Taxation- 

(Law: Code sections 1036, 1084, 1483)

A general property tax is imposed on all real estate and personal property for State, County, and Municipal purposes. (a) Real property includes land, improvements and permanent fixtures affixed thereto. (b) Tangible personal property includes machinery, equipment, furniture, personal effects, vehicles, money on hand or on deposit. (c) Intangible personal property, consisting of accounts and notes receivable, franchises, goodwill, etc., are not taxable to individuals and not directly to corporations; but, as regards corporations, they are indirectly taxed by inclusion in the value of capital stock assessed as a unit. "Since negotiable demand notes are not money on hand or on deposit, they are not subject to ad valorem taxation." (Hedges v. Shipp, 166 Tenn. 451.) "Cash value of life insurance policies are not taxable." (Opinion of Attorney General, January 16, 1936.) "You are advised that stocks and bonds which are taxable under the income tax law, Chap. 20, Acts of the 2nd Extra Session of 1931, are not taxable ad valorem."" (Opinion of Attorney General, January 18, 1936.) 1349

(Ch. 16  Exempt Property- 

Summarized-the property exempt from taxation is as follows: 

1. Public Property. 

2. Religious, Charitable and Educational Institutions. 

3. Cemeteries and monuments 

4. Public roads and streets 

5. Growing crops, certain products of the soil and manufactures. 

6. Personalty up to $1000.00 

7. Property protected by valid charter or contract. 

8. Leaseholds held by certain institutions. 

9. State of Tennessee bonds 

10. County bonds 

11. Municipal bonds 

12. Ceded property 

13. Park lands 

14. Housing authority property. (1) Public property-Includes property belonging to the United States, State of Tennessee, and local governmental units thereof, used exclusively for public, county, or municipal purposes. (2) Certain institutions-Property used exclusively for religious, charitable or educational purposes; but such property is not exempt if any pecuniary profit enures to the personal benefit of any individual or group of individuals. Also, the real property, or part of any real property, belonging to such institutions, not used for religious, charitable, or educational purposes, notwithstanding the use of the income therefrom, is not exempt from taxation. Real property bought in by such institutions, under foreclosure sales to protect endowment investments, is exempt from taxation for one year from the date of purchase. (3) Cemeteries and monuments-This section presumably exempts only the real estate and improvements. 

It does not exempt other property belonging to an incorporated company organized for profit and its capital stock is taxable as in the case of other corporations. "" This statute operates to exempt from taxation the real estate and improvements, and the improvement fund of an incorporated cemetery company, but does not operate to exempt its personal effects. (Forest 

Hill Cemetery Co. v. Creath, 127 Tenn. 686.) (4) Public roads-All roads, streets, etc. thrown open for public travel or use free of charge, are exempt.

Ch. 16) 1351 

PROPERTY TAX 

(5) Crops, products and manufactures—This includes: (a) All growing crops. (b) Direct products of the soil of the State in the hands of the producer or his immediate vendee. (c) Articles manufactured from the produce of the State in the hands of the manufacturer. (a) needs no interpretation. (b & c) the following cases clearly define "Products or produce of the State" and "articles manufactured" that are exempt from taxation. 

(1) The term 'produce of the State' as used in the Constitution embraces whatever is produced or grown in the State, or is the yield of the State, whether it be crops, timber, coal, iron, marble, or wood, or any other article which may be treated as produced or grown within the State from or on the soil, or may be found in the soil.'' (Benedict v. 

Davidson Co. 110 Tenn. 183.) (2) "The term 'produce of the State' as used in the Constitution has been construed to be limited to articles produced or grown from or on the soil or to be found in the soil and therefore excludes animals, though manufactured into food products within the State.'' (Neuhoff 

Pkg. Co. v. Sharpe, 146 Tenn. 293.) (3) Products of the soil of Tennessee are not exempt from taxation after they have left the hands of the producer and his immediate vendee.'' (Morgan & Hamilton Co. v. Nashville, 151 Tenn. 382.) (4) "Logs of a mill operator, grown on Tennessee soil, and lumber, rough and smooth, cut by him from such logs, are articles manufactured from the produce of the State and exempt from taxation." (Benedict v. Davidson Co. 110 Tenn. 183.) (5) "Manufactured articles are not exempt as commodities of commerce, but as articles of manufacture in the hands of the manufacturer; and immunity from taxation does not follow manufactured articles after they have left the hands of the manufacturer.'' (Morgan & Hamilton 

Co. v. Nashville, 151 Tenn. 383.)

Products of the soil of other States-The State of Tennessee cannot discriminate in its taxing laws against the products of another State-as such action would be violative of the Interstate Commerce Clause of the Federal 

Constitution. Therefore, products of the soil of other states (if similar products of Tennessee soil are exempt) in the hands of the producer's immediate vendee in Tennessee are exempt. "A tax discriminates against property the product of the soil of other states brought into Tennessee and at rest within the State of Tennessee and is invalid when like property, produced from the soil of Tennessee, is exempted, since such action places a direct burden upon interstate commerce. "" 

(Darnell & Son Co. v. Memphis, 208 U. S. 113.) 

(6) $1000.00 exemption on personalty-This exemption is allowed each resident taxpayer against taxable

(Ch. 16  

personal property. However, willful conveyance of property to obtain exemptions and evade taxation is not permissible. (7) Property protected by valid charter or contract exemption "Exemptions from taxation are contrary to public policy, and can only be allowed when granted in clear and unmistakable terms, and the benefit of the doubt must be given the state." (Memphis v. Union & 

Planters Bank, 91 Tenn. 546.)

Section 1418 of the Code states that Charter exemptions should be avoided as far as possible, except as to municipal taxes. This provision is in the chapter or article dealing with quasi-public and manufacturing corporations: but it would appear applicable to all corporations. (8) Leaseholds held by institutions of learning exempt -This exemption can only be allowed when the institution is protected by valid charter exemption. In State v. 

Grosvenor, 149 Tenn. 158, the court said: "Clause 8 of the Act is not applicable to an incorporated school not exempted by its charter, but which was exempt by statute." 

(Law covering items 1-8; Code section 1085.) 

(9-11) State, County, and Municipal bonds-are exempt and cannot be taxed by the State, or any county or municipality. (Law: Code sections 1086-1088.) 

(12) Where jurisdiction is ceded-such property is free from any taxation or assessment by State, county or municipality. (Law: Code section 99.) 

(13) Park Lands-in actual use for public park pur poses. (Law: Code section 4186.) (14) Housing authorities-Property and bonds of 

Housing projects created for public use and not used or held for profit are exempt from State, county and municipal taxes, except that any authority may 'in lieu' of taxes pay the cost of any services, improvements or facilities furnished. (Law: Chapter 214-Public Acts of 1937.) Poll Taxes- (Law: Code sections 1082-3) 

Every inhabitant between 21 and 50 years of age, except deaf, dumb, blind or incapable persons, must pay an

Ch. 16) 1353 

PROPERTY TAX 

annual poll tax of $1.00 to the County Trustee, and the revenue therefrom is to be used exclusively for school purposes. Liability for the tax is determined as of the 

10th day of January of each year.

Any person, incapable of labor, desiring exemption from this tax must apply to the quarterly county court. 

As a condition precedent to the exercise of voting, qualified voters must furnish satisfactory evidence that the poll tax has been paid if any has been assessed (Law; code section 2027).

Real Property Defined— (Law: Code section 1351-p. 5) 

All mineral and timber interests and all other interests of whatsoever character, whether for life or a term of years, in real estate, including the interest which the lessee may have in and to the improvements erected upon land where the fee, reversion, or remainder therein is exempt to the owner, and which said interest or interests is or are owned separate from the general freehold, shall be assessed to the owner thereof, separately from the other interests in real estate, which other interest shall be assessed to the owner thereof, all of which shall be assessed as real estate.

Personal Property Defined- (Law: Code section 1355) 

Personal property is assessed under the following classifications: 

Class 1. Household and kitchen furniture, tableware, libraries, jewelry, sewing machines, guns, more than one gun, musical instruments, and all other personal property of a similar character. 

Class 2. Farming implements, machinery, wheeled vehicles, automobiles, tools of all kinds, and all other personal property of a like character.

Class 3. All kinds of live stock, including dogs. 

Class 4. Steamboats, ferry boats, and all other kinds of watercraft. 

Class 5. Money on hand or on deposit in this state or elsewhere not otherwise assessed in this state. 

Class 6. 

nated.

All other tangible personal property not hereinabove desig- Class 7. All personal property which is a part of the capital invested in the business of a merchant, commission, or auction merchant, factors or manufacturers shall not be assessed separately as personalty, but shall be assessed as part of the capital.

(Ch. 16  

Class 8. In assessing steamboats and ferryboats, boats navigating within streams within or bordering on this state, the same shall only be assessed to the extent of the interest therein of any person, company, corporation or firm residing or doing business in this state. The fact that any personal property hereby assessed may be deposited, incumbered, or transferred or pledged as collateral or loaned or out of the possession of the owner, whether the same be in or out of the state, shall not in any wise excuse the same from being listed and reported for taxation. In assessing personal property, the taxpayer shall, in making out his tax schedule, state how much insurance he carries on his personal property. 

It will be observed that only tangible personal property is assessed under this section; but that 'money on deposit' which might be termed a 'credit' or intangible is included. 

It should also be noted that money on deposit in any other state should be listed by residents of Tennessee. The provisions of this section in the main apply to individuals, inasmuch as corporations and merchants are taxed on the capital invested, which includes all personal property, both tangible and intangible. "Money on savings deposit in a bank is taxable." (Hamilton Natl 

Bank v. City of Chattanooga, Supreme Court of Tenn., November 26, 1932.) "Money 'on call' is not money on deposit and therefore not subject to taxation."" (Hedges et al v. Shipp, Supreme Court of Tenn., July 19, 1933.)

As regards merchants, the property or ad valorem tax is assessed upon the capital invested in their business (Code sections 1690-1703) or, on the average amount of merchandise stock carried during the year, whichever is the higher. Such valuation includes not only the tangible, but also the intangible personal property. 

As regards quasi-public and manufacturing corporations, the property or ad valorem tax is assessed upon the actual cash value of the total corporate property or capital stock (Code sections 1404 & 1408). Such valuation includes not only the tangible but also the intangible personal property.

Notwithstanding the separate statutes dealing with the above three types of business, viz: (1) merchants, (2) quasi-public corporations, (3) manufacturers-it is stated in section 1404 that: "All corporations, foreign and domestic, shall be assessed in the same manner. 

---

Ch. 16) 1355 

PROPERTY TAX 

It therefore resolves itself to this-that individual taxpayers do not pay taxes on intangible personal property, but that all corporations do, through the valuation of their capital stock.

In paragraph 8 of section 1355 the law states that personal property deposited, encumbered, or transferred, or pledged, or loaned, or out of the possession of the owner, whether in or out of the State, must be reported for taxation.

It is doubtful whether tangible personal property owned by a resident of Tennessee upon which a permanent, business or taxable situs has been created and established outside the State, can be taxed for ad valorem purposes in Tennessee.

Foreign Corporations- (Law: Code section 4135 and Chap. 106 Public Acts of 

1937)

Tax liability of foreign corporations doing business in Tennessee is the same in all respects as domestic corporations, or those incorporated under the laws of this State. Refunds- 

(Law: Code sections 270: 270.1 and section 15: Act 3, Chap. 108 Public Acts of 1937) 

The Commissioner of Finance and Taxation has, with the approval of the Attorney General, the power to settle, adjust and direct the refund of taxes erroneously or illegally collected.

Particular attention is drawn to the statutory limitation of one year from date of payment of the tax, within which claims for refund must be filed. 

Taxes Must Be Paid: Procedure for Recovery by

Suit- 

(Law: Code sections 1790-1795) 

No writ for the prevention of the collection of any tax is permitted. The remedy-where it is claimed the assessment is wrongfully or illegally made-is to pay the tax under protest and sue the collecting official.

(Ch. 16  

In Bank of Commerce v. Senter, 149 Tenn. 569, the court said: "This and the following sections in this chapter provide a remedy for the taxpayer confronted by an unjust or illegal claim for taxes. The 

State cannot be postponed in the collection of its revenue, and the taxpayer must pay the tax under the conditions prescribed, as a condition precedent to contesting the liability for the tax or any part thereof." 

Voluntary payments, however, cannot be recovered. 

In Cincinnati, N. O. &c. R. Co. v. Hamilton Co., 120 

Tenn. 1, the court said- "Payment, under protest, of taxes alleged to be illegal, before the same have become delinquent and without any demand or threat to levy, merely to prevent the imposition of a penalty and interest which would accrue, is a voluntary payment and the taxes so paid can not be recovered.'' 

In Quick Service Tire Co. v. Smith, 156 Tenn. 96, the court said- "Uncontradicted statements in a letter to a collecting officer stating that the tax is being paid under protest, a check being inclosed to cover the tax demanded, which facts are corroborated by the action of the taxing official in sending a receipt carrying the endorsement that the tax was paid under protest, are sufficient evidence to protect the rights of the taxpayer."

Taxes Barred After Six Years- 

(Law: code section 1494) 

All state, county, school, and municipal property and poll taxes are barred unless the same are collected, or suits for the collection shall have been instituted within six years from January 1st of the year for which the taxes accrued.

Returns To Be Filed— (Law: Code sections 1361-1366, 1371–2)

Taxpayers are required to file schedules setting out in detail all personal property owned on the 10th of January of each year. If the return is not filed by April 20th, then the assessor makes the assessment against the taxpayer. 

Notice of such assessments must be sent to the taxpayer, and protests by the taxpayer must be filed at least 5 days before the first meeting of the Board of Equalizers. 

Failure to protest against the assessment makes the same conclusive against the taxpayer.

Failure to file return of property as required by law is a misdemeanor punishable by fine.

INSTRUCTIONS TO ASSESSOR 

To personally see each taxpayer residing in his county, or his agent or attorney, and take his personal statement (filled out in the blank schedule) of all property of such taxpayer, whether the same be real, personal, or mixed, without regard to any exemptions. 

If any taxpayer is a non-resident, or if the owner cannot be found or scen after diligent search, the assessor shall fill out such statement, sign, and indorse on the same that the taxpayer could not be found after digent search.

In such case, it shall be his duty to examine any person who he may -have reason to believe has any knowledge or information as to the property of the taxpayer. For such purpose, he shall have the power to administer oaths and compel any witness to answer, and it shall be done by questions put to the taxpayer, his agent, attorney, or any assessor or his deputy.

Assessors and deputy assessors shall have like powers and perform like duties when there is any reason to believe or suspect any taxpayer bus withheld or concealed from such schedule any property or failed to 1st any property, which may be done by questions put to the taxpayer, bis agent, attorney, or any other person. 

It shall be unlawful for any assessor or deputy willfully, knowingly, or negligently to assess any property subject to taxation in the names or the initials of any other than the real and true owner thereof, and for each of such offenses he shall be fined not less than five dollars nor more than twenty dollars.

It shall be unlawful for any assessor or deputy willfully, knowingly, or negligently to permit or allow any property subject to taxation to be or remain unassessed or omitted from assessment, or willfully, knowingly, or negligently to assess any property at less than its cash value, or to assess any property or polls solely by substitution or copy from former assessment.

In case the taxpayer refuses or fails to swear to the schedule, so state on the back of schedule; also giving manner of arriving at value. 

DIRECTIONS TO 

Every taxpayer must give a complete description and list of his personal property and all of which he is interested in or over which he has control, and must swear to this list.

Every taxpayer who refuses to give a correct list of property be owns, has an interest jn, or controls, is guilty of a misdemeanor; and swearing to an imperfect or incorrect list is perjury. 

Any person swearing falsely or corruptly or knowingly in any material statement in such schedule or to any statement made as a witness to such assessor or deputy assessor shall be guilty of perjury and indicted for the same. (Sec. 1358, Code of Tennessee, 1932.)

It shall be misdemeanor for any taxpayer or the attorney or agent of any taxpayer to neglect, or refuse to fill out or have filled out the schedule For every taxpayer there must be filled out a schedule which shall be sworn to.

This schedule must be filled out either by the Assessor or by the tax. payer, and must be sworn to by the taxpayer or his agent. 

Failure to comply is a misdemeanor and false swearing is perjury. (Sec. 1368, Code of Tennessee, 1932.)

The value must be fixed by the Assessor. 

Assessors must make report to the County Court Clerk on or befo.e the first Monday in June.

Inquisitorial power is given grand juries in cases where Assessors fail to do their duty, and upon conviction, Assessors are fined and subject to suit on their official bond.

PROPERTY TAX IMPORTANT INSTRUCTIONS TO MERCHANTS 

Every person, firm, company, or corporation transacting a mercantile business within the meaning of the law In the State of Tennessee is required to file this form, properly executed in duplicate, with the County Court Clerk of the County in which such mercantile business is transacted. 

This form should be filed at the expiration of the period of the bond executed by the merchant when licensed to conduct such mercantile business.

One copy of this form will be retained in the office of the County Court Clerk and one copy will be forwarded to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation at Nashville.

These forms will be audited in the office of the Commissioner- just as income tax returns are audited by the Federal Government, and the assessment of each merchant will be raised to the actual value of the property in event it is found an incorrect statement has been made resulting in an incorrect assessment in the first instance. 

Any merchant feeling aggrieved at the assessment fixed by the Commissioner is given the right of appeal to the State Board of Equalization. 

All property in Tennessee is being assessed at its actual cash value and the same standard must be applied to every class of property.

The merchant should swear to this form upon filing same with the County Court Clerk, as no assessments will be accepted and approved by the Commissioner unless proper oath appears on merchant's ad valorem tax schedule. 

IMPORTANT INSTRUCTIONS TO COUNTY COURT CLERKS 

Section 5 of Chapter 113 of the Public Acts of 1921 makes it the duty of each County Court Clerk in the State to furnish to the Commissioner of Finance and Taxation on the first day of each month a report showing the names of all persons to whom licenses to exercise privileges have been issued for the preceding month, amount of State Tax collected, together with such other information as may be called for by said Commissioner. 

Under this authority, each County Court Clerk is required to have each person, firm, company or corporation conducting a mercantile business within his county to file this form in duplicate at the expiration of the period of the bond executed when license was issued to the merchant to transact such mercantile business. 

The Clerk should retain in his permanent files one copy of this form, and on the first day of each month should mail to the Commissioner at Nashville a copy of each form filed by merchants during the preceding month, showing his assessment.

The filing of these duplicate forms with the Commissioner will constitute the report of the County Court Clerk provided by law.

The Commissioner is given authority under Chapter 113 of the Public Acts of 1921 to raise or lower the assessment of any merchant so as to make same conform to the standard of actual cash value. 

County Court Clerks should take notice that the Commissioner will not approve any assessment made at less than actual cash value of the property of the merchant, and will not approve any schedule unless same has been properly sworn to by the merchant filing same, and the original copy of this schedule will be examined in the office of the County Court Clerk by a field representative of the department. 

Railroads, Public Utilities and other Quasi-public corporations must, biennially, file certain information and schedules with the Railroad and Utilities Commission, in Nashville. Further discussion in this connection will be found in the subsection on "assessment of property" in this chapter.

Assessment of Property- When made (Law: Code section 1348)- 

Real Property is assessed every two years-in the odd years.

Personal property and Polls are assessed every year. "Tennessee Constitution, Art. 2-28, concerning the taxation of property, is not self-executing and before any property can be valued and assessed for taxation a proper method and machinery for such valuation and assessment must be provided by the Legislature."' (Sou. Exp. Co. v. Oatterson, 122 Tenn. 279.)

Actual cash value to be used: definition (Law: Code section 1349) Property of all kinds should be assessed at its actual value, which means the amount of money the property would sell for, if sold at a voluntary sale. "The actual cash value is the only practicable basis upon which taxes can be made equal and uniform, and this is clearly the constitutional requirement and legislative intent." (Carroll v. Alsup, 107 Tenn. 257.)

Basis of assessment; to whom assessable; when (Law: 

Code section 1351)- (1) Property is assessed to the owner on the 10th day of January of each year. 1366

(2) Personal property held by executors and administrators should be assessed in the county where decedent resided. If decedent lived in another state, then the property is to be assessed where the personal representative resides. (3) Personal property of minors etc., held by trustees or guardians is assessed where such minors etc. reside, if a resident of the State. If a non-resident, such property is assessable where the guardian or trustee resides. (4) Stocks in banks and other financial institutions are treated elsewhere in this chapter. (5) The property of railroad, gas and electric light companies, including their franchises used within any city, where the principal office is located outside of the city limits, shall be taxed in the city as if the office was situated within the city limits. However, all realty and tangible personalty is taxed in the district where situated. In other words, the excess valuation, if any, over and above the real and tangible personal property would be taxable by the city, town or taxing district, as well as by the county and state. (6) Real property is defined elsewhere in this chapter -Improvements and land can be assessed separately if so owned.

Shares of stock in Financial and certain other institutions 

(Law: Code sections 1391-1403)— 

Shares of stock in the following associations or companies are taxable for state, county and municipal purposes as the personal property of the stockholders, whether they reside within or without the State:- Banks 

Loan companies

Building and Loan Associations 

Insurance companies 

Investment concerns 

Cemetery companies.

These shares of stock, returnable in the county in which the association or company is located, are assessable at their actual cash value: and, in arriving at the assessment value, consideration must be given to the market value or any other evidence of value. "It is my opinion that the mere fact that property has depreciated since January 10, (tax listing date) or has totally lost its value subsequent to the time of assessment would not authorize the County Board of Equalization to exempt or release it from taxation. In my opinion the question is what was its actual cash value on the 10th day of January?" 

(Opinion of Attorney General, June 9, 1933.) 

Real estate and personalty owned by these institutions is assessed as other similar property: and, in arriving at the taxable value of the shares of stock, the assessed value of the real and personal property must be deducted. 

The assessor has power to summon witnesses, to inspect or require the production of books and papers, and consider any other evidence. Where the capital of an institution is not divided into shares of stock, each one hundred dollars of the capital shall be considered as one share assessable at its actual cash value. 

Lists of stockholders and their holdings must be furnished the assessor: but the tax levied is payable by the president or manager as if he were the sole owner of all of the shares.

Where a bank has branches or offices in more than one county, assessment is made by the tax assessors of the

Ch. 16) 1369 

PROPERTY TAX 

county and municipality wherein the principal office is located. These assessments are then divided between the several counties or municipalities proportionately according to the ratio of the total deposits on hand January 10th of each year in each of the branches or offices bears to the total deposits of the institution. 

It is mandatory upon all financial institutions or other companies included herein to keep, at all times, a full and correct list of the names and addresses of the stockholders and the number of shares held by each. 

The tax levied against such shares of stock is payable by the institution or corporation, and such tax constitutes on and after January 10th of each year, a prior lien against such shares of stock. If the taxes are delinquent, the state, county or muncipality may proceed to collect by attachment on the shares of stock in any court of competent jurisdiction.

Quasi-public corporations (Law: Code sections 1404 and 1406)—

Gas works, waterworks, electric light companies and all other corporations quasi-public in their character and which possess rights, franchises, and privileges, shall pay an ad valorem tax upon the actual cash value of its corporate property, including its franchises, easements, incorporated rights and privileges. This value cannot be less than the aggregate actual cash value of both its shares of stock and bonded debt. In arriving at this value, consideration must be given to the market value and any other evidence of value, including gross and net receipts, exclusive of interest paid on bonded debt and dividends on stock.

Real and tangible personal property of such corporations is assessed in the same mode and manner as other real estate and tangible personal property. In computing the value of and assessing the capital stock, the assessed value of real estate and tangible personal property is deductible from the aggregate, the remainder constituting in effect, the 'corporate excess' or valuation of the 'intangible' personal property.

(Ch. 16  

This section does not include the assessment procedures of railroads, street and interurban railways, motor bus and truck, telegraph or telephone companies. 

The assessor has full power and authority to examine witnesses, to inspect or require the production of books and papers, to visit and inspect the property, to obtain and consider any evidence that he may deem material or necessary.

It should here be noted that the quasi-public corporations-gas works, waterworks, and electric light companies -referred to in Section 1404 and discussed in this chapter, are assessed under section 1508 by the Railroad and Public Utilities Commission; however, the basis of assessment is fundamentally the same as enumerated in section 1404. 

Manufacturers (Law: Code sections 1407-1410)— 

All individuals, partnerships, and companies engaged in the manufacture of any goods, wares, merchandise, or other articles of value must pay an ad valorem tax upon the actual cash value of their property-real, personal, or mixed-which is used for the purpose of manufacturing, exclusive of the value of articles manufactured from the produce of the state in the hands of such manufacturer. 

Section 1408 states that manufacturing corporations, either foreign or domestic, shall pay property taxes on the actual cash value of its capital stock, including its franchises, easements, incorporated rights and privileges. 

However, this 'value' cannot be less than the actual cash value of the capital stock and bonded debts outstanding, which is in effect the 'market value' of the shares of stock and bonds. Articles manufactured from the produce of the state, constitutionally exempt, are deductible from the valuation.

Real estate and tangible personal property of any corporations included in this group, is assessed where situated and in the same mode and manner as other realty and personalty. Of course, in computing the assessed value of the corporate capital stock, the value of the real and tangible personal property is deducted and the balance

Ch. 16)

PROPERTY TAX 

1371 represents 'corporate excess' or the value of the ‘intangible' assets. "It was the legislative intention to assess to the corporations the capital stock and corporate property, tangible and intangible, of all manufacturing corporations, whether foreign or domestic, and to exclude the shares of stock in corporations so assessed from further assessment and taxation, either to the corporation or to the stockholders.'' (Tennessee 

Fertilizer Co. v. McFall, 128 Tenn. 645.)

Final analysis of the sections pertaining to the assessment of manufacturers, resolves itself to this: 

(1) Individuals or partnerships— 

Assessment is on the real and tangible personal property as assessed to other taxpayers, exempting articles manufactured from the product of the soil. 

(2) Corporations- 

Assessment is on the value of capital stock and bonded debt outstanding, or the value of the real and tangible personal property, whichever is the higher, excluding of course articles manufactured from the product of the soil. 

In the real property assessment of manufacturing establishments (section 1407) the annual gross income and other sources of value should be given consideration (section 1356). There is considerable divergence of opinion, amongst tax authorities and students of taxation, as to the advisability or practicability of the use of 'income' in the assessment of property: but, obviously, if used at all by assessing officials, it must be used as a factor in all classes of property and not in one particular group or classification.

All other corporations (Law: Code section 1404)— 

Section 1404, although dealing in the main with the assessment of quasi-public corporations, states- "All corporations, foreign and domestic, other than those designated in this section, and in the proviso in this clause, shall be assessed in the same mode and manner as quasi-public corporations set out in this section.",

The corporations, specifically referred to in this section, comprise the following:

Financial and certain other institutions. (b) Quasi-public corporations. 

Manufacturers. 

Corporations assessed by the Railroad and Public Utilities Commission.

(Ch. 16  

Therefore, all corporations, both foreign and domestic, other than those enumerated above, should be assessed by the aggregate actual cash value of their capital stock and bonded debt (as defined in section 1404). This means, in other words, the assessment-for ad valorem tax purposes —of all of the corporate real and personal property, both tangible and intangible. 

Corporations owning property in more than one county 

(Law: Code section 1416)- 

In the case of corporations owning property in more than one county in the state, the real and tangible personal property is assessed where situated. The 'corporate excess' or 'intangible' valuation, if any, is assessable in the county or place fixed by its charter for the meeting of its stockholders, or where the corporation's principal office is located.

Corporations owning property in Tennessee and other states (Law: Code section 1416)- 

In the case of corporations owning property in Tennessee and in other states, the actual cash value of the real and tangible personal property in this state (which is assessable where situated) and the value of the property which has acquired a permanent situs in other states, is deductible from the value of the capital stock, and the 'corporate excess' or 'intangible' value, if any, is assessable in the county wherein the principal office-fixed by its charter-is located. 

Foreign corporations; how assessable (Law: Code section 1417)- All foreign corporations-doing business in Tennessee -are liable, as in the case of domestic corporations, for assessment on the actual cash value of the corporate property in the state. This includes real and personal property, both tangible and intangible. "These cases recognize the principle that choses in action may acquire a situs for taxation other than at the domicile of their owner if they have become integral parts of some local business. The corporation established what has aptly been termed a 'commercial domicile.' 

(Wheeling Steel Corp. v. Fox et al., U. S. Supreme Court, May 18, 1936.)

Charter exemptions to be avoided as far as possible (Law:

Code section 1418)— 

Release from taxation of any company or corporation is not permissible, where the charter exempts its stock and shares. In all cases where, by the terms of the charter, the shares of stock are wholly or partially exempt, or where a rate of taxation is fixed or prescribed in lieu of all other state, county and municipal taxes, the tax levied upon other taxable property shall be assessed. However, this does not apply where it is provided that a stated per cent on each share of stock subscribed shall be paid in lieu of all other taxes. The law further states that the provisions of section 1418 do not apply to municipal taxes.

All property of every description, both tangible and intangible, within the State is assessable by the Commission, biennially in the even years, at its actual cash value and as of the same date as other property is assessed viz: January 

10th. This section does not apply to Tennessee corporations whose principal business is the manufacture of articles from the produce of the soil and transporting such products in their own cars. 

Certain schedules-furnishing the information re-

(Ch. 16  

quested in Code sections 1509-1520 must be filed by each taxpayer with the Commission on or before April 1st. biennially, in the even years. 

Refusal or failure to file the required schedules waives the right to be heard in opposition to the valuation as fixed by the Commission; and, in addition, there is a penalty of $100.00 per day for delinquency. The Commission is vested with the power to summons any person, books, records, etc. and to examine any person in order to ascertain the correct value of the taxable properties. Additional information may be required as deemed proper: but the records of the 

Commission must, at all times, be open to the inspection of the owner of any property assessable under this Statute. 

In making the assessment, the following facts must be given consideration:- :- 

(a) Capital stock 

(b) Corporate property 

(c) Franchises 

(d) Gross receipts (e) Market value of stock

Bonded indebtedness in order that a fair and equitable cash value of the properties be made. There are two types of property belonging to these companies: 

1. Distributable property-not localized. 

2. Localized property. 

Where business is done in Tennessee and other states and in instances where business is done in more than one county, certain property-without an actual situs-is distributable to the respective taxing districts on a mileage basis as outlined in Section 1528 of the Code. Of course property located outside of the State which is not directly used in the business to which the property in the State is devoted, does not enter into the taxable valuation. 

Real property, improvements, buildings and any personal property having an actual situs in Tennessee is described as localized property. It shall be valued separately and assessed in the county, or district, where located. 

All of the properties of gas and electric light companies shall be deemed to be "localized" property and the prop-

erties in the respective counties and towns shall be valued and assessed separately. (Law: Code Section 1530.) There is an exemption of $1000 which is apportioned proportionately.

Under Section 1540 it is the duty of the Governor to convene the Commission if at any time it appears to his satisfaction that any of the properties assessable to the companies referred to are inadequately assessed or omitted from taxation, the Commission having the power to make the proper assessments. No state, county or municipal officials, except the Railroad and Public Utilities Commission, have the power or authority to back assess. 

Merchants (Law: Code sections 1690-1703)— 

All merchants are liable for 'ad valorem' or property taxes upon the capital invested in their business. "An ad valorem tax may be assessed against merchandise brokers whose business consists wholly or partially in negotiating sales between resident and non-resident merchants of goods situated in another state without taxing interstate commerce, and the county may require, as a condition of granting a license, that the tax be paid." (Ficklen v. 

Shelby Co., 145 U. S. 1.) 

The term 'merchant' includes all persons, co-partnerships, agents, or corporations engaged in trading or dealing in any kind of goods, wares, or merchandise. 

Every 'merchant' must obtain a license from the County Court Clerk before commencing in business and such license must be renewed annually. Bond must be furnished in the sum of $500.00 approved by the Clerk, guaranteeing that the merchant will render a true statement annually showing the amount of capital invested in the business. 

Section 1701 of the Code, states: 

"The word 'capital' as used in this section shall be construed to mean the average amount of stock on hand during the year in which it is offered for sale; but if the average stock on hand is less than the capital stock employed by said merchant, he shall pay a tax on the capital stock.” 

Therefore, the assessment or tax base of a merchant consists of the average amount of merchandise stock plus the actual cash value of other tangible personal property and real estate. However, should this tax 'base' be less than the capital stock employed the tax is assessable on the

(Ch. 16  

actual cash value of such capital stock or, in other words, the total invested capital of the entire business. 

In addition to the ad valorem tax described above, all 'merchants' are liable for a privilege tax of 15¢ per annum on each one hundred dollar value of the average capital invested. (See Chapter on Privilege Taxes.)

Section 1702 provides that where a 'merchant' sells any merchandise at auction or on commission, or as agents, then the tax base or assessment on such merchandise shall be an amount equal to one-third of the total annual auction or commission sales.

Section 1703 provides that where a 'merchant' employs capital in any manner of trading in which no stock of goods or merchandise is maintained for sale, the aggregate capital employed in the business constitutes the tax base or assessment.

Housing Authorities (Law. Chapter 214: Public Acts of 1937-Code Section 3647.6)- 

Under Chapter 20, Section 26, extra session 1935, all properties acquired by a Housing Authority were subject to assessment and payment of property taxes: but Chapter 

214, Public Acts of 1937, provides that such property and bonds are exempt from taxation inasmuch as "such housing projects are for public uses and purposes and are not used for, or held for, profit and are governmental functions of State concern." However, Section 2 states that in lieu of taxes or special assessments, Housing Authorities may agree to make payments to any governmental unit for services, improvements, or facilities furnished not in excess of the estimated cost.

Reassessments of Real Property- (Law: Code sections 1385-89) 

Real property is assessed every two years; but in the interim, reassessments may be made, when— (1) Improvements, to the value of two hundred dollars or more, have been destroyed. (2) Permanent improvements, to the value of two hundred dollars or more, have been made since the last assessment.

Ch. 16) 1377 

PROPERTY TAX 

(3) Property, sub-divided since last assessment, shall be assessed to the different owners but the total must be the same as assessed to the original owner. 

Back Assessments or Revision- (Law: Code sections 1486-7, 1496-7) 

Property may be back assessed or reassessed when (a) it has escaped taxation, (b) when assessments have been made at less than its actual cash value by reason of fraud, deception, misstatement or omission of accurate statements by the owner or his representative, (c) when a grossly inadequate assessment has been made. "This statute is not limited to taxes assessed by the county tax assessor, but applies also to the ad valorem taxes on merchants' capital which are assessed as well as collected by the county court clerk.'' and Company v. Haley, 142 Tenn. 382.) (Swift Revision of assessments made by the regularly constituted assessing authorities is not permissible, unless gross inadequacy exists by reason of connivance or fraud in submitting the tax data.

In the case of errors or omissions by former assessors, back assessments are limited to three years— "Section 1487 of the Code of Tennessee provides that no taxes on property for more than three years back shall be assessed and collected where they have not been assessed and not paid in consequence of errors or omissions by former collectors or assessors. This statute controls proceedings to assess property which has been omitted from assessment.' 

(Opinion of Attorney General, September 13, 1935.)

PROPERTY TAXES Boards of Equalization and Review CONTENTS Page Page County Board of Equalization ..1378 State Board of Equalization ....1379 County Board of Equalization- (Law: Code Sections 1419-1433) 

The County Board of Equalization is vested with the powers and duties of equalizing and computing values of property for taxation. 

It is the duty of the County Board to carefully examine, compare and equalize county assessments. It has the power to increase or lower property assessments in order that all property in the county is equalized and assessed upon the standard of the actual cash value thereof; the latter herein defined as the "amount of money the property would sell for if sold at a fair, voluntary sale."

Notice of increased assessments made by the County Board, and opportunity for hearing before the board, must be given taxpayers. "Before the board of equalization has the power to increase the valuation of property the notice, as required by statute, must be given the taxpayer. This is mandatory and any increase levied without it is 

Void.'' 

(St. Louis Basket & Box Co. v. Lauderdale Co., 146 Tenn. 413.)

Any owner of property subject to taxation in the State has the right, in person or by his agent, to make complaint before the County Board of Equalizers that other properties in the county have been assessed at less than its actual cash value or at a less percentage of value than the complainant's own property. 

The Board meets on the first Monday in June of each year with the period limitation as stated in Section 1422 of the Code. Final action by the County Board of Equalizers can only be revised or changed by the State Board of 

Equalization. 

1378

Ch. 16) 1379 

PROPERTY TAX State Board of Equalization— 

(Code sections 1447-1470)

The purpose of the State Board of Equalization is to effect equalization in property assessment values throughout the State at certain uniform standards. The standard value of all properties assessed for taxation is its actual cash value, the latter being defined as the "amount of money the property would sell for if sold at a fair, voluntary sale." 

It is the duty of the State Board to increase or decrease assessments so that the values of all assessments throughout the State conform with the above standard. 

The State Board convenes in Nashville on the second Monday in August of each year and continues in session until equalization is completed. For the convenience of taxpayers, the Board sits for a portion of its allotted time in both the western and eastern sections of the State, the time and place being designated by the Board. Final action must be taken by the Board not later than October 1st; however, special sessions may be held upon call of the chairman.

Any owner of property subject to taxation has the right to a hearing before the State Board upon complaint that his property has been assessed at more than its actual cash value, or that other property has been assessed at a less percentage of value than his own. Complaints and requests for hearings must be made in writing, specifically stating the grounds for complaint, and filed with the Board prior to its annual meetings. It would appear advisable for taxpayers desirous of appealing to the State Board to consult with the County Board of Equalizers or Tax assessor as to the proper procedure. Copy of appeal form is submitted on page 1380.

The State Board of Equalization also hears appeals from back assessments and reassessments made by county trustees or county court clerks. The right of appeal in such matters is given to the State, to the County, and to the taxpayer. Appeals of this nature, however, must be filed within 10 days from the date of back or reassessment. 

County trustees and county court clerks must hear and promptly determine all complaints of this character and

shall then certify their action to the State Board, whose duty it then becomes to hear and settle the controversy. 

Action of the State Board is final and conclusive, but of course is subject to judicial review. "Our assessment acts provide a complete system for the ascertainment of ad valorem taxes. Under them the taxpayer is afforded opportunity to appear before the Board of Equalization and have erroneous or excessive assessments corrected. Failure of the Board of Equalization to observe the requirements of the statute may be reviewed upon certiorari in the circuit courts." (Railroad v. Bate, 21 Lea 577.) "If the taxpayer omits to avail himself of any of these remedies, and the assessment becomes final, the action of the boards of assessment and equalization, in determining the value of the property for taxation, is held to be as conclusive as the judgment of a court." (Ward v. Alsup, 100 Tenn. 745.) "Obviously, therefore, the petition is merely an effort to have the courts review, upon petition for certiorari, the valuation placed upon the property for purposes of taxation by the duly constituted taxing authorities. Nothing is better settled in this jurisdiction, and everywhere we believe, than that the courts will not undertake such a review, nothing else appearing. As said in the cases, value is a matter of opinion, and the opinion of the courts is not likely to be any better than the opinion of the tribunals specially created to fix property values.'' (W. J. Savage Co. v. City of Knoxville, Supreme Court of Tenn., November 18, 1933.)

Collection of Taxes— When payable and to whom; interest and penalty on delin quents (Law: code sections 1545-7, 1559)— 

All state and county property taxes are due and payable the first Monday in October of each year, to the county trustee, except when otherwise provided by law. Interest is chargeable from May 1st following due date; and, in addition, a penalty of one-half of one per cent per month is added beginning with the first of March following delinquency. 

Poll taxes must be paid at the time the property tax is paid.

Distress warrants; when issuable; additional penalty and costs (Law: code sections 1574, 1590)— 

Taxes remaining delinquent for thirty days are collectible by distress and sale of any personal property liable therefor. An additional penalty of 5% upon all delinquent taxes is added upon the filing of suits to enforce the lien to cover the expense of prosecution. In addition sheriff and clerk's fees are added. 

Homestead not exempt from distress or sale for taxes 

(Law: code section 7720)— 

Homesteads are exempt from seizure in criminal or civil cases; but they are not exempt from distress or sale for taxes.

Lien for taxes; damages and costs (Law: code sections 1329-31)- Property taxes of every description, and all damages and costs accruing thereon, are a first lien upon the property, from the tenth day of January of each year, for the taxes of that year.

The tax is on the property and not on the person or owner.

Taxes assessed against leasehold interests or upon any improvements on exempt real estate, constitute a lien only upon such leasehold or improvement interest.

(Ch. 16

Suits to enforce collection (Law: code sections 1591, 1594)—

Suits for the collection of delinquent property taxes are filed between February 1st and March 1st. All lands are subject to sale under court order when the amount due is ascertained.

After the filing of suit, a taxpayer may have the same dismissed by paying the taxes, together with the interest, penalties and costs accrued thereon. 

Subsection 2 of code section 1591 provides that any municipality or county may exempt itself from these provisions by proper resolution.

Relief of persons owing certain delinquent property taxes 

(Law: Chapter 101-Public Acts of 1935)- 

Under this act, all persons owing any property or ad valorem taxes for any or all prior years up to and including the year 1935 were given relief from all accrued interest and penalties thereon, if the tax was paid by October 1, 1937. 

The act also provided for certain other relief in the collection of delinquent property taxes and the enforcement of tax liens. The act, reproduced in full in the law section of this chapter is deemed to be self explanatory. 

Time for filing suits to enforce liens for 1936 and prior years' taxes (Law: Chapter 35-Public Acts of 1937)— 

This act prohibited the filing of suits to enforce liens on unpaid property taxes for the year 1936 and prior thereto until after sixty days from and after January 30, 1937, and

Ch. 16) 1385 

PROPERTY TAX 

no costs or attorney fees incident to a suit could be charged until after that date.

Sale of ad valorem tax certificates (Law: Chapter 206Public Acts of 1937)— 

Under this act, upon the application of the owner of any real property, upon which the taxes have become delinquent, and assent of the purchaser, the county trustee or tax collector, upon the payment to him of all taxes, interest, penalties, etc. due thereon, may issue to the purchaser of such taxes a certificate, which certificate carries with it the same prior lien of the state, county, or municipality. 

These certificates bear interest at the rate of 6% per annum and a penalty of 2% per annum. The reason for the enactment of this statute was to give the delinquent real property taxpayer some relief from the expensive interest, penalties and costs which accrue against unpaid taxes. The act is reproduced fully in the law section of this chapter.

Section 4136: 

Corporation Reports and Fees- 

(a) Each corporation chartered by the state or organized under its laws, and each foreign corporation, qualified to transact its business in the state in compliance with its laws requiring foreign corporations to file their charter with the secretary of state, shall, on or before the first day of July in each year, prepare and file in the office of the secretary of state a written statement, signed by its president or vice-president, and attested by its secretary, or assistant secretary, and sworn to by either its secretary or assistant secretary, or president, which shall contain the following information, to wit: The name and style of the corporation and its principal office or place of business in the state, if it be a Tennessee corporation; and if it be a foreign corporation, its principal office and place of business in the state of its creation, and also in this state; the amount of its capital stock authorized by its charter and the amount of capital stock issued and outstanding; the names of its principal officers, viz., its president, vice-president or vicepresidents, secretary and treasurer, and a complete list of its board of directors; the nature and character of the business in which it is engaged, and also a statement of its gross 1389

(Ch. 17  

receipts for the previous calendar year, arising from business transacted wholly within this state. Every such corporation shall, at the time of filing said statement with the secretary of state, pay to the said secretary of state therefor, in addition to all other taxes, a sum of money as follows: A sum equal to one-half of one per cent of the gross amount of its receipts for the previous calendar year, arising from business done wholly within this state; provided, however, that the minimum payment to be made under this method of computation shall be twenty-five dollars; provided, also, that said corporation may, at their option, pay in lieu of this tax upon their gross receipts from intrastate business, the following schedule of fees: Every corporation with an actual capital stock of $25,000 or less, five dollars; every corporation with an actual capital stock of $50,000 and more than $25,000, ten dollars; every corporation with an actual capital stock of $100,000 and more than $50,000, twenty dollars; every corporation with an actual capital stock of more than $100,000 and not more than $250,000, thirty dollars; every corporation with such a capital stock of more than $250,000 and not more than $500,000, fifty dollars; every corporation having such a capital stock of more than $500,000 and less than $1,000,000, one hundred dollars; and every corporation having such a capital stock of $1,000,000 and over, one hundred and fifty dollars. (b) Taxes paid by any corporation under this statute shall be credited upon the tax imposed upon each corporation known as the excise tax. (c) Every corporation failing or refusing to file said statement and pay any of said fees shall, in addition to the fee, pay a penalty of one dollar for each day's delinquency. (d) It shall be the duty of said corporations to elect, at the time of filing the statements required by part (a) of this section, whether they desire to pay the tax herein before assessed upon their gross receipts arising from intrastate business, or whether they will pay in lieu thereof the tax graduated by the amount of their capital stock and said corporations shall notify the secretary of state of said election at the time of filing such statement with him, or the election shall be with him.

Ch. 17) 1391

(e) All existing remedies of the state for the collection of said tax shall remain in full force, and may be used by the state, at its option, for the purposes of enforcing the collection of said tax.

Section 4137: 

Definition- 

The words "actual capital stock," in the preceding section, shall be deemed, prima facie, to be the corporation's authorized capital stock; but the corporation shall be allowed to show the contrary to be the fact. 4138: 

Inapplicable to State Banks or State Banks and Trust

Companies— The above section shall not apply to state banks or state banks and trust companies, inasmuch as they are now under supervision of a special department, and that part of same fixing the fees to be paid the secretary of the state shall not apply to said state banks for the reason similar fees are paid to the banking department. 4139: 

Distress Warrants for Fees and Penalties— 

The secretary of state is authorized, and it shall be his duty, after the first day of September in each year, to issue a distress warrant for the collection of the fee and penalty due from each delinquent corporation. Said distress warrant may be addressed and delivered to the sheriff of the county wherein such delinquent corporation has its principal office or place of business, or to the sheriff of any county in which the secretary of state has reason to believe property of such delinquent corporation may be found. 4140:

Distress Warrant Returned Because No Property 

Is Found; Charter Shall Be Revoked; Reinstatement of Charter- If any officer cannot find personal property or real estate with which to satisfy said distress warrant and accordingly returns same with officer's return thereon, the charter of such delinquent corporation shall be revoked; not, however, until the secretary of state shall, through a newspaper published in the county of the last known address of such corporation, and if no newspaper be published in that county, then in a newspaper published in an adjoining county, notify said corporation of the return of said distress warrant and that unless the fee and penalty, with the cost of publication, be paid on a certain named date, which shall not be less than fifteen days next after the date of publication, the charter of said corporation shall stand as automatically revoked; provided, however, that at any time within one year after the date of revocation, said charter may be reinstated upon the payment of delinquent fees and penalty, with the cost of publication. 4142:

Section 3859: 

Credit Unions Taxed as Savings Banks- A credit union shall be deemed an institution for savings and shall be taxed in the same manner as savings banks are assessed. At the time of incorporation every credit union shall pay the secretary of state a fee of five ($5.00) dollars, and, inasmuch as there is no fixed capital stock for said unions they shall pay, under chapter 434 of the Acts of 1907 and acts amendatory and in lieu thereof an annual fee to the secretary of state, at the time of filing the annual report, (in) the sum of five ($5.00) dollars.
